△ Third, refutation by way of the non-objectivity of the perceived.

Furthermore, regarding the substantial self-essence that is clung to [by others], since it is neither the object of perception nor the subject of perception, right view is instead caused to sink into the cycle of birth and death.

Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: Regarding the initial inquiry concerning the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*): this adherence to a view of self is a deviation from principle and a fallacious conception.

If the mental factors (*citta-dharma*) that grasp [this view] are not refuted by the subsequent analysis, and since they are not the object of perception (*ālambana*), how can one know that a self exists?

It would be like the eye not seeing; who could then distinguish between blue and yellow? If, however, it were the object of perception, then the vision would not be inverted, because one would be knowing the object of the self as it truly is.
The *Śataśāstra* states: "All noble wisdom knows objects as they truly are; since it is not erroneous, the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) would likewise not be erroneous.
If that were so, the view of self should be like noble wisdom and not the root of birth and death from time immemorial.
If that were so, [the opponent] raises a counter-objection: 'If the view of self is correct, then non-self (*anātman*) must be false. How can you maintain this?'"
Regarding those who hold to a self: the authoritative teachings they trust refute the view of a self, for it causes one to sink into the cycle of birth and death;

they praise the view of non-self, for it enables the realization of nirvana. How could a false view of non-self realize nirvana, while a correct view of a self, on the contrary, cause one to sink into birth and death?

△ Second, establishing the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to demonstrate that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). (2) First, it is shown that the subjective and objective conditions are respectively the seeing and the appearance.

Specifically, it points to the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses that functions as the subjective perceiver.
This is just like a mind that perceives other dharmas, such as the five consciousnesses that perceive form, sound, and so forth.

The initial valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) correctly clarifies that the seeing of the view of self is fundamentally the internal seeing-division; this is because the view of self possesses its own direct aspect (*sākṣāt-lakṣaṇa*).
[It] functions as an object-condition (*ālambana-viṣaya*), just as the five consciousnesses take the five sense-objects as their objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*).
The view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is an existent phenomenon (*dharma*); it does not take a real self as its object, because it possesses an object-condition, like other minds.

"Other phenomena" refers to that which remains apart from a real self, namely the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) that serves as the object-condition. Next, the inference is that the object-condition of the view of self is originally...
The internal image-aspect (nimittabhāga) is the object-conditioned by the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi);

it is merely a reflected image as the direct object-condition, and is certainly not a real self, just like the five sense-objects (pañcaviṣaya) that serve as the image-aspects for the objects of the five consciousnesses. This is the object-conditioned by the view of self.
This is an existent dharma; it is certainly not the doctrine of a real self. Because it is an object of cognition (*ālambana*), this serves as the logical reason (*hetu*).

Since it is like other dharmas, which serve as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), we know that the cognizing subject and the cognized object are precisely the two parts: the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).

Answer: Even if one does not admit the existence of the objective aspect, the fact that the five sense objects (*pañcaviṣaya*) are perceived as perishable and impermanent remains unimpeded;
thus, they can still serve as a valid supporting example for the absence of a real self (*ātman*).

it did not clarify what the object of perception is, nor why it is an object of perception. This concluding passage clarifies: the internal consciousness manifests the various aggregates (*skandha*), which are produced by causes and conditions and are phenomena of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
They exist by depending upon this [consciousness]. What is the fault? The fault lies in [clinging to] the following...
This is merely a variety of conceptual constructions based on one's own deluded sentiments. *Zhongjing* (Mirror of the Essence), Fascicle 59. Question:
If the image that is the object of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is something that exists dependently (*paratantra*), then there should be a real self as a dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Answer: This characteristic arises in dependence upon causes and conditions; it is merely of a dependent nature, a phenomenon that exists like an illusion, and is not the self. Because of that...
To falsely grasp [something] as a self is therefore called "false grasping" (*parikalpita*). This has two aspects in terms of its characteristics:
first, this characteristic arises from causes and conditions and possesses the power to produce the mind; this is the "existent" aspect, which is the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).

Second, regarding the objective aspect of the entity as it is grasped, it is called the "universally imagined" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and this is termed "non-existent. It is like a person in deep darkness who grasps [at things falsely].
Regarding the stone that becomes an ox: the substance of the stone is not devoid of being the objective referent (*ālambana*) of the view of self;
it is like the stone which, while depending on other-dependent characteristics (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), is originally not an ox, yet is grasped as an ox by the deluded mind.

This grasped ox has no substance whatsoever, just as the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is originally not a self, yet is grasped as a self by the deluded mind. This grasped self has no substance whatsoever; there is only the grasping subject.
The mind has no grasping. I mean that regarding this stone, there is only the stone as an object of perception, but no grasped cow;
regarding these objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*), there is only the dharma as an object of perception, but no grasped self.
△ Section Three: The Three Bonds Belonging to the Category of Self-Grasping (3). First, the enumeration of headings:
Now, self-grasping is briefly of two kinds: first, innate (*sahaja*); second, conceptual (*vikalpita*).

*Harṣavāda*: This has already been explained in detail. Herein, the characteristics of the self (*ātman*) as clung to by non-Buddhists and those of other vehicles are collectively summarized and categorized;
namely, the two types of self-clinging: the innate (*sahaja*) and the conceptual (*vikalpita*).
△ Second, the detailed explanation (in two parts): First, innate self-grasping (in three parts). First, explaining the general name:
Innate self-grasping has existed since beginningless time... [it] operates spontaneously; therefore, it is called "innate."
△ Next, the specific characteristics are explained.
This further consists of two types: first, the constantly continuous [state]... (up to) ...arising from the marks of one’s own mind and grasping them as a real self.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: “constantly continuous” means that the subjective grasper and the objective grasped revolve without interruption. “Arising from the marks of one’s own mind” means...

"Characteristics" (*nimitta*) refers to the seventh consciousness. Taking the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its objective essence (*bhāva*), it transforms within itself a reflected image as its "characteristic-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*) object.

When this [seventh consciousness] perceives this [image] and grasps it as a real internal self that is subject to interruption—because its perceiving faculty is sometimes absent or undergoes transformation—it does so in a general sense by reckoning the five aggregates as a whole, or in a specific sense by reckoning any one among those five. This refers to the... [the seventh consciousness].

The six consciousnesses rely upon the five aggregates transformed by the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as their substantial basis; they manifest reflections from within one's own mind as the objective aspect (nimittabhāga).

Taking these as objects, they grasp them as a real self. As for the "five aggregates of clinging" (pañcopādānaskandha), they are so called because they are conjoined with clinging; that is, all desire, greed, and so forth present within the various aggregates.
*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance), *Zongjing* Volume 51. It quotes the *Weishi shuyao* as follows:

"There are two interpretations of the phrase 'arising from the marks of one's own mind. First, it refers to the mark of the reflected image (*pratibimba*). Second, it refers to the mark of that which is grasped (*parikalpita*).

Although they lack substantial reality, they appear before the mind; thus, all explanations regarding the marks of the mind should be understood accordingly. [The commentary] explains: "the reflected image."
These myriad phenomena are reflections of the mind. As for the characteristics grasped [by the mind], all objects lack intrinsic substance; they arise in accordance with grasping.
Because they originate from one's own mind, they in turn serve as the characteristics of that mind.
△ Third, the demonstration of the stage of abandonment.
Because these two forms of self-grasping are subtle, they are difficult to abandon; [only] through the superior contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) can they be eliminated.

Regarding the commentary on the meaning: "In the subsequent path of cultivation" refers to the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) in contrast to the initial path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), namely the stage of *srotāpanna*.

Those who have already transcended [the stage of] the *Huan* (i.e., the *śraddhā-bhūmi*) are those from the first *bhūmi* upward who possess the superior contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

This is because, during the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the contemplation of the emptiness of persons merely severs the portion of the conceptual grasping of a self (*parikalpita-ātma-grāha*);

whereas in this stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one is able to sever the aspect of the innate grasping of a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*). Since the initial Path of Seeing is superior, it is described as "superior."
△ Next, the analysis of the grasping at a self (three parts). First, the explanation of the general name:
The grasping at a self through discrimination (*vikalpa*) is also called "discriminative" because it arises only subsequently, based on present [conditions].

Regarding the "Explanation of Terms": "Furthermore, it is due to the power of external conditions in the present" means that although there is the power of internal causes, one must rely upon external conditions for false teachings to arise.
That is to say, the external condition is false discrimination; this refers to receiving false teachings and thereby giving rise to false mental reflection within.
*Hexiang*: The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source), fascicle 66, states: "This conceptual construction of a self arises dependent upon three conditions:
namely, a false teacher, false teachings, and false reflection. Through the power of long-term perfuming and habitual cultivation by means of these three conditions..."
Consequently, one calculates the other as "other" and clings to oneself as "self. This occurs solely because of the calculation that things exist substantially.

If one were to calculate existence based on substantiality rather than through habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), why would one not cling to both one's own body and the bodies of others at the very moment of birth?
Since one does not calculate self and other at the initial moment of birth—because the habitual perfuming has not yet occurred—it is known that this calculation of existence [arises from perfuming].
Self and others arise from the habitual perfuming of delusion.
△ Next, the specific characteristics are explained:
they exist solely within the sixth mental consciousness (up to) the point where it discriminates, calculates, and clings to them as a real self.

Regarding the "concordant echoes" (*saṃghoṣa*) of the characteristics of heterodox aggregates (*tīrthika-skandha-lakṣaṇa*): these refer to the doctrinal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) propounded by the Vātsīputrīyas and others, as well as the Vaiśeṣikas and others.

Regarding the "characteristic of self" (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*): this refers to the self (*ātman*) that is neither identical to nor distinct from [the aggregates], such as the great self (*mahātman*) and so forth.
△ Third, the demonstration of the stage of abandonment.

Because these two forms of self-grasping are coarse, they are easy to abandon; upon realizing the true suchness of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-tathatā*), they are immediately extinguished.
[Commentary: Regarding "at the time of the initial path of vision," the *Śata-śāstra* states: "The clear realization of the noble truths (*ārya-satya-abhisamaya*) first manifests."
At that time, there arises the True Suchness of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-tathatā*), which is the principle revealed by the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*).

The preceding contemplation on the emptiness of persons refers to the wisdom that performs the observation (*prajñā*), whereas this True Suchness of the emptiness of persons refers to the principle that is the object of observation (*ālambana-dharma*); the texts merely express these two aspects alternately. [The] *Kaimei* [asks]:

Regarding the discriminative (*vikalpita*) and innate (*sahaja*) [afflictions], which are severed first? [The] answer: The obstacles of the discriminative type are severed first at the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), all at once and instantaneously.

[They] are severed. The co-emergent obstacles are severed stage by stage within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), until they can be completely exhausted only upon reaching the moment of the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*).

△ Third, the concluding judgment (in two parts): First, the formal judgment (in two parts): First, judging the presence or absence of the essential nature of the characteristics (in two parts): First, the definitive determination.
Existence and non-existence.
All such aforementioned forms of self-grasping (up to) the aggregates within one’s own mind all exist.
[Exegesis of Terms] First, the correct determination: regarding the existence or non-existence of aggregates external to one’s own mind, these refer to objective entities (*bhāva*). One’s own mind...
The "internal aggregates" (*ādhyātmika-skandha*) refer to the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*). The *Zongjing lu*, fascicle 65, explains:
"That which is the object of the perceiving faculty (*ālambana*) yet is not clung to is all termed 'external to the mind. The seventh consciousness conceives of what is external to its own mind;

only the sixth consciousness conceives of the aggregates as being external to its own mind—or rather, it conceives of them as existing within its own mind where there are no such aggregates. That all things exist [therein] is because they are intimately [connected]."
The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) need not be discussed further, as it is already excluded by the refutation of the notion of a self.

Since images necessarily exist, there is not even the slightest phenomenon that can apprehend another phenomenon; rather, it is only one's own mind that apprehends its own mind. Thus, all [cognitions] take the aggregates (*skandha*) as their objects.
This explains the basis of what belongs to the self (*ātmiya*).
△ Next, the preceding meaning is concluded:
Therefore, all instances of self-grasping are based on the false attachment to the characteristics of the impermanent five aggregates of clinging as being a self.
△ Next, the dependence and pervasiveness [of this grasping] are judged according to their presence or absence.
However, because the various aggregates arise from conditions, [they are]—up to—"due to being falsely conceptualized," they definitely do not exist.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: the aggregates arising from conditions are the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); the conception of a self within the aggregates is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which is non-existent.
△ Next, citing scriptural evidence:
Therefore, the Sūtra says, "Bhikṣus, you should know" (up to) "all arise conditioned by the five aggregates of grasping.
△ Next, resolving difficulties (2): First, directly resolving the difficulties and objections (3). First, resolving the difficulty regarding the matters of memory, recognition, and so forth (2).
The first objection:
If a real self (*ātman*) does not exist, how could there be such things as recollection, cognition, memorization, study, gratitude, and resentment? [Commentary on the terms:

"Recollection" (*smṛti*) refers to the mental awareness of objects previously experienced; "cognition" (*vijñāna*) refers to the present sensory objects; "long-term recitation" and "repeated practice" cause [the mind] to... [retain what has been learned].
They come to ripen, benefiting me or harming me, forming kindness or enmity. As the *Śataśāstra* states: "Furthermore, the mind perishes and arises differently from moment to moment.
If there were no real self, how could such matters as memory, recognition, recitation, and practice exist?"
△ Second, the explanation [of the two points]: First, the refutation of the erroneous view.
Since the substantially existent self (*ātman*) as it is grasped is eternal and unchanging, its substance cannot be separate from its function; therefore, it would necessarily not be eternal.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: Regarding the first phrase, "the subsequent should be as before," "subsequent" refers to the present day, while "before" refers to the past.
"This matter" refers to such activities as recollecting, recognizing, chanting, and practicing, just as when one was an infant and had not yet become proficient in the classics and histories.

In youth one practices; what has not been practiced does not exist, while what has been practiced exists. If the self were permanent, constant, and unchanging, it would have to be as it was later, just as it was before;
there could be no existence later that was not present before, because its essence would be without distinction.

If one were to argue—anticipating and refuting this objection—that although the essence of the self is constantly used, there is no such fault because it undergoes transformation. This reasoning is also...

If one breaks down the relationship between essence and function by asserting that they are identical, then the fault that the essence would be eternal is the same as before. Alternatively, if the essence were to change like the function, it would follow that it is not eternal, which contradicts your own tenet.
△ Next, the principle is revealed.
Now, each and every sentient being possesses a fundamental consciousness (the *ālayavijñāna*)... [up to] ...it is difficult for you to avoid error, whereas it is not so for my school.
Glossary: The fundamental consciousness is the eighth consciousness. This refers to the period from beginningless time until the stage of non-transformation (*aparāvṛtti*). Only...
Because it belongs to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is called "of one kind" (*ekajātīya*). Because it proceeds without interruption, it is called "continuous" (*saṃtāna*).

It is termed the "supporting seed" (*ādhāra-bīja*) because it can maintain both mundane and supramundane seeds. Regarding all phenomena—namely the seven evolving consciousnesses and so forth—when these various phenomena perfume the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), then those phenomena act as the cause;
when the fundamental consciousness gives rise to manifest activity (*pravṛtti*), then the fundamental consciousness acts as the cause. Therefore...
It is said that they act as mutual causes; by virtue of this power of mutual perfuming between the subject and the object, there arise such phenomena as memory and cognition.
Why, then, must one insist upon the existence of a real self? Thus, the following concludes with a reprimand.
△ Next, the explanation of the objection regarding the creation of karma and the experiencing of its results (2). First, the objection:
If there is no real self (*ātman*), who is it that creates karma and who experiences its results?
△ Next, the explanation (2). First, the refutation of the erroneous view.
Since the substantially existent self as it is grasped is devoid of change (up to: if it were subject to change, it would be impermanent).

Regarding the meaning of the terms: the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states: "The substantially existent self is the subject (*dharmin*). It cannot create karma or experience its results, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
The reason (*hetu*) is: 'because it is devoid of change. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like space."
△ Next, the principle is revealed.
However, for all sentient beings, from the mind and mental factors (up to) the creation of karma and the experiencing of its fruits, there is no contradiction with this principle.
[This is] the "Resonance" (*hexiang*). The *Zongjing* quotes the intent of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and asks: "If, according to the six sense faculties, there is no self, who..."
"Who is it that experiences [the results] of what has been created? He replied: "The Buddha taught that by performing good one is born in heaven, and by committing evil one undergoes suffering.

This is simply the natural law (*dharmatā*) of causes and conditions; it is not that 'I' am able to perform or experience these. If one were to say that this 'I' exists apart from causes and conditions, then why would one who commits evil not be born in heaven?
Why instead fall into hell? For how could 'I' possibly desire that hell and thus undergo such suffering?"
"Yes. Since I have committed evil yet do not experience pleasure, we know that the retribution for good and evil arises solely from causes and conditions, and not from a real self" (text).
Supplement: The *Zongjing* states that there are two kinds of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
First, the dominant causal conditions of wholesome and unwholesome karma, which merely induce the maturation (*vipāka*) of rebirth in the heavens or in hell.

Second, the causal conditions of wholesome and unwholesome karma as a similar outflow (*niṣyanda*), whereby those born in the heavens experience jeweled grounds and golden flowers, while those who fall into hell experience forests of swords, copper pillars, and the like. (Text) Cause.
The "conditions" (*pratyaya*) are the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all karmas and the two types of grasping (*dvividha-upādāna*).
△ Third, the resolution of the obstacles regarding saṃsāra and nirvāṇa (in two parts): First, the objection:
"If the self truly does not exist, who is it that wanders through the various realms of saṃsāra? And who is it that, weary of suffering, seeks to attain nirvāṇa?"
Appendix: The *Śata-śāstra-vṛtti*, Fascicle Two, states: "If all phenomena were empty and devoid of self, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa would be lost.
Why? Because it is due to the existence of a self that those who lack wisdom [cling to these distinctions]."
Those who are attached to the cycle of birth and death first perform wholesome and unwholesome deeds, subsequently experiencing their resulting fruits—whether desirable or undesirable.
All wise persons, delighting in *nirvāṇa*, first contemplate the suffering of birth and death;

incited by the scorching heat of that fire, they develop the resolve for renunciation, subsequently abandon evil, and diligently cultivate all that is wholesome until they realize liberation. Thus, all of this is accomplished through me.
△ Second, the explanation [of the two points]: First, the refutation of errors.
Since the substantially existent self as it is grasped lacks both arising and ceasing... (up to)... therefore what they say is "permanent" works to their own detriment.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: Herein, the meaning of "permanence" as asserted by the opponent is refuted.

This means that if the self were permanent like empty space, it would be devoid of arising and ceasing, and likewise devoid of suffering and affliction. Who, then, would transmigrate? Who would proceed toward *nirvāṇa*?
Therefore, what they call "permanence" serves only to bring about their own ruin.
△ Next, the principle is revealed.

Now, as for the class of sentient beings, their mental and physical continuities (*saṃtāna*)—[extending] until they grow weary of suffering and seek to proceed toward *nirvāṇa*—are called "continuities" because they arise and cease without interruption through the power of causes and conditions. Within these continuities...
Arising from delusion, one creates karma and undergoes suffering; the wise person, weary of suffering and longing for its cessation, abandons evil and cultivates good, thereby realizing nirvana.
Next, the conclusion indicates that all is consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra).
From this it is known that there is certainly no real self (up to the point where) fools falsely grasp at it as a self.
△ Next, the refutation of real dharmas (in two parts): first, the interrogation and response regarding their non-existence.
How are the various phenomena (dharmas) existing externally to consciousness known? [This continues] until: because the principle of the external phenomena grasped [by others] does not exist.
*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonances), *Xuantan* (Profound Discourses), Volume 8, states: "That which is supremely subtle, empty, and pervasive is termed the Way (*mārga*).

When the mind wanders outside the Way, it is called an 'external way' (*bāhyamārga*). Thus, only the Buddha’s true path exists; all others are termed external ways. [This refers to] other vehicles (*yāna*).

This refers to the Hīnayāna, which is considered a remnant of the Mahāyāna. Although they have realized the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-nairātmya*), they still cling to the existence of phenomena external to the mind;
thus, they are unable to fully comprehend the correct principles of Mahāyāna Vijñaptimātra (Cognition-Only).

△ Second, the extensive refutation of the attachment to characteristics (three parts). First, the direct refutation of the existence of phenomena external to the mind (two parts). First, the non-Buddhists (two parts).
First, the interrogation:
How is it that what is grasped by the non-Buddhists does not exist?

△ Second, the explanation [of the refutation] (in two parts). First, the specific refutations of thirteen schools (in five parts). First, the Sāṃkhya school (in three parts). First, the statement of their tenets:
Now, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the self (*ātman*) is consciousness (*caitanya*), and that it is real and not conventional, being apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Regarding the phonology and meaning: The *Xuántán* (Profound Discourse) states that the Sanskrit term *saṃkhya* is translated here as "number" (*shù*).

This refers to the number of wisdom (*huìshù*). It is named after the fundamental principles of all phenomena through which they are calculated; because the treatise arises from these numbers, it is called the *Sāṃkhya* (Number) school. Furthermore, the treatise is capable of generating these numbers.
It is also called Sāṃkhya. Those who compose the Sāṃkhya treatises and those who study the Sāṃkhya system are all termed Sāṃkhyas.
Its originator was Kapila. They maintain that the "self" (ātman) is the thinker; by "self," they mean the *puruṣa*, which has thinking as its essential nature.
This is precisely the twenty-fifth truth of the *puruṣa* (self). Regarding the phrase "the enjoyment of *sattva* and so forth":
*sattva* here means "sentient being" (*sattva*) and is also translated as "valiant" (*vīra*). Here, the sense of "valiant" is taken. *Rajas* here means "subtle" and is also called "dust."
Now, taking the meaning of *rajas* (dust): its [Sanskrit] equivalent is *tamas*, which here means "darkness. It should thus be named "the dust of courageous darkness" (*vīra-rajas-tamas*).

If taken in a lateral sense, it corresponds to the old translations "the darkness of joy and sorrow," or "suffering, pleasure, and delusion. The new translations render this as "greed, anger, and delusion," or alternatively as "pleasure, suffering, and equanimity.
In terms of their essential nature, these are the three poisons. These three poisons are themselves the self-nature of the three qualities (*triguṇa*).

Self-nature (*svabhāva*). Anciently it was called "dark nature" (*mīng-xìng*) and is also termed "supreme nature" (*prakṛti*). When it has not yet produced the "Great One" (*mahat*) and the other principles, but merely abides in its own state, it is called self-nature.
Once it produces the Great One and the rest, it is then called supreme nature, because it possesses superior functions. This constitutes the twenty-five [principles].
This is the first of the truths. If the *puruṣa* (the divine self) has a need, those *sattvas* and others accordingly give rise to awakening;
they fashion the *mahat* and so forth for the sake of the *puruṣa*, who then experiences the twenty-three principles, such as the *mahat* that has been produced.

That is to say: from primordial darkness (tamas) arises the Great One (mahat), which is also called "Awakening" (buddhi). From Awakening arises the "I-consciousness" (ahaṃkāra), which is also called "Self-conceit" (asmitā).

From the I-consciousness arise the five subtle atoms (tanmātra), which are also called the five "mere-nesses" (kevala). Their dimensions are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. From these five mere-nesses arise the five gross elements (mahābhūta):
space, wind, fire, water, and earth. From the five gross elements arise the eleven faculties; first, the five organs of cognition arise.

The faculties (*indriya*) refer to the ear, body, eye, tongue, and nose. Next arise the five faculties of action (*karmendriya*), namely the organs of speech, hands, feet, and the passages for excretion and reproduction.
Finally arises the faculty of mental equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). These constitute the twenty-three principles (*tattva*) of the intermediate stage;

including the first and last [stages], there are thus twenty-five (as the text states). Furthermore, "the Great and so forth" refers to the twenty-three factors beginning with the Great One (*mahat*).
The synthesis of the three qualities (guṇas) is real and not provisional. As for the claim that it is "attained through direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*), this refers to their erroneous calculation;
it is a semblance of direct perception.
*Supplement:* The *Qixin penxue*, Volume Five, states: "The 'non-Buddhists' (*tīrthika*) and so forth refers to the Sāṃkhya masters."
Because they rely on the meditative absorption of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) to produce mundane supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they should be regarded as following a false path.

With the knowledge of birth and death (*cyuty-upapāda-jñāna*), they perceive the three matters—the death here and birth there—up to eighty thousand *kalpas* into the future; yet thereafter, they no longer know what those [beings] conceive.
They hold that the nature of darkness (*tamas*) is eternal and arises from this, for among all worldly phenomena, the nature of darkness is obscure and difficult to know. Therefore, it is said:
Prakṛti. From the primordial darkness (mūlaprakṛti) arises intellect (buddhi), and so on, down to the faculty of equanimity (sāmya).
At that time, it is called "the formation of saṃsāra" and the grasping at a single self (ātman). [The self thinks: "I am the master of experience; I contemplate superior objects.
Because Prakṛti transforms into the state of being born for my enjoyment, and because I enjoy it, I am bound by those objects and cannot attain liberation. If I do not contemplate, Prakṛti...
The liberation of the unchanging *puruṣa* is called *nirvāṇa*.
△ Next, the refutation (in seven parts): First, the refutation of what is obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Why is their position irrational? [From here until: How can it be said that it is obtained through direct perception?

Supplement: First, refuting [the notion of] "large" and so forth through the subsequent deconstruction. Regarding the terms "army" (*senā*) and "forest" (*vana*): a collection of people constitutes an army, and a gathering of trees constitutes a forest.
If the people and the trees were dispersed, what would constitute an army or a forest? The *Śata-śāstra* states: "These are merely conventional designations for 'army' and 'forest';
within them, there is no real entity that is an army or a forest. As for the statement regarding "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*), see the *Zongjing lu*, fascicle 4.

The nineteenth fascicle states: "Manifest" (*pratyakṣa*) means that which is clearly manifest; it refers to a directly perceived object that is free from names and words and devoid of false conceptualization.
This is termed "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). "Measuring" (*pramāṇa*) has the sense of establishing through determination;
it means that the mind measures and establishes the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phenomenon regarding its object without error. (Text). This is true direct perception.

Hereafter, all cases shall follow this principle regarding the Mahat and other categories. Since these are composed of many constituent parts, they are not real in the same way that an army or a forest is not real.

How, then, can it be said that they are "objects obtained through direct perception" (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*)? Regarding the categories such as the Mahat: if they are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*) and not real, how can one state the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) as being obtained through direct perception?
One might argue: "The Mahat and so forth are [real] entities because they are composed of many constituent parts; like the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). [But this is untenable.]
[The examples of] an army, a forest, and so forth.
△ Second, the mutual refutation of subject and object:

Furthermore, if dharmas such as "greatness" (*mahat*) were substantially existent (up to the point where they undergo transformation and are therefore impermanent), the same logic would apply by example.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: First, using the established [conclusion] to refute the means of establishment (*sādhana*), it says:

"The great elements (*mahābhūta*) and other phenomena are not substantially existent as composites of the three, because they are like the three primary entities (*sattva*)," and so forth. Next, using the established [conclusion] to refute the means of establishment, it says:
"The three—*sattva* and the others—are also composites of the three; they are identical to the great elements and so forth, just as the great elements undergo transformation."
"Non-permanence as an example is likewise" means that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and other effects arise from their own nature (*svabhāva*).

Because these various effects—such as the great elements—undergo transformation, change, differentiation, and increase, they are non-permanent; they are not permanent like the unchanging nature itself.
"Permanence as an example is likewise" means that, following the above formal argument (*prayoga*), one establishes: "The various dharmas such as the great elements do not undergo transformation."
It is not non-eternal, because it exists substantially. As stated in the *Three Original Treatises* (*Tri-svabhāva-śāstra*), and as the formal argument (*prayoga*) says:

"The three, such as *sattva*, are also transformations and thus non-eternal, because they are [identical to] the *mahat* and so forth; they are analogous to the *mahat* and so forth. The first volume of the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Commentary on the *Śata-śāstra*) refutes this, stating:
"The *mahat* and so forth all take self-nature (*svabhāva*) as their essence. When the *mahat* and so forth undergo transformation, the self-nature should likewise transform. By virtue of this...
This intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) ought to be impermanent, because its essence is not different [from the effects], just like the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth.
△ Third, the refutation based on the identity of essence and function:
Furthermore, each of the three fundamental substances possesses manifold functions; [the same would apply] to the others as well, because their essences are not distinct.

*Hexiang* (Harmony of Resonance): This [section] refutes the Sāṃkhya calculation of three primal essences (*prakṛti*), which each possess various manifold functions such as clarity, agitation, and obscurity, because they undergo transformation into the various phenomena of the "great" (*mahat*) and so forth.
The refutation states: since the functions are manifold, the substance [of the essence] must also be manifold.
One should also understand that because essence and function are one, there are many functions. The *Vyākhyāyukti* on the first fascicle of the *Śataśāstra-vṛtti* states:

"Furthermore, each of the three natures possesses numerous functions such as illumination, agitation, and obscurity. Since it is admitted that they are identical in essence by virtue of their nature..."
[The opponent argues that] according to its functions, it should consist of multiple entities (text). [The author] refutes this attempted defense below. The opponent’s defense states:
"Although the three fundamental substances possess manifold functions, their essence is all-pervasive; thus, there is no fault of having multiple entities. [The author] refutes this, saying:

"Since the three substances are all-pervasive, when they exercise their function in one location and transform all phenomena, they should likewise simultaneously and instantaneously transform them in all other locations as well."
Because the substance of these three things is pervasive and without distinction, the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Commentary on the *Śataśāstra*) states:

"Furthermore, as for the substance of this intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), when one part undergoes transformation, the substance of the remaining immeasurable parts is not different; therefore, they too should undergo transformation accordingly."
△ Four [elements] break down into three, which then combine to form one.
Since you admit that these three things have distinct essential natures (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it should not be said that the three combine to form one.

[Commentary on the Meaning of the Sound]: This means that since your own school admits that the three things have distinct essential natures and characteristics, how could they combine to form matter (*rūpa*)?
[The opponent claims] they are of one identical characteristic. This should not be refuted by the following [objection]:

"If it is argued that when they were not yet combined they were three, but at the time of combination they transform into one, therefore the principle that the resulting form (rūpa) and so forth are one is established"—this is also not correct, because there is no difference in essence between the state of being combined and the state of not being combined.
If it is argued that these two matters differ in essence but share the same characteristic,

and are thus analogous— just as gold, brass, and copper, though three distinct things, are similar in being metal and therefore identical, such that their characteristics remain constant whether joined or unjoined—

there is no such fault. However, this contradicts the refutation of your own tenet below, which states that the characteristic of *sattva* is identical to the essence of *sattva*, and the other two [characteristics] are likewise.
It is likewise. Now you say that while their substances (*tattva*) are different, their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are the same;

does this not contradict your own tenet? The refutation of the substance should follow below through repeated analysis. If you claim that the three things have different substances but identical characteristics, then the substance should be like the characteristic—identical—and the characteristic should be like the substance—unitary.
If that were so, one should say that one [substance] forms one, and three [substances] form three; one should not say otherwise.
The three factors combine to form a single characteristic.
△ Fifth, refuting through the mutual contradiction of the general and the particular:
Furthermore, since the "three" are particulars and the "great elements" (mahābhūta) are the general, because the general and the particular are one, they should neither be one nor two.
Commentary on the Meaning: There are three specific instances [of the "particulars"], while the fact that these three particulars together constitute a single whole is the general case.
The *Śataśāstra* states: "If you maintain that the general and the particular are definitively one, then the general—like the particular—should be three and not one;
or the particular—like the general—should be one and not three. How can there be three particulars that establish a single general?"
△ 6. Refutation based on whether transformation occurs through conjunction or non-conjunction (2). First, the formal refutation:
If these three do not conjoin at the time of transformation... [down to] ...the fundamental distinct characteristics and substance would also necessarily be lost.

Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: If one claims that when the three things undergo transformation, they do not combine to form a single entity, then they would remain as they were before the transformation;
how then could it be perceived that the transformed object is a single thing, such as a color?

If, on the other hand, the three transform and combine to form a single entity, then the essential characteristics of the three original substances would be lost, because their substance and their characteristics are identical.
△ Next, the refutation of the defense.
It cannot be said that each of the three possesses its own three characteristics (up to: "the substance should also be threefold, because the substance is identical to the characteristic").
[Commentary on the Meaning] The first section, the refutation of the three, has two parts. The defense states: "The three entities each possess both general and specific characteristics."

Because of their distinct characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), these three are not yet combined; because of their general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), they appear as one when combined. Thus, there is no fault such as the loss of their essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth.
[The opponent objects: "If the general characteristic is precisely that which breaks down the general, then just as the particular is distinct from the three, the general should likewise be three."
If the three characteristics were distinct, one would not perceive them as one. How then is it that we currently perceive them as a single entity such as "form"?

If you argue that this is refuted by the fact that each of the three [characteristics] possesses its own three [sub-characteristics], they further defend their position by saying: "The substance of each of these three things possesses the three characteristics of *sattva* and so forth;
however, because they are blended together in a state of combination, they are difficult to discern, and thus one perceives only 'this is form. Since this is already [the case]...
This refutes their identity. Since there are three, how can they be seen as one? Once they are seen as one, how can it be known that these three things are distinct?
Furthermore, if each of those three things possesses all three characteristics, then upon mentioning any single one, it should be able to constitute form and so forth;
what would be lacking? Why must they wait for the combination of all three things to be established?

Furthermore, since the characteristics each possess three aspects, their substance must likewise each possess three; for it is logically necessary that the substance is identical to the characteristics.
△ Seventh: Refuting the established [result] by means of non-differentiation.
Furthermore, since the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and other phenomena are all composed of the three [qualities], they would all be without distinction; this would constitute a grave error.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: if one claims that the primary elements and all other phenomena are all composed of the three things, then there would be no difference between the primary elements and the "I" (*ātman*), up to and including the twenty-three factors such as the sense faculties. This would contradict what is posited by your own school.
The distinctions between causes, such as the three [types of] entities, and effects, such as the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth, would all fail to be established.
If that were the case, one sense organ should perceive all objects, or conversely, a single object should be perceived by all sense organs;
consequently, all things in the world—whether sentient or insentient, pure or impure—would be known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and so on.

Since neither [position] is established, the subsequent text states: "This would contradict the distinct natures of the three qualities (*guṇa*) and our own [tenets], and it would also contradict the distinctions among all phenomena in the world;
thus, one would incur faults such as contradiction with one's own teachings and contradiction with the world."
△ The three fetters are not [real].
Therefore, those dharmas they grasp as real are not established; they are merely imagined to exist through deluded conceptualization.
*Hegiang* (合響), Volume 13, states: "From the truth of self-nature (*svabhāva-satya*), all dharmas arise. However—
This is a false conceptualization based on mere sentiment; such speculative reckoning is called a "false cause.
△ Second, the Vaiśeṣika masters (in two parts): First, the statement of their tenets.

The categories (*padārtha*) asserted by the Vaiśeṣikas, such as substance (*dravya*), possess a nature that is substantially real (*dravyasat*) and are apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
*Yinyì* (Explanations of Sounds and Meanings) states: The *Xuántán* (Profound Discourse) says that this is the doctrine of the Vaiśeṣika school.

In Sanskrit, it is called *Vaiśeṣika-śāstra*; this is translated as "Superior" (*shèng*). It establishes six categories of meaning (*padārtha*), which are considered the most superior. Alternatively, it is called "Superior" because it was created by a superior person.
This creator lived at the end of a *kalpa*, when the human lifespan was immeasurable; it was during this time that this non-Buddhist teacher appeared.
In the world, he was named Ulūka, which translates as "owl. By day, he avoided sound and form, concealing his traces in mountains and thickets;
by night, his sight and hearing were suspended as he went forth to beg for food. Because people of the time considered him to resemble an owl bird, they called him the Owl Ascetic (Ulūka-ṛṣi).
He is also known as Ulūka in the *Śataśāstra* (*Bai lun*), and is further titled the Ascetic who Eats Rice from the Navel (*Vrīhimukha-ṛṣi*). [End of] Section Six.

The categories are: (1) substance (*dravya*), (2) quality (*guṇa*), (3) action (*karman*), (4) existence (*sattā*), (5) generality (*sāmānya*), (6) particularity (*viśeṣa*), and (7) inherence (*samavāya*).

Regarding substance: it is the real basis upon which qualities and actions depend; it is called "substance" because qualities and actions do not depend on [other] categories such as existence (*sattā*) and so forth.
There are nine kinds of substances: (1) earth, (2) water, (3) fire, (4) wind, (5) space (*ākāśa*), (6) time (*kāla*), and (7) direction (*diś*).
Eight: the self (ātman). Nine: the mind (manas). "Qualities" (guṇa) refers to the qualities of moral conduct;
there are twenty-four kinds: 1. color; 2. fragrance; 3. taste; 4. touch; 5. number; 6. dimension; 7. distinctness; 8. conjunction;
9. disjunction; 10. thatness; 11. thisness; 12. cognition; 13. pleasure; 14. pain; 15. desire; 16. aversion; 17. effort.
Vigor. Eighteen: the nature of heaviness. Nineteen: the nature of fluidity. Twenty: moisture. Twenty-one: formations. Twenty-two: phenomena.
Twenty-three: non-phenomena. Twenty-four: sound. Action (*karman*) refers to functional activity; it is of five kinds. First: appropriation (*upādāna*).

Second, abandonment; third, contraction and extension; fourth, motion; fifth, existence (*mahāsattā*). Great Existence is unique because the three—substance, quality, and activity—are identical in their possession of existence.
Apart from substance, quality, and activity, there exists a separate category as its essence. It is by virtue of this Great Existence that substance and the others possess existence.
Likewise, the category of "similarity" (*sāmānya*) is also unique; for example, the commonality between earth and earth is distinct from its relation to water.
Thus, there is the distinction between the meanings of "earth" and its various states; earth is not water, and the same applies to water and so forth.
Furthermore, apart from the elements such as solidity (*sāratva*), there exists a distinct substantial entity called the "phrase of conjunction" (*saṃyoga-pada*).

This refers to the collection of dharmas which, by means of the phrase of conjunction—just as a bird flying through the air suddenly reaches a tree branch and stays there without departing—is caused to abide and so forth by that phrase of conjunction.
(Commentary: Regarding the phrase "many real entities" (*aneka-dravya*) and so forth: among the six categories (*ṣat-padārtha*), it refers exclusively to the category of inherence (*samavāya*).
Because it is a conceptual construct (*prajñapti*) and is not apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is said to be "many."
△ Second, the refutation (2): First, the direct refutation (2). First, clarifying that the essence of the various categories is not substantially existent (8).
First, the refutation of permanence and impermanence among the various categories.

The reason why that position is irrational is as follows: (up to) it should not be the case that there exists a real intrinsic nature apart from these [categories]. Regarding the meaning of the terms:

first, concerning the permanent among the categories (*padārtha*), the formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows: "Among the categories, that which is permanent is a subject (*dharmin*) that must be impermanent;
this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it possesses activity (*kāritra*). The similar example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is, for instance, like..."

"Producing fruit. This refers to the sense of being able to produce a fruit. If one does not refute permanence by way of this sense of producing fruit, then one must clarify the *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) inference as follows:
"Among the various categories (*padārtha*), that which is eternal cannot exist as a real intrinsic nature apart from consciousness, because it lacks functional activity, like a rabbit's horn.
One should know that a rabbit's horn is an object grasped through the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) of the mental consciousness."

Although they lack a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are not separate from consciousness. To cite them as examples serves only to dispel the attachment to the notion that things exist substantially apart from consciousness.
Regarding the section on "all non-existents" (*abhāva*) below, it refutes [the opponent's] proof by means of impermanence (*anitya*). The argument states:

Among all categories of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), those that are impermanent do not possess a real nature, because they have material resistance (*sapratighatva*) and are analyzable. This is like an army or a forest; this refutation is based on the presence of resistance.

It truly exists. If there were no [inferential] cognition [establishing it], one might say: "All that is impermanent should not possess a real intrinsic nature (svabhāva) apart from consciousness, because they lack material resistance (apratigha), just like the mind and mental factors.
This explains the "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) nature by way of non-obstruction.
△ Second, refuting [the opponent's view] by means of two phrases concerning actual qualities.
Furthermore, as for that which they grasp as earth, water, fire, and wind—[it is argued that] these are not actually seen as real earth, water, fire, and wind by the eye.

Supplement: In the preceding text, the names and natures of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—as posited by the opponent regarding the cause of tactile contact for the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), were successively interrogated and refuted.
Originally, these four—solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion—are indivisible.
As the *Śata-śāstra* states: "If the names 'earth' and so forth are established based on solidity and so forth, then there is no point of contention."

Because their substance (*dravya*) is not distinct (text). According to the Vaiśeṣika school, earth and so forth are resistant (*sapratigha*) and are categorized separately under the category of substance (*dravyapadārtha*);

whereas solidity and so forth are non-resistant (*apratigha*) and are categorized separately under the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*). Nevertheless, they all admit that these are objects touched by the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).

Since both the resistant and the non-resistant share this same cause [of being tangible], this single cause would then apply to two opposing schools, thereby committing the fallacy of the "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) inconclusive reason.
The fallacy of the inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*). This refers to the first of the six types of inconclusive reasons in the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*. It is as follows:

the property of being permanent and the property of being impermanent both share this same reason. The two formal arguments (*pramāṇa*) are as stated in the text. Regarding earth, water, and so forth, one should establish the formal arguments accordingly, as follows:

The three elements of earth, water, and fire as they are apprehended are the subject (*dharmin*). Your thesis is that they should not be subsumed under the category of "substance" (*dravya-pada-artha*) because they possess resistance.

The reason (*hetu*) is: "because they are seen by the eye-organ," just like blue color and so forth. Furthermore, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is: those very things you apprehend, such as blue color and so forth, are the subject;
your thesis is that they should not be subsumed under the category of "quality" (*guṇa-pada-artha*) because they lack resistance. The reason is: "because they are seen by the eye-organ."

Therefore, just as with the three elements of earth, water, and fire, there would also be the fault of an overly broad scope for the cause of transgression; since the faults would be the same as before, it says, "one should hold them accountable according to this.
Regarding the exclusion of the word "wind" here, the *Śataśāstra* states: "Wind is perceived only by the body, because it is formless. Question:
The first two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have already sufficed for mutual interrogation and the refutation of their tenets; what then [is the purpose] of the latter two?
The meaning of the text is the same as before, except that the word "wind" (vāyu) is absent. What purpose does it serve? Is it not redundant? Answer:

This is because, according to the Vaiśeṣika school, worldly objects and so forth are established without departing from the six categories (padārtha), and they constitute the objects of direct perception (pratyakṣa) through visual observation and tactile contact.
As stated in the sixth fascicle of the *Śata-śāstra* (*Bǎibǎilùn*): "However, that treatise speaks of the jar..."

It is also not logical that objects such as garments exist as objects of perception for the eye and touch for the body because they possess the [real] categories of substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence;
therefore, they are known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by the sense faculties. Why is this so?

Because objects such as jars and garments are merely provisionally designated (*prajñapti*) upon the dharmas of form and so forth by the conceptualizing mental consciousness (*vikalpa-manovijñāna*); how then can they be grasped as being directly perceived?

Regarding the "objects of valid cognition" (pramāṇa-viṣaya): those two causes—the visual perception of the body and tactile contact—comprehensively encompass the five sense faculties and their five objects, all of which are known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

In the present text, although the first two types of valid cognition have already presented the cause of what is touched by the body faculty, the cause of what is seen by the eye has not yet been mentioned.
Therefore, the latter two types of valid cognition are further introduced to complete the set. Thus it is known.

The following concludes the exposition. There is no distinct intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that is not apprehended by direct perception (pratyakṣa). Within the text, the subject (dharmin) and the reason (hetu) are mutually implied across two sections.

First, the preceding two [sections] are concluded. The formal inference (pramāṇa) states: Therefore, it is known that there are no real earth, water, fire, or wind possessing distinct intrinsic natures such as solidity or moisture;
nor are there real earth, water, fire, or wind that are touched by the body-faculty (kāyendriya). This [inference] concerns the earth...

The existence of such phenomena is established by the fact that they are the causes for the body-sense organ (*kāyendriya*) to be touched by shadows; this demonstrates that they are not obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Next, he concludes regarding the latter two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), saying: "Therefore, one knows that the three elements of earth, water, and fire do not exist as real entities.
Nor do they possess distinct intrinsic natures separate from [colors] such as blue. Furthermore, the real earth, water, and fire are not seen by the eye—excluding the term 'wind'."

Wind is not seen by the eye; therefore, this [argument] uses the fact of being seen by the visual faculty as its reason, and establishes it through the presence of attributes such as blue color along with shadows.
In this way, through successive analysis and refutation, the categories of "earth" and so forth, as well as "solidity" and so forth, are not established.

How then could there be a real nature apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Some say this is based on the thirteenth fascicle of the *Zhènhuì xuánlùn* (The Profound Treatise on Resolving Doubts).
At the end of this treatise, it says: "It is not that one sees actual earth, water, or fire with the eye while the word 'wind' is absent;

rather, it is said that this is perhaps a scribal error resulting in a redundant insertion. Looking at the *Zikao lu* (Record of Self-Examination), it also states that the word "wind" is a redundant insertion.
△ Third, regarding the refutation of the category of "real entities" (*dravyapada*), that which possesses resistance (*sapratigha*) is permanent.
Furthermore, among those [entities] they grasp as real categories, such as coarse earth and so forth, these ought to be impermanent.
Supplement: The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: That which possesses resistance within the category of real entities is the subject (*dharmin*); it ought to be impermanent.

Thesis: Because they all possess resistance (*sapratigha*). Reason: [Because they possess resistance]. Homogeneous Example: Like coarse earth and so forth. This refutes [the claim that] space, time, and so on are distinct entities.
Their [erroneous] calculation is that there exists a separate great element of space; however, this is neither the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) space nor the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*).

Furthermore, because the essence of time is substantial, it is called "time" by virtue of being the cause for designating [it] and the cause for the cognition that apprehends it. Moreover, they calculate that space and so forth are...
That which possesses resistance is permanent; earth and the other elements possess resistance and are impermanent. Therefore, earth and the others serve as concordant examples.
△ Fourth, the refutation of the unresisting phenomena within various propositions:

Among the meanings of these propositions, that which is apprehended by the material sense-faculties (up to) is admitted to be apprehended by the material sense-faculties, just like earth, water, fire, and wind.

Supplement: Among the various categories of meaning (*padārtha*), those phenomena (*dharma*) that are apprehended by the sensory faculties (*indriya*) yet lack material resistance (*apratigha*) are, for example, fragrance, taste, and sound as listed among the qualities (*guṇa*).
The *Huìxuán* quotes the ancient commentary (*gūshū*) as follows: "Regarding the essence of these qualities: that which is apprehended by the eye is a single basis termed 'form' (*rūpa*);
that which is apprehended by the nose is a single basis termed 'fragrance' (*gandha*); that which is apprehended by the ear is a single basis termed 'sound' (*śabda*); and so forth."

That which is grasped by the skin is called "the single basis" (i.e., because it relies upon color-form and so forth, the eye and other faculties arise; since color-form is the basis, it is termed "the single basis").

Among these, the three—odor, flavor, and sound—are objects grasped by the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and are dharmas that lack resistance (*apratigha*). Furthermore, the ancient commentary states:

"The specific and general characteristics of earth and so forth, as well as color-form and so forth, do not interchange with one another; they are all objects grasped by the sense-faculties. [Regarding] earth and so forth...

Because there are obstructive phenomena within these real categories (*satpadārtha*), they are cited as concordant examples (*sapakṣa*). The formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) is established according to the text.
△ Fifth, refuting all categories by means of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*):

Furthermore, those [categories] such as substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth, which are clung to by others, are not included among the existent (*bhāva*), and thus are like flowers in the sky (*khapuṣpa*), etc.
Supplement: Generally, there are two broad methods for refutation: first, refutation based on the objects of attachment; second, refutation based on *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only).

In the present text, which refutes the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*), only the former method is employed to generally refute all categories. Within the two positions regarding permanence and impermanence, each has two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In both cases, the first type of valid cognition is used for refutation based on the objects of attachment, while the second type of valid cognition is used for [refutation based on consciousness-only].
Regarding the refutation based on *vijñapti-mātra*: the meaning of the remaining passages consists entirely of refutations directed at what is grasped as real.

Now, this chapter is placed between the two pillars of the six propositions; it synthesizes the preceding and following sections by providing a general refutation of all propositions based on *vijñapti-mātra*.

Nevertheless, among those propositions, the specific focus on refuting the two propositions concerning "substance" (*dravya*) is because, according to the Vaiśeṣika school, substance is [the fundamental category].
It is the basis for qualities and activities (*guṇa-karma*). Furthermore, it is said: "Because this 'Great Existence' (mahāsattā) exists as a real entity (*dravya*) and so forth.

Thus, the *Vyākhyāyukti* on the *Śataśāstra* states: "The categories (*padārtha*) such as 'substance' (*dravya*) as apprehended by the owl-philosophers (the Vaiśeṣikas) are manifested through causes such as 'existence' (*sattā*).
Furthermore, they can only be distinguished when they take 'substance' and so forth as their own basis" (text). From this, [it follows that] it is substantially existent (*dravyasat*).
These serve as the key points for all the categories (*padārtha*). If these two actual categories (*vastu*) are refuted, the others will not be difficult [to refute].

Regarding the statement in the text that "they are not real qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth," this refers to the five categories beginning with quality, which are subsumed under the category of "non-real.

Regarding the statement that "they do not exist as real entities (*dravya*) and so forth," this refers to the five categories beginning with substance, which are subsumed under the nature of "non-existence. Since they are not mutually inclusive, how could they be separate?
Whether existence is apart from consciousness or not apart from consciousness, both belong to the realm of delusion. The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Explanation of the *Śataśāstra*) states:

"The 'reals' (*dravya*) and so forth propounded by the owl-philosophers do not exist, because they lack the nature of existence (*bhāvatva*), just like flowers in the sky. Nor does the nature of existence exist [in them], because they lack reality and so forth, just like the horns of a rabbit.
Therefore, all are empty. The two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are as stated in the text.
△ 6. Refuting the nature of *mahāsattā* (Great Existence).
That which they grasp as "existence" must be distinct from substance (*dravya*) and so forth; therefore, that nature of existence is merely a false conceptualization.

Supplement: First, the direct refutation of the Vaiśeṣika masters’ reckoning of the nature of *mahāsattā* as being a single entity [distinct] from the three categories of substance, quality, and action.
Because it exists as a single entity, there must be a distinct dharma that serves as its essence, separate from substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*).
This is because, by virtue of this "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*), substances and so forth possess existence. Now, first, a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute this;

specifically, taking up the opponent’s position that there is a distinct dharma serving as an essence external to substance, quality, and action, it is refuted by dividing it into two reasons for the argument. [The reason is: "It is admitted not to be non-existent."

As for the claim that "there is a separate entity as its essence, because it is admitted to be distinct from substance (*dravya*) and so forth," this refers to what they call [the universal] being separate from substance, quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*).
Now, it is clarified that this reason contradicts their own thesis (*pakṣa*) and therefore cannot be set aside.

The first syllogism admits the existence of its nature (*sattā*) and refutes its separation from substance and so forth; that is to say, even if one were to grant you the existence of the nature of "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*), it nevertheless...

One may maintain that [the universal] exists apart from substance, quality, and action; however, apart from these, no distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*) can be apprehended.

This is because you yourself admit that an intrinsic nature is not a non-existent thing, as it is capable of possessing substance and so forth—just as, for example, substance, qualities, and the like are not non-existent things.

Furthermore, the formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: even if one were to grant that [existence] is apart from substance, quality, and action, it would still not be an intrinsic nature, because...

Because you yourself admit that [the universal] is distinct from substance (*dravya*) and so forth. That which is called "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*) manifests precisely upon substance, quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*).

As you maintain: "There is a substance because it exists; there are qualities and actions because they exist. Now, since it is distinct from substance and the others, it is like a tortoise's hair—ultimately non-existent.
The two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "Just as... and so forth, this follows the preceding intent and serves as a rebuttal.

To further clarify the refutation of the existence of a "Great Existence" (mahāsattā): according to what you assert, there is a distinct dharma that serves as the essence of the nature of Great Existence, and this is not a non-existent thing.
When examined through this reasoning, apart from the real entities (*dravya*) and so forth, there is no separate nature;
how much less so for the real entities themselves, which are not Great Existence. How, then, could there be a separate nature of Great Existence upon the dharmas such as the real entities?

Because they reckon that substance, quality, and action are identical with existence (*sattā*), this [argument] serves to clarify that apart from substance and so forth, there is no separate nature of existence.

If one were to depart from [substance] and so on, using existence as an example to refute non-existence, it would mean that if there were a dharma distinct from substance and so forth possessing a separate nature of existence, then there should likewise be a separate nature of non-existence apart from non-existent things such as a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns. Since that is not the case...

Not so. Why is this? Because this example does not involve the negation of existence. Therefore, those two statements conclude that [existence] is false. The *Vyākhyāyukti* on the *Śataśāstra*, Volume Eight, states:
"If 'reality' (*tattva*) and so forth were of a different nature from existence, one would be unable to know that reality and so forth exist.
A cognition that apprehends a specific characteristic cannot definitively cognize other phenomena with distinct characteristics. How, then, could this be in the world?"
Regarding phenomena such as "reality" (*tattva*) which lack the nature of existence, does the cognition of existence arise?

If you say that although reality and so forth lack the nature of existence, the cognition of existence arises because they are conjoined with existence, then phenomena such as reality are merely nominally existent;
their essence is not truly existent and should therefore be described as non-existent.
△ 7. Refutation of the Nature of Identity and Difference.

Furthermore, because those [entities] they grasp as real—namely substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karman*)—[lack such a nature], the nature of identity and difference (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

Supplement: The first section generally refutes [the opponent's position] by means of three propositions concerning substance, quality, and activity. In the text, every instance of the word "nature" (*svabhāva*)...
This refers to the category of "sameness-and-difference" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*). The first part restates the opponent's position:

the Vaiśeṣika masters maintain that sameness-and-difference is also a single entity, existing as a distinct substantial reality apart from substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karman*). Now, the Mahāyāna school refutes this based on their own tenets. The passage beginning with "lest this... [proceeds with the refutation].
This is a refutation by means of a formal logical argument (*pramāṇa*). It clarifies the principle that [the opponent's position] is untenable. The word "not" (*mā*) means "it is not permissible.

This term refers to the nature of identity and difference (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*). That is to say, if one maintains that the nature of identity and difference exists as something distinct from substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*), then it would follow that it is not the nature of identity and difference belonging to substances, qualities, and actions.
This is because it is distinct from substances and so forth, just like qualities and actions. In this context, qualities and actions serve as the homologous instance (*sapakṣa*).

Regarding the analogies (*dṛṣṭānta*), they ought to be complete with the three criteria of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As the wording is archaic and profound, it must now be supplemented. The first criterion states: This is the subject (*dharmin*).

Its thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is also not a real nature (*svabhāva*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is distinct from the category of reality (*vastu-pada*). The similar example (*sapakṣa-dṛṣṭānta*) is like qualities (*guṇa*) and activities (*karman*).

The second criterion states: This is the subject. Its thesis is that it is also not a quality-nature (*guṇatva*). The reason is: because it is distinct from the category of qualities (*guṇa-pada*). The similar example... [is like activities].
Regarding "as with substance" (*dravyavat*), the subsequent inference states: "This is the subject (*dharmin*); it is also not of the nature of action (*karman*), this is the thesis (*pakṣa*).

The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is distinct from the category of action. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is: like substance and quality. One must understand that the word "also" (*api*) in the example is placed there for the sake of the two subsequent inferences. Furthermore, the phrase "it should also...
below follows the preceding sense to refute [the opponent's position] regarding the non-establishment of substance and so forth; that is to say, [the refutation of] substance, quality, and action.

The reason they establish both identity and difference is that within substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karman*), there exists the nature of identity-and-difference (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).

As the *Śata-śāstra* states: "When dharmas are compared with one another, some are identical and some are different. Because the essence of a dharma is restricted and distinct, it establishes difference;

because its nature is pervasive and universal, it is called identity. (Text) Now, if the nature of identity-and-difference were distinct from substance, quality, and activity, then [substance, quality, and activity] would be... substance, quality, and activity.

Karma is neither identical nor different. If this were so, it would not only fail to possess the nature of identity or difference, but would also fail to constitute the categories of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*).

Therefore, it is said that "furthermore, substance and the like should be subsumed under non-substance and the like," which contradicts your own school’s tenet that the three—substance, quality, and action—are each mutually exclusive categories.
Moreover, this argument also possesses the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The first inference states: "The category of substance exists."

[The opponent claims: "Dharma is subsumed under the category of 'real entity' (dravya-pada). The reason is: because its nature is different from that of a real entity. The concordant example is like qualities (guṇa) and actions (karma).

The latter two means of valid cognition follow the same pattern as the former. This refutes the universal generality (sāmānya) and particularity (viśeṣa). An ancient commentary states: "Generality and particularity are also one."

This refers to the specific universals (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) of the three categories—substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*)—as well as the specific universals of earth and so forth, and color and so forth (text).
Regarding the section "Earth and so forth," which refutes the specific universals of earth and other such natures:

this means that one should understand by analogy how the specific universals of earth, water, fire, and wind are successively interrogated and refuted; this is to be understood according to the refutations provided in the preceding text. It is fully present [in the argument].

The four measures follow the preceding example. The first measure states: "The nature of earth (pṛthivī-mahābhūta) is the subject (dharmin). It is not the nature of earth; this is the thesis (pakṣa). The reason (hetu) is:
because it is distinct from the nature of earth. The positive example (sapakṣa) is like water, fire, and wind. Furthermore, one should also state that the nature of earth is the subject."

It is not the thesis that is subsumed under the earth-element, because its nature is distinct from the earth-element; this is the reason (*hetu*). The analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like water, fire, and wind—these two sets [of examples].

The latter three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) may be understood by analogy. "As it truly is" (*yathābhūtam*) below refers to the intent of what precedes, wherein both the general and the particular are taken up together to conclude the various preceding cognitions.

"Reality-nature" (*tattva*) and so forth refers to the category of reality (*sat-padārtha*). "Similarity and dissimilarity" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) refers to the various natures such as earth and so on; these are the particular similarities and dissimilarities.
Substance (*dravya*), reality (*satya*), and so forth—these are equal in terms of their qualities and functions; they constitute the general and particular universals (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).

In the subsequent lines, "substance" and so forth represent the general, while "reality" and so forth represent the particular. Just as in the two lines concerning "substance," the former presents the particular followed by the general, whereas the two lines concerning "substance" and so forth present the general followed by the particular.
The translated text is skillful, alternating between the two to clarify them both. To complete the phrasing, it refers to what has been explained above.

Regarding "reality-nature" (*tattva*) and so forth: apart from earth and the other elements, there is no separate reality-nature; that is, upon earth and the others, there likewise should be no separate [threefold] reality-natures.
"Reality-nature" refers in both cases to a distinct nature of identity and difference. To say "apart from earth and the others" means...
