Regarding "there is no distinct real nature" and so forth: this concludes [the discussion on] the various natures such as the stages (*bhūmi*).

Because the stages and so forth are distinct from one another, there would likewise be no distinct real nature for those above the stages; thus, the stages and so forth themselves would also not be mutually inclusive or subordinate.

Furthermore, the "conjunction" (saṃyoga) should likewise not be subsumed under earth and so forth, because it is distinct from the nature of earth and so forth. This constitutes the fourth measure (*pramāṇa*), which is a simple conjunction of the distinctness and identity of natures.
The text is as explained above. Since the nature of substance (*dravyatva*) and so forth does not exist apart from substances and so forth, there is no separate nature of substance apart from them;
thus, within substance and so forth, there should likewise be no separate nature of substance—this constitutes the three propositions regarding substance and so forth.
"Nature" (svabhāva) refers here to both generality (sāmānya) and particularity (viśeṣa). This means that apart from substance and so forth, there is no separate nature of substance and so forth.
This concludes the previous point; lest it be thought that this [nature] is also not the nature of substance, quality, or action, because it would differ from substance and so forth.

Regarding the three types of cognition (pramāṇa), there should likewise be no separate nature of substance and so forth upon substance and so forth; thus, substance and so forth themselves would also not be mutually inclusive. This further concludes the previous point.

"Should be real, etc."—this is not subsumed under "real, etc.," because it is of a nature different from "real, etc. [The phrase] "the three measures" (trividha-pramāṇa) serves as a general conclusion for both the universal and the particular natures.
If one were to depart from the two phrases "real, etc.," this would be a concession;

however, this is stated only in terms of the universal, while the particulars are inherently included therein. Since that is not the case for the two phrases, this is a refutation; therefore, they are identical to the two phrases.
This concludes the demonstration of the provisional designation. The *Vyākhyāyukti* on the *Śataśāstra*, fascicle six, states:

"The Vaiśeṣika tenet that [qualities] such as 'sameness' and 'difference' are objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is logically untenable. The nature of cows, horses, and so forth is a conceptual construction of the mental consciousness;
it is provisionally designated upon phenomena such as form and transcends the objects of the sensory faculties. It is not obtained through direct perception, nor does it pervade all its bases."
Because of their distinction, it is like the substance of a composite (*saṃghāta*).

They postulate that the sixth category, the "composite entity" (*saṃghātapadārtha*), is a single substance that pervades all its substrates, transcends the sense faculties and their objects, and is not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The same applies to the categories of "sameness" (*sāmānya*) and "difference" (*viśeṣa*).
How can they insist that these are objects of direct perception? (Text)
△ Eight: Refutation of the Category of Combination (saṃghāta-pada).

Furthermore, the referent of the category of combination as maintained by them—up to [the point where it is said] "by the aforementioned reasoning"—is also not substantially existent. *Commentary on the Meaning*:

First, the refutation is established through formal inference (*pramāṇa*). The phrase "since they admit... serves as a reductio ad absurdum (*prasanga*). It is not [substantially existent] according to their own admission regarding the referent of the category of combination.

Regarding "attained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)," this is as cited above in the commentary on "sameness and difference. The phrase "even if one maintains" refers to the refutation by means of concession and denial.
"By virtue of the preceding reasoning" refers to the logic of the previous refutation of the five propositions, such as substantiality (*dravya*) and so forth.
△ Next, it is shown that the various categories are not obtained through direct perception (pratyakṣa). (2) First, it clarifies that the various categories are not objects of direct perception:

However, those [categories such as] "reality" (*tattva*) and so forth do not have as their objective condition anything apart from consciousness, because they are admitted to be objects of cognition, like a tortoise’s hair and the like.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: "Existence" (*sat*) and so forth are the subject (*dharmin*). It is not the object of a lower-order thesis. The reason (*hetu*) is stated: "because it is admitted to be an object of cognition.

The concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is "like a tortoise’s hair" and so forth. A tortoise’s hair is an object of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that is not established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it is not obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

By employing this as a concordant example, one causes the opponent to understand the example and thereby realize the negation regarding the property (*dharma*) of the subject. This is based on the single point of being an object of cognition.
[The section on] Valid Cognition concludes by returning to the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Next, it is shown that the cognizing subject is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, true wisdom does not take as its object anything apart from consciousness, because [all things] arise through the conjunction of conditions; thus, true wisdom and so forth [perceive reality as it is].

Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: The wisdom that takes reality as its object is a real dharma; it does not take the lower [inferior] tenets as its object. The reason is stated: "Because it arises from provisional conjunction.
The concordant example is "such as the wisdom of virtue and so forth. To say "arising from provisional conjunction" means that this wisdom arises in conjunction with provisional dharmas.
This establishes that the single cognitive subject (the grāhaka) is subsumed within consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Below, the five other types of wisdom are explained in detail.
The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) may be established accordingly.
△ Next, the conclusion of the refutation:
Therefore, the Vaiśeṣika categories such as "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth are also merely false constructs devised according to subjective sentiment.
Commentary on the Terms: The word "also" (*yì*) is placed here to contrast with the preceding Sāṃkhya system.
△ Third, the eight treatises beginning with Maheśvara (2). First, the refutation of Maheśvara (2). First, the introductory statement.
There are those who maintain that there are two Great Īśvaras whose essence is truly pervasive and eternal, and who are able to produce all phenomena.

Regarding their meaning and terminology, the *Xuántán* (Profound Discourse) states: "These are the ash-smearing heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*) and various Brāhmaṇas who collectively reckon Īśvara to be the cause of all things.
They reckon that this deity possesses four attributes: first, its essence is real; second,"
1. Pervasive; 2. eternal; 3. constant; 4. capable of producing all phenomena.
△ Next, the refutation:
Why is it that their adherence is irrational? (Up to: It would also follow that [effects] arise simultaneously, because the cause is eternal.

Commentary on the Terms: First, the [notion of] permanence is refuted by means of "that which can produce. If something can produce an effect, it must be impermanent. Next, omnipresence is refuted by means of impermanence;

if there is arising and ceasing, then there is no sense of omnipresence. Next, substantiality is refuted by means of non-omnipresence, because that which exists here but does not exist there is not real.
As for the phrase "the essence being already... below, this refutes "that which can produce," meaning that if the essence of that deity is already...
If [the self] were eternal and omnipresent, and possessed all functional capacities, it would necessarily produce all phenomena simultaneously at all times and in all places.
If that were so, it would incur faults such as contradicting worldly experience. [The opponent] anticipates this objection and offers a defense:

"Although its essence is eternal and omnipresent and capable of producing all phenomena, it requires the assistance of various conditions and volitional desire, or the convergence of conditions, before they can arise; therefore, there is no simultaneous production."
The fault of [the theory of] arising: it contradicts [the principle of] non-duality and is refuted by the following. Regarding "a single cause":

because it involves three [factors], it is not the case that a single cause can produce all phenomena; thus, what you maintain is internally contradictory from beginning to end. Alternatively, to refute [your position] by analogy:
the conditions for desire should also arise simultaneously, because the cause, Maheśvara, is eternally present.
△ Next, the refutation of the other seven [categories] follows as an illustration.

The other [schools] that maintain the existence of a single Great Brahmā (*mahābrahman*), time (*kāla*), space (*dik*), and so forth, which give rise to all phenomena, are all refuted in the same manner.
*Commentary on Terms:* "Great Brahmā" refers to the Vedic scholars (*vedavādin*). They calculate that the god Brahmā is the progenitor of all things.
It is able to produce all living and non-living things; therefore, Brahmā is called "eternal" (*nitya*). It is the cause of *nirvāṇa*. Regarding "time" (*kāla*):

this immediately dispels the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who cling to the view that all things arise from time; therefore, time is eternal and is the cause of the myriad things, as well as the cause of *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding "direction" (*dis*): this refers to the calculation of the masters of the theory of direction (*dig-vādins*), who hold that [things] arise from direction.

Human beings are born within heaven and earth; after their death, they return to the *pradhāna* (the primal source). Therefore, *pradhāna* is eternal and singular; it is the cause of the myriad things and the cause of *nirvāṇa*.
What is called the "original limit" (*pūrvakoṭi*) refers to the calculation of the teacher Āṇḍaka:
he asserts that at the very beginning of the world, there was only a great expanse of water. At that time, a great cosmic egg (*āṇḍa*) emerged, shaped like a hen’s egg, surrounded on all sides by...
It was golden in color. At that time, it matured and split into two sections: the upper section became heaven, and the lower section became earth;
from within them, all myriad things were produced. As for what is called "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*), it refers to the calculation of the proponents of causelessness (*ahetuvādin*):
they maintain that all myriad things arise and perish spontaneously, without cause and without condition. Therefore, this spontaneity is eternal, and its production of all things is *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the "cause": those who speak of "space" are the proponents of the *Ākāśakāraṇavāda* (Space-Cause Theory). They assert that space is the cause of all things;
it is a distinct entity, real and eternal, which can successively give rise to all phenomena. Therefore, they maintain that space is the cause of all things.
Regarding the "self": these are the proponents of the *Ātmavāda* (Self-Theory). They maintain that there exists a sentient being (*sattva*), a life-principle (*jīva*), and a living soul (*jantu*).
The nourisher, the one who brings forth, the person (pudgala)—such as these are truly and eternally existent.
Therefore, my eye is able to see all forms. It should be understood that the same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. As for the word "etcetera" (ādi):

"Those such as the proponents of the theory of past actions (*pūrvakṛtavādin*) are all refuted in the same manner" refers to the fact that the objects of refutation are identical to those mentioned previously;
this is explained in detail in the *Xuántán* (Prolegomena).
△ Fourth, the two types of theories on sound (2): First, the introduction.

There are others who hold a biased attachment to the view that the *śruti* (revealed scripture) is eternal; [it exists] until it is manifested by conditions, at which point it possesses the capacity for signification.
Supplement: Within this exposition there are two schools, both of whom maintain that the essence of sound is eternal.

The first maintains that the *śruti* is eternal and does not depend on conditions for its manifestation. The second maintains that all sounds are eternal, but depend on conditions to be manifested. The *śruti* belongs to the outsiders (*bāhya*).
This is a book falsely composed by the Path. The sixth fascicle of the *Vyākhyāyukti* on the *Śataśāstra* states:

"In ancient times, a wise Brahmin secretly composed the *Vedāḥ* (the Illuminating Books) and claimed they existed spontaneously. He permitted only himself to recite them, not allowing others to view them.
Furthermore, the first fascicle of the same commentary states: "By means of inference, it is established that the sound of the *Vedāḥ* was not created by a person; its essence is eternal."
It abides. Furthermore, it is said: "In the beginning, it does not depend on conditions; in the end, it is without destruction.

Its nature is inherently manifest, transcending the objects of the sense faculties, and serves as a definitive authority that never deviates. (This passage) clarifies the provenance of this treatise and the intent of its doctrine of permanence.

(Some claim that "this treatise" refers to the *pañcavidyāsthāna* [Five Treatises on Knowledge]; this is an error. The Five Treatises on Knowledge refer to Inner Science, Medicine, Logic, Grammar, and Arts/Crafts. These are the correct meanings found elsewhere; how could they be non-Buddhist [teachings]?)

...is a biased attachment). Regarding "authoritative cognition" (*pramāṇa*): it refers to a fixed and unchanging meaning. To erroneously reckon this as the "authority of the holy teaching" (*āptāgama-pramāṇa*) is to claim that it can express all phenomena and principles.
There is an attachment [to the following], which is the subsequent attachment. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"The external teachers of the science of sound (*śabdavidyā*) give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine: 'The characteristic of sound is inherently existent; it is without arising and without cessation. However, due to..."
It is only through successive articulations that [the sound] becomes manifest; yet the essence of sound is eternal.
△ Next, the refutation:
Why is it that both [positions] are unreasonable? (Up to: Because things such as jars and garments depend upon a multitude of conditions.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: First, the initial position is refuted. The first volume of the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Explanation of the *Śataśāstra*) states:
"Furthermore, the sound of the *Veda* and other sounds are identical in their nature as sound. Why then is it said that this [Vedic] sound alone is eternal, while other sounds are not?
(*Text*). The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is: The sound of the *Veda* must be non-eternal, because it is admitted to be a signifier (*vācaka*), just like other sounds.
Sound. The following refutes the subsequent position regarding sound. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:

Other sounds must also be non-eternal in their essence, because they depend upon various conditions, just like jars, garments, and so forth. "Depending upon various conditions" means that other sounds necessarily exist in dependence upon various conditions such as space (*ākāśa*).
△ Five. The Lokāyatika Teachers (2). First, the introduction:
There are non-Buddhists who maintain that earth, water, fire, and wind—though impermanent—are substantially real in their essence.
*Hexiang* (合響), *Xuantan* (玄談) Scroll Eight, states: "Lokāyata" is here translated as "Worldly Heretics" (*Shunshijian Waidao*).

They calculate that all phenomena, such as form and mind, take the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as their cause. However, within the four great elements, that which is most refined and intelligent is capable of cognitive reflection;
this constitutes the mental factor (*citta-dharma*), just as with form. Although both are equally "great," it is like a lamp..."

The Radiant [Heaven] is thus; others are not so. Therefore, among the four great elements, there is that which is capable of objective cognition (*ālambana*), and this is certainly without error (text).
The ninth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "Those who reckon the atoms (*paramāṇu*) to be permanent do so by relying on worldly meditative concentration (*laukika-dhyāna*)."
They give rise to such a view because they do not understand dependent origination as it truly is:

they conceive that existence preceded by existence gives rise to the accumulation of results, and that existence preceded by dissolution results in the destruction of results. For this reason, they claim that [existence] arises from the nature of the various subtle particles (*paramāṇu*).
When gross objects arise as effects, they are gradually analyzed until they remain as ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*). Therefore, gross objects are impermanent, while ultimate atoms are permanent (text).
"Gross matter" refers to the "son-atom" (*putra-paramāṇu*); "not exceeding the measure of the cause" means that the cause consists of the "parent-atoms" (*pitṛ-paramāṇu*).
The initial ultimate atom is called the parent; it gathers to produce all forms of matter. Thus, that which is produced [is the son-atom].

It is named "Subtle Particles" (*paramāṇu*). Although these subtle particles are impermanent, they do not transcend their parents [the constituent elements]; therefore, they are substantially existent.
△ Next, the refutation [of the self] (in two parts): first, the refutation of the cause, the subtle particle.
That too is unreasonable. Why? (Up to: How can it be said that atoms are permanent?
[Commentary on the Meaning and Phrases] First, refuting their substantial reality. The *Śataśāstra-śloka* states:
"If an atom has parts, how can it be an atom? The commentary explains: Since it possesses spatial divisions (*digbhāga*), it loses its status as an atom. Such an atom...

Analysis: It should be like coarse objects—neither real nor eternal—which would contradict your own tenets that atoms are partless, permanent, substantially existent, and the creators of the myriad things of the world.
(Text). "Ants marching" (*yǎnxíng*): the sound *xíng* here means *wù*, which signifies a row or a line (as the *Abhidharmakarmasiddhi-śāstra* says:
"like ants marching in a line, etc."). This means that since atoms possess spatial dimensions, they must be like ants forming a line.
[The opponent] states: "The substantiality of the asserted atom must be unreal, because it possesses spatial parts (*digbhāga*), like the trail of ants, etc.

If [the opponent] cannot refute this [argument], [the proponent] states: "The asserted atom must not aggregate together to produce a coarse resultant form, because it lacks spatial parts, like the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Since one can thus refute its permanence, [the proponent] states: "The..."
If one grasps [the atom] as being infinitesimal (*paramāṇu*), how can it be said to be permanent? Since it is capable of producing an effect, it must be like that which is produced from it.
Next, the refutation of the resultant form (*phala-rūpa*) (in three parts): First, the refutation of [the atom] not exceeding the measure of its cause (in two parts): First, the direct refutation.
Furthermore, the produced effect does not exceed the magnitude of its cause; [otherwise,] if it were apprehended by the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*), it would contradict your own tenets.

Regarding the meaning of the sound [of the argument], one first establishes a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to refute [the opponent]: "The produced effect is not called coarse matter (*audārika-rūpa*), because it does not exceed the magnitude of its cause."

If gross matter did not exceed the dimension of its causal atoms, it would be identical to an atom and thus could not be apprehended by the eye and other senses.
Their position—that atoms are capable of producing [gross matter]—is untenable, for that which is produced [from them] cannot be seen, heard, smelled, or tasted.
[The opponent claims: "It is a fruit [of cognition] because it can be seen, heard, smelled, and tasted; therefore, [your argument] contradicts your own tenets.

Because there is no distinction at the point of conjunction, as in the case of gross resultant form (phala-rūpa).

Therefore, there is a contradiction.
△ Next, the refutation of cause and effect occupying the same location.

(Commentary on the Meaning: First, the refutation by means of formal logic (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the effect and the cause must not occupy the same location, as both possess material obstruction.)
Therefore, it is like two atoms. If one were to offer a defense by arguing that when the cause enters the resultant form, the result receives the cause;

The second line [of the verse] provides a further refutation: if there were reception, then separation would be possible; if there were separation, then they would not be one. If there is entry, there must be transformation; if there is transformation, then it is not permanent.
The principle should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the "Resonance with the Sound" (*Ghoṣavat*), the first volume of the *Vyākhyāyukti* on the *Śataśāstra* states:

Furthermore, in order to refute the notion that atoms and their causes occupy the same location, and to demonstrate that the essence of a cause is definitively impermanent, it is said: when various obstructive objects are pressed by other obstructive objects...
If they do not move from their place, they will inevitably undergo transformation and decay.
Thus, the atoms are assailed by their effects, either by mutually accommodating one another or by coexisting as distinct entities, like irrigating a mound of coarse sand with a fine stream;

or else they enter into them and cause them to transform, like pouring a potent medicinal juice into molten copper. If one were to accept the former case (like the stream irrigating the sand), then there would be various...

Since the parts mutually enter into one another, the various constituent parts become separated, like objects that have become detached; thus, they would not produce a common result, and consequently, no gross objects whatsoever would exist.
Furthermore, if it is held that these possess subtle parts just as those [gross objects] do, then their substance must likewise be impermanent, just like them.
If you admit—as stated later—that the substance of the atom undergoes transformation and decay (like medicinal substances or molten copper poured into a mold), why wait for further proof?
The Refutation (Text).

One would then necessarily obtain that [result] in its entirety, because their essence is one; to deny this would contradict the lower [text].

If one does not admit obtaining everything, it contradicts the principle that the essence of the fruit is one. If one admits obtaining everything, it further contradicts the fact that these two are distinct entities.
Therefore, the conclusion of that [lower text] is false. "Advancing and retreating" refers to admitting and denying [the respective positions].
△ Next, the four propositions are synthesized to provide a general refutation. (2) First, the general statement:
Although the categories of non-Buddhists are numerous, the entities they cling to do not exceed four types.
*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance), *Xuantan* (Profound Discourses), Fascicle Eight, states: "To summarize all speculative views, they do not exceed four positions:

This means that the first [position] holds that the effect does not exist within the cause; the third holds that it both exists and does not exist; and the fourth holds that it neither exists nor does not exist.
All other divergent views do not fall outside of these. Furthermore, the eighth fascicle of the *Śataśāstra* states:
"All worldly categories such as form (*rūpa*) are expressed by names and conventions and are known by the mind and wisdom; yet, due to differing attachments, there are briefly four types."
That is to say: existence and non-existence; both being admitted and both being denied. These should be understood respectively as corresponding to the four types of false attachment:
namely, [the attachment to] oneness and non-oneness, and the simultaneous admission and denial of both.

"Harmonizing Resonance" (*hexiang*): "That which possesses the nature of being produced" refers to the dharmas that arise from a source. For example, in the Sāṃkhya system of twenty-three principles (*tattva*), there is the principle of "Being-ness" (*sattā*).

Why is it that their adherence is irrational? (Up to: It should be like sound and so forth, which are not objects of the eye and other [senses].

Commentary on the Meaning: If a phenomenon is not non-existent, it must arise from the nature of existence (*bhāva*). If it were different from the nature of existence, it would be identical to a non-existent phenomenon.

This contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) such as that of the eye, which cognizes objects such as visible form (*rūpa*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

**Thesis:** Visible form and so forth are not the objects of the eye and other [senses]. **Reason:** Because they do not possess the nature of visible form and so forth. **Homologous Example:** Just like sound and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "identity or difference": this is analyzed through the refutation of both concealment (*saṃvṛti*) and manifestation (*prakaṭana*). The first sentence poses the inquiry. "Concealment" means to cover over; "manifestation" means to reveal.

Because the form (*rūpa*), non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and various unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) adhered to by them do not exist according to reason.
Regarding the meaning of the terms, following the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, other vehicles also possess five categories:

In total, there would be seventy-five [factors]. Compared to the Mahāyāna, this is twenty-five fewer.

Regarding "concordant resonance" (*saṃghāta-pratigha*), there are two types of resistance (*pratigha*). First, resistance with visibility (*sanidarśana-sapratigha*), which refers to the object-field of form (*rūpa-āyatana*).

Matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is, in brief, of five kinds: 1. **Extremely condensed matter** (*paramāṇusaṃghāta-rūpa*): This refers to the analysis of the five sense organs, the five sense objects, and the four great elements into their constituent parts until reaching the stage of the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*).

This is its essential nature. 2. **Extremely remote matter** (*paramāvacchinna-rūpa*): It is established by virtue of being separated from obstruction. This includes light, darkness, shadow, and glare, analyzed down to the subtle atom. It is also called "the single manifest color of space" (*ākāśaikavarṇa-rūpa*):

the blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, glare, light, and darkness perceived within the upper and lower spatial realms are collectively termed "the single manifest color of space. Because this manifest color is empty [of obstruction], it is called "the single manifest color of space. 3. **Matter derived from what is received** (*samādānasaṃvara-rūpa*): [This refers to the discipline of vows, such as the Prātimokṣa.]

(1) The discipline and non-discipline received and induced through teachers and instructions; (2) the four types of *parikalpita* (the three natures and the *manovijñāna* which performs universal conceptualization, from which objects arise, and thus are called "arisen from that");

(3) the matter resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), because the objects appearing within concentration arise from it. These five are exclusively derived from what is projected [by karma] and belong to the Hīnayāna.
In the Mahāyāna, both are present. Question: What is the meaning of "having an object" (*sapratigha*)? Answer: It means "obstructive.
When two forms face one another, they mutually obstruct each other, like wood and stone; when they are joined together, their substances do not pass through one another.

To abide facing one another in this way is the meaning of "having an object. Question: Regarding that which is called "form" by virtue of being obstructive, what is its status within the eleventh [category], the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?

Regarding the inclusion of form (*rūpa*): since it lacks resistance (*sapratigha*), how can it be designated by the name "form"? Answer: Although its essence lacks resistance, its name is established based on its relationship to resistant form.

To thoroughly investigate the underlying intent, there is indeed profound significance herein. Herein, it is precisely because of the false attachments of other vehicles that atoms (*paramāṇu*) are held to be composed of resistance (*sapratigha*).

By admitting the existence of spatial parts, one avoids these two faults. Some say that seeing, touching walls, and so forth—[as described] on the feet above—is sufficient.

"If atoms were to combine in their entirety, because they would have no spatial divisions, they could not combine in only a partial portion. In that case, all atoms would occupy the same location.

[Otherwise,] one would contradict and harm one's own school. If that were so, one would have to admit that all categories of meaning transcend the objects cognized by the sense faculties, and thus no distinctions could be established—which would contradict worldly consensus.

this contradicts one's own school and further contradicts worldly discourse. Furthermore, it is said: "Moreover, if atoms lack functional activity..."

△ Next, the conclusion summarizes that by means of spatial division, its substantial existence is refuted;
because it possesses spatial divisions, it can be analyzed and is therefore definitively not substantially existent.
△ Next, the conclusion summarizes the resulting proof that matter (*rūpa*) is not substantially existent.
Therefore, it is established that resistant form does not exist as a real entity.
△ Next, the explanation that resistant form is merely a transformation of consciousness (in two parts): first, the inquiry:
"How could the five consciousnesses lack a supporting basis and an objective condition consisting of form?"
**Exegesis of Terms:** The "basis" refers to the five sense organs; these are the dominant bases (*adhipatīśraya*) for visual consciousness and the others.

The "object" refers to the five sensory fields (*viṣaya*); these are the objects of perception for visual consciousness and the others. These two—the organ and the field—are the actual matter (*rūpa*). Question:
If, as has been refuted above, that which possesses resistance (*sapratigha*) is not real, does it follow that the five consciousnesses have no basis or object consisting of matter at all?
△ Second, the explanation [of the two points]. First, the direct explanation [of the two]. First, the general explanation of the support and object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Although it is not formless (*arūpa*), it is a transformation of consciousness; [it] takes this very characteristic as its support and object-condition.
*Yinyi* (Explanations of Terms): The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source), fascicle 53, states:

"The consciousnesses of the eye and so forth, although they have bases (*āśraya*) and objects (*ālambana*) that appear as form, these are manifestations produced by consciousness itself. They do not exist externally to the mind as separate atoms (*paramāṇu*) that constitute the sense organs (*indriya*) as bases and the objective spheres (*viṣaya*) as objects.
Rather, when the eight consciousnesses arise, it is through the power of internal causal conditions, such as seeds (*bīja*), and so forth..."
Upon the eighth consciousness, there appear transformations resembling the five sense organs and the five sense objects.

The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, rely upon those transformed organs to perceive those original objective entities (*bhāva*). Although they do not directly apprehend them, they must depend upon them for their arising.

In reality, upon the objective matter (*rūpa*) within the fundamental consciousness, the appearances of the five sense objects are transformed and manifest; these [consciousnesses] take those five sense organs as their support, and upon that [original entity].

These two kinds of fivefold sense-objects (viṣaya) serve as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya). If the five consciousnesses did not rely upon that which is transformed by the eighth [consciousness], they would lack an object-condition.
This is because within the object-condition there are both the direct (the image-part, *nimitta-bhāga*) and the remote (the essential nature, *svabhāva*).
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the basis and conditions (2). First, a brief clarification of the basis.
Now, the sense organs such as the eye are not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) [until] they serve as the basis for the arising of visual consciousness and the other cognitions.

Regarding the "Explanation of Terms": This refers to the faculties such as the eye. Although they are transformations of consciousness, they differ from the five objects (*viṣaya*) such as form in that they are apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
They are known to exist by means of inference based on their respective functions, namely, their ability to give rise to the five consciousnesses such as visual consciousness.

As for the phrase "this merely... and so forth, the *Zongjing* says: "These five faculties, although belonging to the category of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), are merely [manifestations] upon consciousness."
The manifestation of functional capacity is not a form produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) existing separately outside the mind.
This term "functional capacity" refers precisely to the activity that gives rise to the five consciousnesses.

Just as one infers the existence of a seed-essence by observing the process of sprouting, since the external forms you cling to are logically non-existent, one must certainly admit that this [manifestation] exists within consciousness and nowhere else.

That which is capable of producing consciousness is called the eye and other sense organs (*indriya*). These serve as the predominant support (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the arising of visual consciousness and the others.
Next, the detailed explanation of the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) (in two parts): first, a general indication of the existence or non-existence of the object-condition.

These consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, take external objects as their objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) [up to] that which is transformed by one's own consciousness as the objective condition.

therefore, the Mahāyāna uses the phrase "admitted by oneself" to distinguish its position, thereby avoiding [the charge of] being [merely] another [school].
