That is to say: you maintain that whatever phenomenon is capable of inducing a cognition resembling itself is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for that [cognition].

In other words, if there is a phenomenon that can draw forth a cognition resembling its own image, do you hold that this phenomenon which induces it is the objective condition for this cognition resembling itself?
△ Next, the refutation:

It is not only that which can produce [the cognition] that is called the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of this consciousness; even conditions such as the auditory organ (*śrotra*) and so forth are also termed its object-conditions.

[Regarding] the meaning of "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*): it must possess two factors: first, the capacity to produce [the cognition]; second, the bearing of the image (*sākāra*). As in the case of an object-condition...

The *Pratyaya-śāstra* states: "The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) refers to that which the cognizing consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises bearing its image, and which possesses substantial reality, such that the cognizing consciousness relies upon it to arise" (text).

Now, to maintain that what can induce the arising of a consciousness resembling itself constitutes the object-condition is to take the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) as the object-condition;
although it has the capacity to produce [the effect], it lacks [the requisite characteristics].
If it possesses characteristics, then both the direct cause (*hetu*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) would all have the capacity to produce [the cognition];
could these also be called the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for this consciousness? In the seventy-first fascicle of the *Zongjing*, the Mahāyāna formal argument (*prayoga*) states:

"The objective condition of your visual consciousness is the subject (*dharmin*). It should not be the objective condition of visual consciousness; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it merely has the capacity to produce consciousness."

Because of this meaning. A similar example is the causal condition (*pratyaya*) of visual consciousness. Furthermore, one may formulate a counter-argument to refute [the opponent’s position] as follows:

Your "causal condition of visual consciousness" is the subject (*dharmin*). It must be like the "object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)" of visual consciousness; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it possesses only the single quality of being able to produce consciousness.
This is just as when the eye perceives a form (*rūpa*). (Text)
△ Second, the refutation of the Sautrāntika masters’ doctrine of the composite (in two parts). First, the presentation of their doctrine:
When the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, cognize form and so forth, they take as their object only a composite that appears similar to those [objects].

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: It is said that when the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth cognize form and so forth, they take only a conventionally designated composite form as their object, because the consciousness arises bearing an appearance similar to that [object].
△ Next, the refutation:
It is not the case that the combined form is distinct from the various atoms (up to: lest the second moon and so forth could produce the five consciousnesses).

[Commentary: The first part clarifies that the combination is not real; the subsequent section, "That which is combined... and below, relies upon the aforementioned unreality to demonstrate its non-existence.

Regarding the objects of the five consciousnesses, do not allow them to fall into the second month [of the logical fallacy]. To provide a supporting analogy, the Master in the seventy-first volume of the *Zhengjingshi* (The Mirror of Correct Principles) says:
"O Sautrāntika teacher, it is not correct for you to take external, composite, conventional form (*saṃghāta-rūpa*) as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Even if you were to grant that visual consciousness takes it as its object because it bears the image of that coarse form, this would still not be the case."
It is called an "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) because you maintain that the composite color has no substantial reality;

it is just like the second moon seen by a person with impaired vision, which lacks substantial reality and cannot produce consciousness, but is merely termed an "object. It cannot be called an "object-condition.
The same applies to the composite color. To refute this, one establishes the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*): Your "composite gross color" is the subject (*dharmin*).
This is stated as the thesis that [the object] is the focal object (*ālambana*) of visual consciousness but not its causal condition (*pratyaya*). The reason (*hetu*) is:

"Because you maintain that it is a mere designation (*prajñapti*) and lacks substantial reality (*asvabhāva*). The corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: "Like a second moon. As the verse in the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* says:
"If one posits a focal object for the five consciousnesses through their conjunction, it is not a causal condition, because its substance is non-existent, just like a second moon."
△ Third, refuting the Sautrāntika’s revised position regarding atoms:
It is not the case that when atoms are in a state of mutual conjunction, the atoms of form and so forth become objects of the five consciousnesses.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: Previously, you calculated that the combination [of atoms] is distinct from the atoms themselves; your attachment lay primarily upon the characteristic of the combination.
Now, you calculate that the atoms exist during the state of combination; your attachment clings to the atoms themselves. You further argue:

"The coarse object resulting from combination is a conventional designation of form (*rūpa*). This is truly as refuted above. That is to say, in the state of combination, each individual atom is capable of constituting [the whole]; this atom—
The "perfectly real entity" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) could serve as the object-condition (*ālambana*) for each of the five consciousnesses and induce their arising.
The Mahāyāna refutes this using the term "non-... (*na*). Thus it says, "It is not [the case that] all," and so forth. The first line of this passage provides the reason:

to arise bearing the aspect of an object is the meaning of being an "object-condition. Since that is not the case here, it is not an object-condition. The subsequent section, beginning with "not all," constitutes the refutation.
There is a characteristic of aggregation (*saṃghāta-lakṣaṇa*) upon the atom (*paramāṇu*).

This does not mean that the atoms themselves possess a characteristic of aggregation that can serve as the respective object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses; for when they are not aggregated, this characteristic of aggregation does not exist.

Since the essential nature of the atom is the same whether it is combined or not, one uses its non-combination to prove its combination. The phrase "not [being] below" refers back to the preceding discussion on combination.
Because they never possess a distinct characteristic [of conjunction], the concluding summary clarifies that they are "harmonized" [as non-conjoined].
Since the essence and characteristics of atoms are conjoined yet as if not conjoined, they are not the objective referents (*ālambana*) of the five consciousnesses.
*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance), *Zongjing* Volume 71, states:

The Sautrāntika school maintains that although the coarse matter resulting from aggregation is conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*), the individual atoms (*paramāṇu*) that constitute it are substantially existent (*dravyasat*) and each functions as a condition (*pratyaya*).
"How could it not also produce the five consciousnesses? The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying:

'Those combined forms and so forth that constitute atoms—even if one were to grant that they act as conditions—they cannot be the objects of perception (*ālambana*), because when the visual and other consciousnesses arise, they do not carry the characteristics (*nimitta*) of those atoms, just as when visual consciousness arises, it does not carry the characteristics of the eye faculty. Those five faculties, such as the eye, can only..."
The five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, arise; however, these five consciousnesses cannot take their own bases, the five sense organs, as objects.

Taking the organs as an analogy, one establishes the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: Thesis: Your "atoms" (*paramāṇu*), which are capable of forming [objects] such as visible form, are not the objects of the five consciousnesses.
Reason: Because the five consciousnesses arise without bearing the aspect (*ākāra*) of those [atoms]. Example: Just as [the atoms of] the sense organs [are not objects of the consciousnesses].

Regarding the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*), the *Ālambanaparīkṣā-kārikā* states: "Atoms are conditions for the five consciousnesses, yet they are not their objects (*ālambana*), because the aspect (*ākāra*) of those [atoms] does not exist within the consciousness, just like the eye faculty and so forth."
△ 4. Refuting the Sarvāstivāda’s Assertion that the Aggregate is Real (2): First, the Presentation of Their Assertion.

There are those who maintain that each individual atom (*paramāṇu*) of form and so forth—up to [the other sense objects]—exists as a real entity, and that these [atoms] constitute the objective referent (*ālambana*).
Regarding "conjunction" (*saṃghāta*): according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, there are two distinct characteristics of conjunction and aggregation.

Conjunction refers to all material forms (*rūpa*) with spatial dimensions (*sapradeśa*) that are above the level of the atom (*paramāṇu*), which mutually conjoin, such as the atoms of earth and water in turbid water mutually conjoining.
Aggregation refers to material forms consisting of spatially extended clusters that come together through successive accumulation.
It is like two lumps of clay which, when struck together, form a mass; whereas if water and sand were mixed, they would certainly not form a mass.

However, when water and earth are mixed, they immediately become a lump of clay that can be fashioned into jars and the like. One can observe that each individual atom (*paramāṇu*) of water and earth possesses the characteristic of aggregation.
(Text). They [the opponents] maintain that when the atoms of form (*rūpa*) and so forth are not yet aggregated, their substance is subtle.
Because they are subtle, they are not the objects of the five consciousnesses. In the state of their collective aggregation, they mutually support one another, and a coarse aspect arises;
since that aspect is not separate from the substance of the atoms, it is substantially real and serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*).

This means that because its substance is real, the visual consciousness relies upon it to arise; and because it is a coarse aspect, it arises bearing that aspect. Since these two factors are both present, [the aggregate is established].

It serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses. This is cited from the *Weishi gushu* (Ancient Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*), Volume 14, which states:

"In the Sautrāntika school, ten bases (the twelve bases excluding the dharma-base and the mind-base) are coarse and provisional while subtle and real (the atom is real; coarse forms and so forth are provisional, as they are formed by the aggregation of subtle atoms).

In the Mahāyāna, conventionally, the coarse is real and the subtle is provisional (all forms and so forth arise from seeds and are transformations of consciousness; thus they are subsumed under the 'objective aspect' [*nimitta-bhāga*]. The coarse and real atom is merely a mental construct)."

The *paryāyika* (provisional) [view] holds that things exist through analysis; thus, the subtle is called "provisional" (*prajñapti*). The Sarvāstivādins and others maintain that both the coarse and the subtle are real (*dravya-sat*), because the atom (*paramāṇu*) is subsumed under its respective qualities such as color, and the subtle is a collection of these qualities derived from the coarse.
The Ekavyāvahārikas and others maintain that both the coarse and the subtle are provisional (*prajñapti-sat*).
Since the Sarvāstivādins hold that both the coarse and the subtle are real, their intention is that [the atom] possesses both components simultaneously.
△ Next, the refutation:
That position is incorrect, because at the stage of collective aggregation, a single consciousness would have to perceive all objects.

[The commentary] explains: The first phrase is a general negation; "collective aggregation" and below state the reason. This refers to the states of being aggregated and not yet aggregated. To the extreme...

The subtle entity is one; as long as it has not yet aggregated into an ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), it is not the object of the five consciousnesses. Now, when in the state of aggregation, could an ultimate atom still be the objective support (*ālambana*) of the five consciousnesses?
If you grant that it possesses a real substance, even if it is an object of cognition, it would not be an objective support. As a verse in the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* says:
"Just as hardness and so forth, though they are conditions for visual consciousness and the others, are not their objective supports; so too, the ultimate atom is granted [to exist]."
[The opponent attempts to] rescue [the position] by means of the characteristic of aggregation (*saṃsthāna*). He argues:

"The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, take as their object the various aggregated characteristics upon the atoms (*paramāṇu*), just as they take objects such as jars or bowls; thus, the specific characteristics of the perceiving consciousness arise, and therefore [aggregation] is the objective support (*ālambana*).
[The author] refutes this: "Although objects such as jars and bowls possess distinctions, they are nonetheless established as atoms."
Because they are equal and without distinction, how could there be a distinct arising of consciousness that takes those marks as its object?

Since the forms of jars and so forth exist separately upon the conventional dharmas of jars and so forth, and are not [ultimately real] atoms (*paramāṇu*), [the opponent] attempts a further defense by saying:

"In the state of aggregation, each atom possesses its own subtle, spherical essential mark; therefore, the consciousness that takes those marks as its object should also have distinctions. [This is now] refuted.
It is said: Since atoms exist in a state of aggregation, each one must necessarily relinquish its individual characteristics of subtlety, roundness, and minuteness.

Once these intrinsic characteristics have been relinquished, how could there be any distinct characteristic produced for an object of cognition? Why, then, would the subtle characteristics of the atom be definitively relinquished in the state of aggregation, while the coarse characteristics are not?

It is because consciousness cognizes subtle characteristics; that is to say, visual and other sensory consciousnesses that take coarse characteristics as their objects certainly do not [cognize the subtle].
This refers to the extremely subtle characteristic of the object perceived by the sixth consciousness. What fault would there be even if it were to perceive such?

It is so that one consciousness does not perceive an object belonging to another realm. Regarding "objects and consciousnesses of other realms": for example, in relation to the ear-consciousness, the eye-consciousness is a consciousness of another realm;
in relation to sound, visible form is the remainder of the object-realm of sound. Thus, they are mutually related to one another.
Regarding the term "the rest": even if a consciousness directed toward one object were to take another object as its condition, what fault would there be?

It would follow that a single consciousness must take all objects as its conditions. If this were so, it would contradict the facts and principles known and perceived in the world, resulting in a great error.
△ Next, the analogy is established.
Even if one were to grant the existence of atoms (*paramāṇu*), such faults as those mentioned above would still ensue; how much more so when there are no real atoms external to consciousness?

[Commentary on the Meaning of the Sound] Even if one grants the existence of atoms, one still incurs the aforementioned errors; how much more so when there are no real [atoms] external to consciousness?
Therefore, it is fully established by reason that the substantial basis of the objective condition for the five consciousnesses is not external form and so forth.

△ Next, it is shown that the internal objective condition is not non-existent (in two parts): first, it is explained that the transformation of consciousness into what resembles form and so forth serves as the objective condition.

From this, it is known with certainty that what is transformed by one’s own consciousness (up to the point of the "seeing" [aspect]) arises in dependence upon those [objects] and carries their characteristics.
Regarding the meaning of the terms: "From this" refers back to what precedes;

because external forms are logically not substantially real, one knows that the transformations of consciousness appearing as the five objects such as form constitute the true *ālambana-pratyaya* (objective condition) for the visual and other consciousnesses, because they possess the "seeing" [aspect].
It arises supported by that [object] and arises bearing its characteristics (*nimitta*), because it consists of two factors. "Bearing" has two meanings:

first, "carrying along," which refers to the cognizing mind directly carrying the essence of the object while cognizing it; second, "transforming and bearing," which refers to the cognizing mind transforming and giving rise to a *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) while cognizing it.
Characteristics (*nimitta*) also have two types: first, the characteristic of essence (*svabhāva-nimitta*); second, the characteristic of appearance (*ākāra-nimitta*). Five...
Consciousness takes an object as its condition. Regarding these two [interpretations of] meaning, it is only the latter sense that applies:

namely, that upon the substance of the five consciousnesses, the forms and characteristics of color and so forth are manifested and carried, thereby serving as the objects of the "seeing-portion" (darśana-bhāga) such as the visual faculty. The *Ālambanaparīkṣā* states:

"Internal form appears as if external; it serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness, because it is admitted that its aspect resides within consciousness and because it is capable of producing consciousness."
△ Next, it is explained that the images manifested by consciousness are not composed of atoms (paramāṇu). (2) First, the direct explanation:
When consciousness undergoes transformation, it does so according to the size of the object; [it manifests] many atoms combined to form a single entity.

Explanation of Terms: This refers to when the five consciousnesses transform into forms and so forth; according to the magnitude—whether large or small—of their respective objective fields (*viṣaya*), they appear immediately upon contact.
The dimensions of the manifested forms are identical to those of their original substrates (*bimba*); they are not produced through a separate transformation.
Rather, a multitude of atoms (*paramāṇu*) aggregate together to collectively constitute a single object.
Appendix: The third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Within an aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*), there has never been the arising of an atom (*paramāṇu*).
When it arises from its own seed, it arises only as a collection—whether subtle, medium, or large.
Furthermore, an aggregate of matter is not composed of an accumulation of atoms."
△ Next, the refutation of objections is explained.
For those who cling to the notion that coarse matter possesses substantial reality [up to] "therefore it is said that the atom (*paramāṇu*) is the limit of matter. (Commentary on the Meaning):
Question: It may be granted that the transformation of consciousness into matter and so forth manifests all at once; why does the Buddha say that atoms exist?
Yes. The answer is: for those who cling to coarse matter as having a substantial personhood, the Buddha taught the atom (*paramāṇu*) so that they might analyze and eliminate it.

Disciples who follow the Teacher in accordance with his teachings use the wisdom of conceptual meditation to gradually divide coarse material forms into seven parts each, until reaching a point where further division is impossible;
this is conventionally designated as an "atom," but it is not said to be substantially existent. Although below this—
He asked again: "Previously it was stated that atoms definitely possess spatial divisions (digbhāga) and are thus analyzable;
why do you now say they are not analyzable? Therefore, he explains: "Although this... and so forth.
△ Next, the conclusion and demonstration:
From this it should be known that all resistant forms (*sapratigha-rūpa*) are manifestations of consciousness and are not composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
△ Next, non-resistant form (*apratigha-rūpa*).
The remaining non-obstructive forms (*apratigha-rūpa*) belong to this same category; therefore, they can be said to be truly existent form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*).

[This claim] is refuted by the preceding examples. That is to say, non-obstructive form belongs to the same class as obstructive form (*sapratigha*); since obstructive form has already been refuted, [non-obstructive form is likewise refuted].
That [resistance] is also not real. Alternatively, there is no counter-argument to establish a formal proof (pramāṇa) to refute it.

Other non-resistant forms (*apratigha-rūpa*) are certainly not real forms, because they are admitted to be non-resistant, just like the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). All other refutations by way of analogy should be understood accordingly.
△ Second, the refutation of manifest and unmanifest form (2). First, the inquiry:
Are manifest and unmanifest form not indeed substantially existent?
[Response: Regarding the term "manifest and unmanifest form": "manifest" (*vijñapti*) refers to that which makes known; it possesses a visible form and characteristics.
Non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is the opposite of this; it consists of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind. *Opening the Ignorant*: Question:
What is the meaning of "informative" (*vijñapti*)? Answer: Because it indicates something, it is called "informative. Question: What is the characteristic of this indication? Answer:

Through the movement of a superior volition (*cetanā*), one initiates actions of body and speech—such as showing reverence or making a request—to make others know what is being done; this is termed "informative. Question: What is non-informative action?
[The meaning is: It is called "unmanifest" (avijñapti) because its function of preventing [unwholesome action] is unknown to oneself or others, and it lacks a manifest characteristic.

Next, the explanation [of the two types of form] begins with clarifying that the two types of form do not exist as substantial entities. This has two parts: first, the actual clarification; second, the refutation of their substantial existence.

Regarding the first [the actual clarification], there is the explanation of the manifest (vijñapti). Regarding the first [the manifest], there is the bodily manifest. Regarding the first [the refutation of its substantial existence], there is the initial counter-interrogation.
This is not substantially existent. Why is this so? Furthermore, if bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) were substantially existent, what would its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) be?
△ Next, the formal refutation (in three parts): first, the refutation of shape (*saṃsthāna*).
If one says that this shape is not substantially existent because it can be analyzed and because the atoms (paramāṇu) of length and so forth cannot be apprehended, [this is a response].
This refutes the position of the Sarvāstivāda school which maintains that shape constitutes bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti). *Huayan chao* 38.2 states:
"The Sarvāstivāda school establishes the correct principle [by] asserting that bodily intimation is a distinct shape; thus, shape constitutes bodily intimation. As [it is said]:...

Regarding the joining of palms and so forth, it is accepted that there are distinct shapes. Shape is itself informative (*vijñapti*), because it informs [others] of good or evil; and what is informative is itself karma.

This form-and-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) is called "bodily karma" because it arises based on the body. The Master [Vasubandhu] refutes this, saying: "If one says it is shape, then it is not substantially existent (*dravyasat*).
Shape—whether long, short, square, or round—is a conventional color (*prajñaptirūpa*) established in dependence upon many manifest colors (*varṇa*)."
Regarding length and so forth: when analyzed, the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) of length and so forth cannot be found.
Next, the refutation of motion:
if one says that this is motion, it is also not truly existent; [if it were,] up to the point where it would follow that cessation would not be cessation because it would depend upon a cause.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: This refutes the Saṃmitīya school’s reckoning that motion constitutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).

If one claims that motion is a manifest form (*rūpa*), it is likewise not substantially existent. It perishes immediately upon arising and does not reach another location, because it lacks the meaning of "motion.

The following section on conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) explains this through successive arguments. How is it that they perish as soon as they arise? Conditioned phenomena do not depend upon... [external causes for their cessation].
Because it is like a flash of lightning that perishes as soon as it appears. How is it that the cessation of phenomena does not depend on a cause?
The coming together of conditions is called arising; the separation of conditions is cessation. If cessation depended on a cause, it would not be cessation.

*He Xiang Kai Meng*: Questions on the Principle that Extinction Does Not Depend on Causes. Question: Please explain the principle that extinction does not depend on causes. Answer: Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) undergo transition and perish from moment to moment; why should they require a cause for their extinction? Question:
I request you to point out a single instance of this. Answer: Take, for example, the human body.

Once it has been produced according to the power of karma (*karma-vaśa*), it perishes in each preceding moment and arises in each succeeding one. From childhood until middle age, it gradually decays and withers until the power of karma [exhausts].
When [the continuum] is exhausted and the subsequent thought-moment does not continue, this is the state of death; how could it wait for the cessation of causes?
△ Third, refuting the production induced by mental factors (*caitta*).
If one says that there is a form which is neither manifest color (*varṇa*) nor shape (*saṃsthāna*), one should know that this applies to the categories of smell, taste, and touch as well.
Supplement: This further refutes the alternative position of the Sarvāstivādins. They claim that there exists a distinct kind of matter called "informative action" (*kāyavijñapti*).

Since it is neither a manifest color such as blue or yellow, nor a shape such as long or short, it is a powerful movement of the mental force of superior volition (*cetanā*) which induces this matter.
It is capable of causing the hands and other limbs to join in palms-together gestures, to bend, to kneel, or to extend and contract for the purpose of grasping.

[The opponent] abandons [the previous position] and asserts that this very matter (rūpa) constitutes bodily informative action (kāyavijñapti). The Master refutes this, saying: "This is also not the case.
If you claim that this produced matter has motion as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then that matter has already been refuted as before.

If you claim that it has the cause of motion as its intrinsic nature, then it is simply the wind element (vāyudhātu). Wind is not informative matter; it is known by touching the body. That touch is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta), whereas the body is pervasive."

Good and evil. What is called bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*)? It is not manifest as odor or taste, because these two objects—odor and taste—cannot be manifested like colors such as blue or yellow;
furthermore, they are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Therefore, it is said that [manifesting] them is "of the same category as tangibility.

One should know that sound is exclusively vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*), and one should know that all five sensory objects are not bodily intimation-action (*kāya-vijñapti-karman*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Bodily and vocal intimations..."
Karma. Because it pervades all three natures, the fifty-third fascicle states: "What is manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*)?
Briefly, there are three kinds: first, defiled; second, wholesome; and third, indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

If, with respect to the ten unwholesome paths of action of body, speech, and mind, because one does not abandon their active manifestation and their predominant power, whatever manifest karma of body and speech exists is called defiled manifest karma. If..."
That which is undertaken through such a vow and is entirely devoid of bodily and vocal informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) is called wholesome informative action.

If it pertains to a portion of the bodily and vocal informative actions involved in the modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) or the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*), it is called neutral informative action.
△ Third, the summary indication:
Therefore, bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti-karman*) is certainly not substantially existent.
△ Next, the presentation of the correct principle.
However, because the mind acts as the cause that causes consciousness to undergo transformation (up to) so as to represent the mind, it is metaphorically termed "bodily intimation" (*kāyavijñapti*).
Regarding the meaning of the term: in the Mahāyāna, this is based solely on the transformation of the mind, which differs from the Hīnayāna. "Mind" refers to the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*);

"consciousness" refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). This means that with the internal sixth consciousness acting as the cause, it causes the eighth fundamental consciousness to undergo transformation.

The color-forms (rūpa-lakṣaṇa) of the hands and so forth arise in a similar succession, appearing as if they possess movement and expression; these are conventionally designated as "bodily intimation" (kāya-vijñapti) with respect to the mind.
It does not mean that there exists a separate substantial entity apart from the mind.
△ Next, regarding the informative intimation of speech (2): first, the refutation of its substantial existence.
The informative intimation of speech is also not substantially existent as the nature of sound, because the external resistant form [of sound] has already been refuted previously.
Explanation of Terms: The first phrase directly refutes [the position]. From "In a single kṣaṇa" onwards, it clarifies the reason why.

Although the sound of a single kṣaṇa exists substantially, it lacks the capacity for signification. Although a continuity of multiple moments can signify, such a continuous phenomenon is a conventional construct and thus not substantially existent.
Since sound was previously refuted as being invisible and possessing resistance (*sapratigha*), one should not persist in clinging to it.
There is indeed the nature of sound, which constitutes vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
△ Next, the correct principle is set forth:
However, because of the mind, consciousness transforms into that which resembles sound... (up to)... it is conventionally designated as vocal intimation; this does not contradict reason.
Harmonizing Resonance. This may be understood by analogy with the preceding discussion on manifest action (*vijñapti*).
Next, the explanation of non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) has two parts. First, refuting its substantial existence:
since manifest action is already substantially non-existent, how could non-manifest action possibly be substantial?
△ Next, the correct principle is set forth.

However, [the nature of] volition (*cetanā*) is established based on the limits of its wholesome or unwholesome intentions and aspirations (*praṇidhāna*); thus, it is a provisional existence (*prajñaptisat*).

[The text continues: "First, the general explanation of volition" refers to the mental factor of volition among the universal (*sarvatraga*) factors. "Aspiration" refers to [the mental factor of] aspiration among the object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) factors.
Regarding the mental factor of desire (*chanda*): this clarifies that it is associated with the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Whether it is a volition (*cetanā*) wishing for the wholesome or a volition wishing for the unwholesome, based on these boundaries and limits of the wholesome and unwholesome, the non-informative (*avijñapti*) is provisionally established. This is explained in the following section.

This means that this non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) is established based on the stage of growth of the seeds of wholesome or unwholesome volitions (*cetanā*) that have initiated superior bodily or vocal actions.
"Growth" refers to the capacity to prevent [unwholesome] initiation, which increases and intensifies further and further. This occurs once these seeds of volition have already been initiated.

Thus, it becomes manifest (*vijñapti*). While it has not yet been emitted, it still resides in the state of the seed; the moment it is about to be emitted but has not yet been emitted is called the stage of increase (*vṛddhi*).
However, this unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is perfumed and established by the manifest color-form (*rūpa-vijñapti*). The fifty-fifth fascicle of the *Zongjing* states:
"Regarding the manifest color-form of the first restraint (*saṃvara*), it refers to the time one receives the precepts in the presence of a teacher. By means of this manifest color-form..."

Therefore, it is only through the manifest action (*vijñapti*) that one perfumes the seeds of good or evil, which possess the capacity for prevention or arousal; this is what constitutes the essence of the *prātimokṣa*, and thus the non-manifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is established.
Second, regarding the manifest form of non-restraint (*asaṃvara-vijñapti*), this refers precisely to the moment when one applies the blade to commit the act of killing.
It is by means of this manifest action that one perfumes the seeds of unwholesome volition (*cetanā*), which possess the capacity for prevention or arousal.
[The text] establishes its unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*). This is an explanation based on the state of ordinary mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), encompassing both wholesome and unwholesome positions.

Alternatively, according to the *Hui-xuan* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), fascicle six, which cites an ancient commentary: it means that within the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one establishes the precepts of concentration and the path (*dhyāna-mārga-śīla*) upon the volition (*cetanā*) that ceases the actual occurrence of bodily and vocal misconduct;
this does not refer to seeds (*bīja*). This is because [the precepts] are said to "follow the movement of the mind" (*anuparivartin*), referring to the actual occurrence of volition.

That may be so. However, seeds are not like this; therefore, that which restrains bodily and vocal misconduct is a provisional designation for "matter" (*rūpa*), as it is that by which matter is brought about.
By means of this power, it obstructs and prevents the materiality of bodily and vocal misconduct—such as killing, stealing, and lying—from manifesting.

Because it obstructs and prevents such materiality, this non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is provisionally designated by the name "matter. (This passage is an explanation based on the state of goodness associated with a concentrated mind. If...
Whether as seeds or as manifest states, both are established based upon volition (*cetanā*); therefore, they do not exist as substantial entities.

Although seeds and manifestations differ, they both take volition as their single underlying factor because it is designated by the meaning of "constructing" (*abhisamskāra*), and the power of volition is preeminent.

The reason the text does not mention the "precepts co-arising with the Path" (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*) is that even when the Noble Path arises, it is capable of preventing [unwholesome actions]; this is precisely the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) which determines [the path].
Since it is not reckoned that there are real dharmas external to the mind, they are not analyzed.
△ Next, the explanation of the objection (in two parts): First, the objection:
"The World-Honored One stated in the sūtras that there are three types of karma; does this not contradict the sūtra by negating the existence of bodily and vocal karma?"

Commentary on Terms: The Sūtras speak of the three types of karma (*trividha-karma*). Now, the Master of the Treatise consolidates these under mental consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*). Is this not in contradiction with the holy teachings?
△ Next, the explanation [of the second point], which begins with a general response that [karma] is not matter (*rūpa*).
It is not denied that they exist; it is merely stated that they are not form (*rūpa*).
△ Next, the substance of karma is explained specifically (in two parts). First, it is explained that volition (*cetanā*) is the substance of the three types of karma:
the volition capable of moving the body is called bodily karma (*kāyakarma*); [omitted] because it moves the mind, it is called mental karma (*manaskarma*).
*Hexiang* (Harmonious Resonance), *Huayan Chao* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka) 38.2, explains: This passage sets forth the substance of the three karmas.
Now, volition (*cetanā*) is of three types: first, deliberative volition; second, determinative volition; and third, impelling volition. The first two types of volition...

This refers to the initiation of bodily and vocal actions at a distance or nearby. The movement initiated by volition (*cetanā*) is precisely what constitutes the essence of the two types of action (bodily and vocal).
Because the first two types of volition are associated with the mind and move the mind, they are termed "mental action" (*manas-karman*).
Therefore, volition as a whole is established as the essence of the three types of action.

△ Next, the explanation of the two types of action—bodily and vocal—is presented in two parts. First, it is shown that they are designated as "paths of action" (karmapatha) because of volition (*cetanā*).
The volitions that give rise to bodily and vocal actions perform various formations; thus, the first seven paths of action also have volition as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Exegesis on Terms: That which is produced through volitional effort is called *karman* (action). Because volition (*cetanā*) is capable of instigating bodily and vocal acts, and because there is something produced, it is designated as *karman*.
This body and speech are the domain traversed and followed by deliberative volition;

they manifest as the causes for good and evil, and universally give rise to the fruits of future suffering and happiness. They are also called "paths" (*mārga*). A path is like a road. Therefore, [as stated] previously...
This clarifies that volition (*cetanā*) is not the sole nature of mental action (*manas-karman*); rather, the essence of both bodily and vocal actions is also volition.
As for the seven paths of action (*karmapatha*), they consist of three of the body and four of speech, comprising both wholesome and unwholesome karma.
△ Next, it is explained that the paths of action (*karmapatha*) are metaphorical designations.

Because they are produced by volition (*cetanā*) manifested through bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*), they are metaphorically designated as "action" (*karman*); and because they are traversed by volition, they are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*).
Regarding the meaning of the terms: the bodily and vocal actions that are produced are not themselves volition (*cetanā*), but are rather set in motion by intermediate volition.

Since volition is designated as "action" (*karman*), these [actions] are established as "action" by way of dependence upon volition. Because they are traversed by volition, they are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*).
△ Next, the transformation of the two types of form as mere consciousness is established.
From this, one should know that external forms do not truly exist, but rather that only internal consciousness transforms and arises appearing as form.

Next, the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are refuted. (3) First, a general clarification that they lack substantial reality and function. (2) First, clarifying their dependence on form.
The designations of mental states (*citta-vasthā*) are conventionally established;
the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are likewise not substantially real (up to: but are merely conventionally established based on the states of form and so forth).

[This is] the "Resonance" (*saṃghoṣa*). First, the heading and inquiry: because acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth are not capable of cognition (*ālambana*), they do not associate with the mind or mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

It should be [understood as] such, because it is not characterized by material resistance (*sapratigha*) and thus does not correspond with form (*rūpa*). Because it possesses arising and ceasing, it does not correspond with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The *Huìxuán* (Meeting the Profundity), fascicle ten, states: "There are two interpretations of this. First, it says: 'The practitioner' refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). There are two types of formations:
first, associated formations (*saṃprayukta-saṃskāra*), which are the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*); second, dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), which are acquisition (*prāpti*)."
[The preceding] and so forth. Now, the term "dissociated formations" (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) is used to distinguish them from "associated formations" (*samprayuktasaṃskāra*).

Second, it is said that one should fully state "non-material dissociated formations" (*arūpaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), which serves to exclude the four aggregates (namely, the mind-king, mental factors, matter, and the unconditioned). This should be reflected upon according to reason.
"Functioning" (*pravṛtti*) is thus incompatible [with its own definition]; this is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Alternatively, it distinguishes [it] from the four aggregates;

this is also a *tatpuruṣa* (determinative) compound (as the text states). "The acquisition (*prāpti*) is not [real]" clarifies that it is not substantially existent. That is to say, these acquisitions and so forth do not possess a substantial ontological characteristic like the dharmas of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
For this reason, it is known for certain that they are not substantially existent. Furthermore, they do not possess any real functional activity distinct from form, mind, and so forth.

Therefore, it is merely established as a conventional designation based on those states (meaning that "this is different from that" cannot be established as having a nature that is either different or non-different).
Next, a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is set forth to demonstrate the absence of a substantial entity or function.

This attainment (*samāpatti*) is certainly not distinct from matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and mental factors (*caitasika*); [it is] like other provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) which lack a real substantial entity (*dravya-svabhāva*).

[Commentary on the Meaning of the Text]: This passage contains three logical measures (*pramāṇa*). The word "this" (*idam*) refers to "attainment" (*prāpti*) and so forth. The first measure grants that it possesses a substantial entity and function, clarifying that it is not distinct from matter and mind.

The syllogism (*prayoga*) is as follows: "This" is the subject (*dharmin*). "It is certainly not [distinct from matter, mind, and mental factors]" is the thesis (*pakṣa*). "Because it is admitted to be included within the aggregates (*skandha*)" is the reason (*hetu*).
As in the analogy of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), or as the mind is shown below to lack substantial reality (*dravya*). The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states:

This [mind] is certainly not substantially existent, because it is not subsumed under mind, mental factors (*caitta*), form, or unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); it is like absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).

Alternatively, as clarified below, it is shown to be a nominal existence (*prajñaptisat*). The formal argument states: This lacks a substantially existent essence, because it is not subsumed under either this [mind] or other real dharmas.
Like other provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*), they are like echoes.
In the Mahāyāna system of dharma-characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), there are one hundred dharmas; in the Hīnayāna, there are only seventy-five.

"The remainder" refers to the seventy-five dharmas remaining [after excluding the provisional ones]. Regarding "the remaining real dharmas" (*dravya-dharma*): this refers to the Hīnayāna, which consists of the single mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the seven remaining [consciousnesses] outside of it.

Aside from the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and the forty-six mental factors (*caitta*), there are the remaining five mental factors; aside from the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), there are the remaining three unconditioned phenomena.

These fifteen dharmas across these three categories each possess both essence and function, and are thus called "remaining real dharmas" (*śeṣa-dravyadharma*). As for the "remaining nominal dharmas" (*śeṣa-prajñaptidharma*):
Apart from the fourteen factors such as acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the Hīnayāna, there are ten other dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

These ten factors are provisionally established based on the states (*avasthā*) of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*); they lack substantial essence or function and are thus called "remaining provisional phenomena" (*śeṣa-prajñapti-dharma*).
△ Next, the specific refutation of acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), and so forth (6). First, the refutation of acquisition and non-acquisition (2).
First, the refutation of the opponent's position (2). First, the inquiry regarding their substantial existence (2). First, the Master’s question.
Furthermore, how can one know that acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) possess a distinct substantial entity and function, separate from form, mind, and so forth?

The "homogeneity of destinies" (gati-sabhāgatā) is called *sabhāgatā*. This refers to sentient beings born together in a single destiny.

Up to those with right view: comparing one with right view to another with right view; from stream-enterers up to arhats and pratyekabuddhas, comparing them to stream-enterers and so forth;

"Homogeneous speech" refers to the discourse that designates [beings] as belonging to the same class. As the *Abhidharmakośa* describes the externalist position:

"If there were no real entity characterized by non-differentiation to be called 'homogeneity,' then among sentient beings who are mutually distinct, how could there arise the cognition that 'sentient being' and 'sentient being' are equal and without distinction?"

Furthermore, it should not be possible to establish [the existence of] *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity). Awakening is equivalent to cognition (*jñāna*), and establishment is equivalent to verbal expression (*abhilāpa*).

Thus, the previous example is refuted: namely, if [it were argued that] they are identical to cognition and verbal expression because they arise from this commonality (*sabhāga*), then *sabhāgatā* would have to exist as a real entity.
If that were so, then grasses, trees, and the like would also possess *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity).

This being the case, it would contradict the sacred teachings (*āgama*), for the various sacred teachings do not state that there is *sabhāgatā* for insentient things. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* asks:
"Furthermore, for what reason is it not admitted that there is *sabhāgatā* for insentient things? [For] grains, rice, beans, gold, silver, mangoes, *panasa* fruits, and so forth..."
There exists a "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*), because [beings] are mutually similar (text). Furthermore, it is refuted by means of a concessive argument regarding the lower [level]:

if that which gives rise to the cognition and expression of "homogeneity" with respect to a particular homogeneity is itself called "homogeneity," then there must further exist another distinct homogeneity that gives rise to that [first] homogeneity.

In this way, there would be the fault of an infinite regress. However, since that *sabhāgatā* does not arise from another distinct *sabhāgatā*, why must this term "common cognition" necessarily arise because of such a *sabhāgatā*?

Furthermore, it has already been established that matter (*rūpa*) is not distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*) [up to the point where it should be understood that, like feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, it is not a real life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)].

Example and refutation: The intent is to clarify that feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth are distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*) and are not the actual life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). If the life-faculty were distinct from consciousness, it likewise would not be the actual life-faculty.
The subject (*dharmin*) is the life-faculty; the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is not the actual life-faculty; the reason (*hetu*) is that it is a real entity distinct from consciousness;
the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like feeling and so forth.
△ Next, the resolution of objections.
If this is so, why does the Sūtra speak of three factors? (Up to: "This consciousness has these as its causes," which will be explained in detail later.

[Commentary on the Meaning of the Sounds]: This consists of three layers of question and answer. The first question is: Since both life-force (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*) are [aspects of] consciousness, why does the Sūtra speak of three?

The following response distinguishes their meanings: although all are consciousness, they are described as being of three types based on their functional distinctions. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source), fascicle 50, explains:
"That is to say, the matter (*rūpa*) within the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the ālayavijñāna, which is apprehended by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), is called 'warmth' (*uṣman*)."

The seeds of this consciousness are called "life" (*āyus*), because they are able to sustain consciousness. Since the manifesting consciousness is itself "consciousness," these three factors are explained as having distinct meanings;
it does not mean that they possess separate substantial natures (*svabhāva*).

Thus, when the body abandons warmth, the other two [factors] are not necessarily abandoned, as in the case of birth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Conversely, when the other two are abandoned, warmth and mind are abandoned accordingly. However...
Now, these three are explained separately according to their specific meanings, yet they constitute a single essence.

Just as the four right efforts (samyak-pradhāna)—which, though distinguished in meaning as the two categories of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas already arisen and not yet arisen—are in fact only a single factor of diligence (vīrya), so too [these three] abide without inferiority.

Furthermore, it is asked: if the meaning is explained as three distinct things, yet there is only a single consciousness, then when one abides in a state of no-mind, since mind is absent, there should be neither vitality (*āyus*) nor warmth (*uṣman*).
How then can the Sūtra say that vitality and warmth do not perish? Is it not answered below that this is because consciousness does not depart?
"Vitality and warmth do not perish. This concludes the preceding [section]. Now follows the third question: "Since consciousness does not depart, how can it be called 'mindless'?

Does that [state] perish? The answer is: "In the state of mindlessness, only the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) cease; it is not said that the eighth [consciousness] ceases. It is proven that this consciousness exists [therein]."
As will be extensively cited from scripture and reasoning below.

This consciousness is sufficient to serve as the substance of the realms, destinies, and births; there is no need to laboriously maintain the separate attachment that a real life-faculty (jīvitendriya) exists.
Supplement: This eighth consciousness is fully capable of serving as the substance for the six consciousnesses of the three realms and the four modes of birth.

This is because it pervades all three realms, whereas the preceding six are excluded as they do not; because it is constant and continuous, whereas the preceding six are excluded as they have interruptions;
and because it is the "ripening fruit" (*vipāka-phala*), which distinguishes it from the ripening-born nature of the preceding six.
△ Next, the correct principle is set forth.
However, based on the seeds that directly produce this consciousness (up to) the determination of its duration, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is provisionally established.
The *Zhongjing* (Mirror of the Essential Teachings), fascicle 50, in its commentary, states: "The word 'this' serves to distinguish [it] from the seeds that directly produce other consciousnesses."

Regarding the term "seed": by saying "consciousness," one distinguishes it from the seeds of associated mental factors (*saṃprayuktadharma*), taking only consciousness itself. Regarding the term "seed":

this distinguishes it from the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*). One does not take the eighth [consciousness] in its active manifestation as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), because that which is excluded here is not the life-faculty.
Now, regarding the seeds of names and phrases produced by one's parents, they are drawn forth by the specific functional capacity for maintaining the body induced by prior karma.
This "specific functional capacity for maintaining the body induced by prior karma" refers, in essence, to that which is牵引 (drawn forth) by the wholesome and unwholesome karma of previous lives.
If the functional capacity of that karma is great, it draws forth these seeds of consciousness so that their duration is determined.
The duration of abiding is determined. If the functional power of karma is slight, then the drawing forth of this consciousness-seed will necessarily have a short duration of abiding.

Based on these determinate stages of long and short duration of abiding, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is provisionally established, causing the duration of abiding for matter, mind, and so forth, to be determined.
It is based on this functional power that it is called the life-faculty; it does not refer to the grasping of birth or manifestation.

Regarding the meaning of the consciousness of formations (*saṃskāra-vijñāna*): by means of these seeds, through the power of karma, there exists the functional differentiation capable of maintaining a body of a single retribution (*eka-vaipākika-kāya*).
This brings about the determination of the seeds; without this functional capacity, the body would simply decay and perish.
When the *ālaya-vijñāna* manifests, it is able to take objects and sustain phenomena such as the eye and so forth by virtue of these seeds; it is also called "the capable."
It sustains. This seed is precisely that which can sustain the manifesting consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

If it were not so, the manifesting consciousness would not exist, nor would there be anything capable of sustaining other factors such as the sense faculties. By virtue of this function, consciousness sustains the body.
