Section Five, Refuting the Three Characteristics of Conditioned Phenomena (2). Part One: Refuting the Errors of Others (2). Part One: Questioning and Answering Regarding Actual Existence (2).
First, the author of the treatise asks:
Furthermore, how is it known that the various conditioned characteristics (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa)—distinct from matter (rūpa), mind (citta), and so forth—possess a real intrinsic nature (svabhāva)?

[Supplement: The various conditioned characteristics, namely arising (jāti), duration (sthiti), change (anyathātva), and cessation (nirodha), are themselves the conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) such as matter and mind.]
Arising, abiding, change, and cessation are the very characteristics of phenomena such as form and mind; they are inherently inseparable from them.

Yet, outsiders (bāhyaka) falsely conceive of these characteristics—arising and so forth—as being separate from form and mind, claiming that their own nature can be apprehended apart from them. The Master of the Treatise challenges this view, citing the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*:

"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are associated with the characteristic of arising in relation to the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), and [associated with cessation] in relation to the posterior limit (*aparānta*)."
It is associated with the characteristic of cessation. Regarding the intermediate state, it is associated with the characteristics of duration and change (as the text states).

If a phenomenon undergoes the complete transition through the three periods of time, this sutra describes it as a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), in order to cause sentient beings to give rise to weariness and fear.
△ Next, the opponent replies: Because it is stated in the sūtras;
as it is stated in the sūtras that there are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned, and so forth, at length.

[Supplement] Furthermore, this opponent cites the sūtra as proof. Regarding the three conditioned characteristics: first, the characteristic of arising; second, [the characteristic of duration]; third, [the characteristic of cessation].

The characteristic of duration-change (*sthity-anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*) and the third, the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*). These three are the characteristics of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*).
Because these characteristics exist, material and mental phenomena are designated as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) dharmas. Furthermore, the Sūtra asks: "Why are the four characteristics not mentioned?

It refers to the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*). This means abiding in those formations (*saṃskāra*), maintaining them, establishing permanence and bliss, and not being separated from them.
Therefore, it is not established among the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*). The *Śata-śāstra* states:

"That is to say, all conditioned phenomena such as form and mind possess the three conditioned characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing" (text). Furthermore, conditioned phenomena are fully endowed with four characteristics;
here, abiding and change are combined into a single characteristic, meaning that the transformation of the characteristic of abiding is itself termed "change. The *Yogācārabhūmi* says: "It is not..."
This distinct characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) exists as a separate entity apart from the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, these two types are collectively subsumed and designated as a single characteristic (text). Now, the opponent, based on the word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) within the cited sūtra concerning the three characteristics of the conditioned, gives rise to a fixed attachment, asserting that characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth definitely exist externally to form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
△ Next, the correct refutation of substantial existence (in two parts). First, a general negation based on scripture:
This scripture does not state that there is a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) distinct from form, mind, and so forth; therefore, it fails as a proof [for such a claim].
△ Next, the refutation by way of the meaning (five parts). First, the refutation that the essence of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*) are distinct.

It is not the case that the use of the sixth grammatical case (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*) necessarily expresses a difference in essence; otherwise, the essence of the characteristics of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) would have to be distinct from the characterized.
Supplement: Regarding the refutation of the "genitive" (shǔshēng) based on the *Kāśyapaparivarta*, it is said that there are eight grammatical cases (vibhakti):

namely, the nominative (tǐ), accusative (yè), instrumental (jù), dative (wéi), ablative (cóng), genitive (shǔ), locative (yī), and vocative (hū). The sixth is the genitive; whatever possesses a relationship of connection is subsumed under the genitive.
Because the opponent takes the word "of" (*zhì*) from the cited sūtra to be the genitive case, they then cling to the characteristics of arising and so forth as being connected [to the self].
Since they are dharmas belonging to matter (rūpa) and mind (citta), the characteristics such as arising (jāti) must necessarily be distinct from dharmas such as matter and mind.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, in recounting the views of outsiders, states: "If the characteristic of arising did not exist, there would be no cognition of 'arising';

furthermore, the use of the sixth case (genitive) would be untenable—for instance, [expressions] such as 'the arising of matter' or 'the arising of sensation'. The intent of my present refutation is that these words [found in the sūtras]...

Since these [terms] belong to the category of nouns (*nāman*), they refer to the three characteristics, such as arising (*jāti*), which are tied to the phenomena of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

Therefore, apart from matter and mind, there is no separate essence of arising and so forth that can be apprehended; it is not the case that the sixth grammatical case (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*) itself expresses a distinct entity.

Thus, one should not say that the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing exist outside of matter and mind, as if one were speaking of "the essence of matter and mind" [as something separate].
How could the substance of matter and mind (*rūpa-citta*) be different from matter and mind simply because of their designations?

Since they are identical to matter and mind, it is not the case that the primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)—such as hardness, moisture, heat, and motion—are distinct from earth, water, fire, and wind.

How could the primary characteristics of arising and so forth be definitively different from matter and mind, existing apart from the characterized (*lakṣya*) objects? Thus, he refutes [the opponent's view] by citing this analogy.

Is it the characterized? If arising, abiding, and ceasing are the conditioning characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the conditioned, they must necessarily be distinct from the characterized phenomena such as form and mind.

By this analogy, the essence of the unconditioned characteristics—being without arising and without ceasing—should likewise be distinct from the unconditioned characterized phenomena (such as space and cessation not through deliberation).
△ Next, [the author] refutes the simultaneous existence of the characteristics (lakṣaṇa), such as arising, and their substratum (lakṣya).
Furthermore, if the characteristics such as arising were to exist simultaneously with their substratum, then the functions of abiding, change, and cessation would not be able to occur together.

*Hexiang* (Harmony of Resonance): The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* of the Hīnayāna states that although the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) are admitted to exist simultaneously, their functions (*kāritra*) occur at different times.
That is to say, the function of arising (*jāti*) exists in the future; once [a dharma] has arisen in the present, it does not arise again.

When all dharmas have already arisen and are currently in the present, the functions of the other three characteristics—abiding (*sthiti*), etc.—only then commence, and not at the time when the function of arising occurs. There is another [point]:...

Third, because of their functions. Although they coexist, they do not contradict one another (text). In this passage, the author first refutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) by means of its functions.
If the natures of the characteristics such as arising were to coexist, they would necessarily exercise their functions simultaneously at all times;

how then could it be logical for a single phenomenon to undergo arising, abiding, and ceasing at one and the same time? The *Śataśāstra* states: "When the nature of a phenomenon arises, it abides and ceases."

It is a delusion and error to claim that the essence [of the characteristics] remains identical even when they have not yet reached the stage of abiding or cessation, for the characteristic of arising has already ceased to exist.

[The following passage] refutes a counter-argument regarding this contradiction: it means that although the essences of arising and the other characteristics coexist, their functions are mutually exclusive.

If they do not arise simultaneously, their essence should likewise be so; why then do you calculate them as co-existent? Furthermore, since they are mutually contradictory, the functions of arising, abiding, and ceasing should not occur together.
How can you insist that they are identical to the present?
△ Third, the refutation of the inherent existence of the characteristics of the agent and the object.

[The opponent claims that] the essences of both the characteristic-agent and the characteristic-object are inherently existent... (up to) furthermore, it would follow that the apprehension of arising and so forth is rendered useless.

[Response: First, the essence is refuted by means of its function. This is because they maintain that the essences of both the characteristic-agent and the characteristic-object are inherently existent.
The refutation says: Since the essence (*tattva*) is fundamentally existent, its function (*vṛtti*) must likewise be so, because there is no distinct nature between function and essence.
The following section refutes a further counter-argument: if it is claimed that although the essence is fundamentally existent, the function requires conditions (*pratyaya*) before it can arise.
Then the causes and conditions upon which it depends must not be inherently existent. Since that which is depended upon is thus, so too is that which depends.
Thus, both the characteristics of the dependent and the dependent-upon arise from causes and conditions; how can you say they are inherently existent?
Furthermore, since [birth and so forth] must depend on the function of other conditions to arise, the "birth" and other factors you cling to would be rendered useless.
△ 4. Refuting the conjunction of the characteristic and the characterized.

[This is because] while the characterized is eternally existent, it would be impossible to find a cause for its difference from [the characteristics such as] arising and so forth when they are conjoined.
(From the *Vyākhyāyukti* / *Pindārtha*). Regarding the meaning of the words, the *Śataśāstra-vṛtti* records their tenet as follows: "They say this: 'In our school, it is taught that all...'"
The four characteristics function by depending upon one another in succession, coming and going through the three periods of time without ever being separated.

Because they are conjoined with birth and the other [characteristics], they constitute the nature of impermanent phenomena which is indestructible; therefore, it is said that they "exist eternally. Thus, while "eternal existence" is not discarded, it does not contradict impermanence and the rest (as the text states).

Now, I shall establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to refute [the claim that] conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) have a "permanently existing" characteristic (*lakṣya*), yet are conjoined with birth and the rest.

Therefore, just as with unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of unconditioned phenomena exist eternally; yet, because they are also conjoined with arising and so forth, they would be like conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

Since both schools [of thought] maintain that arising and so forth are causes that arise simultaneously [with their characteristics], it is said that "distinct causes for this and that" cannot be found.
Since the characteristics of the unconditioned are not conjoined with arising and so forth, how much less could the characteristics of the conditioned be so?
The combination of arising and so forth is refuted here; because it is the combination of arising and so forth, the thesis that "that which is characterized exists eternally" is refuted accordingly.
△ Fifth, the refutation of the contradiction of arising and so forth across the three times.
Furthermore, because the past and future are neither manifest nor eternal, their tenets—whether advanced or withdrawn—are irrational.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: first, a formal inference (*prayoga*) is established to clarify that the past and future are not real. Next, under the heading "Arising" (*jāti*), it is clarified that [the opponent's position] contradicts worldly convention.

First, by way of conformity, it is shown that arising and ceasing contradict worldly convention. If "arising" were defined as "existence," it would necessarily belong to the present; it cannot [belong to the past or future].
Regarding the future: if "cessation" (*nirodha*) were defined as non-existence (*abhāva*), it would belong to the past and not to the present.

If one objects to this by arguing that cessation is not non-existent and therefore belongs to the present, then if cessation is taken to be non-non-existent, arising (*utpāda*) should likewise be taken to be non-non-existent.
Furthermore, if one argues that cessation refers to abiding (*sthiti*) and cessation, they cannot occur simultaneously with arising and abiding.

How could it be possible for them to exist in different worlds? Therefore, the conclusion stated below—that falling back occurs in the future while advancing toward cessation occurs in the present—is entirely unreasonable.
△ Next, the presentation of the correct doctrine (in two parts): First, the four characteristics of a single moment (in three parts): First, stating the purpose of establishing these characteristics.

However, because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) arise through the power of causes and conditions, [the treatise] establishes four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) as provisional designations to distinguish them.
This is consistent with the *Huìxuán* (The Profound Meaning), Scroll Ten, which quotes the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-ṭīkā*: "Characteristics" refers to marks or appearances;

they are called "characteristics" because they serve as signs. By means of these, one identifies a phenomenon as being conditioned. These four are all established upon the basis of manifesting phenomena (*pravṛtti-dharma*)."
Characteristics.
△ Next, the four characteristics are explained and established. (4) First, the four characteristics are explained individually:
that which was originally non-existent and now exists is called "arising" (*jāti*); [the state of existing for a time] until it returns to non-existence is called "ceasing" (*nirodha*).

*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonances): A question on the Profound. How can the names and meanings of the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) be established within a single *kṣaṇa*, such that there is this differentiation?
Since the duration of time is so extremely brief, the principle is difficult to comprehend. Answer: An ancient master used the analogy of a needle piercing paper.

Suppose there is a hundred-fold layer of paper; when a sharp needle is used to pierce it once, the piercing occurs simultaneously across all layers, yet the needle must necessarily [pass through them].
As they pass in succession, there ought to be a hundredfold arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing occurring simultaneously;
yet one must observe that within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), the four characteristics exist with temporal priority and posteriority, and this principle applies to the case at hand as well.
△ Next, distinguishing [the dharmas] from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) by way of time:
because the first three exist, they are all in the present; because the last one is non-existent, it is in the past. *Hehexiang* (Harmonizing the Resonance).

The fifth fascicle of the *Xuantan* (Profound Discourse) states: "The four characteristics manifest simultaneously at the moment of cessation; the subsequent non-existence serves to distinguish them."

In the Hīnayāna, [the characteristic of] cessation arises in the future, while the other three exist in the present. Regarding the question in the *Hui Xuan*: "Since cessation signifies non-existence, it should belong to the future;
why then is it called past? The answer is: it is called past because the state of cessation is non-existent, as that which was present has already fallen away.
However, if one looks toward the arising-phase (*jāti*) and so forth of the immediately succeeding moment, it would instead be in the future.
At the very moment of arising, it still belongs to the present; thus, it differs from the Hīnayāna. Reflect on this.

Supplement: Regarding the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) in Mahāyāna, if categorized according to the theory of time (*adhvan*), arising, abiding, and change belong to the present, while cessation belongs to the past.
If categorized according to the theory of manifestation (*vijñapti*), all are explained as occurring upon the basis of dharmas in their active functioning (*samudācāra*).
△ Third, explaining away external objections.
How can that which is non-existent (the unconditioned) be expressed by means of conditioned characteristics? What fault would there be in this?
*Hexiang* (Huiyan) quotes the ancient commentary, saying: "This is an externalist’s question: 'If cessation (*nirodha*) is non-existent, how..."
It functions as a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) for phenomena that exist in the present. This indicates that the author of the treatise below does not intend to express non-existent phenomena.

Furthermore, regarding those who say that non-existence is established by means of a non-existent cause (*anupalabdhi-hetu*), there is no fault; for they state that non-existence is apprehended through a non-existent [cause].

If that were so, then things such as "tortoise hair" should also be established as characteristics. To this we reply: these are not the same as those [cases], because they do not follow from a subsequent non-existence. Fundamentally...
Since there is no present [existence], it is not a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
△ Fourth, the characteristics indicated by delusion:
arising indicates that a dharma previously non-existent now exists; cessation (up to) indicates that it has perished; and duration indicates that this dharma temporarily possesses function.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: First, the individual [explanations]. "Arising" (jāti) indicates that a phenomenon exists; it was previously non-existent and now exists for the first time.
"Cessation" (nirodha) indicates that a phenomenon will no longer exist at a later time; it currently does not yet exist as non-existent.

"Alteration" (anyathātva) indicates that this phenomenon is not static, but constantly undergoes transition and change. "Duration" (sthiti) indicates that this phenomenon has utility for a brief period, rather than utility over a long duration. Ancient [masters] [have explained it thus].
The Commentary states: This passage precisely explains the reasons for the manifestation of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and what these characteristics signify.
△ Third, it concludes that these are provisional;
therefore, regarding these four characteristics within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), [it says] "this is based on the moment (*kṣaṇa*) to provisionally establish the four characteristics."
△ Next, the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of a single lifetime (*ekādhvika*).
The stages (*avasthā*) of a single lifetime may also be established as provisional (up to: "therefore, the four characteristics are all provisionally established").
Supplement: First, the heading; next, the explanation beginning with "First, there is... The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "That is to say, regarding those various sentient beings, the multitude..."
Within the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*), the initial arising is called "birth" (*jāti*); the final passing away is called "cessation" (*nirodha*).

In the interval between these two, from the stage of infancy and so forth up to the stage of old age, that which is established is called "duration" (*sthiti*). The successive transformations and distinctions among these various stages are called "alteration during duration" (*sthity-anyathātva*).
As the *Kaibong* (Opening the Ignorant) states: "With respect to persons, objects, and so forth, from birth until cessation, there is a period of long or short duration."

Section. Within the span of a single lifetime (*ekakalpa*), these four characteristics are explained; this duration is termed "a single lifetime" (text). Therefore, the following is the conclusion. △ Six:
Refuting the Collections of Names, Phrases, and Syllables (2). First, refuting the errors of others (2). First, questioning and answering regarding their actual existence (2).
First, the Master of the Treatise asks.
Furthermore, how is it known that there exist real *nāma-kāya*, *pada-kāya*, and *vyañjana-kāya*—which express and signify—that are distinct from form (*rūpa*), consciousness (*citta*), and so forth?
Supplement: The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To signify (*quan*) means to possess (*ju*). This refers to possessing the explanation of phenomena (*dharma*) and principles (*artha*).

Regarding "body" (*kāya*): it carries the meanings of substance (*tǐ*), basis (*yī*), and collection (*jù*). A single [unit] is called a "name" (*nāman*). From two names upward, they are termed a "name-body" (*nāma-kāya*). A single phrase is not a "body."

A body [of speech] (*kāya*) is constituted by multiple phrases. A "phrase" (*pada*) consists of syllables (*vyañjana*), which constitute names (*nāman*). A "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) is based on multiple phrases. The *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* states at length: "What is a name-body?
It has the nature of being a metaphorical designation (*adhivacana*) for the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena, such as when one says 'eye' and so forth.

What is a phrase-body (*padakāya*)? It has the nature of being a metaphorical designation for the specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*) among phenomena, such as when one says 'conditioned forces' (*saṃskāra*)."

Regarding the statement "impermanence and so forth," what is a *vyañjana-kāya* (phoneme-group)? It refers to the syllables themselves, for they are able to manifest the two preceding natures (*nāma* and *pada*).
Thus, *nāma*, *pada*, and *vyañjana* are merely specific arrangements (*vaṅka*) within sound; they express meaning but are neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*).

They are conventionally established based on the states (*avasthā*) of form and mind; they are provisional and not real, and are subsumed under the category of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Now, the opponent [says]:
Regarding the proponents who maintain that the collections of names, phrases, and phonemes possess a distinct intrinsic nature existing apart from sound itself:
wishing to refute this erroneous view, the author first poses an inquiry.
△ Next, the opponent replies:
Because it is stated in the sūtras; as the sūtras state that the Buddha attained rare and marvelous sets of names, phrases, and phonemes.
Supplement: The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 14, says: "Based on this scriptural evidence, it is known that these exist separately."
The collections of names, phrases, and syllables that can express various meanings are like vocal sounds; they are real and not provisional.
△ Next, the formal refutation of their substantial existence (in two parts): first, a general negation based on scripture.
This sūtra does not state that there are real entities such as names distinct from form, mind, and so forth; thus, the proof [adduced by the opponent] is unestablished.

△ Second, a detailed refutation based on the meaning (divided into two): first, the direct refutation of the two masters; second, the specific refutation of the master of the *Nyāyānusāra* (first, the refutation of the real existence of names, etc., as distinct from sound).
First, the refutation of the real existence of names, etc., as distinct from sound.
If names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*) were substantially existent as entities distinct from sound, they would—like form (*rūpa*) and so forth—not be actual designators.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the Sautrāntikas state that the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables have sound as their substance and are subsumed under the nature of form.
Why is this? Because they are known to exist separately through both scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*). As for scripture:

The sūtras speak of the "body of speech" (*vāk-kāya*) and the "body of phonemes" (*vyañjana-kāya*). If the phoneme were identical to speech, why would they be mentioned separately? Furthermore, it is said that one should uphold the words and phrases of the true Dharma (*saddharma*).
From such scriptural evidence, we know that there exist distinct sets of names (*nāma*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) capable of expressing various meanings.
Just as speech-sound (*ghoṣa*) is real and not merely conventional, the principle is that it is directly perceived. At times one perceives the sound but not the syllable (*akṣara*);
at other times one perceives the syllable but not the sound. Therefore, one knows they are distinct entities. Regarding the case where one perceives the sound but not the syllable:
this refers to when, although one hears the sound, one does not grasp its meaning. It is observed that there are people who hear another’s speech only roughly and yet...

He questioned him again: "What do you mean by saying that this heard sound of speech does not convey the definitive meaning? It is entirely due to a failure to understand the syllables (*vyañjana*) produced.
How can you then maintain that the syllable is no different from the sound? There are times when one perceives the syllable but does not perceive the sound."

This refers to attaining the meaning [of speech] without hearing the sound. It is observed that there are people who, without hearing another's words, perceive what is being said by observing the movement of the lips and so forth.
This attainment of meaning without hearing the sound occurs entirely because one has mastered the phonemes (*vyañjana*) that are produced.
By this reasoning, it is proven that the phoneme must be distinct from the sound and other such factors. As explained at length therein, the author of the present treatise [now states]:

This is a refutation by means of inference (*anumāna*). If names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) were substantially existent (*dravyasat*) as something distinct from sound, then names, phrases, and phonemes would—like color, odor, taste, and so forth—not be actual signifiers (*vācaka*).
This is because there is no actual signifier apart from sound. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

The collection of names, phrases, and phonemes is not an actual signifier, because it is substantially existent as something distinct from sound; therefore, it must be like color and the other [sensory objects].
△ Second, refuting that sound can produce names, phrases, and syllables (2): First, the formal refutation.
That is to say, regarding the claim that sound can produce names, phrases, and syllables (up to): "This [sound] is sufficient for expression; what use are names and so forth?"

*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance). The *Xuantan yingu shu* (Commentary on the Introduction to the Profound Discourse) states: "In the Sarvāstivāda school, although names (*nāman*) and so forth exist, they possess two meanings:
being manifested by sound and being produced. Now, the Master of the Treatise takes up the meaning of 'production' to refute the meaning of 'manifestation,' employing a refutation by analogy.

The *Huixuan*, fascicle twelve, explains: "'By sound, there are the two meanings of manifestation and production' means that they [the Sarvāstivādins] establish that names, phrases, and syllables exist in the future."
Although all [names] within the storehouse consciousness possess an intrinsic nature, they must depend upon causes and conditions to arise.

With the throat, lips, and so forth acting as conditions and sound acting as the cause, names and so forth arise by virtue of these causes and conditions. Now, the Master of the Treatise takes the sense that [names] are produced by sound and refutes it;
he likewise refutes the sense that they are manifested by sound by way of analogy, because in both cases, [the name] would exist separately from the sound.
Since names and so forth possess substantial reality, both are refuted (text). That is to say, regarding the claim that sound can produce names, phrases, and syllables:

having cited this statement, the following refutes it. Since your school maintains that sound can produce names, phrases, and syllables, there must necessarily be vocal modulations and inflections within that sound;
these very vocal modulations and inflections are sufficient to express meaning. Why, then, would one require something else?
Do "names" (*nāman*) and so forth function as signifiers?

Next, the refutation of the defense (in two parts): first, the refutation of the claim that phonetic rhythms are distinct from names and so forth, and that they exist as real entities separate from sound.

If it is argued that the modulations and inflections of phonetic rhythms upon sound [exist as real entities], then they should likewise exist as distinct real entities separate from the locus of form (*rūpa*).

On Sound and Meaning: Previously, it was established that because there are phonetic modulations (*svara-vakratā*) upon sound, the claim that names (*nāman*) and so forth are produced separately [from sound] is refuted;
this has already been conceded by the opponent. Nevertheless, they still maintain that these modulations exist as real entities (*dravya-svabhāva*) distinct from sound itself.
The Master of Right Reasoning (*Nyāyācārya*) offers this defense: "The modulations upon sound constitute names, phrases, and syllables; their essence is indeed distinct from sound."
Yet it is claimed that [shape] exists as a real entity. This is refuted by the following example: the dimensions of form—namely, length, shortness, and so forth—are merely conventionally existent;
they do not possess a distinct substantial reality apart from the location of the color itself. Sound should be understood in the same way.
△ Next, [the author] refutes the claim that phonetic tones are not the expressive agents, and [establishes] that they must give rise to names and so forth.
If it is argued that "phonetic tones are merely the inflections of sound," then who says that these cannot definitively express meaning?
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: First, the opponent’s defense is restated. The Master of Correct Reasoning (Sthiramati) defends [the position] by stating:

"The modulations of sound within a tone—such as those of stringed or wind instruments—are not themselves real signifiers (*vācaka*). Rather, they must necessarily give rise to distinct names (*nāman*) and so forth. He establishes a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:

"Modulations of sound give rise to distinct names and so forth, because they are not signifiers, just like the sounds of stringed or wind instruments. This [argument] must subsequently be refuted by analogy.

He [the opponent] uses the sound of stringed instruments as an analogy for the phonetic modulations of sounds, arguing that these are not capable of signifying meaning and therefore require the separate production of names and so forth.
The Master [Vasubandhu], however, treats these very sounds with their phonetic modulations as being identical to the sounds of stringed instruments.
Names and so forth are not produced separately [from sound]. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows:

These sounds of articulated phonemes do not produce names and so forth separately, because they are not expressive (*vācaka*), like the sound of strings or pipes. *Hui-xuan* says: "Furthermore, who says that those [sounds] are definitely incapable of expression?"
The above refutes the Sautrāntika masters’ terminology. The phrase "if it can express" and what follows also refutes the Sautrāntikas.
Next, the simultaneous refutation of both the Sautrāntikas and the Sāṃmitīyas (2): first, the direct refutation.
If sound can express [meaning], then why do you not admit that the sound of wind-chimes and the like can also express it?
[This is] a response to the objection. Herein, the Sautrāntika school is refuted in conjunction [with others], because they maintain that names (*nāman*) and so forth are nothing other than sound.

The *Xuantan* (Profound Discussion) states that the *Nyāya* (Principles) school refutes those masters (the Sautrāntikas), saying: "You should not establish the existence of the bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*). This is because...

Sound is the substance [of names]. According to the Sautrāntika interpretation as integrated with Mahāyāna, it is also taught that while names and so forth are conventional, sound is substantially real;

thus, it is said that "names are nothing other than sound. Here, we merely refute this claim of identity. That is to say, if you Sautrāntikas maintain that sound is that which expresses meaning, then sounds such as those from wind-chimes should also possess the capacity for expression.
This is because the word "only" (in the phrase "only sound") serves as a negative emphasis to show that sound alone cannot [express meaning].

Commentary: This section should also refute the *Nyāyapraveśa* (The Entrance to Logic). Since the preceding section has already refuted the Sautrāntika position, the intention of the *Nyāyapraveśa* is to argue that, according to their view, sound itself is the expressive agent;
therefore, they raise this objection: "In our school, sounds—such as those from wind-chimes and the like—are not themselves the expressive agents;
thus, names and so forth must arise separately. [The author] refutes this, saying: "Those wind-chime sounds..."
[The opponent claims: "These [factors] such as [the sound of wind-bells] cannot express [meaning], nor do they separately produce names and so forth.

Since this sound is like the sound of wind-bells and the like, it should likewise not separately produce real name-bodies (*nāmakāya*), phrase-bodies (*padakāya*), and syllable-bodies (*vyañjanakāya*). If one attempts to rescue [the position] by means of the following correct reasoning:

"Those sounds of wind-bells and the like may be unable to produce [names], but now it is only vocal sound that can produce names and so forth. [The author] refutes this, saying: "If it is only vocal sound..."
How can you not admit that sound can produce names (*nāman*) and so forth? Why must you insist that only speech (*vāk*) expresses meaning while names and so forth are produced separately?
This is because correct reasoning (*nyāya*) also refutes the Sautrāntika position of identity (*ekatva*).

Here, for the time being, we shall follow the Sautrāntika view of identity to refute the [Vaibhāṣika] position of a separate substantial entity (*dravya-vyatirikta*). Yet, even identity has never been accepted [by us]. As the *Huìxuán* says: "To clarify..."
He does not immediately refute the Sautrāntika school by clarifying that [the two] are not distinct; rather, he refutes the Nyāya (Siddhānta) school [by clarifying they are not identical].
Since the Mahāyāna possesses both meanings—neither identity nor distinction—he refutes both schools simultaneously.
△ Next, the refutation and conclusion.
By what reasoning is it definitively known that the signifier (*vācaka*) is identical to speech? How can it be known that there exists a signifier distinct from speech?

[Commentary on the meaning of the verses: The first phrase refutes the Sautrāntika school; the second phrase refutes the Nyāya school. Having finished the refutation, the ancient sub-commentary concludes by stating:

Therefore, one should know that there is only the sound of preceding words resulting from beginningless habitual practice; through the power of its specific state (*avasthā*), when a subsequent understanding arises, one says "one hears a name" and so forth.
In reality, the ear and other faculties merely apprehend the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the sound, which perishes in an instant.

It is within this process that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) performs its final interpretive determination, which is designated as a "name" and so forth; these do not exist as separate, substantial entities. This is [the case].
Therefore, you should know that speech is distinct from that which expresses it. Next, the conclusion regarding the distinction between the ignorant and the wise:

while humans and devas alike understand that speech is not different from that which expresses it, only the Devapriya (the "Heaven-Lover") clings to the notion that the expresser is distinct from speech, and no one else does.
*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance), *Huixuan* (Assembling the Profundities), states: "Speech is that which expresses. Whether humans or devas, all alike understand it;
(for both the Sautrāntika and Mahāyāna schools can understand this) they all know that sound is that which expresses.

To stubbornly maintain that the substance of the name is distinct from speech is a view held only by you, O Devapriya (the Master of Nyāya); no other wise person holds such a view. He is called 'Devapriya' because he is foolish."
This fool has nothing worthy of record; he exists only because he is beloved by the gods (*devānāmpriya*). As it is said: "The gods take pity on you," thus he is named Devānāmpriya.
According to another version of the text, *devānuśasta* means that he has received and accepted their teachings.
The *Śūyao* (Essential Pivot) states: "Among those superior in the world, none surpass the gods; among those inferior in the world, none surpass the fool. Thus, he is called a fool.
This is because it was uttered as a jest by the gods.
△ Second, the presentation of the correct meaning (in four parts): First, revealing the distinctions of the conventional.
Now, based on the distinctions in the temporal states of vocal sounds, the collections of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*) are conventionally established.

Regarding the phonology and meaning: following the ancient commentaries, one might raise an external objection, asking: "If the substance of sound (*śabda*) is itself that which expresses (*vācaka*), how can there be a distinction between the three types, such as 'name' (*nāman*) and so forth?
The answer states: "Nevertheless, based on the distinctions in the temporal states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of vocal sound..."
In this treatise, the author establishes the sets of names (nāma-kāya), phrases (pada-kāya), and phonemes (vyañjana-kāya) based on sound.

For example, when the two syllables *cakṣu* are pronounced separately as in the Sanskrit word *cakṣu*, they do not yet denote anything and are thus called the state of phonemes (*vyañjana-vyavasthāna*).

When these two syllables are joined together, they express the essence of the eye and are called the state of names (*nāma-vyavasthāna*). However, at this point, there is no state of phrases (*pada-vyavasthāna*) yet; therefore, the word *asatīva* is added, which constitutes the phrase.
Because that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) regarding the eye is designated as a "phrase-position" (*pada-pada*), names and so forth are established based on these states (*avasthā*).
Next, the distinct functions of the three are revealed:
names (*nāman*) express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), phrases (*pada*) express distinctions (*viśeṣa*), and syllables (*vyañjana*) are the basis for both.
Supplement: The *Bishuōjì* (Record of Revision) states: That which expresses the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is the "name" (*nāman*).

The name is that which expresses; the intrinsic nature is that which is expressed. For example, when one speaks of "form" (*rūpa*), "mind" (*citta*), "water," or "fire," each respectively expresses and represents the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon.
That which expresses the distinctions among phenomena is the "phrase" (*pada*). The phrase is that which expresses all phenomena.

The "differentiated" (*viśeṣa*) is that which is expressed. For example, as with the terms "shape-color" (*saṃsthāna-varṇa*) and "manifest-color" (*varṇa-varṇa*), or "true mind" (*tattva-citta*) and "deluded mind" (*bhrānti-citta*), it is the same for all phenomena.
This is because within each individual phenomenon, one selects and distinguishes them as distinct. Second, the "basis" (*āśraya*) refers to the "text" (*vyañjana*).

These two—name (*nāman*) and phrase (*pada*)—are themselves the "syllables" (*akṣara*). Since these serve as the common support for both of those two factors, by means of this, the name follows in sequence.
First, the sequence of rows; second, the sequential arrangement of phrases; third, the sequential conjunction of words.
△ Third, the explanation of neither identity nor difference:
Although these three do not have a separate substance apart from sound, they differ in terms of the conventional and the real, and thus they are also not identical to sound.
Commentary on Terms: The Master of the Treatise answers the objection. It is said that previously there was a question:

"Although it has been stated above that names and so forth are identical to sound, if names and so forth are non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), they are merely curvatures within form; they are not the sound itself, which is a non-associated formation.

Why is this so? In response, he says: "These three—name, phrase, and syllable—are distinct from sound; although they have no separate substance apart from name and so forth [as mental factors], [they are established as such]."

These [names, etc. are conventional sounds; these are substantially existent. Because the conventional and the substantial are distinct, it is said that names and so forth are not included within the category of sound.
They are merely differentiated sounds; they are designated as "names" and so forth by way of convention because they express meaning.
Since they are dissociated [from mind] and do not arise from a separate seed, it is said that they are simply sound.
△ 4. Reconciling the Contradictions (2): First, the actual reconciliation of the contradictions.
By means of these two analytical knowledges—dharma and nirukti—the inclusion within the aggregates, bases, and elements also differs for each.

Supplement: The seventh fascicle of the *Xuántán* states: An outsider asks, "If names and so forth are identical to sound, what is the distinction between the objects of the two unimpeded understandings of phenomena (*dharma*) and expression (*nirukti*)?
(The *Huìxuán* commentary notes: The outsider's question reveals a contradiction. The thought of the Hīnayāna is this:

If, apart from sound, there were names and so forth that were substantially real, then the two objects could be distinguished. Now, since names and so forth are identical to sound, how can the two objects be distinct? Therefore, he provides this reconciliation. He answers: "Precisely because they take this [sound] as their object, the two..."

The objects differ. The analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) takes conventional designations (*prajñapti*) and so forth as its object (the *Xiaochao* states: "Phenomena" refers to all dharmas; for example, when one speaks of earth, water, fire, and wind, these names are themselves phenomena.
Ancient sages provisionally established names to designate these various dharmas; therefore, the object of the analytical knowledge of phenomena consists of conventional designations and the like).

The analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) takes actual sounds and so forth as its object (this means that one uses verbal expressions to speak of "earth" and other such terms. A king uses such words to distinguish and adorn things; names and their meanings enable people to understand. These sounds of language are real dharmas; therefore, the analytical knowledge of language takes them as its object).
Therefore, it is said that the distinction between the object [name] and the sound is not [real]. Both take the real as their object.

Although the two intrinsic natures—namely, the name and so forth, and the sound—are dharmas that are mutually inseparable, one speaks only of "names" (nāman) because they are directed toward the signified meaning (*abhidheya*); one speaks only of "sound" (*śabda*) because it is mostly directed toward the sensory faculty.

Once the ear has heard the sound, the mind cognizes the meaning. Thus, while the two are said to be different because their respective objects differ, there is no difference in their essential substance (*svabhāva*).

They are distinct. Furthermore, these two objects, as well as names and so forth—the three being distinct from sound—are also different in terms of their inclusion within the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

Specifically, they correspond respectively to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); the base of sound (*śabdāyatana*) and the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*); and the element of sound (*śabdadhātu*) and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

The inclusion of sounds, names, and so forth (the aggregate of form, the sphere of sound, and the element of sound belong exclusively to the aggregate of formations; the sphere of phenomena and the element of phenomena belong to names, phrases, and syllables).

△ Next, following the tracks to resolve contradictions (as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*: "A footprint (*pada*) is a track; just as one seeks an elephant by following its tracks, so too should the term 'track' be understood in its literal sense. Thus, one seeks the meaning through these [tracks].

That is to say, there may be certain Buddha-lands where the Dharma is manifested by a glance, or by raising an eyebrow, and even up to showing a slight smile, and so forth. By means of such things, the Dharma is revealed;

thus, while the capacities that manifest it—such as glancing or raising an eyebrow—differ, the meaning revealed is identical in its fundamental nature. This is fully detailed in the *Xuantan* (Prolegomena) as cited in the *Buyi* (Supplement) below)."
Furthermore, based on this land, names, phrases, and syllables (nāma-pada-vyañjana) are established as three [categories] for things such as subtle odors and tastes.
Regarding the meaning of "sound": a question is asked: "If the bending and curving [of expression] occurs upon sound, then the designation 'speech' would be inconsistent; if it occurs upon form..."
[Objection: It should follow that the *vijñapti* (informative action) is not subsumed under the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*). [Response:

Because there is no *avijñapti* (non-informative action) upon form, it is subsumed under the sense-base of form, whereas upon sound there are names and so forth that are dissociated [from mind] which constitute the teaching. [Question: Since there is curvature (articulation) upon sound, it constitutes the teaching;
since there is also curvature upon form, it too should be able to constitute the teaching. [Treatise says: "For now, regarding this land... and so forth, as cited.

This refers to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. As for the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes contact (*sparśa*), volition (*cetanā*), enumeration (*saṃkhyā*), and so on. Above, [it was stated that] light is form, fragrance, taste, and touch;

here, by mentioning "name" (*nāman*) and "volition" (*cetanā*)—the latter being the mental object (*dharmāyatana*)—it is shown that the remaining five sense objects can all serve as bases for the establishment of teachings. All of these can be provisionally established as the three categories of name and so forth, and they are also categorized as dissociated (*viprayukta*).
Because they are provisional designations made in response to the capacities and desires of sentient beings, they are termed "provisional."
Supplement: The *Xuántán* (Profound Discourse) states: "If one can manifest the principles and meanings, then all dharmas constitute the substance of the teaching (*jiaoti*).
Since sound can manifest meaning, sound is called 'teaching. Furthermore, since the six sense objects (*ṣaḍāyatana*) manifest meaning, the six sense objects are all teaching.
Moreover, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Mahāmati, as you have said, because there are verbal expressions, there are all dharmas; this treatise..."
It is not the case that all buddha-fields lack verbal expression. What is called "verbal expression" is merely a conventional designation.

There are some buddha-fields where the Dharma is revealed by a glance; or by raising an eyebrow, or by moving the pupils of the eyes, or by showing a smile, or by a frown, a sigh, a cough, a mindful recollection, or a physical movement.
It is through such means as these that the Dharma is revealed, as in the world of the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha).
By partaking of fragrant food, one manifests samādhi; in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, through listening to the wind in the trees, right mindfulness is perfected.
The lute and flute can transmit the mind; through "meeting the eye" (direct perception), one preserves the Way. Therefore, it is not that all phenomena exist solely by virtue of verbal expression.
△ Third, the collateral refutation of the attachment to latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), etc. (2): First, the direct refutation (2): First, stating the attachment.

There are those who maintain that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are distinct from the mind and mental factors, and are subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from the mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).

Regarding the meaning of this term, the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra* states: "The Mahīśāsaka school asserts that the latent dispositions are neither mind nor mental factors, and they lack an object of perception (*ālambana*).
They are distinct from the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*; 'active' because the afflictions manifest, thus termed 'active outbursts'). The *Yogācārabhūmi* states that all afflictions possess..."

[The opponent argues: "Because all that manifests are called 'envelopments' (paryavasthāna), the nature of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) is dissociated from the mind, whereas the nature of manifest envelopments is associated with the mind;
this is precisely our position."

Supplement: "Anu" (anu-) has the meaning of "co-arising. "Śaya" (śaya) has the meaning of "seed," referring to the seeds of afflictions that lie dormant within sentient beings, hidden within the *ālayavijñāna*.
Because they either persist or increase in their faults, they are called "proclivities" (*anuśaya*).

These are precisely the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness, which is itself maintained by the eighth consciousness; however, other vehicles consider them not to be associated with the six manifest [consciousnesses].
Because they are associated with consciousness (*vijñāna-saṃprayukta*), they are also grasped as being included among the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Next, this is refuted:
that too is unreasonable, because they are designated as "greed" and so forth; just as manifest greed and the like are not dissociated, so it is here.

Supplement: Because the seeds of greed and so forth are designated by the same names as greed and so forth, they must necessarily be associated with a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*), just like the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of greed and so forth.
How, then, could they be called non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*)? The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 89, states:
"The heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the category of afflictions that adheres to the physical basis is called 'latent tendency' (*anuśaya*); it is capable of..."
Because the seeds give rise to all the entanglements of the afflictions (*kleśa-paryavasthāna*), it should be known that these are further established as sevenfold.
Based on the distinction of the category of those who have not yet abandoned desire, the latent tendencies of attachment (*rāga-anuśaya*) and aversion (*pratigha-anuśaya*) are established.

Based on the distinction of the category of those who have already abandoned desire, the latent tendency of attachment to existence (*bhavarāga-anuśaya*) is established. Based on the distinction of both categories, pride (*māna*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are established.

The latent tendencies of view and doubt are thus collectively subsumed within all afflictions (as the text states). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The subject (*dharmin*) is the grasped latent tendencies;

the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they are not non-associated [with the mind]; the reason (*hetu*) is "because they are named greed and so forth"; the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "like manifest greed and so forth."
△ Next, the remaining [categories] are illustrated by example.
The adherence to the existence of other distinct non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) should all be refuted according to the same principle as before. Supplement:

Illustrating the refutation of the remaining ten types—namely, *pravṛtti* (evolution), *niyama* (determination), *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity), *jāti* (birth), *jarā* (aging), *sthiti* (duration), *anityatā* (impermanence), *nāmakāya* (sets of names), *padakāya* (sets of phrases), and *vyañjanakāya* (sets of phonemes)—as well as *āśu* (velocity) and *anukrama* (sequence).
Regarding the categories of time, direction, number, and the natures of conjunction and non-conjunction (the meaning of which is explained as in the *Kaimeng*),

one should follow the same logical principles used to refute the fourteen dharmas mentioned previously to negate the existence of a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in things distinct from form, mind, and so forth.
This concludes the refutation of the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
△ III. Refuting the Non-conditioned Dharmas (2) A. First, the direct refutation of their substantial existence (2) 1. First, a general negation based on reasoning:
It is logically untenable that non-conditioned dharmas exist as determinate, substantial entities apart from form, mind, and so forth.

"Harmonizing Resonance": Regarding all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), namely the three types—space (*ākāśa*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—other vehicles maintain that these possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) independent of matter, mind, and so forth.
Now, the Master of the Treatise refutes this entirely based on reason.
△ Second, the specific refutation based on meaning (in two parts): First, the formal refutation (in two parts). First, the general refutation by analogy with conditioned phenomena (in two parts).
First, the refutation by analogy that unconditioned phenomena do not definitely exist apart from form, mind, and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the established existence of phenomena, there are briefly three types [up to] the point where one cannot maintain that unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena definitely exist.
[This is] the "Resonance" (*saṃghoṣa*). In order to refute unconditioned phenomena, it first cites conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena as a supporting example.

The *Zhengjīng* (Mirror of Correctness), fascicle 58, explains: "As with form, mind, and so forth" refers to the objects of the five groups of consciousness and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). [It means] knowing others...

"Mental phenomena" (citta-dharma) refers to the knowledge of others' minds. This refers to the five sense objects such as form (*rūpa*), as well as the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). This is stated in terms of their collective aggregation rather than their individual distinctions.
As for the question of whether these are objects known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by which consciousness: they are not objects known [by that consciousness].

Just like jars, clothes, and so forth, although these are currently seen and utilized, they are not objects of direct perception because they are conventional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*); they exist merely as present entities.

Regarding the objects of enjoyment: if one asks, "In this context, under which type of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the mind that takes jars, clothing, and so forth as its object subsumed? The answer is:

it is not subsumed under valid cognition. Because it does not directly apprehend the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena, and because it is not an inference (*anumāna*), it is subsumed under non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).

As for the five material sense faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*), such as the eye and ear, they are not obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor are they known by ordinary people in the present world.
Regarding the statement, "There exist these [faculties] such as the eye and ear," each is inferred to exist by means of its respective function of producing consciousness;

this is the "reasoning of proof" (*upapatti-sādhana-yukti*). Because one infers the existence of a cause based on the perception of an effect, the "effect" refers to the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that have been produced.

By means of inference (*anumāna*), one knows that the various pure material faculties (*rūpa-indriya*) exist. This is not known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or through the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

The object of the eighth consciousness in the Mahāyāna is also apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). With the exception of the Buddha, it is universally accepted as being established by treatises rather than being commonly known to the world;
therefore, it is said that its existence is known through inference (*anumāna*). The following section on unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) provides a formal analogy that makes this clear.
△ Next, a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is established to demonstrate that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the true nature of form and mind.
However, because all unconditioned phenomena are of the nature of objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), they lack any real unconditioned nature apart from form, mind, and so forth.

**Commentary on the Meaning of Terms:** The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the object known by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). It is also the nature manifested by the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividhaśūnyatā*) regarding matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

Therefore, it should be understood as the true nature (*dharmatā*) of matter and mind. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Thesis (*pakṣa*): All unconditioned phenomena are existent things (*dharmin*). Reason (*hetu*):

Because they are of the nature of being objects of knowledge (*jñeyatva*), or because they are the nature manifested by matter, mind, and so forth. (Note: "Should not" in the original refers to the fact that the reason does not fall below the level of the thesis; here, it indicates that the reason is established as being coextensive with the subject.)
It is analogous to form, mind, and so forth.
△ Next, the specific refutation based on the distinction between the one and the many (2): First, the general inquiry.
Furthermore, space and so forth are one, yet they are many.
△ Second, the detailed explanation (in two parts): First, refuting that [space] is a single substance (in two parts). First, refuting space:
If its substance were one and pervasive of all places, then where there is [an object], it should intermingle with it; where there is no [object], it should not be pervasive.

*He-xiang* (Harmonizing Resonance): The first phrase restates the thesis being critiqued. The section beginning with "pervading all" refutes the oneness of the essence by means of its pervasive containment.

This means that if the essence of space were one, and since that essence of space pervades all locations and is capable of containing phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), then the space that is contained should, following the various phenomena that contain it, become multiple in essence. Why?
Therefore, at the place where one [substance] is conjoined, others are not conjoined.

For example, when a square vessel is conjoined with space, other circular vessels and the like cannot occupy the space within this square vessel; thus, each of those other circular vessels and so forth has its own space with which it is conjoined.
How then could they not be multiple? If it were otherwise—that is, if one were to claim that while one is conjoined, the others are not—then these various phenomena [would be contradictory].
They should mutually pervade one another, just as space pervades square vessels; it should likewise pervade all other circular and such vessels.

The same principle applies to the pervasion of square vessels within circular ones and so forth. Since it is stated that they are "not one," it follows logically that what is conjoined with one would not be conjoined with others.
This is how the reasoning must proceed. If you argue that space does not conjoin with phenomena, then it should not be capable of containing them.

Regarding "sensation" (*vedanā*): like cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and so forth, it is not even space; how then can one speak of its essence being unitary? The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

Space should not be that which contains, because it does not conjoin with phenomena, just like other unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Furthermore, below the section on "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth, the critique proceeds by interrogating the two meanings of existence and non-existence.
If one asserts existence, then form and space would be mixed and intermingled; if one asserts non-existence, then form and space would be separated.
It is not pervasive. How then can their essence be one?
Next, the other two [positions] are refuted:
when the dharma of a single section and a single chapter is being severed, [the opponent argues that] it is logically necessary for their essence to be one.

Explanation of Terms: "Section" (*bhāga*) refers to a division, such as the section of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) or the section of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhāga*). "Category" (*prakāra*) refers to a type, such as superior, middling, or inferior.
Because one eliminates the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) through the discernment of wisdom, it is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

If one were to maintain that because its substance is unitary, one would obtain [the cessation] of all sections and all categories simultaneously, then upon attaining the cessation of one section or one category, one should necessarily attain the cessation of all other sections and all other categories; for the cessation through discernment does not depend on individual discernment.

Cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is that which is manifested by the absence of conditions. If one maintains that its essence is a single entity, then at the time when a single phenomenon is obtained as non-arising due to the absence of conditions, it would follow that one obtains cessation not through deliberation with respect to all phenomena.
△ Next, the refutation of the multiplicity of its essence.

If its essence were multiple, there would be various categories [extending to] unconditioned space (*asaṃskṛta-ākāśa*), and it would further follow that it must be multiple and all-pervasive in order to accommodate and contain [all things].
(Commentary on the Meaning) The first section provides a general refutation of the three types [of space]; from "unconditioned space" onwards, there is a specific refutation of unconditioned space.
△ Next, the analogy for the remaining [two]. First, refuting by analogy with the preceding case:

the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) entities, asserted as substantially existent and separate from mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) by other schools, should be refuted in accordance with the previous example.
*Hexiang* (Harmony of Resonance). *Huayan Chao*, Volume 21-1, states:
"As for the fact that the Hīnayāna mostly speaks of three [unconditioned phenomena], this refers to what the *Abhidharmakośa* and other treatises say:

'The untainted refers to the Truth of the Path and the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena—namely, space and the two types of cessation' (the latter being those previously refuted). As for saying 'mostly,' the *Vibhajyavādins* maintain there are four: first, space; second, non-"

1. Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); 2. Cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*); 3. True Suchness (*tathatā*). The Mahāsāṃghika school asserts nine unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), namely these three plus four:
the nature of the links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-aṅga-svabhāva*) and the nature of the links of the Noble Path (*āryamārgāṅga-svabhāva*). The Mahīśāsaka school also asserts nine;
in addition to the aforementioned three, they add the immovable (*āniñjya*) and the three natures of the path links and the links of dependent origination (which are precisely what is refuted here).
△ Next, this proof is established by means of refutation.
Furthermore, since all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are admitted to lack cause and effect, they should not exist as something distinct from mind and so forth, just like a rabbit’s horn.
△ Next, the correct meaning is revealed (in three parts): first, the general statement.
However, the sūtras state that there are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), such as space and so forth, which are briefly of two kinds.
Supplement: The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "That which is without arising or cessation and is not bound to causes and conditions is called unconditioned.

The tenth fascicle of the *Huìxuán* states: "Briefly, there are four explanations: first, 'neither arising nor ceasing,' because it distinguishes [the unconditioned] from the four marks [of conditioned existence]; second..."
There is no going and no coming, because it does not belong to the three periods of time. Third, there is neither "that" nor "this," because it is entirely free from self and other.

Fourth, there is no gain and no loss, because it neither increases nor decreases; this reveals its unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta*). Because it is devoid of these four kinds of activity and lacks any fabrication, it is called "unconditioned.
Alternatively, it is called "unconditioned" by way of distinguishing it from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
△ Second, the detailed explanation (in two parts). First, [the explanation of] that which is provisionally established based on the transformation of consciousness.
1. That which is provisionally established based on the transformation of consciousness... up to: that which is provisionally described as permanent because it is without change.
*He-xiang* (Harmonious Resonance), the first heading. This refers to what was previously explained.

Regarding the phrase "having heard it said, etc.," this means that at the time of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one hears the names of the six kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), such as space (*ākāśa*). Following what was heard, one discriminates the characteristics of space and so forth.

From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) up until the stage prior to the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), by the power of repeatedly perfuming with a contaminated mind (*sāsrava-citta*), [the seeds of these characteristics are established].
Therefore, when the mind and its associates arise, they manifest as resembling the characteristics of unconditioned phenomena such as space;

or, because Bodhisattvas on the stages, having realized True Suchness through fundamental wisdom, subsequently manifest appearances resembling space and so forth through their subsequently attained wisdom.

Whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), all depend upon the transformation of consciousness. This explanation provided below [regarding space] is that it is a provisional existence (*prajñaptisat*).

The fifty-eighth fascicle of the *Zongjing* states: "This has no objective essence; it is merely what is transformed by the mind. Like atoms and so forth, it transforms to resemble the appearance of space and other such forms.

As for the manifestation of its substance, in the Mahāyāna, one speaks provisionally of the existence of empty space solely in reference to the appearance-part (*nimittabhāga*) transformed by the mind."

Therefore, it is not that there is emptiness apart from the mind. Question: If one says that the transformation of consciousness produces the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), and yet calls this "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*), then since it is a characteristic that follows along with consciousness, how can it be established as unconditioned? Answer: This is said to be the transformation of consciousness;
it is conventionally designated as unconditioned, but in reality it is not unconditioned. The unconditioned is an eternally abiding dharma.
Therefore, that which now relies on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nature takes as its essence only the "solitary-image" (*kevala-pratibimba*) aspect that accords with consciousness.
This is because it is similar before and after, without change, and possesses only a single category of characteristics such as space.

It is conventionally designated as "unconditioned," yet these six unconditioned states are, for Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), transformations of consciousness that are still contaminated (*sāsrava*). If [this occurs] after the stages...
The attainment of wisdom-transformation is itself untainted (*anāsrava*).
△ Next, the provisional establishment based on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): (1) first, indicating the name of the nature of phenomena;
(2) the provisional establishment based on the nature of phenomena [up to]: it is called the "nature of phenomena" because it is the true principle of all phenomena.

**Explanatory Notes on Terms** *First, the heading; "that which is empty" below is the explanation.* Regarding "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*): "Dharma" refers to various phenomena such as form and mind.
"Nature" refers to the essential substance upon which those dharmas depend—namely, the *tathatā* (suchness) revealed by the two kinds of emptiness.
It is far removed from attachments to existence and non-existence, identity and difference, and so forth. As it is the true principle of all dharmas, it is called "dharma-nature."
△ Next, the essence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is presented.
Because it is free from all obstructions, it is called "space" (*ākāśa*), [and so on], up to: there is a real, eternal dharma called "Suchness" (*tathatā*).
*Commentary on Terms and Meanings:* 1. **Unconditioned Space:** That which is manifested by being free from the obstructions of all dharmas of form and mind.

1. Truth (*tattva*). 2. The unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskṛta*). This is the truth manifested by the arising of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) which effects the cessation of all obstructive defilements through discernment.
3. The unconditioned state of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskṛta*).

This refers to those phenomena that, by their very nature, are pure even without the power of deliberation—that is, self-nature purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*). Alternatively, it refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that do not arise due to the absence of conditions.
The state of non-arising that is fully attained is the principle of purity; manifesting these two meanings is termed the unconditioned of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskrta*).

Fourth is the unconditioned of the immovables (*āniñjya-asamskrta*): the fourth dhyāna, which is free from the three calamities, the eight difficulties, [the four feelings of] sorrow, suffering, joy, and pleasure, as well as vitarka, vicāra, out-breathing, and in-breathing.
The truth revealed by the sudden relinquishing of suffering and pleasure is the unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*) of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).
From the fourth dhyāna upward, up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), neither the sensation of equanimity nor coarse perception functions; thus, the realization of truth is attained.
These five lower [categories] define the essence, namely the five kinds of unconditioned phenomena, all of which are *tathatā* (suchness); suchness is their very essence.
There is nothing else external to this; it consists of six kinds of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena. Each of these relies upon the actual qualities of true suchness (*tathatā*).
As clarified below regarding true suchness as an unconditioned phenomenon, these five unconditioned phenomena are provisionally established as space and so forth upon the basis of true suchness.
However, because the essence of true suchness is neither "like" nor "unlike," even the name "true suchness" is a provisional designation. It is, for example, like [the following]:
The "insect" is named "oil-eater" (*taila-bhakṣaka*). It is a provisional name for "oil-eater" because it does not denote its actual substance. True Suchness (*tathatā*) is likewise.
This negates the denial [of Suchness] by explaining the name according to its meaning. Qingliang says: "True Suchness is also a provisional designation because its substance cannot be apprehended.

This is said to negate those with the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*), while asserting that Suchness exists as a negation. Among the Hīnayāna schools, such as the Mahīśāsakas, they cling to it as being determinately and substantially existent.

Therefore, it is said to be "empty" (meaning that one's emotional attachments are emptied). This does not mean that the unconditioned essence itself is empty (the essence of True Suchness is not empty). Do not say it is "illusory.

"Illusory" excludes the *parikalpita* (imagined nature), while "illusory" [in this context] selects the *paratantra* (dependent nature); this directly reveals True Suchness, which is the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature).
It is called *tathatā* (Suchness) because it is a dharma that is without falsehood or inversion. The phrase "not as in the lower [teachings]" concludes the distinction from other schools.

Regarding the phrase "not by the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) and so forth," the *Huayan jing shuchao* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) explains: "The treatise maintains two meanings. The first meaning distinguishes it from the Small Vehicle regarding the deficiency of conditions.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Ultimately, there is an obstruction to what is to arise; this is a specific attainment not resulting from discernment (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
"Cessation. Regarding "that which is to arise": it refers to dharmas that are destined to arise in the future. When conditions assemble, they arise; when conditions are lacking, they do not arise.

At the time when they do not arise, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This non-analytical cessation obstructs dharmas that are to arise, causing them never to arise again;

this is called "ultimate" (*atyanta*). As for "obstructing a separate acquisition," this refers to non-analytical cessation having a real substantial nature (*dravya-svabhāva*), which arises as a distinct entity during the state in which conditions are lacking.

Because it is attained. Non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is not attained through analytical cessation; rather, it is named non-analytical cessation because it arises solely from the absence of conditions.

The treatise clarifies this by citing a specific instance: "For example, when the eye and the mind are focused exclusively on one form, other forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles [are subject to non-analytical cessation]."
The five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) and so forth, which depend on those objects, abide in the future and never arise at all.

Because they cannot take past objects as their domain—since the conditions for such perception are incomplete—they attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Regarding "contact" (*sparśa*) and so forth:

the term "and so forth" includes those factors within the mental phenomena (*dharma*) that exist simultaneously with their corresponding cognitive subjects (*ālambaka*) and serve as their objective domains (*ālambana*), such as the object of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
This refers to the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).
△ Third, the conclusion and demonstration:
Therefore, the various unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not definitively real entities.

△ Second, establishing the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to reveal that there is only consciousness (2): First, it is shown that the dual grasping is the aspect of the object (*nimittabhāga*) and the aspect of the subject (*darśanabhāga*).

[The various phenomena] grasped by non-Buddhists and those of other vehicles [are only consciousness], because they are capable of being the grasper, just like the cognition that takes this [consciousness] as its object.
*He-xiang* (Harmonizing Resonance): The preceding text has completed the refutation of the "real self" (*ātman*) as clung to by non-Buddhists and followers of other vehicles.
