The meaning is the same; therefore, there is no contradiction.
△ Next, regarding the explanation based on the direct cultivation of the Mahāyāna:
furthermore, from the stage of the Immovable (Acalā-bhūmi) upward, this [text] also refers to those Bodhisattvas by the name of Arhat.

Commentary on Terms: From the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*) upward—that is, the Bodhisattvas of the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages—all afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

As for the statement that "co-nascent obstructions (*sahaja-āvaraṇa*) never again function," this is because they have already permanently distanced themselves from all manifest entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).

Regarding the phrase "the swift flow of the Dharma": it refers to the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). Sentient beings, adrift and submerged by the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*), undergo the death of transformation (*pariṇāmiki-cyuti*).
Like a torrential stream that flows spontaneously, because one attains mastery over its swift current;
because one can initiate all practices within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), such as initiating all the perfections (*pāramitā*) within the single practice of giving;
and because one advances further at every moment, flowing moment by moment into the ocean of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). By these meanings, it is proven.
Attaining stages such as the Immovable (Acalā) is called "non-retrogression.

Below this, [the text] explains the abandonment of the name "ālaya," along with self-view, self-love, and so forth—namely, the four afflictions associated with the manas, which are innate self-clinging—from the eighth stage upward.
The fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons arises and manifests in a continuous succession; no longer conceiving it as a self, the name *ālayavijñāna* is relinquished.
Therefore, within this verse, he is also called an *arhat*.
△ Second, refuting divergent interpretations (2): First, the formal refutation (2). First, the introduction:
There is an interpretation stating that bodhisattvas from the first bhūmi upward... [up to] ...are therefore also called *arhats*.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: Does this master’s intention clarify that it is not only those from the eighth bhūmi and above who are called "non-retrogressive"? Bodhisattvas from the seventh bhūmi and below are also called non-retrogressive.

This is because they have already realized the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the two-fold emptiness of birth and phenomena; they have already attained the two-fold wisdom regarding birth and phenomena;

and they have already severed the two obstacles of afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) and the known (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) which are characterized by conceptual discrimination. Consequently, whether they practice any one of the various modes of conduct...
Adornment. Although they manifest both acquired and innate afflictions for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they ultimately do not incur any fault.
Because these various meanings exist, the first stage (*bhūmi*) and those above it are also called "non-retrogressive. Below this, the text explains the abandonment of the name *ālayavijñāna*.

This refers to the first stage (*bhūmi*) and those above it. Although the innate afflictive obscurations (*sahaja-kleśāvaraṇa*) have not yet been completely severed, this consciousness no longer conceives of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-love (*ātma-sneha*), and so forth, nor does it again grasp [the ālayavijñāna] as its own internal self (*adhyātman*).

For this reason, it also abandons the name "ālaya" (storehouse), and that state is also called "Arhat. Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* cites scriptural evidence below regarding the fault of not giving rise to afflictions (*kleśa*). Afflictions...
Just as there are various poisons, right knowledge is like a medicinal incantation. Although afflictions may arise, because they are subdued by right knowledge, they do not constitute a fault.
Although they have been suppressed but not yet severed, they are as if already severed; such a person is also called an Arhat.
△ Next, the refutation:
That [position] is irrational; from the seventh stage downward (until it is admitted), it contradicts what is taught in the various treatises.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: this refers to the seventh stage and below, wherein the innate self-grasping (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) within the seventh consciousness has not yet been permanently eliminated.

Because it has been severed, one should not abandon the designation "ālaya. If one were to object by providing a lower-level example—that if one claims that merely severing conceptualized views of self, craving, and so forth constitutes abandoning the ālaya, then those such as the *srotāpanna* (stream-enterers) should also be said to have abandoned it—then we grant that [they have indeed abandoned it].
This would contradict what is taught in the various treatises, for among those treatises, one never finds it stated that the *srotāpanna* and others abandon the *ālayavijñāna*.
△ Next, the refutation of the defense (in two parts): first, the statement of the opponent's position.
Regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*) arising in Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*): how could one possibly use them as an analogy for this [case of the stream-enterer]?
Regarding the phonology and meaning, Jiu says: "Bodhisattvas on the stages manifest the arising of afflictions for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;
because they possess correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), it does not constitute a fault. The stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) is not like this; how could they be considered equivalent?"
△ Next, the refutation:
"The afflictions arising within those six consciousnesses... (up to) "...therefore it is known that their explanation is irrational. [Commentary on the Meaning of the Words]:
This refers to innate (*sahaja*) afflictions, which pervade the first seven consciousnesses. Within the first six consciousnesses, there are both intermittent (*vyavakīrṇa*) and innate [afflictions].

The arising [of the seeds] may be explained as stated above. However, within the seventh consciousness, during states of contaminated mind, it spontaneously and simultaneously clings to and stores [the seeds].

How could this not be the same as that? Regarding "contaminated states," this refers to those Bodhisattvas who, at the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), have already forever and completely abandoned the two obstacles of conceptual discrimination (*parikalpita-āvaraṇa*), yet have not yet subdued or eliminated the two obstacles of innate nature (*sahaja-āvaraṇa*). Therefore, in these [states],...

On the stages of realization (*bhūmi*), the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) states arise alternately. During the state of a non-outflowing mind, the seventh consciousness does not again grasp and store [the ālayavijñāna] through self-view, self-love, and so forth;
yet, because it continues to function spontaneously and constantly even when emerging from the non-outflowing state, it has not yet abandoned its status as the "storehouse" (*ālaya*).
This concludes the refutation below.
△ Next, [the text] distinguishes that what is abandoned is merely a designation.
However, when an Arhat cuts off this consciousness... (until) at that time he enters nirvana without remainder.
Supplement: The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source), fascicle 50, states: From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, there is no longer the designation "ālayavijñāna";

there is only the "vipākavijñāna" (retribution-consciousness). Furthermore, the seventh consciousness constantly grasps the vipākavijñāna as its object. Moreover, the eighth consciousness originally lacked the name "ālaya";
it was due to the seventh consciousness grasping the views of the eighth that it was divided into a self, thereby causing the eighth to acquire [that name].
If the name *ālaya* is not grasped, it is merely called the *vipākavijñāna*. Therefore, an Arhat only relinquishes the name *ālaya*, but does not relinquish [the consciousness] itself.
This is because the substance of the eighth consciousness, as that *vipāka*, has not yet been emptied;

it still maintains the innate factors (*sahaja-dharma*) and clings to seeds. Since there are many names for the eighth [consciousness], it is said that "all" [is relinquished] when the consciousness is relinquished.
[Objection: All Arhats, upon realizing the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), should immediately enter nirvana without remainder.
Why? Because there would be no maturation-result (vipāka) for the consciousness-substance that maintains the seeds; the wisdom of the final body would have nothing capable of sustaining it.
This implies, conversely, that as long as the seeds of maturation have not been completely severed, one cannot discard the maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna). Therefore, he says "do not."
△ Second, a general clarification of the eighth [chapter]’s alternative names (2): First, an extensive explanation of the various names (2): First, an explanation of the meaning of the names (2):
First, the general heading.
Although the eighth consciousness is possessed by all sentient beings, it is established under various names according to its specific functions.
Regarding these names and meanings: the "eighth consciousness" is so called because it pervades all stages, whether noble or ordinary;

thus, while it is possessed by all—be they ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), those in training (*śaikṣa*), or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—seven distinct names are established based on its functions such as accumulation and maintenance.
Supplement: Regarding the establishment of distinct names based on their meaning, the *Xiaochao* states:
"Among sentient beings, there are those who possess this name and those who do not."
△ Next, the detailed explanation (in four parts). First, the explanation of the four names beginning with "mind" (*citta*).
That is to say, it is called "mind" (*citta*) because of various phenomena (*dharma*), and so forth; these various names apply to all states.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) explains that the meaning of "accumulating" (*citta*) is the meaning of "mind.
The meaning of "arising through accumulation" is also the meaning of "mind," because it can accumulate and produce various seeds, or because it can infuse seeds into this consciousness;
since it both accumulates and gives rise to all phenomena, this consciousness is called by the name "mind. *Ādāna* is translated here as "grasping."
"Holding" means holding all the various material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*). Regarding "the basis of the knowable" (*jñeyāśraya*): "basis" refers to the eighth consciousness;

"the knowable" refers to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*)—defiled, pure, and both. Since seeds (*bīja*) and manifestations (*vṛtti*) serve as the basis for those [three natures], it is called the "basis of the knowable.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "Because it is that which should be known, it is called 'the knowable' (*jñeya*); 'basis' (*āśraya*) means the support (*niśraya*). This term "support" [is used here].

One selects only those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that are subject to defilement (*saṃkleśa*) or purification (*vyavadāna*), and does not select the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because the latter lacks the sense of having a basis (*āśraya*).
This basis is the *ālayavijñāna*, also called the "seed-consciousness" (*bījavi-jñāna*), which is able to maintain the seeds of both the mundane (*laukika*) and the supramundane (*lokottara*).
That which maintains the impure (*sāsrava*) seeds is termed "mundane," while that which maintains the pure (*anāsrava*) seeds is [termed "supramundane"].
It is called "supramundane. Question: What is the difference between the meaning of "seed-consciousness" (*bīja-vijñāna*) and "mind" (*citta*)? Answer:

It refers to the eighth consciousness in its active manifestation (*pravṛtti*), which is also called a "seed. Because it is that which is a seed capable of producing active manifestations, it is termed "seed-consciousness.
From the perspective of its functional capacity to produce the seeds of phenomena through its active manifestation, this eighth consciousness is termed "seed."

Regarding "consciousness" (*vijñāna*): as for what was previously called "mind" (*citta*), it is merely a name for the sense of accumulation and arising; these [terms] below conclude the four names mentioned above, which apply universally to both the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
△ Next, the name *ālaya* is explained.
It is also called "the storehouse that encompasses all" (up to) "because it has the sense of being a repository for the defiled dharmas. Regarding the phonetics and meaning:

this name applies to two [categories]. It is not [the case that] those below the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) [possess it]; this correctly reveals the name *ālaya-vijñāna*, which exists only in [the state of]...
There are two categories: ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*).
△ Third, explaining the name "ripening consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*):
it is also called ripening consciousness because it is capable of projecting birth and death (until: because there are still dharmas that are ripened and indeterminate).

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: This name, "vipāka-vijñāna" (retributive consciousness), applies generally to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), practitioners of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), and Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
It excludes only the Tathāgatas, because the Tathāgata’s nature consists solely of untainted goodness (*anāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) and thus lacks any tainted retribution (*sāsrava-vipāka*).
Because it is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharma.
△ Fourth, the explanation of the name "Stainless Consciousness" (*vimala-vijñāna*):
It is also called the Stainless Consciousness, which is supremely pure... corresponding to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
Commentary on Terms: It is called "stainless" (*vimala*) because it is not the basis for afflictions.
"The most supremely pure untainted phenomena" refers to all the merits possessed within the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*).

This stainless consciousness is named "only the Tathāgata," because those of the three vehicles and ordinary beings have not yet attained the thoroughly purified eighth consciousness. As in the sūtra passage below, this cites the merits of the Tathāgata.
Established by the *Guṇavyūha-sūtra*. Supplement:

The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the School), fascicle 50, states: "The ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is permanently relinquished in a single moment until the end of the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*).
Within the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), it immediately becomes the stainless consciousness (*vimalavijñāna*), which is named *amala*."
The eighth consciousness within the state of fruition is purely and exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).

Because it does not contain the seeds of any defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) and does not serve as the support for the manifestation of defiled seeds, it is associated solely with the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and is termed the "stainless consciousness" (*amala-vijñāna*).
△ Next, the excluded [synonyms] are distinguished.

Because the name *ālaya* carries a heavy fault [of being associated with the defiled], it is not applied [to the pure state]; because [the term] "mind" (*citta*) and so forth apply generally to both ordinary beings and noble ones, they should be explained according to their respective meanings.

**Commentary on the Meaning:** Question: Since the eighth consciousness already possesses various names that apply throughout the stages of both ordinary beings and noble ones, why does the root verse [mention only certain names]?
It is taught that only the *ālaya* is [so named]. The commentary explains this by saying it is because its faults are grave.
That is to say, it mutually contains and conceals the defiled (*saṃkleśa*) dharmas, and it is also grasped by sentient beings as a self; thus, it is the root of tainted (*sāsrava*) birth and death.

The names for the others are not like this, and therefore it is said their faults are grave. Furthermore, it is because it is abandoned at the very beginning; that is to say, prior to the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), one has merely abandoned the *ālaya*, but not yet...
It is called "abandoning the rest" because one first abandons this [emptiness]. Since there are these two meanings, the verse specifically mentions it.

"When about to attain Bodhi" refers to the final mind following the Vajra Path. That which is abandoned at the time of entering the Nirvāṇa without Remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*)—following the Vajra Path and the maturation-emptiness (*vipākāśūnyatā*)—refers to the time when the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) dissolve their bodies and extinguish their wisdom. It is stainless and...

Equanimity (*upekṣā*). Because it can give rise to the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and other untainted wholesome dharmas (*anāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) that endure until the end of the future, the four mental factors—faith, diligence, mindfulness, and equanimity—are present throughout all stages;
they are explained according to their respective functions based on the meanings of defilement and purity.

Appendix: Regarding the statement that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas discard the substance of the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) at the time of entering nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), this is discussed from the perspective of the specific teachings of the Hīnayāna. If viewed from the standpoint of the Mahāyāna, however, it has in fact never been discarded.
It must be completely severed. The seeds of maturation (*vipāka-bīja*) are only emptied of their substance after the Bodhisattva’s Vajra Path.

Here, however, we are considering the perspective of the Hīnayāna, where at the limit of the "extinction of the body and cessation of cognition" (*pudgala-nirodha*), it is provisionally said that the substance is abandoned; yet in reality, this is merely the abandonment of the name.
That which is called *ālaya-vijñāna* abandons its name as "maturation," while what is called "consciousness" abandons its substance. This is truly because the *ālaya* is the cause.
The name is derived from its meaning as the "Three Baskets" (Tripiṭaka). Within these Three Baskets, the seventh consciousness has a heavy tendency toward grasping;
if it does not grasp, it abandons the "Basket" (kṣaya), and is thus named the *vipākavijñāna*. It is so named because it receives the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).

Furthermore, since it also contains inferior untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, it cannot be said to be entirely empty in its essence. Because it is not called *bodhi*, it is therefore said that its essence is abandoned.
△ Next, the two stages of the final reversion are established.
Now, the eighth consciousness generally comprises two stages (up to) because the mirror-like wisdom universally cognizes all phenomena.

[Commentary on the Meaning and Phonology] The first phrase provides a general heading. Regarding "First, there is... and so forth: this specifically clarifies that within the stage of outflows (*sāsrava*), it is exclusively non-existent.

It is subsumed under the nature of obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta). Its associated mental factors consist solely of the five [beginning with] contact; its objects of perception consist solely of the three spheres of apprehension and location.

Within the untainted state (anāsrava), it is subsumed solely under the nature of the wholesome (kuśala) and is associated with the two lower types of clarity (vidyā). These have been previously listed and set forth.

Next, a single verse is provided to explain and establish [the categories]. The first line explains the five omnipresent mental factors (*sarvatraga*). The five lines beginning with "constant joy" (*nitya-rati*) explain the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*) in their respective order.
The single line "extremely pure" (*suviśuddha*) explains the eleven factors that are wholesome by nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*).

The phrase "untainted" (*akliṣṭa*) and below serves to distinguish them from the non-associated [factors], because they are not defiled; thus, they do not associate with the roots or the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and they are free from distraction (*avikṣepa*).
Therefore, it does not correspond with the four indeterminate dharmas. This also explains below the designation of "associated" (*saṃprayukta*);

while [other minds] are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), this one belongs exclusively to the wholesome (*kuśala*). The following explains the object-condition (*ālambana*): because if it did not universally take all things as its object, it would not be the Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
The explanation of the verse is hereby complete.
△ Next, the proof that the foundational consciousness (ālayavijñāna) exists (three parts). First, the inquiry and response providing a general outline:
"How should one know this eighth consciousness? ... because the sacred teachings and correct reasoning serve as the authoritative standard."
Commentary on Terms: Regarding the Hīnayāna, it has been traditionally understood that there are only the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth.
Now, having heard the Master extensively clarify the functioning of the eighth [consciousness] as an object-condition, and its establishment under various names, one may understand this to be so;

yet how does one know that there exists a distinct self-nature apart from the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth? The Holy Teaching answers this below. The *Zongjing* commentary explains: "This eighth..."

The eight [liberations] are not objects perceived by worldly direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); they are known to exist solely through the authority of sacred scripture (*āptāgama*) and correct reasoning (*yukti*).
Next, the specific explanation according to teaching and reasoning (in two parts): first, citing the teachings (in two parts): first, citing Mahāyāna (in two parts): first, citing the sūtras.
Scriptural Proof for the Existence of the Eighth [Consciousness] (2): The First Three Sūtras and Four Verses (4). First, citing a verse from the Abhidharma (2).
First, the citation of the verse.
This refers to the Mahāyāna Abhidharma, which [extends] up to the realization of the various realms of existence (*gati*) and *nirvāṇa*.

**Commentary on the Terms:** *Abhidharma*: This is translated as "Incomparable Dharma" (*anuttara-dharma*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* explains: "The beginningless time" means there is no initial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).
"Realm" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of "cause. That is, it refers to the seeds; what is the cause of these seeds? It is said to be all [phenomena].

The Dharma. Regarding "the equal support of all dharmas" (the self-witnessing division of the eighth consciousness): because it is capable of sustaining [them], and because it is not of the nature of a cause.

The meaning of being able to sustain is the meaning of being a support (*āśraya*), whereas the meaning of not being a cause is not the meaning of being a support. This is because the natures of the supported (*āśrita*)—which are the three natures—and the support (*āśraya*)—which is unobscured-neutral—are each distinct.
Regarding the phrase "by this there are the various realms of existence (*gati*) and the attainment of nirvāṇa": this refers to the defilement of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*) and so forth.
In the hells and other realms, if apart from the ālayavijñāna, the cessation of all afflictions (*saṃkleśa*), such as birth and so forth, would be impossible;
this ultimate cessation is called nirvāṇa. If apart from the ālayavijñāna, it could not be realized.

△ Second, the explanation of the meaning (in two parts). First, the direct explanation (in three parts). First, the explanation based on its two functions (in two parts). First, a brief determination of the verse text:

This eighth consciousness has a subtle intrinsic nature [which serves as] the function of providing support for both the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*) and the process of cessation (*nivṛtti*).

Commentary on the Meaning of the Verses: The first two lines generally reveal the intent of the verse. Below, in the verse itself, the distinct functions of the beginning and the end are specifically judged.

△ Next, the detailed explanation of the meaning of the verses (in two parts): First, the function of causes and conditions (in two parts): First, the explanation (in two parts): First, the direct explanation of the cause.
Condition (*pratyaya*).
"Effect" has the meaning of "cause," which refers to the seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*) [up to] its serving as the support for all phenomena; therefore, it is called a condition.
Regarding the meaning of the term: the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the School), fascicle 47, explains that the word "element" (*dhātu*) signifies cause. That is to say:

The eighth consciousness, from beginningless time until now, is able to maintain the seeds of all phenomena—both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), including those of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
Furthermore, it provides the power for these contaminated and uncontaminated seeds to arise as actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*).

Thus, the eighth consciousness serves as the support (*āśraya*) for all seeds; its function as the basis for their arising constitutes the meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*). This refers to the eighth...

The eight consciousnesses are capable of transforming into the body and the receptacle world, serving as the support for sentient beings and for all outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) manifest phenomena.
They act as the basis by being able to grasp and maintain the physical body of the five sense organs and the manifestations of the preceding seven consciousnesses.

Because it serves as the co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), the eighth consciousness is able to serve as the augmenting causal support for all currently manifest phenomena, such as form and mind.
Next, the function of this support is explained in turn.
This means that because it can maintain all seeds (up to: it also takes the seventh consciousness as its co-existent support). [Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms]:

This means that because the eighth consciousness is able to maintain the seeds, and because it serves as the support for the present life, it transforms itself into the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), the sense faculties (*indriya*), and the body (*deha*), and acts as the support for those seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). The phrase "because it can" [below] provides a specific explanation.

Regarding its basis: first, it is clarified that [the ālayavijñāna] serves as the support for the five sensory consciousnesses; furthermore, it serves as the support for the two consciousnesses below—the sixth and the seventh.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Because the ālayavijñāna exists, the manas exists; because this manas serves as a support, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is able to function.
It is, for example, like the five groups of sensory consciousnesses functioning by depending on the five sense organs, such as the eye."
It is not that the five sense-faculties do not exist; the same applies to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). It is not that the mind-faculty (*manas*) does not exist (text).

Below [the section on] the *manas*, a formal inference (*prayoga*) is established again to clarify that the sixth and seventh consciousnesses possess simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*). The *manas* and the mental consciousness are the subject (*dharmin*); they depend upon a simultaneous support.

Thesis: Because it is subsumed under the category of evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). Reason: Because it is of the nature of consciousness (*vijñānatva*), like the seventh consciousness. Example: Like the visual consciousness and others. Furthermore, the eighth [consciousness] has a further support;

the seventh and eighth are the subjects (*dharmin*), and the thesis is that they likewise have the seventh as their simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*). Reason: Because they are of the nature of consciousness. Example: Like the seventh consciousness.

This refers to this consciousness acting as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

it is because this eighth consciousness exists [that] even the requisites for the various realms are given the name "realms."

In relation to birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the seeds of afflictions and karma act as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), while the seeds of suffering act as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for birth and death.
Because the eighth consciousness can maintain these three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it causes the continuity of birth and death for sentient beings. Although...

The following section clarifies doubts regarding the term "delusion" (*moha*). A doubt arises as follows: Since delusion, karma, and suffering are all phenomena of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), why does the verse state only that "birth in the various realms of existence" (*gati-janman*) is suffering?
There are two ways to explain this. First is an explanation based on the predominance of the result; second is an explanation that encompasses both cause and result.
That which leads [to rebirth] refers to delusion and karma; that which is led [therein] refers to suffering. Furthermore, the "birth" and its "requisite conditions" are themselves delusion and karma.
Because it can provide the provisions for the various realms of existence and bring them to completion.
△ Third, the conclusion:
All afflictions, karma, and births depend upon this consciousness; thus, it functions as the support and basis for the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*).
△ Next, the explanation of the support for the process of reversal and cessation (3): First, the heading.
Regarding "the realization of nirvāṇa," it is because this consciousness exists that the realization of nirvāṇa exists.
△ Next, the explanation:
It means that because this eighth consciousness exists, one realizes *nirvāṇa* at the stage of ultimate exhaustion. Regarding the meaning of the terms:

it refers to the originally existing untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*). Because they are sustained by this consciousness, [they function] in accordance with the dharma of cessation and reversal (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
From the stages before and after the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), through successive perfuming and arising, until the ultimate attainment of *nirvāṇa*, it causes the practitioner to realize it;
thus it is said that it "causes the practitioner to attain realization. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the School) states:

"The eighth consciousness does not merely serve as the supporting basis for the phenomena of the impure process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*); it can also simultaneously serve as the supporting basis for all pure phenomena conducive to the cessation of suffering (*nivṛtti*)."

[This is] the explanatory text (*vṛtti*). Herein, the following provides a detailed analysis and interpretation. Specifically, regarding the phrase "attaining nirvāṇa" within this verse, it refers exclusively to the path capable of realizing [nirvāṇa], and does not refer to nirvāṇa itself.

This is because nirvāṇa is the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) cause of clarity (*prakāśa-hetu*) for the pure *dharmadhātu*, and that which is clarified does not exist in dependence upon this consciousness.
Thus, this [explanation] is based solely on the capacity to realize. Alternatively, from "or this" below, it is based on the object realized.

Commentary on the Proof: Alternatively, this passage speaks only of the *nirvāṇa* that is realized, because that which is truly sought through the arousal of the mind and the practice of the path is solely *nirvāṇa*.
That is to say, the term "attainment" (*prāpti*) refers to that which is realized.

Alternatively, it may speak of both cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), because the path is that which brings about cessation, and cessation is that which is brought about; both are therefore subsumed under the category of "that which leads to cessation," namely, *nirvāṇa*.

Below, the meaning of the paired exposition is presented: that which is capable of attaining is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and that which is capable of severing is the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
△ Third, the conclusion:
both the object realized and the abandonment achieved all depend upon this consciousness; thus, it serves as the supporting basis for the process of cessation and return to tranquility.
Explanatory Notes on Terms: "That which cuts and that which is cut" refers to the path that cuts and the afflictions that are cut.
"That which realizes and that which is realized" refers to the path that realizes and the cessation that is realized.
△ Next, the explanation is given in terms of defilement and purity.
Furthermore, within this verse, the first line demonstrates that [the opponent's position] is logically untenable based on the *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses), and so forth.

**Commentary on the Meaning:** Regarding the phrase in the first line, "the *dhātu* (element/ground) existing from beginningless time," *dhātu* has the meaning of "nature" (*svabhāva*). It refers to the very nature of consciousness itself.

The nature [of reality] is beginningless. The phrase "always existing" refers to all phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth. "Basis" (*āśraya*) indicates that it serves as the support for both defiled and purified phenomena.
Because of this, there are the various realms of existence (*gati*), which are the basis for defilement; and the realization of *nirvāṇa*, which is the basis for purity.

Regarding the detailed explanation of the downward progression of defilement: the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is the agent of transition, while the truths of afflictions, karma, and suffering are the objects [of transition].
The realms of rebirth constitute the cause and effect of these two mundane worlds (*loka*). The Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) is that which realizes the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*);
the Nirvana thus realized constitutes the cause and effect of these two supramundane realms. The following concluding passage clarifies the nature of this eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Because it is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta), it serves as the support for both defiled and pure phenomena. The first seven evolving consciousnesses, however, involve both wholesome and defiled natures;
therefore, they cannot serve as the support for both simultaneously.
△ Third, the explanation by way of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Alternatively, it should be understood that the first phrase reveals the essence of this consciousness as being, respectively, the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*. [Supplementary Note:
The meaning of the three natures will be explained later in the eighth fascicle. Third, the manifestation [of the consciousness] in relation to the three [natures].
Regarding that which has the seed-nature (*bīja-svabhāva*) as its basis:
the second phrase refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as its basis, because all phenomena arise in dependence upon conditions.

The third phrase refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as its basis, because the various realms of existence (*gati*) exist through the power of imaginative construction, and the essence of those born in those realms is the eighth [consciousness]. The fourth phrase refers to...
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) serves as the basis, because both types of perfected natures are realized by depending upon the eighth consciousness.
Next, the conclusion of the proof:
the various meanings explained in this verse could not exist apart from the eighth consciousness.
△ Next, the preceding verse from the sutra is cited again (2). First, the citation of the verse:
That same sutra further states: "Therefore, O Victorious One, I have revealed it as the *ālaya*."

△ Second, the explanation of the meaning (in two parts). First, the direct explanation (in two parts). First, the explanation of the first three phrases (in two parts). First, the explanation according to the sense of "containing" (*ālaya*).
Because this fundamental consciousness possesses all seeds... [up to] ...because the support and the supported arise and perish together.
Commentary on the Phonetics and Meaning: Because the text of the verse is arranged in reverse order, the prose commentary provides an explanation by rearranging the phrasing.

This means that because the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness maintains all seeds, it is able to contain and store all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*). Based on this sense of "containing and storing," the name *ālayavijñāna* is established.

This is not like the Sāṃkhya school, which asserts that the *pradhāna* (primordial nature) transforms into the *mahat* (the Great One). (Note: The term *yinyì* [音義] refers to a traditional genre of Buddhist lexicography and exegesis that explains the phonetic values and doctrinal meanings of specific terms.)
Although cause and effect differ, their essence is one; although the fruit is subject to arising and ceasing, the cause is eternal. Now, this is not the case, and thus it is said:
"How could it be so? This is because the entity of the seed that can produce [the fruit] is not identical to the entity of the manifest fruit.
Furthermore, because the various phenomena that depend [upon it] and the consciousness which serves as their basis arise and cease together, this differs from false attachments.
It can manifest correct reasoning.
△ Next, the explanation according to the meaning of the Three Baskets (*piṭaka*):
Because it mutually contains and stores defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), this consciousness is called the *ālaya*.
△ Next, the explanation of the fourth phrase (2): first, the explanation in terms of those on the stages (*bhūmi*).
For the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have already entered the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*)... [up to] ...therefore my World-Honored One correctly reveals and teaches it for them.
Commentary on Terms: There are six types of direct realization (*abhisamaya*). Regarding the explanation of "true" [realization] in the ninth fascicle below:
it refers to the fact that the "similar direct realization" prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) has not yet severed the afflictions, and thus is not called "true realization and understanding.

Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), however, have already attained two kinds of superior wisdom and therefore understand this subtle consciousness as it truly is, even though they have not yet exhausted its ultimate source.
Having already attained partial awakening, the World-Honored One correctly reveals [the teaching] for them.
Next, the general explanation for those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) follows:
"Alternatively, all bodhisattvas are called 'victors' (jina) because they seek that transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); therefore, it is also taught for their sake."

Explanation of Terms: Those who possess faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*) have not yet attained realization. Regarding "relying on the teaching to give rise to faith and understanding and effecting the transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*):
this refers to the fact that this consciousness (*vijñāna*) can maintain the seeds of both defiled and pure phenomena, and it serves as the basis for those defiled and pure phenomena.

The Noble Path transforms it so that one abandons the defiled and attains the pure. This refers to Bodhisattvas in the stage of Provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*) and others; although they have not yet realized this in actuality...

Having understood this, they are able to rely upon the teaching with faith and understanding; they exert great vigor regarding the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) because they seek the fruit of that transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
For their sake, my Blessed One has also taught this.
△ Next, the conclusion of the proof:
The various evolving consciousnesses do not possess such a meaning.
△ Third, citing verses from the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (2): First, the citation of the verses.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* also states this (up to): "Lest they conceptually grasp it as a self.
Regarding the meaning of the terms, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* explains: "Profound" (*gambhīra*) means that the cognitive wisdom of those who are wise in the world cannot fathom its depths.
"Extremely subtle" (*sūkṣma*) means that it is difficult for śrāvakas and others to understand. Therefore, it is not [taught] for the sake of śrāvakas.
Regarding "hearing" and so forth: this consciousness is revealed because they do not seek the subtle *sarvajñajñāna* (the wisdom of omniscience).
"All seeds like a torrential stream" means that they continue in succession from moment to moment without interruption, like a rushing torrent of water.

"I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant" means that for those who harbor the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), I do not disclose it, fearing that they would engage in conceptual construction and calculation.
For my sake. △ Second, the explanation of the meaning (in two parts): First, the direct explanation (in three parts). First, the explanation of the first phrase:
Because it is able to maintain the seeds of all phenomena... [up to] ...it cannot be fully penetrated, it is therefore called "extremely subtle."
*Saṃghoṣa*. *Ādāna* is translated here as "grasping and maintaining. The *Zongjing lu*, fascicle 50, states that there are three types of grasping and maintaining:
first, grasping and maintaining the sense-faculties and the body so that they do not decay; second, grasping and maintaining the seeds so that they are not lost;
third, grasping and taking up the continuity of rebirth, which refers to a sentient being at the final moment of their existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
In the very first moment of the eighth consciousness at the time of taking birth, there is the sense of grasping and the continuity of linking [to a new existence].
"Linking" (kṣepa) means binding or belonging. In the womb of the parents, one takes birth in a single instant and immediately becomes bound to them;
it is like a lodestone attracting iron. The two drops of the parents' semen and blood are like the iron, and the eighth consciousness is like the lodestone.

In a single kṣaṇa, it immediately grasps and maintains [the body]. Simultaneously, the seeds of the faculties, objects, and so forth also arise as manifest activity from within their own consciousness;
this is called "grasping and linking rebirth" (saṃdhāna-pratisaṃdhi). As the Blessed One said:
"If the ādāna-vijñāna did not enter the mother’s womb, it would not coalesce to form the kalala and so forth. Those who lack the nature [of Buddhahood] are... [text ends]

The icchantikas do not believe that the eighth consciousness is the self-nature of all phenomena; because if the eighth consciousness did not exist, there would be no Buddha-nature, they are called "icchantikas of no nature.
It is because non-Buddhists do not believe this consciousness to be the root of all phenomena [that they are so designated].

Some cling to the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), while others cling to the principle of great existence (*mahāsattā*). Clinging to annihilationism or eternalism, they are thus adrift and submerged, unable to achieve liberation.
Therefore, they cannot fathom the depths or attain tranquility. This refers to those śrāvakas who likewise do not believe in the eighth consciousness;
they know only the six consciousnesses and the three poisons as the root of defilement and purity, sinking into emptiness and stagnating in quiescence, remaining unaware [of the ultimate truth].
Because of this knowledge, one cannot penetrate it.
△ Next, the second phrase is explained:
"These are the true seeds of all phenomena (up to) which are constantly uninterrupted, like a torrential stream."
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: Regarding "the seeds of reality," they are so called because they directly produce manifest phenomena (*pravṛtti-dharma*).

As for "being like a torrential stream," although all the seeds within the eighth consciousness encounter various conditions and, being struck by them, give rise to the visual consciousness and the other sensory cognitions, the substance of this consciousness itself remains constantly uninterrupted, just like a torrential stream.
Alternatively, it refers to the fact that the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of the seeds never cease.
Because it is like a torrential stream.
△ Third, the explanation of the final two phrases:

"Ordinary beings" refers to those who lack the nature [of Buddhahood], and "the ignorant" refers to those who incline toward tranquility; (up to: for this reason, our World-Honored One did not expound [this teaching] for them.
Commentary on Terms: Hearing the most profound and subtle principles, they are unable to realize or understand them, and instead give rise to false attachments, recklessly conceiving them as a self.
Because they have not heard the holy teachings in the past, these innate [afflictions] constantly arise; now, hearing the sound of the Dharma, their conceptual discrimination increases further.
This discriminative clinging is the cause of the evil destinies; it obstructs the Noble Path and prevents it from arising.
Therefore, our World-Honored One did not expound upon it.
Next, the conclusion of the proof.
Only the eighth consciousness possesses such characteristics.
△ Fourth, introducing a verse from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* (2): First, the citation of the verse.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* also states: "...constantly giving rise to the waves of various consciousnesses, which manifest and function in their active transformation."
Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: These eight lines of verse consist of four lines that are purely metaphors, followed by four lines that combine the teaching (dharma) with the metaphor.

The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is like the ocean; objective conditions are like the wind. The character "constantly" (*nityam*) joins with the preceding [phrase] to mean there is no interruption.
The arising of the various consciousnesses is like the waves; the waves are the functioning of the ocean, and the various consciousnesses are the functioning of the storehouse consciousness.
△ Next, the explanation of the meaning:

The various consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and others, lack the qualities of the great ocean... [omitted] ...therefore we know that there exists a separate eighth consciousness-nature.

(Commentary on the Meaning and Phonetics): This clarifies that the various consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and others, arise and cease with ease and are subject to detachment; they do not possess the constant continuity like the great ocean.

The subsequent arising of the waves of consciousness serves as a counter-illustration that reveals the eighth consciousness possesses such characteristics; thus, the following section provides the concluding proof.
Next, the extensive evidence for its existence is indicated:
within these and other immeasurable Mahāyāna sūtras, the eighth consciousness is specifically taught through inference.
△ Next, it is demonstrated that the Mahāyāna is an authoritative scripture (āptāgama). (2) First, an inference (*anumāna*) is established as proof:
All Mahāyāna sūtras conform to the doctrine of selflessness; therefore, like the *Ekottarika-āgama* and others, they are subsumed within the category of authoritative scriptures.

Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: This refers to those such as the Śrāvakas who exclusively believe in the Hīnayāna, holding that the *Ekottarika Āgama* and other such sūtras constitute authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), while they do not believe in the various Mahāyāna sūtras.

If one does not take those Hīnayāna sūtras they themselves accept as a homologous example (*dṛṣṭānta*) to prove that the Mahāyāna sūtras are authoritative scripture, then even if one were to extensively cite a thousand sūtras, if they— [the opponent]...
If one lacks faith, bestowing [teachings] upon them is fruitless. Therefore, to support the Mahāyāna, one must first establish its existence;

only then can others be freed from doubt and develop deep faith. In this text, the first two lines clarify that the meanings realized by the Mahāyāna accord with [the principles of] non-self and so forth;
the next two lines clarify the emptiness of persons and the rejection [of false views], and they clarify the Four Noble Truths while praising the Buddha-dharma.

The first two lines clarify the praise of the internal and the censure of external [appearances], such as the aggregates (*skandha*). The second two lines clarify that [the former] expresses what is correct and excludes what is erroneous.
"Delighting in the Mahāyāna" and below conclude the principle explained above: it is a non-perverted delight. Regarding "the Mahāyāna," it is accepted as being revealed and shown.

The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows: All Mahāyāna sūtras are the subject (*dharmin*). They are included within the category of authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), which is the thesis (*pakṣa*).

This is because they all conform to selflessness (*anātman*), and so forth, up to the reason that they are included among the *sūtras*. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is, for instance, the *Aṅgula* [Sūtra] and others.
△ Next, citing seven reasons as proof (2). First, citing the seven reasons of the noble Maitreya (2). First, the general statement:
Furthermore, the noble Maitreya proves that the Mahāyāna sūtras are truly the word of the Buddha by means of seven kinds of reasons.
Supplement: Having already cited the present Śākyamuni above, we now cite the future Maitreya to prove that the Mahāyāna was spoken by the Buddha.
△ Next, a specific explanation in seven parts: (1) First, the lack of prediction.

First, because [the Buddha] did not previously record them: if the Mahāyāna sūtras (up to) had predicted in advance all such terrifying events, then when the Tathāgata was still present, regarding those terrifying matters that would arise in the future and destroy the True Dharma...
*Yinyi* (Phonology and Meaning): If there are terrifying events that will arise in the future and destroy the True Dharma, [they were not recorded] while the Tathāgata was in the world.

All were previously granted predictions [of their future enlightenment], as the Buddha taught: "In the age of the Final Dharma, there will be various Māra kings who enter my Dharma, don my kashaya robes, and destroy my True Dharma until the Dharma is inevitably extinguished. Regarding such matters as these, the Buddha had already bestowed predictions in advance.
If Mahayana sutras were not spoken by the Buddha, why did the Buddha not likewise predict that they would destroy the True Dharma after his parinirvāṇa?

Regarding "the Dharma": it refers to those matters that inspire fear, which [the Buddha] had previously predicted. The formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: The Mahāyāna sūtras are the subject (*dharmin*);

the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they are truly the word of the Buddha; the reason (*hetu*) is that they were not previously predicted [in the Śrāvaka canon]; the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like the Sūtras of the Hīnayāna.
The remaining six reasons for the formal inference are to be understood by analogy.
△ 2. Both [traditions] are practiced together.
Because both traditions are practiced together, how could one know that the Mahāyāna teachings alone are not the Buddha’s word?
△ 3. It is not the domain of others.
Third, because it is not the domain of others, that which is taught in the Mahāyāna is [the word of the Buddha]; therefore, Mahāyāna sūtras are not non-Buddha-spoken.
Regarding the meaning of the terms: what is taught in the Mahāyāna sūtras is extremely profound and inconceivable; only those possessing great faculties are capable of receiving it.
This is because it is not the sphere of deliberation for those of heterodox or external views, nor has it ever been taught within their teachings, even if they were to speak of it.

They do not believe it; how much less would they believe what he [the Buddha] taught? Therefore, one knows that the Mahāyāna is truly the word of the Buddha, and is not something not spoken by the Buddha.
△ Fourth, it should be universally established.
Fourth, because it must be universally established: if one claims that the Mahāyāna is the word of the Buddha, this principle is universally established.
[This is because] whether it be the present Buddha or other Buddhas, they are equally Buddhas. If one were to claim that the Mahāyāna was spoken by another Buddha...
This was not spoken only by the present Śākyamuni Buddha. Since the Way is the same for all Buddhas, one should believe that the Mahāyāna sūtras are what the Buddhas have taught.
Their principles are thoroughly established and admit of no dissent.
△ 5. The existence or non-existence of the five aggregates.
Because the five aggregates either exist or do not exist, if one asserts that there is a Mahāyāna [but it is] not the teaching of the Mahāyāna, this would be contrary to reason.
Glossary: If one admits the existence of the Mahāyāna, one must believe that this Mahāyāna teaching was spoken by the Buddha; otherwise, it is devoid [of authority].
Because it is impossible to seek the Mahāyāna apart from this teaching, if there were no Mahāyāna, the Śrāvaka vehicle would likewise not exist. Why?
Because apart from the Mahāyāna, there is no principle of attaining Buddhahood; who, then, would appear in the world to teach the Śrāvaka vehicle?
Since we acknowledge that the Śrāvaka vehicle was spoken by the Buddha, we do not disparage the Mahāyāna; this is not [the case].
The Buddha’s teaching is not contrary to correct principle.
△ Sixth, because it possesses the capacity for antidote:
since it possesses the six capacities for antidote, one should rely on the Mahāyāna sūtras and believe that this is what was spoken by the Buddha.

Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: This refers to the practice of the Hīnayāna, which can induce true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) and serve as an antidote to the afflictions (*kleśa*); one should have faith that this is the Buddha’s teaching.

Furthermore, if one practices diligently according to the Mahāyāna, all such practitioners are able to induce non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which can correctly counteract all afflictions;
therefore, one should have faith that this is what was spoken by the Buddha.
△ Section Seven: Differences in Meaning and Text.
Because the meaning differs from the text, that which is taught in the Mahāyāna (up to) "therefore the Mahāyāna is truly the Buddha’s teaching. [Commentary on the Phonology and Meaning]:

The principles and patterns taught in the Mahāyāna are exceedingly profound; those who hear them should appropriately recognize them silently within their own minds and attain realization through direct mental penetration.
To realize the principle through the forgetting of words, one must not merely grasp the literal text while neglecting its meaning; otherwise, one slanders that which is not the Buddha’s word.
Since such profoundly deep teachings could not have been proclaimed by anyone other than the Most Holy One, we know that the Mahāyāna is truly the Buddha’s teaching.

As that treatise states regarding this point (up to): "Because the established [position] and its counter-argument differ in their phrasing."
△ Next, citing other schools (2): First, the general statement.
In the sūtras of other schools as well, the *ālayavijñāna* is taught with an underlying intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) as having a distinct intrinsic nature.
[Supplement]: This citation of the underlying intentions taught by the four schools of the Hīnayāna is intended to prevent them from giving rise to conceptual attachments.
Therefore, it was indicated obliquely rather than stated explicitly. Now, in the subsequent text, the Master of the Treatise explicitly identifies these as all referring to this eighth consciousness.
△ Next, specific citations (four): first, the Mahāsāṃghika school.
This refers to the *Āgama* of the Mahāsāṃghika school (up to the point where it states that the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth do not possess such meanings).
Regarding the meaning of the terms: the Sanskrit *Mahāsāṃghika* is translated here as "The Great Assembly.

It is said: Regarding the two fundamental divisions, as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, at the time of the first council, five hundred people were selected;
these constitute the Sthavira school of Kāśyapa within the cave. Those not included in this number are called the Mahāsāṃghika, who were outside the cave.

*Āgama*—here translated as "Sūtra"—refers to the sūtras contained within the Vinaya-piṭaka; that is to say, it refers to what was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) within those sūtras.
The eighth is called the *mūlavijñāna* (root-consciousness), because it is the support for the visual and other consciousnesses,
just as the trunk and so forth are supported by the root of a tree. Since the visual and other consciousnesses do not possess such a status as a support,
this serves to reveal that only the eighth consciousness possesses this meaning of being the "root."
△ Next, the Sthavira school.
Regarding the *Vibhaṅga* of the Sthavira scriptures (up to): "Only this [ignorance] is constantly and universally the cause of the three realms of existence.
*Yinyi* (Sound and Meaning): The Sanskrit term is *sthavira*. This is translated as "old elder" (*lǎosù*). In the Qin language, it is "Sthavira" (上座). It refers exclusively to Kāśyapa.
...and so forth. Elder monks gathered together and collectively produced the Vinaya-piṭaka sūtras; these are the sūtras within this very collection.

As for the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it refers to those who composed treatises to explain the sūtras; that is to say, both those sūtras and their commentaries were taught with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).

This eighth [consciousness] is named the "appropriating consciousness" (*ādāna-vijñāna*). From "only this" onwards, it is revealed that only this eighth consciousness is constant and uninterrupted, pervading...

△ Third, the Mahīśāsaka school:

The Mahīśāsakas state that this is called the "aggregate that exhausts birth and death" (*saṃsāra-kṣaya-skandha*)... (until) only this consciousness is named the aggregate that exhausts birth and death.

*Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings): According to the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra-śāstra*, this school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda. *Hui-xuan* states: "Regarding the Mahīśāsaka school:
its founder was formerly a king who transformed and governed the common people upon the earth. Later, he abdicated his throne, left the household life, and practiced the Way;
the school is named after this original act. It is called the Mahīśāsaka. *Wu-xing* explains: "In that regard..."
Within this section, there are three kinds of aggregates (*skandha*): first, the aggregate of a single moment, which refers to phenomena that arise and perish within a single *kṣaṇa*;
second, the aggregate of a single lifetime, which refers to phenomena that persist continuously until death;

and third, the aggregate that exhausts birth and death, which refers to phenomena that persist continuously until the attainment of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*). These are called "exhausting birth and death" because they continue until that point.

The *Zongjing* commentary explains: Because this eighth consciousness pervades the three realms and nine stages and is eternally present, wherever there is birth and death, it constantly and universally serves as the basis.
It is only when one reaches the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) of the Mahāyāna and the final afflictions are exhausted that it is relinquished;
therefore, it is called the "aggregate that exhausts birth and death" (*saṃsāra-kṣaya-skandha*). Below this, the text clarifies that [this aggregate] is distinct from the eighth consciousness.
This is precisely the eighth [consciousness]. For apart from this consciousness, those aggregates that exhaust saṃsāra (*saṃsāraparyantika-skandha*) could not be found.

"Without the lower" excludes other aggregates, as they are not the aggregates that exhaust saṃsāra. "Without form" excludes the various forms of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which are interrupted;

this excludes the aggregates of form in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) and so forth. "The cessation of others" excludes feeling, perception, and formations, while including them within the aggregate of consciousness.
The preceding seven consciousnesses and the non-associated formations lack a distinct intrinsic nature; this is to distinguish them from the non-associated formations.

It is like a worldly treasury. As for the "arising of active manifestations," this refers to all active manifestations of form and mind within the three realms and five destinies, whether contaminated or uncontaminated; all of these arise from the eighth consciousness.

It functions as the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), which is able to gather the seeds of all phenomena so that they are not lost, and furthermore, it is able to give rise to the functional capacity for the manifestation of those seeds.
Because it has continued without interruption since beginningless time, it possesses exclusively the meaning of "gathering" and "arising.
Thus, one knows that the eighth consciousness’s self-witnessing division and the seeds within consciousness serve as two causes; this is precisely what is meant here by "gathering" (*saṃgraha*).

Two meanings arise: first, it serves as the supporting cause (*ādhāra-hetu*), which is the meaning of "accumulation" (*samudaya*); second, it provides the power that causes [the effect] to arise, which is the meaning of "origination" (*utpāda*).
If [it were] not so... [then], according to the principle, one proves the existence of the eighth [consciousness].

This refers to the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) which, in states such as the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), are not minds arising from the accumulation of seeds that are either defiled or pure.
Supplementary Note: The *Zhongjing* (Zhengfa nianchu jing lun), fascicle 50, states: "The first seven are called evolving consciousnesses. 'Evolving' (*zhuan*) means to transform or shift."
This is not fixed; it refers to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the three objects (*viṣaya*). It is easily shifted and indeterminate (text).
Regarding "the meditative absorption of cessation" (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth, the term "and so forth" includes the five states of mindlessness (*acittaka*).

They are categorized as being more easily transformed and discarded, like a flash of lightning; their nature is not stable, they cannot be perfumed, and they cannot maintain seeds.
Therefore, the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are not the "mind" described in that sutra as the locus where defiled and pure seeds accumulate.

The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: the various evolving consciousnesses are the subject (*dharmin*); they cannot maintain seeds, because they are not the locus where defiled and pure seeds accumulate.

The fundamental tenet regarding the arising of the mind is that it occurs within states such as the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and the like, because there is an interruption [of the mental continuum].

Furthermore, due to the distinct categories of faculties, objects, attention (*manasikāra*), and wholesome states (*kuśala*) and so forth, the mind easily slips away and arises; it does not abide firmly, being comparable to a flash of lightning and the like.

Although the ten sections preceding and following this cite sūtras as evidence, their primary aim is to reveal the underlying principle (*yukti*). Since the intention is to reveal this principle, it cannot be established by mere scriptural authority (*āgama*) alone, but must rely on inference (*anumāna*).

Consequently, one would be unable to determine right from wrong or to verify the heterodox from the orthodox; thus, the application of inference (anumāna) is advanced so that the opponent is silenced and cannot help but develop faith.
Therefore, in the *Pòjiǎn wén* (Refutation of Objections), the three-membered syllogism is employed at every turn to establish conclusions through inferential measurement.
If there is no confusion, then the correct principles of the Mahāyāna will manifest of themselves.
△ Next, the eighth [consciousness] is explained as the mind that maintains the seeds (2). First, the direct explanation (2). First, the positive exposition.
This consciousness is of a single class, constant, and uninterrupted—thus corresponding to the meaning of "mind" (*citta*) as it will be explained there.

[Supplementary Note: To distinguish this from the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*): "of a single class" means it is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), thereby distinguishing it from the different categories of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).

"Constant" distinguishes it from that which is easily abandoned. "Uninterrupted" distinguishes it from that which is intermittent. "Firmly abiding" distinguishes it from that which is not firmly abiding.

This consciousness possesses these aforementioned characteristics; therefore, it is able to maintain the seeds. For this reason, only the eighth consciousness accords with the meaning of the "mind that accumulates and arises" (*ālayavijñāna*) as taught in that sutra.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: This eighth consciousness is a real entity (*dharmin*); its thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is stable, enduring, and capable of being perfumed (*vāsya*).
Because one category [of consciousness] is eternally uninterrupted, it serves as the cause, just like the *eraṇḍa* seed and so forth.

Since they are not the basis for internal seeds, how could they possibly maintain seeds? The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:

**Thesis:** Form and the non-associated factors are phenomena that, by principle, cannot be perfumed (*vāsya*), and thus how could they maintain seeds? **Reason:** Because they are not of the nature of mind (*cittatva*). **Example:** Like sound, light, and so forth.

△ Next, the refutation of divergent interpretations (5). First, the refutation of the view that the categories of consciousness receive perfuming and maintain the seeds (2). First, the presentation [of the opponent's position].
Some say that since the six consciousnesses have existed from beginningless time [up to the present], why is it necessary to insist on the existence of an eighth consciousness-nature?
[Supplementary Note: This is what is clung to by the Hīnayāna. In their school, they admit only a single mind-king;

its functions are six, which are called the six consciousnesses. As for the statement that they depend on the various states of the sense organs and objects throughout preceding and succeeding moments, this refers to a single mind.

O King, as the six faculties, the six objects, mental attention, and the three natures—wholesome and so forth—undergo transformation through their preceding and succeeding states, the six consciousnesses are formed.
Although the entities (vastu) undergo transformation, the types (jāti) remain undifferentiated;

this means that the entity is the very substance (svabhāva) of consciousness, while "type" refers to similarity—that is, the category of consciousness. This implies that the substance of the preceding moment of consciousness brings forth the category of the subsequent moment of consciousness.
It is like the resonance of an echo: although the original sound has already ceased, the lingering resonance still persists; it belongs to the same category as that sound.

The nature of consciousness is likewise: although the substance of consciousness relies upon the sense faculties, objects, and so forth, and undergoes modification and transformation across successive states, its essential category remains without distinction of good or evil, being of a single flavor and without differentiation—this is the transformation of the preceding moment.
Regarding this matter: that which is perfumed by subsequent moments of consciousness as a single, undifferentiated class is the "perfumable" (bhāvyam).

It is capable of maintaining seeds, and thus the relationship between cause and effect is established. Why, then, must one insist on the existence of an eighth consciousness with a nature of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) as that which receives the perfuming and maintains the seeds?

He asks: "What is the reason that there is no meaning [in his claim]? (up to: "It should be unable to sustain the real seeds of internal dharmas."

[Commentary on the Meaning] The first phrase is a general inquiry. "If it is... and so forth constitute the specific refutation. First, the refutation of the wholesome and unwholesome: the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states, "The category..."
If it were either wholesome or unwholesome, it would not be susceptible to perfuming, because it is admitted to be determinate (*vyākṛta*), just like analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

do not let it be that the entity is wholesome or unwholesome while the homogeneous character is indeterminate. Why? Because since the entities possess the distinctions of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), the homogeneous character should be the same.
Because distinct categories must necessarily share the same nature as distinct entities.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: within the state of non-mind (acittaka), since the six consciousnesses are absent, this category [of seeds] certainly does not exist.

△ 3. The Refutation of the Theory that Matter and Mind of Their Own Kind Serve as Seeds for Subsequent Moments (Part 2). First, the introduction:
Some maintain that matter and mind of their own kind arise without interval; [they argue that] the previously stated proofs are therefore unestablished.
Commentary on Terms: The masters of the Sautrāntika school maintain that from a preceding moment of matter, a subsequent moment of matter arises without interval;
and from a preceding moment of mind, a subsequent moment of mind and its associated mental factors arise without interval.

It is asked: When one passes away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), or passes away from the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), or emerges from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), these physical and mental factors have long since ceased.

Once the followers of the Two Vehicles have entered the nirvana without remainder, then at the point of death there is already no matter or mind; by what seed, then, would the subsequent aggregates arise? Therefore...

The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* concludes its refutation by stating: "Since matter and mind arise sequentially from one another, there can only be the conditions of equal-immediate antecedent (*samanantarapratyaya*) and object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*);

They grasp at the principle of the emptiness of dispelling characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) as the final goal; this merely destroys the emotional attachments of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

It is a protective negation (*paryudāsa-pratiṣedha*) that wards off errors, yet they instead negate the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), treating them both as the mere appearance of empty flowers. △ Next, the eighth [topic] clarifies that this is the true maturation (*vipāka*). (3) First, it is shown that there is a true maturation by way of the bodies of sentient beings and their environment.
One must necessarily admit the existence of a truly matured mind (*vipākacitta*); otherwise, based on what dharma could the status of a sentient being be perpetually established?
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: First, it is explained in accordance with principle.

Because of the reasoning above, one must certainly admit the existence of true *vipāka* (maturation), which is the fruit that compensates for projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*), capable of transforming the body and the environment to serve as the support for sentient beings. Next, following the section on the body and environment, it is explained by way of contrast to exclude the sense organs, the body, and the receptacle world;
this is because these do not exist apart from mind and mental factors. "Non-associated phenomena" (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) refers here to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Because the sense faculties, the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are not constantly present, if this mind did not exist, what would transform the body and the vessel-world?
Furthermore, based upon what dharma would one perpetually establish the existence of sentient beings?
△ Next, regarding the experience of physical pleasure and fatigue, it is shown that there truly exists a distinctively matured result (*vipāka*).
Furthermore, whether one is in meditative absorption or not, how could such physical sensations exist at that stage?

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: This means that when one is in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is no discursive thought (*vitarka*); when one is not in concentration, there is discursive thought.
When there is no discursive thought, the body subsequently experiences a sense of ease and the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) arises.

When there is discursive thought, the body subsequently experiences weariness and the feeling of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*) arises. The manifestation of these bodily sensations occurs entirely through the presence of true maturation (*vipāka*).
If this did not exist, such a thing would not occur.

in states where non-Buddhas give rise to other wholesome minds and so forth (up to) when they are permitted to arise, because those are non-Buddha sentient beings.

Oṃ. There still remains a portion of innate clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) that has not been exhausted, and the maturation (*vipāka*) still persists.

the concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like the time when [others] are asserted to give rise to those [minds].

therefore, they too are not the realms of existence. Thus, in summary, none of them can be [the basis for the realms of existence].

△ Third, the proof by way of the Tathāgata not being comprised within the realms of rebirth (*gati*).
Because the Tathāgata is not subsumed under the realms of rebirth, having forever severed all seeds of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: For the reasons stated above, the Buddha does not belong to the realms of rebirth (*gati*), because his karmic maturation (*vipāka*) is already empty.

Nor is he subsumed within the three realms (*dhātu*), because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been eternally exhausted. The two truths of suffering and its origin constitute the cause and effect of the three realms; since the Tathāgata has already abandoned these, he is not included therein.

"Realm" (*dhātu*) carries the sense of "cause," referring specifically to the seeds of the outflows and the seeds of all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*); since these have been eternally severed, [the Buddha] is beyond them.
△ 3. Summary and Conclusion of the Proof.
Since the actual destination of rebirth consists solely of maturation (*vipāka*), one knows that there exists this separate eighth consciousness.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: the five faculties, such as the eye (the *paramārtha-indriya*), along with their physical bases (the *rūpa-pratibhāsa-indriya*), have already ceased in the past and have not yet arisen in the future.

△ Next, the eighth [consciousness] is established as that which possesses appropriation (upādāna). (2) First, the formal establishment:
