△ Next, the distinction:

This statement is intended to show that the evolving consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, are merely the mind of maturation (*vipāka-citta*); therefore, this explanation is given.

Regarding the meaning of the words: The phrase "these evolving consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, do not possess such a quality" does not indicate that they are capable of appropriation (*upādāna*).

Only the ripening consciousness (*vipākacitta*). Why? If it were claimed that only the ripening consciousness functions as the appropriating agent, then since the ripening [consciousness] of the Buddhas has already ceased, would they not lack appropriation?
However, the stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) is also capable of appropriating the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) of the Buddhas.
Therefore, this statement does not indicate that only the ripening consciousness is the appropriating agent. If so, why [is it said otherwise]?

It was previously stated that only the *vipāka*-citta (maturation-consciousness) is capable of appropriation (*upādāna*). However, this statement was made because it is only the *vipāka*-citta that is capable of appropriating the contaminated physical body (*sāsrava-rūpa-kāya*).
△ Next, distinguishing the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and others as not being capable of appropriation (three parts): first, distinguishing the various evolving consciousnesses.

This means that because the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise from present conditions, they are unable to grasp and maintain the contaminated physical body (*sāsrava-rūpakāya*).
Regarding the phonetic meanings: herein there are three syllogisms (*pramāṇa*), all of which take "the inability to grasp and maintain the contaminated physical body" as the thesis (*pakṣa*).
The first syllogism generally clarifies the evolving consciousnesses; the subsequent two syllogisms specifically address their arising from conditions according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
"Arising" excludes that which is not projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*). "That which is not projecting karma" excludes that which is not of a single category;

that is to say, it refers to the two natures of wholesome and defiled, which are summoned by their own power and are not projected by karma—just as the unconditioned state of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is pure by its very nature (*prakṛti-viśuddha*).

It is not manifested by the abandonment of afflictions through the power of wisdom; it is not "pervasive" (vyāpin) because it excludes that which is not pervasive; it is not "continuous" (anubandhin) because it excludes that which is not continuous.
Therefore, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) cannot grasp and maintain the contaminated physical body (*sāsrava-rūpakāya*).
Appendix: Regarding the manifestation of present conditions. It arises by depending upon present conditions; that is to say, visual consciousness arises through nine conditions, and so forth.

the evolving consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, take the various conditions in the present life as their causes. As it is said:
Due to the power of the eye, its object, and attention (*manasikāra*), the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise.
Next, to distinguish them from the mental factors (*caitta*):
the term "consciousnesses" (*vijñāna*) also includes the mental factors, because they are necessarily associated [with consciousness], just as the term "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) does.

This statement is made for fear that someone might claim that while the evolving consciousnesses themselves cannot appropriate, their mental factors might be able to do so; therefore, it further specifies [the subject].
△ Third, the exclusion of the material faculties (*rūpindriya*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
This is because the various material faculties and the non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*), being like space and so forth.

[The term] "resonance" (*pratirava*) refers to the five material faculties; they are that which is appropriated (*upātta*), yet they lack the sense of an appropriator (*upādātṛ*). [They are thus] non-associated formations.

Among these, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth lack a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Although the faculties possess the function of illuminating objects, they lack the sense of being a subjective cognizer;
therefore, like the non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), they have no object of cognition (*ālambana*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

The subject (*dharmin*) is the various material faculties and non-associated formations; the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they cannot be appropriated as a body possessing material faculties, because they lack an object of cognition.
The cause is like the analogy of space and so forth.
△ Third, the summary conclusion establishing the proof:
Therefore, there must separately exist a mind capable of appropriation, and that mind is precisely this eighth consciousness.
△ Five: The Sustenance of Vitality, Warmth, and Consciousness (3). First, citing sūtras to prove their existence:
Furthermore, a sūtra states that there are three—vitality, warmth, and consciousness—[up to] because consciousness would not be able to endure for a long time [if it were not sustained].
Harmonizing the Resonance. First, citing the sutra: "If there were no... and so forth, proving that [the ālayavijñāna] exists.
Second, a detailed explanation based on the meaning (in two parts). First, distinguishing that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) do not maintain life-force, warmth, and consciousness.

This means that the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are intermittent and subject to transformation; therefore, they cannot be established as that which sustains life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

In terms of logical structure: The evolving consciousnesses are the subject (*dharmin*). They cannot be established as that which sustains life-force, warmth, and consciousness—this is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
The reason (*hetu*) is: because they are intermittent and subject to transformation, lacking the function of constant maintenance. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like sound, wind, and so forth.
△ Next, the eighth [consciousness] is explained as that which sustains life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). (2) First, the formal establishment:
Only the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is uninterrupted and non-transformative; therefore, it can be established as that which sustains life-force, warmth, and consciousness.

Commentary on Terms: Regarding the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation-consciousness), because it is the opposite of the various meanings mentioned above, it can be established as that which sustains life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Life-force and warmth are explained as in the first fascicle. Since these two persist for a fixed duration and necessarily function without interruption, they serve as a common analogy (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
The formal logical argument (*prayoga*) may be understood accordingly.
△ Second, the explanation and establishment (in two parts): First, the direct explanation.
The Sūtra states that these three factors mutually support one another; [if it were otherwise], how could the theory of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) possibly accord with correct reasoning?

Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: One might fear that someone could say, "The Sūtra speaks of 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*); this term may refer to the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
By what reasoning is it definitively known to be the eighth consciousness? Therefore, the commentary explains: "The Sūtra states that three factors mutually support one another.

While vitality (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*) belong to a single homogeneous category and are uninterrupted, consciousness alone is not so. How then can it be the same as those? Because it possesses the function of constant maintenance. Thus it is said.
How could it accord with correct principle for the intervening evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and the uninterrupted life-force and warmth to serve as mutual supports?
△ Next, resolving objections (2): first, the objection.
Although it is taught that these three factors mutually support one another, why do you not allow that consciousness alone can arise intermittently?

[Regarding the meaning of the terms: In the Mahāyāna school, it is accepted that *uṣmagata* (heat) does not pervade the three realms, because in the formless realm there is no body and thus no characteristic of heat.
The Hīnayāna school cites *uṣmagata* as an example and objects, saying: "Since the three factors are mutually dependent, and since you accept the factor of heat..."
It does not pervade the three realms. Why then do you not allow that consciousness (*vijñāna*) also functions with interruptions?
△ Second, the explanation [of the two points]: first, the explanation by way of the locus where the three factors are complete.
This does not constitute a fault or difficulty against the preceding principle (until: "therefore, the principle previously stated is thoroughly established").
*Yinyì* (Explanatory Notes on Terms): This means that [the opponent’s] objection fails to hit the mark; therefore, it is said that this is not a valid critique.
Previously, the eighth [consciousness] was established based on the sūtras as that which sustains life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

This is strictly in reference to the fact that at this [level of existence], these three factors are fully present and function simultaneously and without interruption, such that they can constantly sustain one another. If, however, in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) the factor of warmth were absent, then this warmth would no longer exist [there].

It is constantly maintained as a function. By means of the principle that these three factors operate simultaneously and without interruption, the preceding [passage] demonstrates that the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) used in the Sūtra does not refer to the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), but correctly clarifies that the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) possesses the function of constant maintenance.

Now, you cite the fact that the factor of warmth (*uṣman*) is not omnipresent as a challenge; how could this undermine the principle established previously? Why is that? Because when warmth is relinquished, the other two [factors] do not [remain].

Because it is abandoned. Therefore, what I previously stated—that the maintenance of vitality (*āyuḥ*) and warmth (*uṣman*) constitutes an uninterrupted retribution (*ānantarya-vipāka*)—is established as the ultimate principle.
Next, this is explained by way of the fact that warmth does not pervade all locations.
Furthermore, among the three dharmas, there are two: vitality (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*). [Question: At that time, which consciousness is able to sustain that vitality? [Answer:
Warmth is the eighth [consciousness]’s objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*), which is a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*). Vitality is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*);

it is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*) for its own distinct continuum based upon the seeds of the eighth [consciousness] in their actual manifestation (*pravṛtti*). This continues until the maturation (*vipāka*) is exhausted. These two— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]

Since it is always associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), one knows that this consciousness is certainly not untainted (*anāsrava*). This establishes the principle, demonstrating that these three dharmas are necessarily all associated with outflows.
Regarding the phrase "if born in the formless realm" (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is a formal refutation based on the fact that "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) is not universal.

That is to say, when an *anāgāmin* saint is born in the formless realm and gives rise to an untainted mind as the sixth [consciousness], if this [storehouse] consciousness were absent at that time— [The text continues: ...at that time... (the argument follows).
Which consciousness is able to sustain that life-span? It cannot be an untainted (anāsrava) mind, for it would not maintain tainted (sāsrava) seeds.
△ Third, the summary conclusion establishing the proof:
For this reason, we know that there exists a ripening consciousness (vipākavijñāna); [from here until] that consciousness is precisely this eighth consciousness.
△ Section Six: The Mind at the Time of Birth and Death (3). First, citing sūtras to prove its existence:
Furthermore, a sūtra states that for all classes of sentient beings, the mind at the time of birth and death would not exist [if it were otherwise].

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: First, the scripture is cited. It states that for sentient beings, at the time of taking birth and at the time of death, the evolving consciousnesses such as the visual consciousness certainly do not manifest.
They necessarily abide in a state of distracted mind; they possess a mind and are not without a mind, nor is it a state of meditative concentration.
The phrase "If there were no... serves as a reductio ad absurdum to prove its existence.
△ Second, the detailed explanation according to the meaning (2): First, the correct elucidation of the mind at the time of birth and death (2): First, the elucidation of the correct principle (2):
First, distinguishing that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are not the mind at the time of birth and death.
This means that at the time of birth and death, the body and mind are昏昧 (obscured and dull); [this state] must be recognized as being like other times. Regarding the phonology and meaning:

first, by means of the obscuration and dullness of body and mind, it is demonstrated that there are no evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: "At the time of birth and death..."

When the manifesting consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are clearly understood to be necessarily not arising, it is because the body and mind are dull and obscured, as in the states of sleep without dreams or extreme fainting.

Furthermore, below this, the absence of manifesting consciousnesses is demonstrated by the fact that their mental aspects (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) cannot be known. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

In this state, the six types of evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) necessarily do not manifest, because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) and objects of perception (*ālambana*) cannot be known,

as in the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*). By contrast, it is revealed that in the six lower states, they must be knowable, as in ordinary times when one is not in the state of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
△ Next, the eighth [consciousness] is explained as the mind at the time of birth and death.
Because the true *vipākavijñāna* (retributive consciousness) is extremely subtle, it is designated as the "mind of birth and death," which does not contradict correct principle.

Heliang asked: "If that which is called 'non-existent' refers to the fact that the aspects and objects of the six consciousnesses cannot be discerned during the state of birth and death, then why is it not also non-existent that the maturation (vipāka) of the state of birth and death—its aspects and objects—likewise cannot be discerned?"
Answer: It is the true retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). Because it is extremely subtle, both its mode of activity (*ākāra*) and its object (*ālambana*) cannot be discerned.

This does not mean that it is "without mind" (*acitta*); rather, it is called "indiscernible" because this retributive consciousness is the recompense for projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), serving as the sovereign lord of the total retribution (*sāmānyavipāka*).

It continues uninterruptedly throughout a single lifetime (*ekajīvitaparyāya*), remaining eternally without transformation. This very consciousness constitutes both the state of distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*) and the state of having mind (*sacitta*); it is not a state of being without mind.
A concentrated mind; this is what is called the mind at the time of birth and death.
△ Next, the refutation of divergent views (2): First, the divergent views (2). First, the introduction:
Some say that the five consciousnesses are definitely absent in this state (until...), and therefore the mental consciousness is also absent at the stage of taking rebirth.

Explanatory Notes on Terms: "Initial" refers to the stage of taking birth; at this point, the five consciousnesses definitely do not exist. "Inferior to the mental consciousness" means that there is no sixth consciousness.
"Caused by the five consciousnesses" means having the same objects as the five consciousnesses—namely, the present five sensory realms—and being simultaneous with them;

this refers to the simultaneous mental consciousness. "Caused by the instruction of others" means that based on the instruction of another person, one gives rise to either false or correct reflection. This...
This refers to the state of dispersion. Regarding the claim that the independent *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) is necessarily the cause:
this refers to the state of meditative absorption within the various *dhyānas* and *samādhis*, wherein the independent *manovijñāna*—meaning the arising of the sixth *manovijñāna*—is present.

Since these three causes for the state of birth cannot be found in those states, there is likewise no *manovijñāna* at the moment of taking birth. How, then, can it be said that [the *manovijñāna*] undergoes birth?
At the end of life, one must necessarily abide in a state of distracted consciousness (*vikṣipta-citta*).
[Supplementary Note: At the stage of taking birth, there is no conscious awareness; this is identical to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.

However, to falsely claim that there is no conscious awareness because three causes cannot be found constitutes a divergent theory, as it fails to believe in the existence of the eighth [consciousness].
The seeds within consciousness serve as the cause, yet [the opponent] separately posits the three causes, such as the five sensory consciousnesses, as the cause;
therefore, this is refuted by the Mahāyāna.
△ Next, the refutation [of the second position]. First, the direct refutation.

If that were so, when sentient beings are born in the formless realm, there would necessarily be no inducement for either meditative or non-meditative states of mind to arise, as there would be no basis for their occurrence.
[Note on Meaning]: "If that were so" (*yadi tarhi*) restates the previously held position; it means that at the moment of taking birth, because the various causes are absent...
Mental consciousness would not arise. If sentient beings were born within the formless realm, mental consciousness would never arise again thereafter.

Why? Because a concentrated mind must be induced by the preparatory application of a distracted mind, and a distracted mind must be induced by the five sensory consciousnesses or by the instruction of another;
yet in that realm, neither the induction of concentration nor distraction exists, as there is no means for them to occur.
[It] arises. Since the three causes are absent, it will never arise again.
△ Next, the refutation of the defense:
If one were to claim that it necessarily arises through the power of habitual practice (up to this point), then this is simply the aforementioned cause; why labor to state it separately?
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: First, the opponent’s defense is cited. That defense states:

"Although that realm lacks the power to induce either concentrated or distracted minds, nevertheless, due to the force of habitual practice from former lives, those concentrations subsequently manifest spontaneously. This initial point is now refuted.

If it arises due to habitual practice, why would it not manifest at the very moment of initial birth? Why wait for a later time? Furthermore, one may use the lower realms as an analogy to refute [the opponent's position]:

since it is admitted that in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) a concentrated mind manifests suddenly through the power of habitual practice, then in the desire and form realms (*kāmadhātu* and *rūpadhātu*), at the time of first taking birth, the consciousness habituated [to concentration] should likewise manifest; why should this alone not be the case?

If it is argued that at the moment of initial birth, because of mental dullness and obscurity, the mental consciousness does not immediately manifest—this is precisely what was stated previously regarding the dullness and obscurity of body and mind, wherein the evolving consciousnesses do not appear; why then labor to state this separately?
△ Next, other schools.
There are other schools who maintain that the states of birth and death, etc., do not apply to the consciousness that is universally established (*prasiddha*), and thus it is not so.
[Regarding] the sounds and meanings: the preceding section provides the narrative; one should know that the following section applies generally.
△ Second, the specific explanation of the mind at the time of death (in two parts). First, the presentation of the thesis:
Furthermore, at the time of death, due to wholesome and unwholesome karma... [up to] ...the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are unable to maintain the body.

*Yuyi* (Explanation of Terms): The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: Furthermore, for one who has committed evil deeds at the time of death, consciousness departs from the upper parts of the physical basis (*āśraya*), and a sensation of coldness arises sequentially from the upper parts, whereby [the body] is gradually abandoned.
Conversely, for one who has performed virtuous deeds, consciousness departs from the lower parts of the physical basis, and a sensation of coldness arises sequentially from the lower parts.
It gradually arises; in this way it is gradually relinquished, even unto the location of the mind. One should know that the final consciousness is relinquished solely at the location of the mind.
From this point, the sensation of cold pervades the entire basis.
Supplement: The fifty-first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "For what reason is it illogical for consciousness to exist at the time of death if the ālayavijñāna does not exist?
It is because at the time of death, either from the upper parts of the body, consciousness gradually departs and a sensation of coldness gradually arises;
or from the lower parts of the body, consciousness gradually departs and a sensation of coldness gradually arises."
It is not that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) sometimes does not arise; therefore, we know that only the *ālayavijñāna* is capable of maintaining the body through appropriation (*upādāna*).
If this were abandoned, the sensation of coldness would immediately arise in the bodily parts, and the body would be devoid of sensory awareness. The mental consciousness is not like this.
Therefore, it is illogical if the *ālayavijñāna* does not exist.
△ Second, the explanation and establishment (in two parts). First, the refutation that the evolving consciousnesses do not produce the sensation of cold.
Because the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, have distinct bases, the sensation of cold should not arise from them gradually.
Commentary on the Terms: "Each has its own distinct basis" means to exclude those that are not universal bases;

that is, eye-consciousness relies on the eye-faculty, and so on, up to body-consciousness relying on the body-faculty. "Or does not function" means that at times, due to a deficiency in conditions, it does not manifest.
"Does not abide in the body" refers to the sixth consciousness, which does not rely on the five material faculties but relies solely on the mind-faculty. Regarding the object...

Regarding "concentration" (*samādhi*): whether it be matter or mind, or objects of the past, present, or future, because it universally takes all things as its object and is constantly continuous, being fully resident within the body—as the Sūtra says:
"That mind is always present in the various sense faculties, following after their respective objects without ever abandoning them.
Since the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, possess these characteristics, they should not be regarded as insentient.
Contact arises gradually from that.
Next, the eighth [consciousness] is explained as being able to produce cold contact.
Only the *vipāka*-mind, by the power of prior karma, [continues] until—though it transforms and takes objects—it is not appropriated (*anupātta*).

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: Only the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-citta*) is capable of appropriation (*upādāna*). When it relinquishes the locus of appropriation, the sensation of coldness arises. Why?
Because life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are inseparable; where there is no consciousness, there is no warmth.

The place where the sensation of coldness arises—like the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*)—is insentient (*acetana*). Although this consciousness undergoes transformation, it nevertheless takes that [coldness] as its object.
And it is not appropriated.
△ Third, the summary that establishes the proof:
Therefore, one knows that this eighth consciousness definitely exists.
△ Section 7: The Basis of Dependent Origination (3). First, citing sūtras to prove its existence:
Furthermore, a sūtra states that "consciousness conditions name-and-form" (up to the point where it says) that the self-substance of that consciousness would not exist [if this were not so].

Exegesis on Terms: First, the scripture is cited from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: Question: For what reason are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) established as being mutually conditioned?
Answer: In the present life, consciousness takes name-and-form as its condition; furthermore, in the subsequent life, name-and-form takes consciousness as its condition.
Why is this so? Because when there is a continuity [of existence] within the mother’s womb, [these two function reciprocally].

This is because they are explained as being mutually conditioned. With consciousness as a condition, the semen, blood, and so forth within the mother’s womb are grasped by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and through their conjunction, they form the nature of the *kalala*. This is how name-and-form acts as a condition, further causing that consciousness to abide therein.
This is the meaning of these two phenomena being mutually dependent and evolving simultaneously. If [the latter] were absent...
Establishing the proof.
△ Next, the detailed explanation according to the meaning (in two parts): First, citing the sūtra for explanation.
That is to say, within that sūtra, it provides this own explanation: [omitted] "...they always function simultaneously and are never separated from one another."

**Explanatory Notes on Phonetics and Meaning:** The four aggregates other than form (*rūpa*) are feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

*Kalala* is translated here as "impure mixture," referring to the impurity of the parents' red and white elements which form a mixture; this constitutes the first stage. It is equal to the remaining four stages.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "In the beginning is the *kalala*, which is translated as 'thin curd'; next arises the *arbuda*, which is translated as 'blister'."
From this, *peśī* arises; this is translated as "soft flesh. From *peśī*, *ghanā* arises; this is translated as "firm flesh.

The fifth stage is *praśākhā*; this is translated as "limbs and joints. These five stages are all included within the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). This fifth stage is also subsumed under the link of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The three subsequent stages are all the link of the six sense bases: the sixth is the stage of hair, body hair, and nails; the seventh... [is the stage of the formation of the sense organs].

Regarding the stage of the faculties (*indriya*) and the eight stages of form (*rūpa*): if one takes a single lifetime, all are subsumed under name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Consequently, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) all belong to name-and-form;
thus, it says "and so forth. As for "like bundles of reeds": it is like setting up two bundles of reeds so that they lean against each other at both ends;

only then can they stand upright. If one is removed, the other falls eastward; if the other is removed, this one falls westward. Name-and-form and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are mutually dependent in this same way.
It is likewise so.
△ Next, the explanation of the treatise (in two parts). First, explaining that the eighth consciousness is the condition for name-and-form (nāmarūpa) (in two parts). First, the direct explanation:

The evolving consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, are subsumed within "name" (*nāman*); if this [eighth] consciousness did not exist, what could be designated as "consciousness"?
*Yinyi* (Explanations of Terms), Volume 47 of the *Zongjing*: It quotes the Hīnayāna as saying, "I take the six consciousnesses to be the support for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);

why is an eighth [consciousness] required? The Master of the Treatise says: "The six consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, are already subsumed within 'name' (*nāman*) because they constitute the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
However, it is necessary to have an eighth [consciousness] to serve as the external branch of consciousness that acts as the support for name-and-form."
Eighth, if these did not exist, what would be designated as "consciousness"?
[This is like] the echo of a response. The *Huayan chao* states: "If one says that the four aggregates are 'name' (nāma) and the kalala and so forth are 'form' (rūpa)..."
Thus, the consciousness that serves as the basis for actualization is also solely the *ālayavijñāna*.

Furthermore, it is said that since the four non-material aggregates (*skandhas*) constitute "name" (*nāman*), the member of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is already present within the member of "name"; therefore, the eighth consciousness is established as the member of "consciousness."
△ Next, the refutation of the defense:

It cannot be said that [the intermediate state] is called the "aggregate of consciousness" (vijñāna-skandha), because during the sixth stage, the kalala, the five sensory consciousnesses do not exist.

Regarding the meaning of the terms, Qingliang says: Fearing that one might further defend [this position] by claiming it is called the "aggregate of consciousness" because it consists of the five [consciousnesses] such as the eye-consciousness...
This refers to the limb of consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is the sixth [limb]. Therefore, it is refuted by stating, "nor can it be said," and so forth.

This indicates that during the *kalala* stage within the first seven days, the sense faculties (*indriya*) are not yet complete and objects (*viṣaya*) have not yet appeared before them; this is according to both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.

This is because it is universally accepted that the first five consciousnesses do not exist [at that stage]. In the Mahāyāna, the sixth consciousness is designated as the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) within the context of "name.
△ Next, the evolving consciousnesses are distinguished from being the condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Furthermore, because the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) arise intermittently, how could they be said to always serve as the condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)?
△ Third, summary conclusion establishing the proof:
Therefore, the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the eighth consciousness.
Supplementary Explanations of Pronunciations for the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only), Scroll Three.

Pronunciation Guide: *Ying* (pronounced *ying*): [The character for] "infant. *Chou* (pronounced *chou*): [The character for] "counting" (*suan*). *Meng* (pronounced *meng*): [The character for] "dimness"; it refers to the eyes being unclear. *Shi* (pronounced *shi*): [The character for] "speed"; it refers to a horse moving swiftly. *Shen* (level tone): [The character for] "depth"; it refers to water gathering and being profound. It is the opposite of "shallow" (*qian*).

Yě (pronounced ruì; meaning profound clarity and thorough understanding). Hūn (rhyme with hūn; pronounced hūn; meaning the mind is not clear). Chuàn (rhyme with chuàn; pronounced chuàn; meaning to pierce or to thread through).
Luò (rhyme with luò in the departing tone; pronounced luò; meaning to patrol or to obstruct).

△ The Essential Nature of the Eight Consciousnesses as Food (3). First, citing sutras to prove its existence:
Furthermore, a sutra states that for all sentient beings... [omitted] ...because that essential nature of consciousness as food would otherwise not exist.
*Yinyì* (Explanatory Notes on Phonology and Meaning). First, the scripture is cited: "Food" (*āhāra*) has the meaning of "sustaining and benefiting" and the meaning of "maintaining.

Because of this food, it is able to maintain the bodies and lives of sentient beings within the three realms; therefore, it is said that "all depend upon food for their existence. The phrase "If there were no... below serves as proof for the existence of the eighth [consciousness].
△ Second, the detailed explanation according to the meaning (in two parts). First, a general clarification of the characteristics of the four nutriments (in two parts). First, the general statement:
The Sūtra states that there are four kinds of nutriment.
Supplement: The second fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "There are six kinds of supports (*niśraya*).
The sixth is the support of nutriment (*āhāra-niśraya*), which refers to the four nutriments: first, edible food; second, contact-food; third, volitional-food; and fourth, consciousness-food.
Because they sustain the bodies of sentient beings, they are called 'supports. Furthermore, the fifty-seventh fascicle states: 'The Sūtra says there are four...'"
All types of food are capable of nourishing the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

That is to say, by means of these four kinds of nutriment, one nourishes the five material sense faculties, the mental faculty (*manas*), as well as all the primary elements upon which those faculties depend.
△ Next, the detailed explanation (in four parts). First, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
1. Edible food has "transformation through decay" as its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), because when it has decayed, matter (*rūpa*) is no longer functional.

*Saṃghāta* (composite) refers to "divisions" (*kavaḍa*). This is because each individual portion can be swallowed and consumed. Regarding its characteristic of transformation and decay (*vipariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*):
this means that such composite food must necessarily undergo transformation after being swallowed before it can function as food. This is intended to provide a further explanation below.
"Bound to the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) means that composite food exists only in the desire realm. "Fragrance" (*gandha*) refers to a pleasant aroma.
Odor; taste refers to tastes such as sweet and pungent; touch refers to tactile sensations such as cold and heat. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Therefore, edible food is subsumed under three bases (*āyatana*); it functions as food at the time of transformation and decay. The sixty-sixth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"By means of odor, taste, and touch, if they are properly digested and transformed, they can nourish [the body]; if they are not properly digested and transformed, then..."

It serves to diminish [the body]. When various types of food, at the time of swallowing, cause the mind to rejoice and the sense faculties to be gladdened, at that moment it is not called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), but is instead called "contact as nutriment" (*sparśa-āhāra*).

Once it has been consumed and is being digested and transformed in a state of well-being, increasing joy and pleasure—at the time of this digestion and transformation, it is then called edible food. (Text) By this, those that are not [edible food] are excluded below.

Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that the sense-field of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) is not established [as food], because it only brings about benefit or harm when it reaches the stage of transformation through taste, potency, and maturation.
Although the color of food may be beautiful, its color serves no purpose at the time of transformation. This is for the sake of enlightening the ignorant.
Question: What constitutes the essence of this edible food? Answer: It has the three objects—odor, flavor, and tangibility—as its essence. Question:
Why do the two objects of form and sound not constitute its essence? Answer: The visual and auditory consciousnesses apprehend their objects through contact at a distance (*viprakṛṣṭa-grahaṇa*).

Since the objects of form and sound do not come into contact with the sense organs, they cannot nourish the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the various organs; therefore, they do not constitute its essence. [The same applies to] the olfactory and gustatory [consciousnesses].

The three [types of nutriment] pertaining to the body apprehend their objects through contact; because the object and the sense faculty meet, they are able to sustain the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the faculties.

Therefore, the three types of sensory objects (*viṣaya*) specifically constitute the essence of nutriment. Question: What is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*)? Answer: Its characteristic is transformation and decay (*vipariṇāma*).

This means that it is only at the time when odor, taste, and touch undergo transformation and decay that they are able to nourish and develop the sense faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Qingliang asked: "Does food act only in relation to the body faculty, or does it also relate to the other faculties? He replied: "First, it nourishes the body faculty; once that has been sustained, [it subsequently benefits the others]."
Subsequently, they nourish the remaining faculties so that consciousness may arise with clarity and sharpness.

Supplement: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle five, states: "Furthermore, as for the enjoyment of food and drink, it refers to the maintenance of the life-span of sentient beings—both those about to be born and those already born—within the three realms.
In this regard, one should know that there are three [factors]: contact (*sparśa*), mental volition (*manas-karma*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)."
Because of the various kinds of food, the life-span of all sentient beings within the three realms is sustained.
Only one kind of food—edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra)—sustains the life-span of sentient beings in the desire realm. Furthermore, among the sentient beings in the hells, there is a subtle edible food;
namely, a subtle moving wind within their internal organs. By virtue of this cause and condition, they are able to endure for a long time. [As for] the hungry ghosts...
Among animals and humans, there is coarse, substantial food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) which they consume by dividing it into portions.
Furthermore, there is subtle food, namely that of sentient beings dwelling in stages such as the *kalala*, as well as the various devas of the desire realm;
once they have consumed this, all substantial food flows into every limb and joint of their bodies and is immediately digested, leaving no remainder.
Excrement and urine.
△ Second, the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*).
Second, the nutriment of contact has the characteristic of contacting objects (up to: ...and because it is superior in providing nourishment through equanimity that is conducive to benefit).

*Yinyì* (Explanation of Terms): "Contact" (*sparśa*) refers to one of the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-citta-dharma*). Its characteristic is that it enables the mind and its concomitants to come into contact with their objects.

There is an interpretive gloss [in the commentary] stating: "Regarding 'tainted contact' (*sāsrava-sparśa*)," this distinguishes it from contact associated with untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*).

Regarding "that which can grasp and receive joy and so forth, serving as the function of nutriment," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 57, states: "Contact is able to grasp and receive either joy..."

Whether it be pleasure (*sukha*) or equanimity (*upekṣā*), [the latter] encompasses both the adverse and the favorable; this [equanimity] is associated with joy (*prīti*) and pleasure, and thus constitutes a portion that is favorable and beneficial.

By means of this, it is further able to provide benefit and support to all consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). Because it provides such benefit and support, it is further able to nourish the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

This is distinguished from the [other types of] contact (*sparśa*) mentioned below. The *Zhengjing* (Mirror of Orthodoxy), fascicle 50, states: "The essence of this nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) pervades all eight consciousnesses. Although it pervades them..."

Regarding the association with the various consciousnesses, for those belonging to the six consciousnesses, the meaning of "nutriment" (*āhāra*) is particularly predominant. This is because the objects they contact are coarse and manifest;
because they can specifically sustain the feelings of joy and pleasure (*sukha*); and because they can produce equanimity (*upekṣā*) that is beneficial to the body.

This constitutes the sense of being "predominant. In contrast, the contact associated with the seventh and eighth consciousnesses has subtle objects and is entirely incapable of producing the feelings of joy and pleasure.

Although one may give rise to the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), it is neither detrimental nor beneficial; for this reason, it is shown that contact (*sparśa*) gives rise to sorrow and suffering, and not to an equanimity that accords with benefit.
Thus, it is not the essence of nutriment (*āhāra*), as it does not provide sustenance (text). For example, seeing forms and becoming attached to them is called "nutriment";
likewise, watching plays and the like while fasting all day without hunger—all these are instances of the meaning of the nutriment of contact.
△ Third, nutriment of mental volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*).
It has the characteristic of aspiration through the mental faculty (*manas*). This is because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses a preeminent aspiration toward its objects.

*Supplement:* "Mental volition" refers to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) mental engagement with volition (*cetanā*). If it resides in the stage of the mind (*manobhūmi*), it is capable of engaging with objects.

Volition (*cetanā*). Among these universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), volition and among the object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyata*), desire (*chanda*)—these two always function together, because [volition] is able to aspire toward those desirable objects.
Because of this aspiration, it is able to nourish the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Although volition functions together with desire, why is it called "the nutriment of volition" alone? *Kaimeung* (Opening the Ignorant) asks: Why is desire not considered a nutriment? The answer: Because it is merely deliberation (*vitarka*).
[The mind] benefits the faculties because it possesses the capacity for volition. Question: Please cite the matter of how reflection serves as nutriment. Answer:

It is like using suspended sand to treat hunger or longing for plums to quench thirst; these all derive from the nourishment provided by reflection to increase the magnitude of the faculties—this is precisely what is meant. Question:

Since reflection is also a universal mental factor (sarvatraga) and is present in all eight consciousnesses, which consciousness’s reflection is [the one under discussion]? Answer: That of the sixth consciousness is predominant.
△ Fourth, the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).

"Fourth" refers to the nutriment of consciousness, which has the characteristic of maintaining [the body]. This is because it possesses the preeminent power of maintaining a continuous stream of a single category [of existence].
Supplement: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 94, states: "Fourth is the nutriment of consciousness, which is able to maintain and appropriate all..."
Regarding the faculties (*indriya*), the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*):

because consciousness is able to appropriate (*upādāna*) the faculties, the primary elements, and consciousness itself, it causes those faculties, the primary elements, along with life-force (*āyus*) and heat (*uṣman*), to abide without departing from the body. For this reason, it is said that consciousness is the cause of their abiding (text).
The *Kaimeng* states: "By the power of the functional influence (*sāmarthya*) of the three aforementioned nutriments (*āhāra*), consciousness is able to nourish and sustain them."

The sense faculties (*indriya*) and the great elements (*mahābhūta*) constitute the food of sustenance (*āhāra*). (Text) This consciousness (*vijñāna*) excludes its own substance (*svabhāva*), which is the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).

Question: Since the term "consciousness" refers to all consciousnesses in general, and since the meaning of "consciousness" is the same for all, why is only the eighth consciousness designated as "consciousness-food"?
Answer: It is because the eighth consciousness alone is a single, continuous stream, and its function of grasping and maintaining [the body] is particularly predominant.
△ Section Three: A Summary of the Three Categories (2). First, a summary according to the three aggregates (*skandha*).
Accordingly, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that these four nutriments (*āhāra*) are called "nutriments" because they cause [the body] not to perish and sustain it.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: Regarding the inclusion [of the four nutriments] within the three aggregates (*skandha*), five bases (*āyatana*), and eleven elements (*dhātu*), the *Qingliang Chao* states: "Edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) belongs to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Contact (*sparśa*) and volition (*cetanā*) belong to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Consciousness-food (*vijñānāhāra*) is like the [aggregate of] name (*nāman*). Edible food consists of the three bases of odor, taste, and tangibility; contact and volition consist of the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*);

and consciousness consists of the base of mind (*manāyatana*). Edible food is subsumed under three elements; contact and volition under the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); and consciousness under the seven mental elements."
The elements (the six consciousness-elements and the mind-base element). These four are the lower fetters.
△ Next, judging according to the three realms:
edible food has utility only in the desire realm (up to: it functions based on consciousness and follows the presence or absence of consciousness).
Commentary on the Terms: That which is called the "desire realm" (kāmadhātu) is so designated because it possesses food, sleep, and sexual desire.
Since these three do not exist in the form and formless realms, edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra) is functional only within the desire realm.

Although the two factors of contact (sparśa) and volition (cetanā) are subsumed under the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika) and thus pervade all three realms, they are absent where there is no associated consciousness; therefore, they follow the six consciousnesses.
They are thus categorized as existing or non-existing. Because the food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) is all-pervasive, it is omitted here from discussion.
Supplementary Note: Regarding whether [the other foods] exist or not in accordance with consciousness: for example, in the First Dhyāna, the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue are absent;

consequently, the two foods of contact (*sparśa*) and volition (*manasikāra*), which are associated with those two consciousnesses, are also absent. Only those associated with the eye, ear, body, and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) exist.
The two sustenances of contact (*sparśa*) and volition (*manasikāra*) should be understood as follows: from the second dhyāna upward, the first five consciousnesses are absent;

there are only the sustenances of contact and volition associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). In the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), the sixth consciousness is absent, and thus there are no sustenances associated with it.

Although there are the sustenances of contact and volition associated with the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, their function as sustenance is not predominant; they possess only the sustenance of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).

△ Second, a specific explanation of the nature of the consciousness-nutriment (vijñānāhāra). (2) First, distinguishing that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are not the nature of the consciousness-nutriment. (2) First, the formal distinction:
The evolving consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, are intermittent and subject to transformation... [omitted] ...all sentient beings subsist by depending upon nutriment.

Commentary on Terms: First, the headings are presented; that is, there is no further explanation below. First, it clarifies that there are interruptions in the state of mindlessness. "Even if" and so forth:
next, it clarifies that there are transformations in the state of having a mind.

This means that the faculties which serve as the basis are not identical, the objects which are perceived are not uniform, the natures are either wholesome or unwholesome, the realms consist of the three realms, and the stages consist of the nine stages. Such various factors undergo transformation.
Because it is easy [to refute]. "All those who hold... and below: this concludes the refutation of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Next, the refutation of divergent views (4): First, the refutation of the claim that past and future consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) and so forth serve as nutriment.
This is because they do not exist during states without mind (*acittaka*), and because past and future things—such as space (*ākāśa*) and the like—are not of the nature of nutriment.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: Their calculation is as follows. They argue:

"Even though consciousness does not manifest during the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), because there is consciousness and mental factors (*caitta*) belonging to the past and future, one takes these very things as nutriment. Why would this be unacceptable?

Why must the eighth [consciousness] necessarily be posited as the nutriment of consciousness? Therefore, they establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to refute this, stating: "The consciousnesses and so forth of the past and future are the subject (*dharmin*)."
The position that the state of being without mind (*acittaka*) constitutes nutriment is not tenable. The reason is that it is neither present nor permanent, and lacks both essence and function;

thus, it is like a flower in the sky (*khapuṣpa*). The phrase "even if it were" introduces a concessive refutation: even if past and future consciousnesses possessed essence and function, they would nonetheless not be present.
Nor is it of the nature of nutriment. For that which functions as nutriment must necessarily be present.
Second, the refutation of the mind in meditative absorption (*samāhita-citta*) and so forth as being nutriment:
one cannot say that the mind in meditative absorption and so forth [is nutriment], because it has already been fully established that what is past is not nutriment.

Regarding the "Explanation of Terms": as for the phrase "the mind and mental factors of entering meditative absorption," this refers to the preparatory minds and their associated mental factors prior to the actual absorption.

Fearing that others might further speculate that these preparatory minds and so forth constitute the nutriment for sentient beings in a state of non-consciousness, [the author] refutes this by stating:
"Nor can it be said... and so forth.
△ Third, [the opponent] breaks [the argument] by claiming that non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) function as nutriment.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that non-associated dharmas such as the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) are not substantially existent.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: One might fear that [the opponent] will again argue as follows:

"Since the Sūtra states that the food of dhyāna-joy (*dhyānāhāra*) exists, and since the two concentrations—the non-conceptual (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)—are formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), they may indeed serve as the food for those who have entered these two concentrations.

Therefore, [the author] refutes this by saying, "Furthermore, it cannot be said... and so forth. Why? Because formations dissociated from mind are not included among the four types of food, such as edible morsels (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).

Because [these factors] are subsumed [within other categories]. Furthermore, non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are provisionally established based on the states (*avasthā*) of matter and mind;
apart from matter and mind, they do not possess a real substantial entity.
△ Fourth, the refutation of the sixth consciousness as nutriment (in two parts): First, the introduction.

There are those who maintain that even in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and similar states, the sixth consciousness still exists and can function as nutriment for that sentient being.
△ Next, the refutation [of this view], first consisting of a general censure and a reference to the detailed exposition.
That position is irrational and shall be refuted in detail later.
[In the] detailed refutation following the "resonance" (pratirava), only the existence of a sixth consciousness within the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is refuted.
△ Next, a specific refutation based on meaning (three parts): first, the refutation of untainted consciousness (*anāsravavijñāna*) as nutriment.
Furthermore, they should explain that for those born in the two higher realms (up to the Peak of Existence), [the sixth consciousness] cannot serve as nutriment for their bodies and lives.

Regarding the commentary on the meaning of "they should explain": this is a rhetorical question. "They" refers to those who claim that the sixth consciousness exists within the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and serves as its nutriment.

If a person who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is born into the two higher realms and gives rise to an untainted (*anāsrava*) sixth consciousness, the tainted sixth consciousness no longer exists.

At that time, one must explain what serves as its nutriment. Fearing that they might calculate that the untainted mental consciousness itself serves as the nutriment, [the text] refutes this by stating:
"Untainted consciousness, etc. (and so forth). One should understand that this refers to the state prior to the realization of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

All physical life is entirely comprised of outflows (āsrava). Even if one were to sustain that physical life with an outflow-free mental consciousness (anāsrava-manovijñāna), it would constitute a contradiction between the obstacle and its antidote;
therefore, it is said that "it destroys existence."
△ Next, the refutation of the existence of contaminated seeds as food:
It is also untenable to maintain that within uncontaminated consciousness (until the point where it is said) it cannot maintain contaminated seeds.
[Commentary on the Meaning]: Fearing that the opponent might offer this defense: "Within uncontaminated consciousness, there exist contaminated seeds; these very contaminated seeds..."
It can serve as food for them; therefore, it does not destroy the contaminated body and life. The refutation states:

"Nor can one cling to [them] as equal," etc., which expresses the underlying intention: namely, that uncontaminated consciousness is like nirvāṇa—pure and untainted—and cannot sustain those contaminated, defiled seeds.
Since the contaminated seeds do not even exist, what could serve as its food?
△ Third, the refutation that body and life-sustenance mutually serve as food for one another.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that sentient beings of the higher realms [possess such things], because their *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous character) and so forth lack substantial reality.

Regarding the meaning of the term: furthermore, fearing that one might offer a defense by saying, "Sentient beings of the higher realms sustain their lives with their bodies, and sustain their bodies with their lives," [the author] provides this refutation.
They thus take one another as food. [The opponent] refutes this, saying: "Because those two—bodily food and life-sustaining food—are not included among the four nutriments;

furthermore, in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), no physical body currently exists, and since there would be nothing capable of sustaining the life of those sentient beings, what would serve as their nutriment?
Since the homogeneous character (nikāyasabhāga) and so forth lack substantial reality (*dravya*), just like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), they likewise cannot sustain the body."
△ Next, it is explained that the maturation (vipāka) is the substance of the consciousness-nutriment (*vijñānāhāra*). (2) First, the direct explanation:
From this, it is definitively known that [it] is distinct from the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*)... [until] all sentient beings subsist by depending on nutriment.
△ Next, the general resolution of objections.
[The text states: "Sentient beings are established solely by relying on the appropriated aggregates" (up to) "it should be known that all are spoken of in reliance upon manifestations.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Words:* Question: All sentient beings subsist by relying on nutriment (*āhāra*), and the Buddha likewise relies on nutriment; therefore, he must be a sentient being.

Regarding "sentient beings" (*sattva*): the commentary explains that the designation "sentient being" is established solely based on the presence of outflows (*āsrava*). Since the Buddha is without outflows, he is not included among sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is asked: the Sūtra states that the Buddha is the supreme among all sentient beings; is this not then a sentient being? The commentary explains:
when it is said that sentient beings dwell by relying on nutriment (*āhāra*), one should know that these are all spoken of in terms of conventional manifestation (*saṃdarśana*).
△ Third, the summary conclusion establishing the proof.
Since the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is of the nature of the supreme nutriment, that consciousness is precisely this eighth consciousness.
△ Ninth, the existence of mind during the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). (3) First, citing scripture to prove its existence.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that for one who dwells in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) must not be absent from the body.
Regarding the meaning of the terms: the first citation refers to the sūtra. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Great Canon), fascicle 47, explains:

"For a noble one who has entered the attainment of cessation, the activities of body, speech, and mind are all extinguished. Inhalation and exhalation are the preparatory applications (*prayoga*) of the body; sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*) are..."
Mental application (*citta-prayoga*) consists of vitarka and vicāra, which are the application of speech. These three types of application are associated with the sixth consciousness;
because they are all extinguished within the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), yet life-force (*āyus*) does not perish, it resides upon the seeds of the eighth consciousness.
There is a function that maintains the continuity of the physical form and mind of a single lifetime without interruption, which is called "life-force" (*āyus*). It is also not separate from "warmth.
Warmth is the eighth [of the ten] objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness; thus, both of these dharmas are inseparable from the eighth consciousness.

Since one is within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the six groups of consciousness, as well as bodily, vocal, and mental formations, are all non-functional; yet, the presence of life-force and warmth therein clarifies [the existence of the eighth consciousness].

"Knowledge" refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). It serves as the basis for life-force (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*). "If it were not... and so forth, proves the existence of the eighth consciousness.
Next, the detailed explanation based on the meaning (in two parts): First, clarifying that the eighth consciousness exists within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

First, clarifying through the meaning that there is consciousness in the absorption of cessation (in two parts): First, clarifying that the eighth consciousness within the meditative state is the consciousness that does not depart from the body.

This refers to the fact that the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the eye-consciousness and other sensory cognitions are coarse and mobile. (Up to: On what basis is it said that consciousness does not depart from the body?

Regarding the meaning of the terms: first, to explain in accordance with the principle, for one who abides in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) must necessarily cease. If this were not the case, it would conversely imply [the opposite].

It is certainly the eighth consciousness that does not depart from the body. If this is not admitted, then according to what meaning is it stated in that sūtra that consciousness does not depart from the body?
Next, [the author] refutes the claim that consciousness is said not to depart from the body because it arises again at a later time.

If it is argued that at a later time that consciousness arises again—just as life-force (*āyus*) and heat (*uṣman*) are in fact not separated from the body—the commentary on the words and meanings first restates this position, fearing a defense might be offered:
"In the case of one who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), at the initial moment of entering the concentration, those six consciousnesses are extinguished;
yet when subsequently emerging from the concentration, the six consciousnesses arise again, like a tertian malaria. Although the malaria temporarily subsides, the root of the disease remains."
[The consciousness] still remains; this is called "not departing from the body. That consciousness is likewise so. This is then refuted below:

if it were to arise again later and thus be called "not departing from the body," then the Sūtra should not have stated that "mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) have ceased. Why? Because consciousness and perception (*saṃjñā*), etc., necessarily arise and cease together.
If you claim that consciousness ceases and then arises again later, [and thus] is called "not departing from the body," then even though mental formations have ceased, later...

It also arises again. Why then would consciousness not be called "not separated from the body"? Vitality (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and the sense faculties (*indriya*) should likewise arise again after having ceased, just like consciousness.
If that were so, then at the very moment one enters meditative absorption, one would be no different from a corpse; this would constitute a great error.
We have seen that when a person's lifespan, warmth, and faculties have ceased, they may yet be reborn;
therefore, one must admit the existence of an eighth [consciousness] which truly does not depart from the body, and thus there is no such fault.
△ Next, refuting the claim that there is no consciousness at all in the meditative absorption of cessation (3): First, refuting the total absence of consciousness.
Furthermore, if within this state there were no consciousness whatsoever... how could it be said that one is "dwelling in the meditative absorption of cessation"?

Regarding the explanation of the terms: it is said that within this state, all those consciousnesses are extinguished. If the eighth consciousness were not admitted, then there would be no consciousness at all.

If there were no consciousness whatsoever, it would be like an insentient object such as a tile or a stone; how then could the sūtras describe one who is in the meditative attainment of cessation as a sentient being?
△ Next, the refutation of the absence of the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
Furthermore, if the ripening consciousness were absent at this stage, [rebirth] would be impossible, because there is no rebirth apart from relying upon another body. [Query:
To what would that [consciousness] belong? [Response: Within the state of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is not admitted that there exists anything capable of maintaining [the continuity].
Regarding consciousness: for one who dwells in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the sense faculties, vitality, and warmth are all utterly destroyed.

As for the consciousness spoken of in the sūtras as "not departing from the body," to which does it belong? For what reason? Because once consciousness has departed from this body to take up residence in another body, it never again returns to be born in this body.
Supplement: The previous position held that if consciousness were absent, all consciousnesses would be entirely non-existent; therefore, it was refuted by using tiles and pebbles as an analogy.

This [current] position holds that while consciousness is absent, there is merely no *vipāka* (maturation); it demonstrates that the sixth consciousness exists and arises again upon emerging from meditative absorption;
therefore, it is refuted by the argument that consciousness must maintain the sense faculties, life-force, and warmth.
△ Third, the refutation of the absence of a seed-holding consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Furthermore, if there were no seed-holding consciousness at this stage (up to the point where) it has already been refuted that [the mind] receives perfuming and maintains seeds. [Commentary:
The first section directly refutes [the position] by showing that subsequent consciousnesses lack seeds; the section beginning with "past" refutes it through a series of successive arguments.
△ Third, establishing the logical proof (*pramāṇa*) to demonstrate that consciousness exists in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
However, within such mindless states as the attainment of cessation, [consciousness] definitely exists; in reality, it does not depart from the body.
