Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: If it is argued that because the verse of the *Mūla-śāstra* states that at the stage of an Arhat there is no afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*), the seventh [consciousness] does not exist, then by the same logic of that verse—which also states that at the stage of an Arhat one "abandons the storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*)—the eighth pure consciousness would likewise not exist.
Since that [text] does not say that the essence of the eighth stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) does not exist, how can you claim here that it does not exist?

The supramundane *manas* exists; therefore, we know that when the verse states that it is "non-existent" in three states, this is said with reference to the defiled *manas*, not that the pure essence is absent.
△ Next, the contradiction with correct reasoning (4): first, the equality-wisdom (*samatājñāna*) would lack a basis.

Furthermore, various treatises state that the seventh consciousness is transformed [into the mirror-like wisdom], because it is admitted that in a Buddha it functions constantly like the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).

Regarding the meaning of the terms: first, the scriptural citations are presented; they will be explained below. First, the remaining wisdoms are explained in accordance with the doctrine, namely the three wisdoms such as the wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).
Below this, the consciousness is challenged by way of a counter-argument: consciousness is the supported (*āśrita*), while wisdom is the support (*āśraya*); it is not possible... [below].

Refuting the [opposing] position: If it is claimed that the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) depends upon the six evolving consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*), then since those six consciousnesses which serve as its support (*āśraya*) are subject to interruption, the supporting wisdom of equality would likewise have to be interrupted.

This is not logically tenable. Why? Because the treatises maintain that the wisdom of equality of all Buddhas functions constantly, just like the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), for it is without interruption. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: the wisdom of equality...
This is a formal argument (*dharmī*). It is established that there exists a pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) which necessarily has a basis (*āśraya*) with which it is associated.

The reason (*hetu*) is: because there can be no supported (*āśrita*) apart from its support. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like the other three types of knowledge (*jñāna*). Furthermore, the formal proof (*pramāṇa*) states: The Knowledge of Equality (*samatājñāna*) is the subject;

it cannot be said to be based on the six evolving consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-parāvṛtti*). The reason is: because it is admitted that the Buddha acts perpetually. The example is like the Mirror-like Knowledge (*ādarśajñāna*). The first formal proof is thus established.
The proof: Next, regarding true refutation.
Second, the eighth consciousness has no basis.

Furthermore, in the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*), if the seventh consciousness did not exist—[omitted]—there must necessarily be this basis, because its nature is like that of the other consciousnesses.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the eighth consciousness in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) has a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), because it is of the nature of consciousness, just as with other consciousnesses.
△ Third, the view of self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) lacks a support.

Furthermore, as with those individuals who have not yet realized [the truth], because they have not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), the commentary first mentions the grasping at a personal self (*pudgalātmagrāha*).
By this, it should also be understood by analogy that there is grasping at a phenomenal self (*dharmātmagrāha*).

This consciousness is then contrasted [with others] to reveal that there is a seventh [consciousness], namely, the ever-active grasping at a phenomenal self. That which serves as its support is precisely the seventh consciousness.
If this consciousness did not exist, upon what would that [defiled mind] depend?

It cannot be said that it depends on the eighth consciousness, because the view of a self in phenomena (*dharmanairātmyadṛṣṭi*) is itself a form of wisdom (*prajñā*), whereas the eighth consciousness lacks wisdom; therefore, it cannot be its support. For this reason, the following encourages faith:
they merely rely on the sacred teachings which all state that there are three states; when these are absent, it is only the manas—the support of the afflictions—that is absent. One should...

I maintain that the three stages [of the path] are not devoid of the manas associated with the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because those [stages] have not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
△ Fourth, the sixth consciousness lacks a support.
Furthermore, in various treatises, it is stated that "the five [consciousnesses] have the same nature" (*pañca-samāna-dharma*)—up to "the six also always have a support" (*ṣaḍ api nityam āśritāḥ*).

This should be understood accordingly. [Supplementary Note: First, by following the principle that mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) has a support, the existence of a seventh [consciousness] is revealed. Regarding "the five having the same nature":
this means taking the first five consciousnesses as the analogies (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the sixth consciousness. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: "The sixth mental consciousness..."

There exists a dharma that is necessarily co-nascent and possesses a non-common support (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*). This is established because it is subsumed under one of the six well-known consciousnesses.

The reason is identical to the example of the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, which relies on the eye-faculty, up to the tactile consciousness, which relies on the body-faculty.

This precisely uses the five consciousnesses as a homologous example (*sapakṣa*) to prove the existence of a seventh [consciousness], establishing that the sixth consciousness relies upon the seventh. That is to say:

The sixth is the mental faculty (*manas*). This is clarified by contrast with the subsequent discussion on the Noble Path (*āryamārga*). Regarding the thesis (*pakṣa*) that the sixth [faculty] is without support (*anāśrita*), there is a fault in the reason (*hetu*).

That is to say, when the noble path of the two vehicles, the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) gives rise to the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanājñāna*), if the pure seventh [consciousness] does not exist to serve as the support for the sixth, then there is the fault of the non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) within the thesis. Why? Because when the noble path arises...

If there were only the sixth consciousness associated with the wisdom of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and no seventh consciousness serving as its co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), then the subject-property (*pakṣadharma*) in the latter part of the thesis would not be universally established (*prasiddha*). The "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*)—namely, the subject-property of the thesis—specifically refers to the seventh consciousness.
Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) would incur the fallacy of being "uncertain due to commonality" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*). For what constitutes the "universally established six consciousnesses"?

Because they are subsumed under the category of "one of the five," the five consciousnesses necessarily have a basis (*āśraya*). However, regarding the sixth [consciousness], in the state of outflow-free (*anāsrava*) realization, it does not necessarily have a basis.
Consequently, an opponent raises this objection: "Are the six [consciousnesses] equal to the preceding five in that they all necessarily have a basis at all times?
Or is it the case that you establish the thesis that the sixth has a basis while the preceding five do not?"
If the sixth [consciousness], being untainted (*anāsrava*), likewise lacks a support (*āśraya*), how can you establish the thesis that the first five [consciousnesses] are without support?
Whether they have a support or lack one, they all share this same reason; thus, you commit the fallacy of the "common indefinite" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*).

If you claim that the five sense-faculties are the same as the sixth mental faculty (*manas*) for the purpose of a formal analogy, the syllogism would be: the sixth mental faculty is the subject (*dharmin*); it is the sixth...

The school that maintains that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises simultaneously [with its objects] and has a non-common support (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*) is fully established [in its position], because it is subsumed under one of the six sense organs.
The reason (*hetu*) is identical to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), such as the five sense organs; the sixth, the mental organ (*manas*), is precisely the seventh, the *manas* (ego-consciousness).

Thus, by means of the common property of the five sense organs, the existence of a seventh [organ] is proven to serve as the support for the sixth. If there were no seventh organ, the thesis would suffer the fault of being unestablished (*aprasiddha*) regarding its specific distinction.

The subject (*dharmin*) presented in the prior member (*pūrvapakṣa*) serves as that which is to be qualified; it specifically refers to the seventh [consciousness]. Since the existence of a pure seventh consciousness is not admitted, the subject presented in the prior member is not established (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, within the reason (*hetu*), there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because the subject in the prior member lacks a seventh consciousness to serve as the locus for the sixth.
If the seventh does not exist, how can the sixth have a locus? Thus, the "homogeneous instance" (*sapakṣa*) mentioned in the commentary is untenable.

Although the faculties and consciousnesses are distinguished, both interpretations are sound, and there is no contradiction in their being presented together. Alternatively, one might raise an objection by analogy using two phrases:

"If the sixth [consciousness] lacks a support, then the five [consciousnesses] should likewise be so. To this, it is replied: "The two phrases 'the five are constant' and 'the six are always present' establish the supports for the five; the same should apply to the six as well."
△ Second, the presentation of the correct principle (in two parts). First, clarifying that while there is no defilement, there is purity.
Therefore, it is certain that there exists a non-defiled manas (until: "it is not the case that there is no eighth [consciousness]; this too should be so").
Supplement: Regarding the statement that "it does not exist," this is spoken with reference to the *kliṣṭamanas* (defiled mind). This serves to reconcile the meaning of the verse.
As it is said, the following provides an example to prove its existence.
△ Next, the distinction between the defiled and the pure is explained (2). First, the general explanation of the defiled and pure manas briefly has three types (2).
First, the heading:
"These distinctions of the manas briefly have three types" (up to) "...associated with the wisdom of equality."
△ Next, the explanation of (the three): First, the manas associated with the view of a personal self (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Initially, it pervades the mental continuums of all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), [giving rise to] the consciousness that conceives of a person as a self (*pudgala-ātmadṛṣṭi*).
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: The *manas* associated with the view of self and other (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*) is continuously present at all times for all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
For those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it arises intermittently, as explained below.

For a certain class of bodhisattvas—namely, those of gradual enlightenment (*anupūrva-abhisambodhi*), including those in the stages of training (*śaikṣa*) of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage—it does not manifest during the state of untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*). If, however, [it manifests]...

In the state of the mind with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*), that manas takes the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object and gives rise to the view of a self among persons (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

The *Kaibao* commentary states: "The state associated with the view of a self among persons is entirely characterized by outflows; when these are transformed into the state of being without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are no longer this state."
△ Next is the manas associated with the view of a self in phenomena (dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi).
Subsequently, it is common to all ordinary beings and śrāvakas [up to] that point; taking the ripening consciousness (vipāka-vijñāna) as its object, it gives rise to the view of a self in phenomena.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: The manas associated with the view of a self in phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) exists continuously at all times in all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, because they have not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena.

It arises intermittently within all lower levels of clarity, that is, from the eighth bhūmi of the Mahāyāna onwards, regardless of whether one’s progress is gradual or sudden, for all bodhisattvas, when the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena manifests.

In the preceding stage, it does not manifest. If one is in a stage where the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*) is not present before them, that mind takes the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) as its object and gives rise to the view of a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
(From the eighth stage upward, the storehouse consciousness has already been abandoned; therefore, in those stages, the seventh consciousness takes only the ripening consciousness as its object.)
△ The seventh consciousness (manas), associated with the wisdom of equality,
subsequently pervades the mental continuums of all Tathāgatas, arising as the wisdom of equality from the ripening consciousness (vipākavijñāna) and so forth.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: The manas associated with the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is perpetually continuous because all Tathāgatas have eternally severed the two obstacles and fully realized the two kinds of emptiness.
[The following] clarifies that for Bodhisattvas, it arises intermittently:

when a Bodhisattva is in a state where the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*) does not manifest—namely, during the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—then it does not manifest. Regarding phenomena...
In the stage where the wisdom of emptiness manifests, that mind takes the stainless *vipāka-vijñāna* as its object and gives rise to the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).
Regarding "stainless *vipāka*": when the Wisdom of Equality arises, it takes the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object;

because it momentarily possesses reflection and lacks the characteristic of self, and because one observes that the grasping [of self] has perished, it is called the "stainless Vajra Path. While the preceding *vipāka* has not yet become empty, it still...
It is called "maturation" (*vipāka*). Therefore, it is termed the "stainless maturation.
Supplement: Regarding the phrase "that which takes the stainless maturation consciousness and so forth as its object," to what phenomena does "and so forth" (*ādi*) refer? The *Zongjing* states:

The seventh cause is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and takes only the self as its object. The untainted (*anāsrava*) takes the eighth [cause] and the fruit of true reality (*tathatā*) as its objects, because it is accepted that these take all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) as their objects.
△ Next, the specific explanation of the manas associated with the two types of grasping—of self and dharmas (3). First, the explanation of the basis of the view (2).
First, the explanation that the view of self relies upon the grasping of dharmas.
Regarding the stage at which the view of a person (*pudgala-ātman*) arises (up to): "Just as one who is confused at night might mistake a stump for a person.
*Yinyi* (Exegesis of Terms and Meanings) states: The *Zongjing* says that this demonstrates that the initial stage necessarily entails the subsequent stage, because the former is brief.

At the stage where the view of a person arises, there must necessarily be a view of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*), because the view of a person necessarily arises based upon the view of phenomena. It is like a person walking at night.

First, one mistakes a branch or a stump for a person; here, the stump is a metaphor for the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), and the person is a metaphor for the clinging to a self (*ātma-grāha*).
[Question]: Why do these two types of clinging arise simultaneously? [Answer]: Because the clinging to a self necessarily arises based upon the clinging to phenomena;
therefore, they arise together. [Question]: What is the reasoning behind this? [Answer]: It is because one first clings to [the object] as a phenomenon...

They truly exist; only subsequently do they grasp at them as having functions such as acting and experiencing (the *Zongjing* says: "The dharma-self has its own nature and superior functions," while "the person-self has mastery and agency").

Therefore, they must exist simultaneously. Furthermore, it is asked: between the two attachments to self and dharmas, which is broader and which is narrower? The answer is: the attachment to dharmas is broad, while the attachment to self is narrow. It is asked: why is this so? The answer is:
one who is deluded regarding the person must necessarily be deluded regarding its dharmas, but one who is deluded regarding dharmas is not necessarily deluded regarding the person.
Question: For what reason? Answer: That which can maintain its own essence is all termed "dharmas. Only that which possesses constant and singular function is termed a "person" (pudgala).
Next, it clarifies that the two views rely upon a single wisdom.
Although the functions of the two views—the view of a self (*ātman*) and the view of phenomena (*dharma*)—are distinct, they do not contradict one another;

therefore, this case should also be understood in the same way. **Commentary on the Meaning:** Question: Since the functions of the view of a self and the view of phenomena are each distinct, how can they arise together without contradiction?
Answer: Although the functions of the view of a self and the view of phenomena are distinct, their essence is no different; they both rely upon the same wisdom. Therefore, [they may coexist].
There is no contradiction. For example, although the substance of visual consciousness is one, it simultaneously possesses multiple functions, such as discerning blue, yellow, and so forth;
likewise, although the substance of tactile consciousness is one, it possesses multiple functions, such as discerning cold, warmth, and so forth.
Since these share a single consciousness as their common basis, there is no contradiction.
△ Next, the subduing and severing of the two types of grasping (2). First, a general explanation of the arising and ceasing in the three vehicles (2).
First, at the stage of subduing the grasping at a self, only the grasping at phenomena arises.

In the case of the noble paths and the meditative absorption of cessation belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) of the two vehicles, the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) and the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*) have already been suppressed.
Regarding the meaning of the terms: there are three categories within the stage where the grasping at a self is suppressed. In the text, these three categories are first listed individually;

at the end, each is concluded with only two phrases that collectively summarize and establish them. First, regarding the two vehicles: within the stage of training (*śaikṣa-avasthā*), during the noble path and... [the absorption of cessation].
When meditative concentration (*samādhi*) manifests before one, only the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) arises, while the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*) has already been suppressed.
When concentration and wisdom arise, they are mutually exclusive with their respective obstacles and remedies.

Third, for Śaikṣa Bodhisattvas of gradual awakening, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), only the grasping at phenomena arises, because the grasping at a self has already been suddenly suppressed.

In the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), all those [afflictions] are fruits of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) that manifest before one; furthermore, they give rise only to the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), because the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) has already been suppressed.
Next, even in the stage where the grasping at a self is severed, the grasping at phenomena still arises.

The two vehicles in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and these gradually enlightened [bodhisattvas] likewise give rise only to the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), because their grasping at self (*ātman-grāha*) has already been severed.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: this stage of severing the grasping at self consists of only two categories. Namely, the two vehicles in the stage of no-more-learning, who give rise only to the grasping at phenomena because the grasping at self has already been severed;

and the gradually enlightened bodhisattvas who have turned their minds toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), who possess the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*).
When [the object] is not present before them, they likewise give rise only to attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), because their attachment to a self (*ātman*) has already been severed.
△ Next, the specific explanation of the arising and ceasing of Bodhisattvas (in two parts): first, the formal explanation.
This is because it is not contradictory that all Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward still give rise to attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Regarding the commentary on the meaning: this specifically clarifies that Bodhisattvas at the profound stages give rise to attachment to phenomena.

"All" refers to the self-attachment (*ātman-grāha*) of Bodhisattvas, whether sudden or gradual, which is either eternally non-active or has already been suppressed. The following explains the sense of "non-activity. In the case of the gradual [path], it is eternal...

They are abandoned and do not function. Through sudden [realization], they are permanently suppressed and do not function. If the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) does not manifest, the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*) still arises. Question:
Although the fruit of the knowledge of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*) does not manifest, the knowledge of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmyajñāna*) does manifest;

since grasping is exhausted when this knowledge arises, how can it still arise? Explanation: The knowledge of the emptiness of persons and the grasping at phenomena do not stand in direct opposition to one another; therefore, they are not mutually contradictory.
△ Next, the scriptural evidence is cited.
As it is said in a sutra: "From the eighth stage upward... [omitted] "...otherwise, afflictions would also have to be present.

(Commentary on the Meaning and Phrases): First, the text is cited; next, the meaning is explained. The cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is precisely the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). This is because...

Regarding the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*): afflictions arise based on the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Although they do not manifest [actively], the cognitive hindrance still remains;
therefore, it is said that "only the cognitive hindrance remains. However, this refers to the manifest state, not the seeds.

This proves that the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) arising from the eighth bhūmi upward is in its manifest form, not as seeds. Otherwise, if one were to claim that even for Bodhisattvas at these profound stages...

If the seeds are not manifest, then the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) should also be said to exist [in that state]. Why? Because the seeds of the afflictions have likewise not yet been severed.
△ Third, the determination of its affiliation with the *manas* of dharma-grasping (in two parts): first, a general determination of its nature according to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

The manas associated with the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is called "unobscured" (*anivṛta*) because it does not obstruct the wisdom of the followers of the Two Vehicles. Regarding the meaning of the terms:
this manas, which is associated with the view of a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*), is severed along with the afflictions (*kleśa*) by those of the Two Vehicles.
The mental factors associated with the grasping at the reality of phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) that do not seek the emptiness of phenomena do not obstruct the wisdom of the emptiness of persons;
therefore, they are not termed "defiled. They are categorized solely as non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Conversely, the mental factors associated with the grasping at the reality of phenomena in Bodhisattvas obstruct the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena; therefore, they are termed "defiled" and are also called "obscured neutral" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
△ Next, an inference (*anumāna*) is established to determine that [the mental consciousness] belongs to the category of "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
It is subsumed under "born of maturation" because it arises from the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*); [this applies] up to those not otherwise subsumed, all of which are included herein.
Commentary on the Terms (*Yinyì*): This refers to the manas that is concomitant with this dharma-grasping (*dharmagrāha*).

Although it arises from and is bound by the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), it is subsumed under "that which is born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) rather than being a "fruit of maturation" (*vipākaphala*). Why? Because it arises at all times from the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

This is explained below by citing an analogy: the term "fruit of maturation" is restrictive in its application, whereas the term "born of maturation" is pervasive. It is like the case of "predominant [condition]" (*adhipati*).
Regarding conditions (*pratyaya*): those not subsumed under the other three conditions are all subsumed under the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). This name is likewise so.

Furthermore, regarding that which is not subsumed under the true matured fruit (*vipāka-phala*), it is all subsumed under the category of "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "Born of maturation" is the subject (*dharmin*). Thesis (*pakṣa*):
Those not subsumed under the others are all included within this [category]. Reason (*hetu*): Because this name is pervasive. Example (*dṛṣṭānta*): As in [the case of]... [end of fragment].
The Dominant Condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
△ Next, proving the existence of the seventh [consciousness] (3): First, the general introduction through question and answer.
How should one know this seventh consciousness? ... because the holy teachings and correct reasoning serve as the authoritative standard (*pramāṇa*).
*Yinyi* (Explanation of Terms): The Hīnayāna [schools] maintain that what is called "mind" (*manas*) is merely the sixth consciousness entering the past;
since there is no separate entity for a seventh [consciousness], they raise this question.

Next, the distinct clarification through teaching and principle (in two parts). First, citing the teachings (in two parts). First, the direct citation (in four parts). First, a general citation from the Mahāyāna.
The Threefold Meaning of "Vehicle," "Realization," and "Name" (3). First, citing the sūtras:
The Bhagavat states in various sūtras that the three distinct meanings are designated as "vehicle," "realization," and "name," with "discernment" being designated as "consciousness."

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms (*Yinyi*): The ancient sub-commentaries explain that the above provides a general interpretation according to the Hīnayāna, which states that the future is called "mind" (*citta*), the past is called "intellect" (*manas*), and the present is "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Although there are various distinctions, they possess no separate substantial entities. Now, a scriptural passage is cited as proof.
△ Next, the explanation of the meaning.

Although these three meanings apply generally to all eight consciousnesses (up to the point where they are said to be coarse, active, intermittent, and functioning as discernment), the *Yinyi* (Phonology and Meaning) states that Qingliang’s commentary says: "That which is perfumed by all manifest activities; this is the accumulation of all dharmas."

The seeds serve as the basis for the present life and act as the cause capable of producing all things, because they give rise to all phenomena. Regarding the phrase "conditioned by the ālayavijñāna, etc.":
while in the causal state, the impure [consciousnesses] take only the self as their object; in the causal state, the pure [consciousness] takes the eighth consciousness and suchness as its objects.
This is because it is accepted that, in the resultant state, it takes all things as its objects. As the treatise states, "coarse and agitated" refers to what is easily [discerned].

"Understanding" (vijñāna) is named for its coarse transformation; "movement" (citta) is named for its fluctuation; and "interruption" (manas) is named for its lack of continuity. Each has its own specific object of perception, and thus receives its distinct name.

Furthermore, it is said that if one understands the mind in terms of its arising and gathering, the eighth consciousness alone is called "mind" (citta); if one understands the mind in terms of its accumulation, [it is called "thought" (manas)]."
All eight consciousnesses are termed *citta* (mind). If "intentionality" (*manana*) is used to define *manas*, then only the seventh is termed *manas*.
If "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*) is used to define *manas*, then all eight consciousnesses are termed *manas*.

If "discerning distinct objects" (*vijñapti*) is used to define *vijñāna* (consciousness), then only the first six are termed *vijñāna*, because they discern the distinct objects of the six sense-fields. If "discernment" (*vijñapti*) is used to define...
Consciousness (*vijñāna*). All eight consciousnesses are termed "consciousness"; this is the meaning of the specific explanation, as detailed in that [text].
△ Third, the proof of establishment:
As stated in the *Lankavatara-gatha*: "[That which] can cognize the characteristics of all objects is called 'consciousness'."
△ Second, citing the Mahāyāna scriptures generally to prove the existence of the seventh consciousness.
Furthermore, because various Mahāyāna sūtras specifically state that there is a seventh consciousness, it exists as a distinct entity.
Supplement: The fact that various [sūtras] specifically state that there is a seventh consciousness does not mean that the sixth consciousness has entered the past; it refers to [the seventh].

This refers to the *manas* (mind). Therefore, the statement "there is something distinct" is the direct answer to the previous question regarding whether consciousness exists as a distinct entity apart from the eye and other [senses].

Commentary on the Meaning: *Zhongjing* (Mirror of the Source), Fascicle 52. The Hīnayāna proponent says: "In our school, we take the physical mass of flesh as the basis for the sixth consciousness.
Why must you insist that there is a separate seventh consciousness? The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying:

"It cannot be said that the sixth consciousness depends upon matter (because the physical mass is a material phenomenon). The sixth consciousness must depend upon the mind (*manas*). Some say: [This is so because...]
Because the mind (manas) is not of the nature of form (rūpa). Furthermore, it is said that the sixth [consciousness] possesses three kinds of discrimination:

recollective (anusmaraṇa), conceptualizing (abhinirūpaṇa), and intrinsic (svabhāva) discrimination. If one were to allow that the sixth consciousness depends on form as its basis, it would be identical to the first five [sensory consciousnesses], which lack both recollective and conceptualizing discrimination.
△ Third, [the author] refutes the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) position that the sense organs exist prior to consciousness and serve as its support.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that the five consciousnesses lack [a simultaneous basis], for like the mind and mental factors, they are necessarily simultaneous.

Commentary on Terms: Regarding the "Mirror of the Source" (Zongjing), the followers of the Hīnayāna offer this defense: "In our school, the five consciousnesses arise with the sense organs preceding them;

thus, the five organs of the preceding moment give rise to the five consciousnesses of the succeeding moment. The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying: "As for a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), it is like a sprout depending on a seed to arise;
the sprout and the seed exist at the same time. Or like a shadow relying on a body to be produced; the shadow and the body exist together. So too, consciousness arises depending on the organ."
In principle, they must be simultaneous, for there is no preceding momentary faculty that gives rise to a succeeding momentary consciousness.
Since the five consciousnesses possess simultaneous faculties, it should be proven that the sixth consciousness likewise possesses a simultaneous faculty; this is precisely the seventh consciousness.
△ Third, the conclusion by means of formal inference (*pramāṇa*).
By this reasoning, it is established that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is included within one of the six well-established consciousnesses.
Regarding the meaning of the terms: "to manifest its own name and locus" means that the consciousness which relies upon the eye is called "eye-consciousness," and so forth.

The consciousness that relies upon the mind is called "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*). This explicitly reveals its own name, as well as the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) and so forth. Regarding "not included in the immediate":

it is not subsumed under the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Regarding "arising through predominance": this means that the faculty serves as the predominant generative condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the consciousness.
Regarding "subsumed by any one": this means being subsumed by any one among the six [bases]. As for "measure" (*pramāṇa*): [it refers to the extent of the object].

It is said: "The universally established mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the subject (*dharmin*). It must necessarily have the following thesis (*pakṣa*): 'Because it is subsumed within one [category] with the six universally established consciousnesses,' this is the reason (*hetu*).
'Like the visual consciousness and so forth' is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)."

Since it lacks substantiality, how could it possess the function of deliberation to be called "mind" (*manas*)?
△ Next, the refutation of the metaphorical designation as "mind" (in two parts): First, the refutation of the metaphorical designation.
If it is argued that this is a metaphorical designation, that reasoning is also incorrect; since there is no actual deliberation, upon what could a metaphorical basis be established?

Commentary on the Terms and Meanings: Fearing that they might argue, "That which is called 'mind' (*manas*) is merely a conceptualization," one should know that this is a provisional designation and does not possess a real substantial entity.

The refutation states: If "mind" is a mere provisional name established by virtue of correct conceptualization, then in the absence of correct conceptualization, upon what could that provisional designation be established?
△ Next, [the author] refutes the notion that it has previously possessed deliberation (*samanvāhāra*).

If one were to claim that because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) previously possessed deliberation while present, it is called "mind" (*manas*) even now despite having already ceased, [we respond: *Yinyi* (Commentary on Terms):
The opponent attempts to rescue the position by saying: "The mental consciousness previously possessed deliberation while it was present; although it has now ceased, it may still be given that name."
[Question: Why is it necessary to specifically designate the seventh [consciousness] as the *manas* (the thinking mind)? [Response: To refute this, it is said:
When the sixth consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) resides in the present, although it possesses the function of thinking, at that time it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and not "mind" (*manas*).

It is only when it has passed into the past that it is designated as "mind. This is because the followers of the Hīnayāna maintain that what is present is called "consciousness," while what is past is called...
Because it is the mind (manas).

Therefore, one should know that there exists a separate seventh [consciousness], the manas; [from] "until" "having ceased, it relies upon this to metaphorically establish the name 'mind'."
Commentary on the Meaning: Therefore, one should know that the existence of the seventh consciousness must be accepted, because it possesses the function of cogitation and is thus named *manas*.
If it were merely the equal-and-immediate *manas*, it would only be designated as "mind" (*manas*) by way of metaphorical establishment based upon this [seventh consciousness].
△ Section 4: Distinction Between the Two Mindless Absorptions (2). First, citing sutras to prove their existence:

Furthermore, the Sūtra states that if the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭa-manas*) did not exist, there would be no distinction between the absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

△ Second, the explanation that establishes the meaning of the sūtra (in two parts). First, the formal explanation (in two parts). First, clarifying that there is no seventh consciousness and that the two meditative absorptions are not distinct.
That is to say, both of those two absorptions equally cease the six consciousnesses; [from] "one exists" to "one does not exist," how could those two be different?

Commentary on the Terms: This means that in both the Cessation Attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and the Non-conceptualization Attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the six consciousnesses and their associated mental factors (*caitta*) are equally ceased.

There is no difference in their substance or number; their substance is the substance of the mind, and their number consists of the mental factors. Since these six kings [the consciousnesses] and their subjects [the mental factors] are equally ceased in both attainments, they are said to be "no different.
The phrase "If there were not... below clarifies that in the Cessation Attainment, there is no afflicted manas (*kliṣṭa-manas*), whereas in the Non-conceptualization Attainment...

Because there is the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are distinct. If the seventh consciousness did not exist, one attainment would possess it while the other would lack it;
how then could there be any difference between the two? Next, [the text] refutes the notion that there is any other distinct cause for the difference between the two attainments.

If it is argued that [the distinction between the two meditative attainments] depends on factors such as preparatory effort (*prayoga*), realm (*dhātu*), and stage (*bhūmi*), and that if these were absent, their cause would also be absent—[the opponent’s] response is as follows:
The difference between the two attainments is due to distinctions in preparatory effort and so forth;
what does this have to do with the seventh consciousness? The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that there are five differences between these two attainments: first, the basis (*āśraya*); second...

1. Essential nature; 2. three types of designation; 3. mental attention (*manasikāra*); 4. realm and stage (*dhātu-bhūmi*). Among these, the preparatory application (*prayoga*) refers to that fourth [type], namely mental attention, realm, and stage.
Regarding the phrase "just as with the name, the basis, etc.": "basis" (*āśraya*) refers to the support; "etc. (*ādi*) refers to the other two types. The reasoning is also [found] below.
Regarding the refutation of the cause for differentiation: "because this exists" means that because this seventh consciousness exists, the five [factors] are established.

The distinction is as follows: if, preceded by the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the perception of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-saṃjñā*), one causes the cessation of the non-perpetually active mind and mental factors, and this is established under the name "non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*) with the cessation of perception as its primary feature, this meditative absorption belongs exclusively to the fourth dhyāna. If, however, it is preceded by the perception of cessation (*nirodha-saṃjñā*)...
Preceded by mental attention (*manasikāra*), it causes the cessation of non-perpetually active mind and mental factors, as well as the perpetually active defiled mind and mental factors;

thus, it is designated "cessation. Although it belongs to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it is comprised within the untainted (*anāsrava*). This constitutes the distinction of its preparatory application (*prayoga*) and its level (*dhātu-bhūmi*).

As for the distinction of its basis (*āśraya*): this meditative attainment of cessation is produced by the disciples of the Buddha through the power of relying on the teachings of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Therefore, the state of non-perception arises from the power of false teachings as propounded by various non-Buddhists; the other two [attainments] may be understood accordingly.
These five distinctions all exist because of the mind.

Supplement: Regarding the distinction of their essential natures (*svabhāva*): the essential nature of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) belongs to the contaminated (*sāsrava*), while the essential nature of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) belongs to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the distinction of their provisional establishment (*prajñapti*): based on the seventh consciousness (*manas*) which is obscured (*nivṛta*), and taking the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*)—which is free from conception—as the locus of true liberation, the attainment of non-conception is provisionally established.

Based on the seventh consciousness which is unobscured (*anivṛta*), and taking the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) as its object, [the attainment of cessation] is [provisionally established].
I provisionally establish the attainment of cessation.

△ 5. Defilement in the Heaven of Non-conception (2): First, citing sūtras to prove its existence.

△ Second, explaining and establishing the meaning of the sūtra (in two parts). First, the direct explanation (in two parts). First, clarifying that the state without mind and without perception (*asaṃjñika*) is not defiled.
That is to say, because those [beings] lack the six evolving consciousnesses for a long period of time... [up to] ...it would not be something censured and loathed by the noble ones (*ārya*).
Regarding the meaning of the terms: the self-grasping of ordinary beings exists only within the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.

Since those gods lack the six evolving consciousnesses for long periods of time, if one does not admit the existence of the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭamanas*) in them, they would be devoid of self-grasping throughout their entire lifetime.
It has never been observed that an ordinary person bound by all fetters lacks self-clinging throughout the course of a single lifetime.

Since those gods lack self-clinging for such a long duration, they should be as pure and untainted as nirvana; consequently, they would not be objects of censure and aversion shared by the noble ones.
△ Next, it is explained that there would be successive faults if [the storehouse consciousness] were absent.

Since [the storehouse consciousness] exists at both the beginning and the end, such a fault does not arise. (Up to: Having already refuted the irrationality of other dharmas receiving perfuming, [the argument continues:]...

**Commentary on the Meaning of Terms:** Regarding their defense, they claim: "The six consciousnesses of those devas, along with their associated mental factors (*caitta*), cease during the first half-aeon and arise during the second half-aeon.

Since the sixth consciousness exists during both the first and second half-aeons to give rise to the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*), there is no such fault [of failing to account for the continuity of self-grasping].

[Their intention is that because the sixth consciousness arises to grasp a self, this itself constitutes the defilement (*saṃkleśa*) of those devas; why must there necessarily be a seventh consciousness? Below this, the refutation begins: "First..."
"Even though [the self] exists later, there is a fault because it does not exist during the intervening four hundred and forty-nine kalpas.

To this, he further attempts to rescue [his position] by saying: "Because there is attachment to a self in the past and future, such a fault does not occur. He then refutes this, saying: "That is not so..."
The past and the future are neither manifest nor permanent, like flowers in the sky and so forth; because they lack manifest permanence, there is a logical fallacy.

"That which is obtained" [is] below; this is a repeated refutation of its irrationality. "That which is obtained is non-existent" means that those sentient beings, prior to the attainment of the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), seek the fruit of non-conception;
thus, the seeds perfumed [by that seeking] bring about the maturation (*vipāka*) of that celestial realm. [This refers to] the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭa-manas*).

Consequently, the coarse and fluctuating perceptions and so forth that constitute the basis for the grasping at a self do not arise; within this state, the "retribution of non-conception" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) is provisionally established.

If this consciousness did not exist, the maturation (vipāka) of those gods would not be possible. Since the retribution of non-conception that is obtained would be absent, the sentient beings who possess that non-conception would also not exist.
Fearing that they might offer the following defense: "There is no [such thing as] non-conception..."

Maturation (*vipāka*) is a factor dissociated from thought (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Is it not, then, existent? Factors dissociated from thought are provisionally established based on the states of matter (*rūpa*) and mind;
they are not substantially real, as has already been refuted previously.

As for the non-existence of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), it is because it is that which is grasped and stored by the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and so forth, as one's own internal self; and it is that which stores all phenomena of both the defiled and pure categories, causing them—
Because it is never lost, it is for this reason that the name *ālaya* is established. Without this "grasping and storing" (*ālīyante*), that consciousness would not exist.

Since there is no grasping and storing, the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of all defiled and pure phenomena would likewise be non-existent. Why? Because it has already been demonstrated in the preceding text that other phenomena cannot receive perfuming, as it is logically impossible.
△ Next, the conclusion and demonstration.
Therefore, there must be a distinct defiled *manas* (up to: "for this reason, the noble ones alike revile and loathe it").

Commentary on the Meaning: The *Zongjing* says: "There is a seventh [consciousness] which gives rise to the grasping of a self; because it belongs to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it emerges [from meditative absorption]."
After emerging from meditative concentration, one sinks again into the cycle of birth and death and gives rise to various afflictions; the noble ones censure such a person.
If the seventh consciousness did not exist, they would not censure them, for there would be no fruit of transgression.

That is to say, when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) possess minds of the three natures, the giving and other [virtuous acts] they initiate cannot eliminate signs.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: This refers to the class of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

At times when the mind is of the three natures—wholesome, defiled, or neutral—the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), though externally performing wholesome, unwholesome, or imperturbable (*āniñjya*) karma, are accompanied by the seventh [consciousness] which continuously clings to a self.

Because of this constant internal clinging to a self, the wholesome karma such as giving that arises within the six consciousnesses fails to realize the emptiness of its own essence and instead grasps at it.
Regarding the characteristics.
△ Next, the proof (three parts). First, citing the text:
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the defiled manas... [until] once the manas has ceased, one is liberated from the bondage of characteristics.
Commentary on the Meaning: The intent of the treatise states that the afflicted *manas* serves as the universal support for the six preceding defiled consciousnesses.

As long as it has not been extinguished, it prevents the six consciousnesses from attaining liberation from the bondage of characteristics (*nimitta-bandhana*) and the bondage of views (*dṛṣṭi-bandhana*). Once the afflicted [manas] has been extinguished, [liberation is attained].
Only then does one attain liberation. "Phenomena" (nimitta) refers to the objective division (*nimittabhāga*); "discernment" (*vijñapti*) refers to the subjective division (*darśanabhāga*).
△ Next, the explanation of the meaning:
regarding the term "bondage by phenomena" (*nimittabandhana*), it means that because one lacks mastery over the characteristics of objects, it is called bondage by phenomena.
**Commentary on the Meaning of Terms:** Regarding "bondage by characteristics" (*nimitta-bandhana*):

This refers to the fact that because the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) constantly clings to a self, it causes the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) to be unable to realize that their objects—dependent natures (*paratantra-svabhāva*)—are neither existent nor non-existent, but are like illusions produced through dependent origination.
Consequently, they are constrained by the two parts of perception and appearance (*dṛśya-darśana-bhāga*), and thus cannot attain mastery; for this reason, it is called "bondage by characteristics."
△ Third, the proof through three stages.
Based on this meaning, there is a verse (up to): "As long as it has not been extinguished, the consciousness-bondage is never released.

△ Next, the explanation regarding the formation of the outflows (*āsrava*). (II) First, the exclusion of the six consciousnesses and others from being able to form the outflows. (IV) First, the exclusion.
Afflictions.

Furthermore, during moments of wholesome or non-obscured neutral mind—lest [the path] become untainted (*anāsrava*) merely through the understanding of another—the seventh [consciousness] would constantly arise as a self.
(Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms): Furthermore, during moments of wholesome or non-obscured neutral mind, if the seventh [consciousness] did not constantly arise as a self...
If this were accepted, then those wholesome states and so forth would not be associated with outflows (*sāsrava*). Why?

Because within one's own continuum, the afflictions existing among the six consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously with those wholesome states and so forth. "One's own continuum" refers, for example, to a subsequent moment of visual consciousness.
This continues from the previous discussion regarding eye-consciousness and so forth. Suppose they offer this defense:

"Although present afflictions do not coexist with wholesome states and the like, they nonetheless become 'with-outflows' (sāsrava) due to past and future afflictions. Refutation: This is illogical, because the existence of past and future objects as causal conditions is not established by reason.
As for "the afflictions of others," this refers to the afflictions of another person. For example, although the mind of a donor may be wholesome, [it becomes defiled] due to the recipient...

This is because there are delusions within the mind [of the recipient], which cause the mind of giving to become *sāsrava* (tainted). "Another's understanding" refers to the other's untainted (*anāsrava*) pure understanding.
The meaning is that it is not due to the afflictions of the recipient that my mind as the giver causes my wholesome mind to become tainted.
If that were so, even if the recipient were an untainted pure field, it would still be able to cause my mind as the giver to be... [tainted].

If a mind with outflows becomes free from outflows, one knows that it is only because of the seventh consciousness’s constant internal grasping at a self that wholesome and indeterminate states become possessed of outflows.
△ Second, distinguishing the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, it cannot be said that there exists a separate *anuśaya* (latent disposition), because it has already been fully established that such a thing does not exist as a real entity.

Regarding the meaning of the term: one might fear that [the opponent] would further argue that there is a distinct dharma called *anuśaya*, which is different from mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*), is subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*), and arises manifestly in a continuous stream during states such as wholesome ones; for this reason...
Because [the categories of] wholesome and so forth establish the existence of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). As previously stated, "Furthermore, it cannot be said... and so on;
this is because it is already fully established that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are not substantial entities, as clarified in the second fascicle.
△ Third, the exclusion of the seeds of outflows (*āsrava*).
It cannot be said that [the uncontaminated mind] arises from contaminated seeds, lest one also conclude that the uncontaminated mind under training (*śaikṣa*) becomes contaminated.
[Commentary on the Meaning]: Furthermore, there is the fear that the opponent might offer this rebuttal: "Wholesome states and so forth, though contaminated, arise from contaminated seeds."
Because [the seeds] would become contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is further denied by saying, "nor can it be said," and so forth. Why?

Because those seeds would have no prior cause for becoming contaminated. The intended meaning is that for contaminated seeds to be established, they must necessarily be grasped as a self by the seventh consciousness.

They coexist with the active manifestation of wholesome states and so forth, thereby perfuming and forming the seeds of outflows (*āsrava*). If the seventh consciousness did not exist, those seeds would previously have lacked a cause for becoming seeds of outflows;
how then could outflowing phenomena arise from such seeds? It is not by means of the lower [consciousnesses]. Furthermore, he provides an example to refute this:

it is not by means of the seeds of outflows that the manifest wholesome states and so forth become outflowing phenomena; otherwise, one would fall into the error of contradicting the training (*śikṣā*).

An untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) can also become tainted (*sāsrava*). Why? Because within the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), there still exist tainted seeds within the untainted mind of one in training;
thus, it is an untainted mind that has manifested within a state that is [otherwise] tainted.
△ 4. Distinguishing the Impure Inducement.
Although karma such as giving is induced by afflictions (*kleśa*), how does it subsequently become *sāsrava* (outflowing)?

Regarding the meaning of the sound [of this term]: Furthermore, they [the opponents] maintain that at the time of a wholesome mind and so forth, although it is not accompanied by afflictions, it is nevertheless preceded by these [afflictions].
[The opponent argues: "Because they are incited by afflictions (*kleśa*), meritorious actions such as giving (*dāna*) become outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas. The commentary explains:

"Although acts of giving and so forth are incited by afflictions, at the moment the karmic action of giving arises, the afflictions have already ceased. Because they do not arise simultaneously, [the afflictions] are not the primary cause for being outflow-tainted.
Why? Because the term 'outflow-tainted' signifies that which co-exists with the outflows (*āsava*). Furthermore, the text below provides a counter-example by way of interrogation.

Refutation: If it is argued that virtuous states of mind such as giving (*dāna*) are *sāsrava* (with-outflows) because they are induced by afflictions (*kleśa*), then how could the sixth consciousness, when initiating an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) karma that does not depend on present conditions and is not induced by afflictions, itself become *sāsrava*?
The point is this: becoming *sāsrava* occurs through association with outflows, which is precisely due to the simultaneous grasping of a self by the seventh consciousness.
△ Next, the correct explanation of how the sixth and seventh [factors] mutually benefit one another to constitute outflows (āsrava). (3) First, the direct explanation:
Now, all outflows arise from association with one’s own [body]... (omitted)... Just as it is for ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), so it is for those in training (śaikṣa).
Commentary on the Terms: "All that is with outflows" (*sāsrava*) refers to the wholesome, the indeterminate, and so forth. "One's own body" excludes the delusions of others.

"Manifestly active afflictions" (*paryavasthāna*) excludes latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and seeds. This refers specifically to the self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) and so forth associated with the seventh consciousness, which arise and perish simultaneously;
this excludes those that do not arise together. "Mutually augmenting" refers to what is produced within the six consciousnesses.

At the time of practicing giving and so forth, because [the sixth consciousness] arises and ceases simultaneously with the manifest self-clinging of its own seventh consciousness, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses mutually benefit one another, whereby they become outflowing (sāsrava). Consequently, this further perfumes and produces seeds of outflowing dharmas.

The two phrases concerning ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) serve as an analogy for those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*). That is to say, the noble ones (*ārya*) who have attained the first, second, or third fruits still have innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) that have not yet been permanently exhausted;
therefore, they are considered "with outflows" (*sāsrava*), being the same in this regard as ordinary beings.
*He-xiang Kai-meng* (Harmonizing Resonance, Opening the Ignorant). Question: Regarding the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not defiled.

By what means do they become outflows (*āsrava*)? Answer: Because they arise simultaneously with the seventh [consciousness] afflictions, they mutually augment one another; thus, they become "with-outflow" (*sāsrava*).
This is what is meant by the statement that the wholesome and so forth are "with-outflow" because they are associated with the seven outflows.

△ Next, the refutation of the objection is explained. Although the contaminated (*sāsrava*) states of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are not associated with outflows (*āsrava*), they nonetheless constitute "contaminated" in accordance with principle; thus, there is no contradiction in reasoning. *Commentary on the Meaning:* The objection states: One in training (*śaikṣa*) has not yet exhausted the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), and because their states are associated with outflows, they constitute "contaminated. However, [the states of] one beyond training are not so. Why? Because they have already abandoned the grasping at a self. Furthermore, since they are not associated with the outflows, how can they be called "contaminated"? This is the objection. The response is as follows:

although the outflows themselves are not present within them, because these states are produced by the power of past outflows, they are designated as "contaminated. This is like the designation of the "contaminated" for the *anāgāmin*’s fruit and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Therefore, there is no fault. Furthermore, the term "contaminated" is established based on the presence of the outflows; it does not mean that the outflows must be currently manifesting. For example, when one says "this person possesses wealth," it means they have acquired wealth through effort, not that they are currently holding a specific coin in their hand. It is the same here. Thus, even though the outflows are not currently manifesting, because they are produced by the power of past outflows, they are designated as "contaminated. Consequently, there is no contradiction in principle.
