When they speak of "at one time," they mean a single moment within a continuum of many moments (*saṃtāna*), just as it is said that "one mind" does not refer to a single arising-and-ceasing.
Here, however, we rely on a single moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), in which it is certainly impossible for [multiple factors] to coexist. Therefore, there is no contradiction between our positions.
△ Next, the Master’s view that [the three natures] may coexist (3). First, the formal explanation:
There is an interpretation that the six consciousnesses can coexist with all three natures; thus, the objections previously raised are rendered futile in this case.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: *Sūer* (sudden/arbitrary) refers to the mind that arises immediately upon encountering an object for the first time when hearing the Dharma;

this belongs to the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). *Dēngliú* (outflowing/continuous) refers to the mind that contemplates an object moment by moment with a uniform continuity between preceding and succeeding states; this encompasses both the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), or may be manifold.

"Manifold" means arising simultaneously with the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). "Or few" means two, three, or four [consciousnesses] arising together. Those that are capable of arising together are... *sūer*.

"Because those [mental factors] of the same category can arise simultaneously. That is to say, when the five consciousnesses perceive objects and encounter the five sense-objects appearing all at once—perhaps the visual consciousness arises as a sudden encounter (*ābhoga*), while the auditory consciousness arises as a homogeneous flow (*nisyanda*) that is wholesome, and the remaining consciousnesses arise as a homogeneous flow that is unwholesome;

or perhaps the auditory consciousness arises as a sudden encounter, while the remaining consciousnesses arise as a homogeneous flow, and so forth. This is what is meant by the simultaneous arising of the three natures within the five consciousnesses."

Regarding the meaning: although the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the five sensory consciousnesses necessarily arise together, their natures—such as being wholesome and so forth—are not necessarily identical.

Therefore, it is possible for the three moral natures of the six consciousnesses to arise simultaneously. The meaning of this distinction will be seen in the following passage. As for the previous objection being rendered futile:
The former masters said: "If the five consciousnesses function in all three natures, then the mental consciousness at that time must also necessarily correspond to all three natures;

thus, they claim this contradicts reason. Now it is said: although the mental consciousness functions together with the five, its nature is not necessarily the same as theirs. Thus, the former objection is established in vain against this position.
△ Second, citing scriptural evidence (in two parts): First, citing the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (in three parts).
First, the citation of the text: Therefore, the *Yogācāra* states: "If one encounters the condition of sound... [omitted] ...if there is an expectation, it will only emerge at a later time."
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: When the various practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*) are correctly entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the five consciousnesses do not function.

If they encounter an object-condition consisting of sound and emerge from that absorption, this is merely the arising of the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) as a residual derivative co-arising with the wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) associated with that absorption;

it is not the case that [the auditory consciousness] alone is associated with that absorption. This indicates that it is necessary for the auditory consciousness to be accompanied by the mental faculty (*manas*) in order to apprehend [the sound].
Having perceived the sound, he subsequently emerges from meditative absorption. It is not only the mental consciousness associated with that absorption that can perceive this sound.
If one were to claim that there is only the mind and no ear-consciousness, then a solitary mental consciousness existing solely within absorption would be unable to hear the sound;
because it does not apprehend this auditory object, one should not emerge from absorption. Therefore, the five [sensory] consciousnesses and the sixth [mental consciousness] [must coexist].
This serves as a clarification; it does not mean that one has emerged from meditative absorption [at the moment] the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) arises.

Since meditative absorption is associated with the mental faculty (*manas*), there might be the concern that the ear-consciousness apprehending sound would immediately cause one to emerge from absorption. However, it is not necessary for one to emerge only after the ear-consciousness has arisen simultaneously with a consciousness associated with absorption.
The commentary states: One does not emerge from absorption at the very moment of apprehending the sound; rather, it is necessarily the ear-consciousness that perceives the sound.
Thus it is said. At that time, if the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has a desire, one subsequently emerges from meditative absorption;

therefore, the sixth consciousness serves as the basis for the discernment of the first five. Since the mind remains in absorption, both consciousnesses must necessarily apprehend this sound together before one can emerge from absorption.
△ Next, the explanation of the meaning:

When the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) suddenly hears a sound while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*)... [up to] ...it is not necessarily of the same nature as the five wholesome states, etc.
(Commentary on the Meaning): This refers to the ear-consciousness that first arises to hear a sound while one is in meditative concentration. According to principle, it should not be wholesome. Why?
In the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the sudden, adventitious mind (*sahaja-citta*) is necessarily indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Since the five sense-consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness only reach their full perfection upon attaining the ultimate fruit, once the transformation of the basis has been realized, even the sudden, adventitious mind is exclusively of a virtuous nature (*kuśala*). The following concluding summary expresses this point: [text omitted].
Since the indeterminate ear-consciousness arises in association with a wholesome mind that is concentrated (*samāhita*),
this proves that the mental consciousness concomitant with the five [sensory] consciousnesses does not necessarily share the same moral quality— such as wholesomeness— as those five consciousnesses.
△ Third, the proof from three sources.

In various places, it is stated that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) co-arising with the five [sensory consciousnesses] also takes the five objects as its domain, yet it is not said that they must be of the same nature (sajātīya).
△ Next, reconciling this with the *Saṃgrahābhidharmasamuccaya*.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states that the five consciousnesses do not exist during the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*). This is said based on the majority of cases.
**Supplement:** An objection is raised: The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states that there are no five consciousnesses in the state of meditative equipoise.

How then can it be said that an auditory consciousness, which arises simultaneously with a mental consciousness associated with concentration, is able to hear sounds? **Explanation:** [The response follows...]
That [statement] was spoken primarily with reference to one remaining in meditative absorption (*samāhita*), whereas this is said in relation to the brief period after emerging from absorption;

therefore, they do not contradict one another. *Samāhita* is translated here as "equipoise" (*ting-ying*); it is a name for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), meaning that by practicing calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) in a balanced and non-biased manner, one draws forth spiritual qualities.
Within the state of equipoise, wholesome concentration and wholesome wisdom [arise] together with the sixth consciousness.
They are associated, supple, upright, and for the most part abide without the arising of the five consciousnesses.
△ Third, the summary and indication:
If the three natures (trisvabhāva) all operate within the five consciousnesses... [omitted] ...therefore, it is possible for the three natures to coexist within the six evolving consciousnesses.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: "Exclusive focus" (*piānzhù*) refers to exclusive emphasis and concentrated attention.

For example, if the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) focuses exclusively on what is wholesome, then the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) follows that exclusive focus and likewise becomes wholesome.

Alternatively, if other consciousnesses focus exclusively on what is unwholesome or neutral (*avyākṛta*), then the mental consciousness also becomes unwholesome or neutral. Thus, it is known that the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) are compatible with the six consciousnesses.
Both. △ Next,

having already undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and attained the stage of mastery, it is comprised solely of a virtuous nature (*kuśala-dharma*), because the seeds of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca-bīja*) have been eternally and completely eradicated.

Supplement: This clarifies the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*). It is comprised exclusively of the nature of goodness (*kuśala*). That is to say, within the stage of the Buddha’s fruition, the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is transformed into the stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*).

At that time, because it has become untainted (*anāsrava*), there are no [defiled] sense organs (*indriya*); thus, the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) that are produced also become untainted mental faculties (*manas-indriya*).
Because they are purely untainted, the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) that is produced is likewise purely untainted. These five faculties are termed...

The Buddha’s untainted form (*anāsrava-rūpa*) and the eight consciousnesses termed the Buddha’s untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) constitute this state. Form refers to the adornment of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and merits;

mind refers to the mental complex associated with the four wisdoms of enlightenment (*catur-jñāna-bodhi*). Both are subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) and are devoid of anything unwholesome.

Since the seeds of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca-bīja*) have been eternally extinguished, there is no indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state; therefore, they are associated with the wisdom of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna*).
The category of mind (*citta-kalāpa*). The categories of mind associated with the attainment of knowledge (*jñāna-samprayukta-citta-kalāpa*) are exclusively of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*).
Next, the explanation of the latter two gates (2): first, a brief indication of the mental factors (*caitta*), followed by a detailed explanation of those associated with feeling (*vedanā-sahagata*).
(3) First, the provisional treatise poses the question.
With how many mental factors (*caitta*) are the six consciousnesses associated?
Next, the verse of the root treatise answers this.
The verse says: "These mental factors—universal, [particular,] afflictive, secondary afflictions, and indeterminate—are associated with the three feelings."
Supplement: The fifty-fifth fascicle of the *Zongjing* states:

"The first three lines of the verse enumerate the general names for the six categories of mental factors (i.e., the section on the association of mental factors). The final line correctly explains their coexistence with feeling (i.e., the section on coexistence with feeling)."
△ Section Three: Commentary on the *Trimśikā* (Part Two). First, a brief explanation of the six classes of mental factors (*caitasika*). (Two) First, the general heading. The treatise says:
These six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are, in general, associated with six classes of mental factors, namely the universal (*sarvatraga*) and so forth.
Supplement: The second fascicle of the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states:

"The meaning of 'correspondence' (xiāngyìng) refers to the fact that although the mind and its mental factors (fǎ) are distinct—where 'mind' refers to the sovereign mind (cittarāja) and 'mental factors' refer to the mental concomitants (caitta), they are called 'distinct' because the sovereign and its attributes differ—one knows that their characteristics of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) and their characteristics of objectification (*ālambana-lakṣaṇa*) are identical based on the distinctions between the defiled and the pure.

That is to say, if the sovereign mind cognizes a defiled mental factor, they are the same; if the sovereign mind objectsifies a pure mental factor, they are likewise the same. The characteristic of cognition is the identity of the subject that knows, while the characteristic of objectification is the identity of the object known."

△ Second, the detailed explanation (in two parts). First, the explanation of the names and meanings of mental factors (citta-saṃprayukta-dharma) (in two parts). First, the explanation based on three meanings:
"They always arise dependent upon the mind and are associated with the mind" (*yāvat*)... [up to] "...just as things belonging to a self are designated by the name 'mine' (*ātmīya*)."

*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance) states: "That which possesses these three meanings is called a *caitta* (mental factor). Why is it said that they 'always arise dependent upon the mind' (*cittāśrita*)?
Answer: Because they must have the mind as their support (*āśraya*) in order to arise. Question: "What does it mean to be 'associated with the mind' (*cittasaṃprayukta*)?

Answer: Contact (*sparśa*) and the others are always associated with the mind; therefore, they are called mental factors (*caitta*). Since it is said they are "associated with the mind," [it follows that] the mind is not associated with itself.
Because they are associated (*saṃprayukta*). Mind is not a mental factor (*caitta*). Why? Because association occurs with another nature (*parabhāva*), not with its own nature (*svabhāva*).

Question: How many meanings does "associated with mind" have? Answer: There are four meanings, namely: identity of time (*kāla*), identity of basis (*āśraya*), identity of object (*ālambana*), and identity of function (*kārya*).
Matter (*rūpa*) and so forth, in relation to mind, do not possess these meanings; thus, matter is not a mental factor. Question: What is meant by "belonging to"?

[Question]: Regarding the mind (*citta*): when one examines contact (*sparśa*) and the other [mental factors] to see with which mind they arise, they belong to that specific mind because contact and the others are dependent upon it.
Since it is said that they "belong to" the mind, and the mind-king (*cittarāja*) does not itself belong to the mind, the mind is not a mental factor (*caitta*).
The illustration is clear as stated in the text.
△ Second, the explanation by way of auxiliary matters (in two parts): First, the direct explanation.
The mind apprehends only the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of its objects, like a master painter and his disciples drawing a model and filling it with colors.
*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance): The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source), fascicle 55, states: "The characteristics of the mental concomitants (*caitta*) are as follows:

the mind grasps the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of an object, merely grasping them in their totality without further discrimination. For example, when one says 'perceiving blue,' the mind merely grasps 'blue' in its totality without further discrimination.
The mental concomitants, however, grasp both the general and specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of that [object]; therefore, the word 'also' is used. It is like a painting."
Regarding "the master and the student acting as model and color-applier": "master" refers to the *ācārya* (teacher), and "student" refers to the disciple.
Just as when the master creates a model by drawing the form, the student applies the colors; because the colors are applied to the model, they do not depart from it.

Likewise, when taking the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), at the time of applying the colors, one causes them to appear beautiful. Similarly, when taking the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) take [them].

The object is likewise. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is able to discern the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of an entity; it is not said to grasp specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), because it is the primary [subject].
If it were to grasp specific characteristics, it would then be a mental factor (*caitta*).
Appendix: Regarding the designation of "mental factors" (*caitasika*) as those that assist and accomplish the mind’s activities, the first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Those companions refer to the various mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) that are co-existent and associated with that [mind], namely:
attention (*manasikāra*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and other co-existent and associated mental factors."
△ Second, citing scriptural evidence (in two parts): First, proving the universal and specific object-conditions (in two parts). First, proving the universal [mental factors].
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that consciousness is able to discern... [omission] ...this indicates that mental factors also take general characteristics as their objects.
"Harmonizing Resonance" (*hexiang*)—that is, the single phrase "the distinct characteristics apprehended by all mental factors"—pervades the five preceding and following phrases.
The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source), fascicle 55, states: "The single dharma of attention (*manasikāra*) alone is able to discern numerous distinct characteristics.
Because the power of attention causes the mind and its mental factors to apprehend objects, it possesses this 'general apprehension of many' due to its superior efficacy."

Regarding the distinct characteristics of the dharmas: the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* takes attention (*manasikāra*) as primary, whereas this treatise takes contact (*sparśa*) as primary because its conjunction is predominant.
Each is based on a single specific meaning. Contact is able to grasp three types of aspects: the agreeable, the disagreeable, and that which is neither.
Feeling (*vedanā*) subsumes the aspects of loss, gain, and that which is neither. Perception (*saṃjñā*) is able to discern the aspects that serve as the causes for verbal expression.

This is because it apprehends the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the objective sphere’s boundaries. That is to say, by thinking "this is blue, not non-blue," and so forth, one gives rise to verbal expression;

thus, the characteristic of *saṃjñā* (perception) is the cause of verbal expression. *Cetanā* (volition) discerns correct causes, incorrect causes, and those that are contrary to both, which are precisely the characteristics of correctness, incorrectness, and so forth within the object;
this is the cause of karma. (Text). This indicates that mental factors (*caitasika*) also take the aggregate as their object.
"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the meaning of this term as it is explained within various passages.
Next, regarding the proof of distinct objects:

other sources further state that desire (*chanda*) can also discern [objects], up to and including concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), which also discern characteristics such as gain and loss.
△ Next, we take the four categories beginning with the wholesome as an illustration.

By this, it is understood that when wholesome, defiled, and other mental factors arise toward an object, they all apprehend both the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the focal point.

[Commentary on the Meaning]: Since the universal (*sarvatraga*) and the object-specific (*viniyata*) mental factors already apprehend the specific characteristics of their objects, by extension from this, one should know that the remaining wholesome and defiled factors do likewise.
The four categories of mental factors (*caitta*) all apprehend both the general and specific characteristics of their objects.
Next, the classification of the six categories is explained: first, the headings and enumeration.
Although the names and meanings of the various mental factors (*caitta*) do not differ [in their essential nature], thus six stages comprise fifty-one [factors].

Supplement: The first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that fifty-three mental factors are obtainable, namely from attention (*manaskāra*) up to and including vitarka and vicāra as the final limit.
In addition to the eight universal secondary mental factors (*anuvṛtti-caitta*), it further adds improper desire (*mithyā-chanda*) and improper resolve (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*).

Because of the inclusion of *adhimokṣa* (resolute belief), there are fifty-three. Now, in this treatise, since *chanda* (desire) and *adhimokṣa* already exist among the object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya-citta*), and because they also pertain to both the wholesome and the defiled, *mithyā-chanda* (wrong desire) and *mithyā-adhimokṣa* (wrong resolute belief) are subsumed; thus, there are only fifty-one.
△ Second, the Explanation of the Meaning (in two parts): First, clarifying the general name for the six stages.
[This is because it] can certainly be found within all states of mind... [up to] ...because it is not determinate with respect to the wholesome, the defiled, and so forth.
△ Next, the distinctions among the types are explained.
However, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* combines six into five (up to) these five stages, by which the distinctions among the types are established.
Supplement: Regarding the combination of six into five in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the text of the first fascicle, [the afflictions] are greed, anger, and ignorance.
Following the six root afflictions—pride, views, and doubt—the three types of secondary afflictions (anuśaya)—small, medium, and great—are enumerated;

thus, the two classes of defiled phenomena, the roots and the secondary afflictions, are combined into a single category. Regarding the "four kinds of universality": "all natures" refers to the three natures, namely the wholesome and so forth;
"all stages" refers to the nine stages within the three realms; and "all times" refers to all present [moments].
"At that time, all [mental factors] are present together; that is to say, they are associated with the eight consciousnesses.

Among the five universal [factors], those that possess four [characteristics] are so called because they pervade the three natures, pervade the nine stages, and arise at all times, as they are common to all eight consciousnesses.

As for the specific-objective [factors], they possess only two [characteristics]: they pervade the three natures and the nine stages, yet they do not exist at all times, because their four objects..."

Because they arise individually, there is no simultaneous occurrence of all [mental factors]. Since desire and the other [afflictions] do not pervade the mind, when the wholesome is singular—meaning it is present across all stages—it is universally wholesome;
thus, because the three natures are mutually exclusive, there is no simultaneous occurrence of all [factors] in that state.

Furthermore, since the eleven [factors] do not arise at the same time, there is no occasion where all are present. This is because the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, being with-outflow (*sāsrava*), lack these [wholesome factors].

"None are present in all [minds]; the four defiled ones are entirely absent" means that they do not pertain to the nature of the wholesome, do not pervade all levels (*bhūmi*), and do not arise simultaneously;

thus, these eight [mental factors] are absent from the eight consciousnesses. "The indeterminate ones are not necessarily unique" means that they pertain only to the three natures, as they are not fixed within any specific nature, such as the wholesome or the defiled.
Sleep exists only in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*); vitarka and vicāra do not pervade the three realms; and none [of these] exist [in the higher realms].
All [six consciousnesses] do not arise simultaneously; there is no time when they are all exclusively attended by the six consciousnesses, nor is there any simultaneity of all [of them].
△ Next, the detailed explanation of the association with the three feelings (in two parts): first, the state before the transformation of the basis (in two parts);
first, clarifying that the feelings associated with the six consciousnesses are not identical (in two parts); first, the general heading.
These six evolving consciousnesses are easily detached and indeterminate (up to: because they all experience agreeable, disagreeable, and neutral objects).
Regarding the meaning of the terms: *Zhongjing* (Mirror of the Essence), Fascicle 55, states:

"These six evolving consciousnesses are easily detached and indeterminate" means that their substance is always easily detached and never fixed. "Easily detached" carries the sense of interruption and transformation. It is not... [text ends].
Because the mental activities of joy, sorrow, and equanimity arise alternately within meditative concentration, all three are associated with the three types of sensation (*vedanā*).
Next, the specific explanation (in six parts): First, clarifying the characteristics of the three sensations.

Experiencing the aspect of a favorable object that brings harmony and pleasure to body and mind is [the pleasant sensation]. ... [omitted] ... that which is neither oppressive nor pleasing is called the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*).
△ Second, explaining that each of the three [types of sensation] is further divided into two.
Thus, these three sensations are each divided into two (up to: because even painful sensation arises from the untainted).
Commentary on the Meaning: Within the division into two, there are two kinds of "two," namely: body and mind, as well as tainted and untainted. Question:
The untainted noble dharmas (*anāsrava-āryadharma*) bring about the eternal exhaustion of all suffering and are subsumed within the Path (*mārga*) and Cessation (*nirodha*).

How, then, can they also be associated with painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*)? The explanation states: This is because those who cultivate the untainted must necessarily undergo hardships and subject their mental resolve to suffering before they finally attain them.
Therefore, painful sensation arises from the untainted.
Supplement: Qingliang says: That which arises based on the physical sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) is called "bodily sensation" (*kāyikavedanā*);
that which arises within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) from the mental organ (*manas*) is called "mental sensation" (*caitasikavedanā*).
△ The three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) each further divide into three. Alternatively, each divides into three:

namely, those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), [those abandoned by meditation], and so forth; furthermore, there are the three consisting of the learner (*śaikṣa*), the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and that which is neither.

Supplement: Within the division into three, there are two kinds of triads. The first consists of each being divided into three; this is the characteristic of abandoning the delusions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*).

The three feelings associated with [afflictions] abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) are [the first type]. The three feelings associated with innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The three feelings associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*) are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*). Next, each [of these] generally pertains to the three stages;

that is to say, the three feelings of those in training (*śaikṣa*), and so forth. Those that are "neither" refer to those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), namely the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), or the stages of the provisions (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*).
These are the ordinary beings of the inner and outer stages.
△ Fourth, the three [categories] are collectively divided into four.
Alternatively, they are collectively divided into four: the wholesome, the unwholesome, the obscured-unspecified, and the non-obscured-unspecified. These are the four types of feeling (*vedanā*).
Explanation of Terms: This means that pleasant feeling is wholesome; painful feeling is unwholesome; and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is neutral (avyākṛta) in both respects.
△ Five: Each of the three [categories] is divided into four. (3) First, the heading.
There is an interpretation that each of the three feelings (vedanā) is further divided into four.
This refers to the three feelings associated with wholesome states of mind; the same applies to unwholesome states and the two types of neutral (avyākṛta) states.
Next, the explanation of the second [point] begins with the formal exposition.
The spontaneous greed and delusion arising simultaneously with the five consciousnesses (up to the point that) they are all capable of being associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).

Regarding the meaning of the terms: this section provides a detailed explanation according to the specific difficulties. The obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) is capable of being associated with the feeling of suffering;

this refers to two types of spontaneous afflictions (*kleśa*) that arise simultaneously with the five consciousnesses and those within the realms of pure suffering (*ekāntaduḥkha-gati*), because they do not incite unwholesome karma.
These are not unwholesome; they are subsumed under the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). All of them can be associated with painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*).
Next, the scriptural evidence is cited (2): first, from the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If [afflictions] arise spontaneously (*svarasena*), they are associated with all faculties (*indriya*) of the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
Supplement: This is from the fifty-ninth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi*. Question:

Of these various afflictions, how many are associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), and so on, up to how many are associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)? Answer: If they arise spontaneously, there is one.
"All afflictions are found to manifest within the three types of feeling;

therefore, those that pertain to all groups of consciousness are associated with all faculties, while those that do not pertain to all groups of consciousness are associated with all faculties of the mental stage" (text).
Now, this passage is cited as proof that among the six consciousnesses, the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) is associated with all three types of feeling.

All groups of consciousness refer to the first five consciousnesses, which are bodily sensations (*kāyika-vedanā*). The mental ground refers to the sixth consciousness, the mental faculty (*manovijñāna*), which is mental sensation (*caitasika-vedanā*).
Thus, there are two types of sensation: bodily and mental. Spontaneous afflictions (*kleśa*) are associated with these three types of sensation.
△ Next, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

Add the following to address the objection: Someone might raise the difficulty, saying, "To 'observe' means to investigate, which carries the sense of discernment (*pravicaya*).
Since there is no discernment within a state of mental dullness (*mūḍha-citta*), how can it be said that such a person takes an object as their focus? The intent of the response is this:

Although that dull-witted person, while in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), possesses concentration (*samādhi*) but lacks wisdom (*prajñā*), they nonetheless possessed a modicum of hearing (*śruta*) during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).

Regarding the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*): at present, based on the time of preparatory application (*prayoga*), there is a slight sense of wisdom; therefore, it is said that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) takes the object of observation as its focal point.

Alternatively, according to another interpretation, based on the lower [stage], with respect to the object of observation, meditative concentration and wisdom are both predominant, while each possesses a small portion of the other.
There is concentration without wisdom; now, because it refers to the majority of cases, it is said that samādhi takes the object of observation as its focal point.

As in the passage on "forgetting through play" (*līlā-vismaraṇa*), which cites an instance to provide proof: this deva is included within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Or, in the section below, it clarifies the object of observation.
There is wisdom without concentration.
△ Second, the arising of two:
at times two arise, namely, when one gives rise to both concentration and wisdom regarding that which is desired; [counting these] together, there are twelve.
Regarding the "Meaning of Terms": "arising from two" refers to either: (1) arising desire and resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) toward two objects that are desired and determined;

or (2) arising desire and mindfulness (*smṛti*) toward two objects that are desired and previously experienced; or (3) [arising desire and mindfulness] toward two objects that are both desired and being observed.
One may give rise to desire and concentration; or, regarding two objects that are either desired or observed, one gives rise to desire along with wisdom;

or, regarding two objects that are determined and previously practiced, one gives rise to resolve and mindfulness; or, regarding two objects that are determined and being observed, one gives rise to resolve and concentration;
or, regarding two objects that are determined and being observed, one gives rise to resolve and wisdom; or, regarding objects that have been previously practiced...
One contemplates two objects, giving rise to mindfulness and concentration; or, regarding the two objects previously practiced for contemplation, one gives rise to mindfulness and wisdom;
or, regarding a single object of contemplation, one simultaneously gives rise to both concentration and wisdom. In this way, there are ten such pairs in total.
△ Three [applications] arise; three [objects].
At times, three arise, namely: regarding the desired [object], up to the arising of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—altogether there are thirteen.
Regarding the meaning of the terms: "or three arise" means that regarding the three objects that are desired, determined, and previously practiced, desire arises.
Resolve and mindfulness: either one gives rise to desire, resolve, and concentration regarding the three objects of observation that are desired and determined;

or one gives rise to desire, resolve, and wisdom regarding the three objects of observation that are desired and determined; or one gives rise to desire, mindfulness, and concentration regarding the three objects of observation that are desired and previously practiced;
or one gives rise to desire and mindfulness regarding the three objects of observation that are desired and previously practiced.
Wisdom (*prajñā*). Or, regarding the two objects of interest and observation, one gives rise to desire, concentration, and wisdom;

or, regarding the three objects of observation that have been determined and previously practiced, one gives rise to resolve, mindfulness, and concentration; or, regarding the three objects of observation that have been determined and previously practiced, one gives rise to resolve, mindfulness, and wisdom;
or, regarding the two objects of observation that have been determined, one gives rise to resolve, concentration, and wisdom; or, regarding those [objects] previously practiced...
Regarding the two objects of observation, one gives rise to mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Thus, there are ten sets of three in total.
△ Fourth, the arising of four:
at times, four arise; that is, regarding what is desired (up to) the arising of the latter four types, making five sets of four in total.

Regarding the "Meaning of the Terms": As for the phrase "arising from four," it refers to either: (1) the arising of desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and concentration (*samādhi*) with respect to the four objects of observation that one delights in and has previously practiced;
or (2) the arising of desire, resolve, mindfulness, and wisdom (*prajñā*) with respect to these same four objects;

or (3) the arising of desire, resolve, concentration, and wisdom with respect to the three objects of observation that one delights in and has determined upon; or (4) [the arising of these qualities] with respect to the three objects that one delights in and has previously practiced and observed.

Regarding the objects: one arouses desire, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; or, regarding the three objects previously practiced and contemplated with certainty, one arouses understanding, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Thus, there are five sets of four in total.
△ Five arise as five.
At times, five arise together; that is to say, within an object of observation that is pleasing, determined, and previously familiar, all five types arise simultaneously.
△ Next, the summary.
Thus, regarding the four [foundations], there are thirty-one phrases in total, comprising the five [mental factors] such as desire (*chanda*), both collectively and individually.
Regarding the meaning of the terms: this is the concluding summary of the number of phrases. When the five types arise together, they constitute one phrase in total.

As for the individual cases, when one [factor] arises, there are five phrases; for two and three [factors], there are ten phrases each; and for four [factors], there are also five phrases. Thus, the total is thirty-one.
Eleven phrases.
△ Next, the non-arising is explained.
There are cases where, even in states of mind, all five do not arise (up to) those associated with the *ālayavijñāna*; instances of this kind are numerous.

Regarding the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Terms): In states such as those involving the four objects that are not desired, as well as the mind of sudden encounter (*sūer duòxīn*) and its association with the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), these five [mental factors] do not arise at all. Their instances are manifold.
△ III. Analysis by Way of Various Gates (3). First, the gate of association with the various consciousnesses (2). First, regarding the latter three consciousnesses:

the seventh and eighth consciousnesses [are associated] with these five object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya-ka*), because whether they have undergone transformation or not, neither is obstructed.

Regarding the "Explanation of Terms" (*Yinyi*) concerning the presence or absence [of mental factors] according to their respective stages as previously explained: this refers to the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*).

Prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it possesses only wisdom (*prajñā*), while the eighth consciousness lacks all five [mental factors]. Once the basis has been transformed, both possess all five kinds.

As for the sixth consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), in all stages—whether the basis has been transformed or not—it is possible for these five to arise simultaneously. In all the various sacred teachings (*āgama*), none...
Because it is excluded.
△ Next, regarding the first five consciousnesses (in two parts): First, one master holds that there are none of these five.
Another interpretation holds that these five [mental factors] are all absent in the five consciousnesses, because they cannot engage in inference and lack discernment.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: This master asserts that the first five consciousnesses have no distinct objects (*viṣaya*). The five explanations of their meanings can be understood according to their respective order.
△ Next, the second master asserts there are five [distinct objects]. (2) First, these may exist in the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

There is an interpretation that the five consciousnesses may possess these five [mental factors] (up to the point mentioned). The remaining three are to be understood accordingly; there is no fault in their having wisdom (*mati*).

Regarding the meaning of the terms: this is the correct doctrine of Dharmapāla. That is to say, the five consciousnesses may be accompanied by the five [factors] beginning with desire (*chanda*), and so forth.

Although they lack [the others], they are established in sequence as follows: because they exclude meditative equipoise (*samāhita*). As for "etc. (*ādi*): previously, a question was raised stating that the treatise says the five consciousnesses are... [text truncated].
"Since its nature is distracted and unstable, how could it possess concentration? To this, the commentary states: "It excludes *samāhita*," and so forth.

Regarding *samāhita* and *samādhi*, according to the *Qingliang Chao*, the explanation is as follows: The Sanskrit term is *samāpatti*, which is translated here as "equipoise" (*samādhi*). This refers exclusively to states involving mental activity (*sacittaka*), yet it encompasses both concentrated and distracted minds.
The Sanskrit term is *samāhita*, which is translated as "equipoise" (*samāhita*); this applies to both [concentrated and distracted] states.
"Mind" and "mindlessness" refer to being free from dullness and agitation; this is called *samāhita* (equipoise). That which gives rise to virtuous qualities is called *samādhi* (concentration).
The primary intent here is to clarify the exclusion of both "having mind" and "being mindless" regarding the meditative absorption that induces such virtues;
it speaks of "intrinsic distraction" (*svabhāva-vikṣepa*) in order to exclude the concentration of a distracted mind. Therefore, he spoke in this manner.

[It is] known. It is possible for the five consciousnesses to be associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because that which is free from lethargy and excitement is termed "equipoise" (*samāhita*), and that which gives rise to virtuous qualities is termed "inducing" (*āvedha*).

Thus, while it is only the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that can cultivate meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—which is the mental factor of concentration (*samādhicaitta*) in the sense of focusing one-pointedly on a single object—the five consciousnesses may also possess it. The following passage cites scriptural authority:

regarding the statement in the sacred teachings that the eye and other [faculties] possess wisdom, among the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the two powers of the divine eye and the divine ear are precisely these two consciousnesses.

Regarding the associated wisdom: since the visual and auditory consciousnesses are already accompanied by discernment (*prajñā*), the same applies to the remaining three; thus, there is no fault in their possessing discernment.
Next, it is certain that [discernment] exists in the stage where the basis has been transformed (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
In the state prior to mastery, these five may be absent; [from that point] up to the state of mastery, all five consciousnesses possess the wisdom of performing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

Regarding the meaning of the terms: this refers to the state of mastery. In the Tathāgata’s five consciousnesses, each is associated with the five faculties such as desire (*chanda*) and so forth, being supremely predominant and not weak or inferior. The explanation of the meaning is easy to understand.
△ Next, the section on the correspondence with the various feelings (2): First, the inquiry.
With which feelings are these five object-specific mental factors associated?
△ Next, the explanation (2): First, the view of the first master that some are associated while others are not.

There is an interpretation [which holds] that in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are three [types of feeling], excluding the feelings of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*). This is because the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) lack the capacity for discernment and certainty. Regarding the meaning of the terms:

it means that in the desire realm, there are only the three feelings of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). These are associated with the three feelings, excluding the feelings of sorrow and suffering.

The remaining four [consciousnesses] are associated with the four feelings beginning with joy, excluding only the feeling of suffering. This explanation is identical to the previous solution regarding the absence of the desire realm and so forth in the five sensory consciousnesses.
The first master [holds this view].
△ The second master [holds that] it is associated with all five feelings.
There is an interpretation stating that it is associated with all five feelings (up to) because, by virtue of this, it is associated with the five feelings such as desire (*chanda*) and so forth.
**Explanation of Terms:** The first phrase provides a general indication that [the five faculties] are associated with the five types of feeling, beginning with desire (*chanda*).

In the section "The treatise states that the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya*) exists in the realm of desire," it explains that there is grief in the realm of desire. In the section "Purely feeling... it explains that there is suffering (*duḥkha*) in the realm of desire. In the section "The treatise states that craving (*tṛṣṇā*)...

it provides dual proof that both grief and suffering coexist with desire. In the section "Since the faculty of suffering... it explains that the four faculties beginning with resolve (*adhimokṣa*) are associated with suffering, while [the remaining ones] are also associated with joy (*saumanasya*).
And so forth; these follow the previous explanation. The following concludes the section.
△ Third, concluding by analogy with other categories:
These five should further be analyzed according to various categories such as nature (*dhātu*), realm (*dhātu*), and training (*śaikṣa*), as appropriate for reflection.

Explanation of Terms: "Nature" (svabhāva) refers to the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth. "Sphere" (dhātu) refers to the desire realm, the form realm, and so forth. "Training" (śaikṣa) refers to those in training, those beyond training, and so forth.
Since these five possess four of the "all-inclusives," the first two all-inclusives are thus the three natures.

It pervades all three realms. Furthermore, since it is not obstructed whether the sixth consciousness is transformed or untransformed, one should know that such categories of examples exist within the stages of training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth, as can be inferred by analogy.

△ Second, the mental factors of the wholesome state (3). First, concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent one:
Having already explained the two categories of universal and object-specific mental factors, what are the characteristics of the mental factors of the wholesome state?
△ Next, the root verses are cited in response. The verses state:
"Good [factors] are said to be faith, shame, and dread; (up to) diligence, serenity, non-negligence, equanimity, and non-harming.
△ Third, the final commentary provides the explanation (in three parts): first, the direct explanation of the verse text (in two parts); first, the general introduction.
The Commentary states: Only those mental factors that coexist with a wholesome mind are called "wholesome minds. These consist of eleven factors, namely faith, shame, and so forth.

Next, the detailed explanation (in two parts): first, the explanation of faith and the others (in eight parts); first, the explanation of faith (in two parts); first, clarifying the correct principle (in two parts);
first, the direct explanation (in two parts); first, a brief clarification.
What is faith? It is characterized by conviction in reality, virtue, and capability (up to its function of counteracting lack of faith and delighting in the wholesome).
Regarding the phonetic meanings: "reality, virtue, and capability" refers to the bases of faith; "profound endurance and aspiration" refers to faith in cause and effect.
That which can purify the mind is precisely faith in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); this cites both cause and effect as the intrinsic nature, taking them as its essence.

Non-belief is the affliction to be remedied; delighting in the wholesome is the beneficial dharma sought; this cites both that which is to be remedied and that which is sought as the objects of faith and practice.
△ Next, the sequential explanation.
Now, the distinctions of faith are briefly of three kinds... [up to] ...delighting in the cultivation of mundane and supramundane virtues.
*Yinyi* (Exegesis): First, it clarifies the arising of patience toward reality. The actual reality of all phenomena refers to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). All phenomena...

The "true principle" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This is because, although the teachings expounded by the Buddhas upon their appearance in the world consist of immeasurable gateways, when summarized, they do not transcend these two.
Therefore, one should have deep faith that they truly exist, accord with them through patient acceptance (*kṣānti*), and never oppose them.

Following the section on the two types of faith in existence, next is the clarification of generating delight toward the qualities. Regarding the true and pure qualities of the Three Jewels: the Buddha...

The true purity of the Buddha’s qualities refers to his freedom from delusive defilements, his permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity, as well as his four powers of knowledge (*jñāna-bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
The true purity of the Dharma refers to unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), quiescent phenomena such as the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and suchness (*tathatā*).

The true purity of the Saṅgha refers to their bodies adorned by ethical discipline and meditative concentration, and their possession of the six points of harmony (*ṣaḍ-abhedyāni*). These Three Jewels are that which all sentient beings delight in.

Because it is the basis [for liberation], one should have deep faith, joy, and reverence for it, never feeling satiated. Third, regarding the three types of faith—superior, middling, and inferior—the latter clarifies that which gives rise to aspiration.
As for "worldly and world-transcending virtues": worldly virtues refer to the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, the four dhyānas, the eight concentrations, and so forth;
world-transcending virtues refer to the Four Noble Truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, the six perfections, the four means of integration, and so forth.
Regarding "able to attain and able to accomplish," Qingliang says: "Believing in oneself and others, one attains now and accomplishes later.

This means being able to attain pleasant fruits and able to accomplish the noble path; therefore, one should have deep faith in its efficacy and give rise to aspiration, expecting that it will certainly be attained.
From "By this" onwards, he next explains the function of faith. "Not believing in that mind" refers to not enduring [the truth] regarding reality and so forth.

This serves as the antidote to the desire for pleasure and the mind of defiled attachment; it also simultaneously remedies the karma of indolence that relies upon them, for those who delight in realizing and practicing mundane and supramundane virtues.
△ Next, the critical analysis (in two parts). First, the analysis of its own characteristic (in two parts). First, the question:
"Patience" refers to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), which is the cause of faith; [the author] now explicitly states what the specific characteristic of this faith is.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: this refers to profound patience (*kṣānti*) and aspiration (*chanda*). These are its cause and fruit, not its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). What, then, is its intrinsic nature?
△ Next, the answer follows.
Is it not appropriate to say that the nature [of faith] is the purity of mind?
△ Next, distinguishing the purity of mind (in two parts): first, the question.
This still does not clarify the statement regarding "the purity of that mind" (up to: the objection that the pure factors associated with the mind are likewise [purity]).
Supplement: This still does not clarify the statement that "the mind is pure. Why is this? If purity were the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) itself, then the mind would not be a mental factor (*caitta*).
In that case, this faith (*śraddhā*) should not be designated as a mental factor. This objection is raised using the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound analysis.

If it is held that [faith] causes the mind to become pure, how does it differ from shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*)? This objection is raised using the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound analysis. If one says...

This is a dharma that is pure simultaneously with the mind. How does it differ from [the mental factor of] shame (*hrī*) and so forth? It is because it is a dharma that arises at the same time as the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
This is the response to the objection regarding its proximity.
△ Next, the answer follows.
This nature is clear and limpid, capable of purifying the mind and so forth; because faith is the direct opposite of those [defilements], it takes purity as its characteristic.

Regarding the meaning of the term *śraddhā*: in the answer, following the sequence of the primary question while implicitly including the subsequent one, it means that the essence of faith is itself clear and limpid, and is also capable of purifying other mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*).
Now, the name is established based on its predominant function; therefore, it is said to "purify the mind."

Regarding "Purity" (*śuddhi*), the *Zongjing* says: "Only faith is that which purifies; all other virtues, such as the wholesome [mental factors], are that which is purified. Therefore, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is taken as the primary factor; one speaks only of the purity of the mind, not of the mental concomitants (*caitta*). This is illustrated by the analogy of water below.

As for the passage concerning "shame" (*hrī*) and so forth, there is no fault of redundancy with the preceding discussion of shame and the rest. That is to say, while the dharmas of shame and the like share the common meaning of being "conducive and beneficial," each possesses its own distinct substance (*svabhāva*).

However, these [other factors] do not have purity as their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); because this [purity] has purity as its defining characteristic, it is not identical to shame and the others.
The fault of mutual confusion. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "All those below" again cites the object of negation to show that this [faith] has purity alone as its characteristic.
△ Next, the erroneous interpretations are refuted.
Some say: "Faith is associated with longing" (up to) "...by this it should be known that mental purity is faith."

Regarding the definition of faith as "taking delight" (*anurāga*) as its characteristic: Qingliang states that this is the tenet of the Sthavira school of the Hīnayāna. This should be understood as a general critique. He refutes it by saying:
"If faith were defined by taking delight as its characteristic, it would not be exclusively wholesome. Taking delight is itself a 'particular object' (*viṣayaviśeṣa*) [mental factor];

therefore, desire (*chanda*) should also pertain to all three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral). Furthermore, since the truths of suffering and origination are real entities that serve as the objects of faith..."
It is not a dharma that is desirable or delightful; therefore, one should not give rise to faith by taking this as an object.

As for those who maintain that "conformity" (*anuloma*) is its characteristic, Master Qingliang’s commentary identifies this as the tenet of a divergent teacher within the Mahāyāna. This should be understood as a critique extending downward [to other schools], stating:

it should not be exclusively wholesome, because conformity is itself resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) and desire (*chanda*). If it conforms while maintaining a definitive certainty, that is simply resolute conviction.
Because it is explained thus: if one complies with what is cherished and desired, that is precisely desire (*chanda*);
for apart from those two factors, there is no characteristic of compliance. This concludes the demonstration below.
△ Second, the explanation of *hrī* (shame) and *apatrāpya* (moral dread). (2) First, the direct explanation. (2) First, *hrī*. What is *hrī*?
It relies on the power of oneself and the Dharma... [it serves as] the antidote to shamelessness (*ahrīkya*) and brings rest to all unwholesome conduct.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: First, the body and function are explained; this refers to the subsequent sequential interpretation.

Qingliang says: "Regarding 'one's own dharma' (*svadharma*): 'one's own' (*sva*) means one's own person; it refers to the superior power of generating respect for oneself. 'Dharma' (*dharma*) refers to the teachings;
it refers to the superior power of generating veneration for the teachings. By virtue of these two powers, one honors the worthy and capable and reveres those who are good."

To feel shame for one's transgressions and evils, such that one does not dare to commit them; this specifically opposes *anapatrāpya* (lack of shame), while generally it brings all unwholesome conduct to rest.
Next is *hrī* (moral dread).
What is *hrī*? It relies on the power of the world [to restrain oneself]... [it serves as] the antidote to *anapatrāpya* and brings all evil karma to rest.
*Yinyì* (Explanations of Terms and Meanings): First, the correct [commentary] explains the essence and function. This refers to the subsequent sequential interpretation. Qingliang says:

"Relying on the world" means relying on the world's censure and defamation by others, as well as one's own sense of shame regarding unwholesome dharmas, and thus refraining from [unvirtuous actions], and so forth.
It is named after the world. It is characterized by intense revulsion and loathing. That which possesses evil is called "violent. The essence of defiled phenomena is called "evil.

Regarding these two types of phenomena, one treats the light [evils] with aversion and does not associate with them; one rejects evil karma and does not commit it. It is through this intensity that [the name is established].
It is the antidote to lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*) and brings to rest all unwholesome conduct.
△ Next, the analysis (three parts): First, the summary and clarification according to the *Abhidharmasamudaya*.
Because the sense of shame regarding faults and evils is the common characteristic of both [shame and dread], various holy teachings provisionally designate it as their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the "Meaning of the Terms": This refers to the two dharmas of shame (*hrī*) and dread-of-blame (*apatrāpya*). Each possesses both general and specific characteristics.

However, the statement that both consist in "feeling shame for faults and evils" refers to their general characteristic, not their specific characteristics. As clarified in various sacred teachings and the *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (Treatise on the Manifestation of the Holy Teachings), the *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) states:
when that treatise explains that feeling shame for faults and evils constitutes the two characteristics, it is referring to the general characteristic.
[The ear] is so called from the perspective of its conventional designation as a substance; in reality, it consists of the elements such as earth and so forth, which are its specific characteristics.
△ Next, the formal distinction between the general and the specific (in two parts): first, refuting the external schools' attachment to the general as being the specific.

If one maintains that shame (*hrī*) and modesty (*apatrāpya*) are two distinct characteristics (up to the point where it) further contradicts the treatise’s statement that these ten pervade all wholesome minds.

[Commentary on the terminology]: This means that if one maintains that the faults and evils [of transgression] constitute two distinct characteristics, then both of these dharmas would take shame as their essence;
consequently, there would be no difference in essence between *hrī* and *apatrāpya*. Due to this, these two dharmas [would not be distinct].

They arise simultaneously. Furthermore, an example is cited: "It is not [the case that] feeling, perception, and so forth, possess this property. Therefore, one should know that the five—feeling, perception, and the others—each have their own distinct substance (*dravya*).
They pervade all phenomena; when they arise, they arise together, without any sequence or the quality of being non-associated (*viprayukta*).

This is illustrated by the case of shame (*hrī*) and dread (*apatrāpya*), which both pervade wholesome minds and are not non-associated; therefore, one should not maintain that [the dissociated factors] are universal.
[They] take [these] characteristics as distinct entities. If one anticipates the following objection, an external defender might say:

"Although the sense of shame regarding transgressions and evils is a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), *hrī* (shame) depends upon one's own dharma, whereas *apatrāpya* (embarrassment) depends upon the world. Now, based on one's own dharma and the world, the powers of self and others differ."

One might attempt to establish two distinct categories; therefore, he cites and refutes this [position], saying: "If [the factors] were established through dependence, their essence would necessarily be unreal, which contradicts the scriptures.

Furthermore, fearing that one might offer a defense by claiming: "Although their essence is substantially existent, they merely arise individually," he refutes this, saying: "This also contradicts the treatise, for the treatise states:
'Among the eleven wholesome dharmas, with the exception of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), the remaining ten are universally present in all wholesome states.'"
Because it is the mind, it does not arise separately.

△ Next, the refutation of the internal school’s position regarding the distinctness of characteristics while being common to both (2). First, the refutation of the distinctness of characteristics while being common to both (2).
First, the refutation.
"Veneration and slight rejection are the distinct characteristics of these two [types of objects]. (Up to: Since both faults are identical, why is the blame directed only at one side?

Commentary on the Meaning: The objection states: If the author of the treatise has already said that veneration and slight rejection are the distinct characteristics of those two, then it follows that veneration is the contemplation of a virtuous object, while slight rejection is the contemplation of a non-virtuous object; thus, the objects of focus (*ālambana*) are respectively virtuous and non-virtuous.
Since their objects are distinct, these two dharmas should not arise simultaneously. Otherwise, they would incur the two faults of either not arising together or arising separately.
Since they are identical [in nature], why do you dogmatically cling to the view that they must arise separately?
△ Next, the explanation.
Who says that the objects of these two dharmas differ? (Up to: "It is simply that for wholesome minds, the objects of perception have no distinction.
*Yinyi* (Explanation of Terms): The first phrase provides a direct answer; the second phrase poses a further inquiry; "wholesome minds" and below explain the meaning.
△ Second, the refutation that there is a distinct meaning regarding the pervasion (2). First, the refutation. [Objection:
Is it not the case that I have also stated this principle?

[Commentary on the Meaning of the Sound]: The intention of the refuter is as follows: The previous statement that "when a wholesome mind arises" and so forth, up to "the object of cognition has no distinction," [is intended to show...]
[The opponent asks: "Is it not the case that I have stated that shame (*hrī*) and embarrassment (*apatrāpya*) are two distinct characteristics? Does this point not also apply here?
[The author] next refutes [this]:
Since you maintain that the intrinsic characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of shame and embarrassment are identical, by what logic can they possibly ward off the objections previously set forth?

Commentary on the Terms: Regarding the phrase "since their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are identical," this refers to the fact that both shame (*hrī*) and modesty (*apatrāpya*) take the sense of "feeling ashamed" as their essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Thus, the objection raised previously—that shame and modesty should have no distinction in essence—contradicts the scriptural passage stating that there are ten universal wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-citta-mahābhūmika*), and so forth.
△ Third, further aligning with the sacred teachings (*āgama*).

However, the sacred teachings state that "self and other" refers to what is beneficial or harmful to oneself; thus, "self and other" are designated based on this. [Regarding the] phonology and meaning:
An opponent from a non-Buddhist school asks: "If the two distinctions are not established in dependence upon self and other, how then [does the sacred teaching]..."
The teaching explains that this involves regarding oneself and others; therefore, the commentary states: "In the Noble Teaching, 'self' and 'other' are not as you conceive them.
For [the Teacher], one's own phenomena are called "self," while those of the world are called "other.

Alternatively, that which is honored and esteemed—being beneficial to oneself—is called "self," while that which is despised and rejected—being detrimental to oneself—is called "other. As for what you conceive, it is merely one...
Shame is established as two distinct types by observing oneself and others; are these not, therefore, nominally existent?

What the Holy Teachings refer to as the two different natures of "veneration" and "rejection"—that which is beneficial and that which is detrimental—is precisely this distinction between self and other.
Alternatively, if one takes the world of one's own phenomena as the basis, it is termed "self" and "other. How could this be the same as your own tenet that [these] do not truly exist?
△ Third, the explanation of non-attachment and so forth (in two parts): first, a general clarification.
The phrase "non-attachment, etc. includes non-hatred and non-delusion, as they serve as the direct antidotes to the three unwholesome roots.
Regarding the meaning of the term *mūla* (root): it carries the sense of "that which can produce.
These are called the three roots because they are preeminent in producing wholesome dharmas and because they directly counteract the three unwholesome states of attachment, hatred, and delusion.

△ Second, the detailed explanation (in two parts). First, the explanation of the first two [wholesome roots] (in two parts). First, the detailed explanation (in two parts). First, non-attachment (*alobha*). What is non-attachment?
Its nature is non-attachment toward existence and the requisites for existence; its function is to counteract attachment and to bring about the performance of wholesome deeds.
*Yinyi* (Explanatory Notes on Pronunciation and Meaning): Qingliang says: Some claim that there are three subsequent "existences" (*bhava*).
The fruit of maturation (*vipāka*) consists of existence itself and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).

Within these two, not giving rise to craving or attachment is the nature of non-greed (*alobha*), which serves as the specific antidote to greed. Performing various kinds of wholesome deeds is its general function.
△ Next is non-hatred (*adveṣa*).
What is non-hatred? It has the nature of being free from resentment toward suffering and the instruments of suffering; its function is to counteract hatred and to produce wholesome states.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: *Qīngliáng* says that "suffering" refers to the three types of suffering, and "instruments of suffering" refers to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
That which can produce suffering refers to wrong views and the like, for they slander the untainted (*anāsrava*). These also produce suffering.

Among these two [types of causes], not giving rise to hatred is the nature of non-hatred (*adveṣa*). Its specific function is to counteract hatred, while its general function is to perform all manner of wholesome deeds.
△ Next, the general clarification:
When a wholesome mind arises, regardless of what object it encounters... (up to) ...therefore, these two types both pervade the wholesome mind.
[Commentary on the Meaning and Phonetics]: It may be asked: Since these two roots of goodness have different objects of perception (*ālambana*), they should not arise simultaneously.

"Not universal" refers to wholesome minds. The commentary explains: when a wholesome mind arises, regardless of the object it encounters, it is free from attachment and aversion toward existence (*bhava*) and suffering (*duḥkha*), etc.
One establishes non-attachment and non-hatred by observing existence and so forth; it is not necessary for those [objects] themselves to serve as the focal objects.

This is like the previously mentioned *hrī* (shame) and *apatrāpya* (dread), which are established by observing good and evil, rather than having good and evil as their focal objects. Therefore, these two types [of wholesome minds] both [possess them].
The universal wholesome mind.
△ Next, the explanation of non-delusion (in two parts): first, the direct explanation.
What is non-delusion? It has clear understanding regarding all principles and phenomena as its nature; its function is to counteract delusion and to perform wholesome deeds.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists in the clear understanding and thorough knowledge of the principles of the various truths (*satya*) as well as all actual phenomena (*vastu*).
Its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*) consists in specifically counteracting delusion (*moha*) and generally performing all manner of wholesome deeds.
△ Next, the critical examination (in two parts). First, according to one master, non-delusion is precisely wisdom (*prajñā*).
There is an interpretation that non-delusion has wisdom as its intrinsic nature; [it is] like the view among the afflictions, which is therefore explained separately.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: This master’s concise intention is that non-delusion (*amoha*) has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its intrinsic nature and possesses no separate substantial entity.

Why? Because the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that the substance of this non-delusion consists of the "resultant" (*vipāka*), "instructional" (*śruta*), and "realizational" (*bhāvanā*) wisdoms, which are determined through scriptural authority and inferential reasoning.

These three types of wisdom—resultant and so forth—are, respectively, the innate (*upapatti-labdha*), the heard (*śruta-mayī*), and the cultivated (*bhāvanā-mayī*) wisdoms. (Some say that the term "innate" refers to the resultant.)

The single term "wisdom" (*prajñā*) explains two types of wisdom: that which arises from hearing the teachings and reflecting upon them (i.e., *śrutamayī-prajñā*), and that which is realized through cultivation (i.e., *bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Regarding the phrase "Although this is... and so forth:

it means that an objection might be raised, "If this is identical to wisdom, since it is already included among the 'object-specific mental factors' (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*), why is it mentioned again? The explanation states: Although this is indeed wisdom, it is mentioned here to demonstrate that within the category of wholesome factors (*kuśalapakṣa*), there is a superior efficacy.

Non-delusion (*amoha*) is exclusively wholesome, whereas wisdom (*prajñā*) permeates both the wholesome and the defiled, just as the afflictions (*kleśa*) include views (*dṛṣṭi*), even though these views are themselves forms of wisdom.
[Included] within [the category of] grasping because it is exclusively defiled; yet it is separately established as two [types]. This case should be understood in the same way.
△ Next, the second master [asserts that] it is not wisdom (four points). First, the formal explanation that it possesses a substantial entity.

There is an interpretation that non-delusion (*amoha*) is not identical to wisdom (*prajñā*). [This is because] it is subsumed under non-hatred and non-delusion, but not under the faculties (*indriya*).
Regarding the meaning of the term: non-delusion is not wisdom; it possesses a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as the direct antidote to delusion (*moha*).

For example, just as non-attachment (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adveṣa*) possess their own separate entities because they are subsumed under the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), this [non-delusion] should likewise be so. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "All..."
The Buddha’s great compassion (mahākaruṇā) is subsumed by the absence of hatred and delusion; it is not said that compassion is subsumed by the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya).
Since the absence of delusion can subsume great compassion, how could it be identical to wisdom? This is seen in the text in scroll fifty-seven.
△ Third, refuting the previous interpretation.
If that non-delusion has wisdom as its intrinsic nature... (up to)... the three are conventionally existent, while the rest are all real. [Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms]:
This means that if non-delusion were identical to wisdom, then non-delusion would lack an essential substance. Great Compassion should be understood accordingly.

The ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and so forth, are likewise subsumed under the faculties such as wisdom (*prajñā*), because they are not comprised within non-hatred (*adveṣa*) or non-delusion (*amoha*).
Furthermore, if non-delusion lacked substantiality, it would not be a real entity (*dravya*), which would contradict the treatise’s exposition of the eleven wholesome factors (*kuśaladharma*).
Only non-harming (*avihiṃsā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and heedfulness (*apramāda*)—these three are conventional (*saṃvṛti*). The remaining eight are all substantially existent (*dravyasat*).
△ Third, connecting this with the previously cited treatise:

However, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that wisdom (*prajñā*) is their essence; [this applies] up to the point where it says that the principle for expressing the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of faith must necessarily be so.

Regarding the "Explanation of Terms" (*Yinyi*): "Citing those causes and effects, etc. means that the wisdom born of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is the cause of non-delusion (*amoha*), while the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) is the fruit of non-delusion.
However, when the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that "wisdom (*prajñā*) is its essence," this refers to those three types of wisdom as the causes and fruits of non-delusion;
it merely clarifies the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this non-delusive clarity and understanding. As for [the example] with...
The following example clarifies this; the underlying meaning may be inferred accordingly.
△ Fourth, establishing that [ignorance] possesses a substantial entity:
because greed, hatred, and delusion are associated with the six consciousnesses... (up to) ...therefore, since there is no delusion [in this state], it should not exist separately.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: This refers to the three unwholesome roots, such as greed (*lobha*), and so forth. Because they give rise to evil with particular intensity, their remedies (*pratipakṣa*) are both general and specific.
The general remedy is the wholesome faculty of wisdom (*prajñā*) among the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-viniyata*). The specific remedies are the three types of wholesome roots.

If one were to claim that non-delusion (*amoha*) is simply wisdom, it would not be appropriate for it to be specifically opposed to delusion (*moha*). Therefore, non-delusion, like the preceding two [roots], possesses its own distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and is specifically opposed to delusion.
Explanation.
△ Fourth, the explanation of diligence (*vīrya*). First, a brief clarification:
Diligence refers to the application of vigor (*vīrya*) toward wholesome and unwholesome categories; its function is to counteract indolence and to bring wholesome qualities to fulfillment.
Commentary on the Terms: Virtuous factors should be cultivated, and unwholesome factors should be abandoned.

Within these two matters of cultivation and abandonment, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is valor and intrepidity. Its functional activity (*karman*) is to counteract laziness and to bring wholesome matters to completion.
*He-xiang Kai-meng* (Opening the Ignorant through Harmonious Resonance). Question: Are "diligence" (*qin*) and "vigor" (*jingjin*) one and the same, or are they different? Answer: They are different.

Diligence pertains to all three moral natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral), whereas vigor is exclusively wholesome. Question: Since they are different, why is it said that "diligence" refers to vigor, as if they were designated as one? Answer:

It is because when referring to that which belongs to a specific portion [of diligence]—namely, that which is of a wholesome nature—they are treated as one. Question: Regarding the cultivation and abandonment of the wholesome and the unwholesome: Answer: With respect to the wholesome.
Cultivating the wholesome factors and abandoning the unwholesome factors. Question: What is the meaning of *vīrya* (diligence)? Answer: *Vīra* means external exertion; *dhṛti* means firmness.

To be courageous without timidity and steadfast without fear is the meaning. Question: What is the meaning of *paripūri* (fulfillment)? Answer: To bring wholesome matters to completion is called fulfillment.
