Therefore, the three roots are termed "performing the wholesome," and this is called "fulfillment" because they are able to fulfill those [wholesome qualities]. Question: One hundred...
Regarding the statement that after the faculty of faith (*śraddhā*) comes diligence (*vīrya*): why is it that diligence is taught only after these three faculties? Answer:

The sequence of causes and conditions follows a specific order, and the establishment of the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) system likewise follows a sequential order; therefore, they are not the same. Question: What is the nature of this causal dependence? Answer:
Faith is the basis for desire (*chanda*), and desire is the basis for diligence (*vīrya*). For this reason, diligence is taught immediately after faith.
Question: Why are they established according to this sequence? Answer: The faculties are established based on diligence (*vīrya*).
Since the four factors—the three beginning with equanimity (*upekṣā*) and their basis—must logically be explained together, the text explains diligence only after the three faculties.
△ Second, the sequential explanation (in two parts): First, a general statement that it is exclusively virtuous.
"Vigor" (*vīrya*) signifies superior progress and distinguishes it from all defiled phenomena; this immediately demonstrates that vigor is subsumed within the nature of virtue alone.

*Yinyì* (Explanations of Terms): "Courageous" (*yǒng*) refers to valor. It serves to signify superior progress and thereby excludes that which is unwholesome, obscured, or non-arising, as these lack the capacity for excellence.
*Jìngliáng* says: "Courageous" clarifies that [the mind] is high and superior in every moment;

it is not like defiled phenomena, which, even if they increase, are all termed "regression" when compared to the various wholesome categories, and cannot be called "progress. "Fierce" (*hàn*) refers to being forceful and aggressive. By...

"Pure" (*viśuddha*) signifies being "exclusively pure" (*kevala-viśuddha*). This immediately excludes the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), because although it may be pure, it is not exclusively pure due to its susceptibility to being interspersed with other states.
Since it excludes that single nature, it reveals that [the category] is comprised solely of the wholesome (*kuśala*).
△ Next, the specific distinctions are explained in detail.
These distinctions are briefly of five kinds (up to) because of the differences between the uninterrupted, the liberated, and the progressive [paths].
Regarding the meaning of the terms: from "armor-like diligence" (*saṃnāha-vīrya*) up to "tireless diligence" (*aparikheda-vīrya*), these are what the treatise reveals as the distinctions.

This is an alternative title. That is, in the lower part of the sutra, it provides the alternative titles for the assembly of the sutra. Regarding "donning the armor" (*saṃnāha*): it receives its name from a metaphor.
Just as a person entering battle must first don armor to defend against bows and arrows, so too one seeking *bodhi* must first make a vow to prevent falling back or losing [the goal].
This refers to what the sutra calls "vigorous effort with power. Regarding "application" (*prayoga*): although one has generated [the resolve],...
The mind, by means of the embankment of aspiration, is free from loss or regression. Nevertheless, according to one’s inclination, one must apply oneself with diligent practice;
this is what the Sūtra refers to as "possessing diligence and vigor. Regarding the phrase "without inferiority" and so forth:

it means that whatever wholesome deeds one performs according to one’s inclination, one practices without negligence until seated upon the sublime seat of Bodhi, even at the cost of personal exhaustion.
To feel no discouragement in the face of suffering is called "absence of dejection. To have a mind that does not waver when confronted by the afflictions of others is called "absence of retreat.
To cultivate wholesome qualities with constant diligence and without weariness from the present until reaching enlightenment is called "absence of satiety.
These three phrases correspond respectively to the three types of vigor described in the Sūtra as "courageous" and so forth.

This is the progression. Based on the preceding commentary, the intent of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* is established. Below this section on the five distinct [categories], the specific meanings are again summarized;

there are four such distinctions in total. First, the five are explained in terms of practice: first, the practice of initial resolve; second, the practice of one's own stage, as indicated by the subsequent "inferior" [category].
Third, the practice of one's own level; fourth, the practice of a superior level; and fifth, the practice of excellence.

These correspond respectively to the five types of diligence mentioned above. Alternatively, the first is "inferior," while the second concerns the cultivation of the five types of clear realization (*vidyā*):

first, cultivation upon initial resolve; second, long-term cultivation; third, uninterrupted cultivation; fourth, intensive cultivation; and fifth, exhaustive cultivation. These should be understood in their respective order.

Alternatively, [the stages] are supported by the lower [stages]. Regarding the five [stages], they are explained according to their positions: first, the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*); second, the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*);

third, the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*); fourth, the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*); and fifth, the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*). These should also be understood in their respective order. One might ask:
"While diligence can be understood for the preceding four stages, how can it also be applied to the ultimate fruit of culmination? The explanation states:

The ultimate goal of the two vehicles is the aspiration for great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*); the ultimate goal of the Buddhas is to benefit sentient beings. Therefore, at this stage, there is "tireless vigor" (*anikṣiptadhura-vīrya*).
Alternatively, [the stages] are divided into five according to the path: first, the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) of the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*);

second, the path of preparation of the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*); third, the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*); fourth, the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); and fifth, the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
The Path is likewise to be understood according to the sequence above. Regarding the preceding four stages, had each been explained individually, it might have obstructed the primary meaning;
therefore, they are merely assigned and briefly elucidated here. Let the wise examine this in detail.
△ Fifth, the explanation of *praśrabdhi* (pliancy).
"Pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*) refers to being free from heaviness and rigidity (*dausthulya*), thereby causing the basis (*āśraya*) to become transformed into a state of ease and comfort.
*Kaimeng* (Opening the Ignorant) states: It is called "pliancy" because being free from heaviness is "light," and being harmonious and flowing is "pleasurable. It is capable of...

"Capable" means being able to endure and being able to undertake. "Transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti) means causing the body and mind, which are the basis, to abandon their heaviness (dausthulya) and attain tranquility (praśrabdhi).
This following passage provides an explanation: that which obstructs meditative concentration is precisely lethargy (styāna).
The basis is the body and mind.
△ Sixth, the explanation of non-negligence (in two parts): First, the direct explanation (in three parts). First, the brief clarification:
Non-negligence consists of diligence and the three roots [of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion], and its function is to serve as the foundation for all mundane and supramundane wholesome deeds.

Commentary on Terms: Non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion, along with diligent vigor, prevent the arising of the evils to be abandoned and cultivate the increase of the virtues to be practiced;
this is the intrinsic nature of heedfulness (*apramāda*). Its functional activity is to counteract heedlessness (*pramāda*) and bring virtuous dharmas to fulfillment.
△ Next, the sequential explanation:
This means that these very four dharmas, regarding the matters of abandonment and cultivation (up to the point of) being devoid of functions other than those four, have no separate utility.

[Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms]: That is to say, it is precisely the four dharmas beginning with diligence (*vīrya*) that can prevent and cultivate; this is called "heedfulness" (*apramāda*). It is not [something else].
"Having a separate substance but no distinct characteristic" clarifies that it lacks substance. "Having no distinct function" reveals that it lacks function.
△ Third, resolving objections:
Although faith, shame, and so forth also possess this capacity [to motivate], they are not the basis for this [vigor] because they do not universally stimulate all faculties.

Regarding the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Terms), it says: "Fa (Fang) states that faith, shame (*hrī*), remorse (*apatrāpya*), and so forth, are all capable of both preventing [unwholesome states] and cultivating [wholesome ones].

Why then is 'heedfulness' (*apramāda*) not established based upon them? The commentary explains: "Although faith, shame, and the others also possess this capacity, compared to these four dharmas, their functional power is weak and inferior.
Because they are not roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and because they do not universally exert stimulation, they are not the basis for heedfulness."
△ Next, the section on discernment (in two parts): First, clarifying that guarding and cultivation do not constitute its characteristics and functions (in two parts). First, the objection:
Is it not the case that guarding and cultivation are indeed its characteristics and functions?
Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: The objection states: Since there is the name "guarding and cultivation," how could it not involve guarding and cultivation?
This is precisely the characteristic function of non-heedlessness; why then do you say that it lacks both essence and function?
△ Next, the explanation:
How do guarding and cultivation differ from the three roots of diligence? (Up to: "In this case, one would have to wait for yet another [factor], which would lead to the fault of infinite regress.
Commentary on the Meaning: The explanation states that guarding and cultivation are not different from the three roots of diligence. If it is argued that those four [roots] must depend upon...
Only through non-negligence (*apramāda*) does activity arise; this [non-negligence] would have to depend on something else, leading to the fallacy of infinite regress.
△ Next, the four dharmas are explained as having the function of prevention and cultivation (2): first, the objection.

Diligence merely universally stimulates all wholesome factors, while the faculties merely serve as the general support for all wholesome factors. How, then, can it be said that those four factors possess the function of guarding and cultivation?

This implies that the functions of guarding and cultivation must necessarily belong [to the specific powers]. *Yinyi* (Exegesis): Diligence merely universally stimulates all wholesome dharmas; the faculties merely serve as the universal basis and sustenance for all wholesome dharmas.
How, then, can it be said that these four dharmas possess the function of guarding and cultivation? The intent is to clarify that guarding and cultivation definitely pertain [to the powers].
This is the essential function of negligence (*pramāda*).
△ Next, the explanation:
"What are the characteristics of its defensive cultivation? (up to: "Therefore, non-negligence (*apramāda*) certainly has no separate substantial entity."

Commentary on the Terms: The first phrase is a rhetorical question. "If [it is] universal," and so forth, refutes it through reasoning. "In this way," and so forth, concludes that there is no separate entity.
The intent clarifies that everything from being universally supported to ensuring non-forgetfulness is not, in itself, the function of *apramāda* (heedfulness).
Thus, one knows that the prevention [of unwholesome states] and the cultivation [of wholesome ones] have no separate entity; they are simply the four dharmas.
△ Seventh: Explanation of Equanimity in Practice (2). First, the direct explanation (2). First, a brief clarification.

What is equanimity in practice (*vyāyāma-upekṣā*)? It consists of the three roots [of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion], and its function is to counteract restlessness (*auddhatya*) and to establish tranquility (*śamatha*).

Commentary on the Terms: Regarding "equanimity of formations" (*saṃskāropekṣā*): this refers to the equanimity within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) that constitutes wholesome dharmas;

it is called "equanimity of formations" to distinguish it from the equanimity subsumed under the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*). "Evenness of mind" means not following after lethargy or agitation.
"Rectitude of mind" means being free from crookedness or partiality. "Abiding without effort" means dwelling in a state of tranquility.
△ Next, the sequential explanation:

This refers to how these four dharmas cause the mind to become detached [from its objects], distinguishing the differences in relinquishment (*upekṣā*) throughout the initial, middle, and final stages.

*Hexiang* (Combined Resonance) and *Kaimeng* (Opening the Ignorant) ask about the meaning of "causing the mind" and so forth. The answer is: it is by means of relinquishment that the mind becomes detached from lethargy (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*).
The initial mind is equanimous; the subsequent mind is upright; and the final [mind] is effortless.
△ Next, the distinctions are clarified:
through non-negligence, one first eliminates defilements (up to) that which brings about tranquility, because the mind is thus equalized.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: Question—Since both heedfulness (*apramāda*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) take the four factors as their essence, how is one to know the distinction between these two?
The explanation states: Through heedfulness, one first eliminates defilements;

equanimity, moreover, causes the mind to abide in tranquility. This clarifies that the elimination of defilements belongs to heedfulness, while causing the mind to abide in tranquility belongs to equanimity.

This is precisely the cultivation of equanimity (*upekṣā*). These two have distinct meanings; there is no separate explanation for their distinct natures here, because they are identical to the four dharmas, just as with heedfulness (*apramāda*).
[From] *Hexiang* and *Kaimeng*: Question: Since they are identical to the four dharmas, why is it necessary to establish them separately? Answer: If they were not established separately...
Because it establishes this capacity [of non-harming].
△ Eighth, the explanation of non-harming (in two parts): First, clarifying the correct meaning (in two parts): First, a brief explanation. What is non-harming?
Toward all sentient beings... [it] has the function of counteracting harming and taking compassion as its activity.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: This is precisely that absence of hatred (*adveṣa*). It consists in not causing injury, harm, or affliction toward sentient beings;
thus, its intrinsic nature is non-violence (*avihiṃsā*), which serves as the antidote to violence. Its functional activity consists of compassion and sympathetic pity.
△ Next, the sequential explanation:
This means that non-hatred toward sentient beings [is so called] because those two [benefit and happiness] are superior for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings.
Regarding the meaning of the terms: First, non-harming is clarified; its essence is non-hatred, yet it is merely a name provisionally established based upon that [non-hatred].
Below, "non-hatred" (*adveṣa*) and so forth: next, the distinctions are revealed. Non-hatred is the opposite of hatred; non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) is the opposite of harming.

Non-hatred is loving-kindness (*maitrī*); non-harming is compassion (*karuṇā*). This is the distinction between these two. Non-hatred has a substantial nature (*dravya*), whereas non-harming is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*).

Why is it established separately? It is to reveal the distinct characteristics of the two, loving-kindness and compassion. What does "revealing them" mean? It means benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings. These two...
Because it is superior.
△ Next, the refutation of divergent interpretations (in two parts): First, the introduction.
Some say that non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) is not identical to non-anger (*avyāpāda*). [The text continues: "What is the characteristic of this? It is said to be the absence of harming or afflicting."
Regarding the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Terms): A divergent interpreter says that non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) does not have non-anger (*adveṣa*) as its essence;

rather, the nature of being virtuous and wholesome (*kalyāṇatva*) is the essence of non-harming. He further inquires: "What are the characteristics of this nature of being virtuous and wholesome? The divergent interpreter replies: [as follows].
That is to say, it is non-affliction.
Next, [the author] refutes [the opponent's view]:

"The same applies to non-hatred (*adveṣa*); how could there be a separate intrinsic nature? (up to: Because loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) are virtuous and wholesome, they are non-hatred."

Commentary on the Phonology and Meaning: The refutation of the [opposing] view states: "If one is free from anger toward sentient beings and does not inflict harm or affliction upon them, how could one possibly be devoid of this nature of non-harming?

Next, the explanation of the word "and" (及): (1) First, the direct explanation of what is manifested by "and," such as joy (*muditā*) and so forth. (a) First, the explicit clarification of the meaning of "and."

Furthermore, it reveals that although the eleven distinct mental factors (*caitta*) have different meanings, they do not differ in essence; therefore, they are not established separately [from the wholesome roots].
Regarding the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) in the verse: it serves to indicate that, in addition to the eleven wholesome dharmas, there are other wholesome mental factors.

That is to say, including the roots and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), there are twenty-six types in total. Eleven [of these] have already been countered by the wholesome factors such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth.
As for the remaining fifteen types that were not individually countered, they are now indicated by the word "and" (*ca*). One might ask:
"Since the other wholesome mental factors (*caitasika*) have distinct meanings, why are they not established separately in the verse? The commentary states: "The factors such as *pramodya* (joy)..."
The wholesome states (*kuśala*). Although their names and meanings differ, their essence is not distinct; therefore, they are omitted here.
△ Next, the detailed explanation of joy and so forth (six sections). First, the five beginning with joy.
*Prasāda* (joyful interest) refers to a portion of non-hatred (*adveṣa*) that arises together with desire (*chanda*). [It extends] up to being the appropriate opposite of a portion of hatred.
Regarding the phonetic meaning: *prasāda* means joyful delight; it arises together with wholesome desire toward an object worthy of joy, and is free from malice or resentment.
This takes a portion of non-hatred as its essence. It is also free from indignation, enmity, vexation, and envy.
Its essence consists of a portion of non-hatred (*adveṣa*), as it corresponds to the four minor derivative afflictions— anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*),
vexation (*pradāśa*), and envy (*īrṣyā*)— which have a portion of hatred as their essence.
△ Second, the three beginning with aversion (*arati*).

Disgust (*nirveda*) refers to a portion of non-attachment (*alobha*) that is concomitant with wisdom (*prajñā*). (Up to: Because it is the appropriate direct opposite of a portion of attachment (*lobha*).

Regarding the phonology and meaning: "disgust" means wearying detachment. It refers to arising together with wholesome wisdom; toward objects that should be found disgusting, one does not give rise to defiled attachment.
Its essence consists of a portion of non-attachment. It is neither stinginess nor pride, and both are likewise portions of non-attachment.

[The latter] serves as the essential nature [of the former]. This is because, according to their respective correspondences, the two minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*) of stinginess (*mātsarya*) and pride (*mada*), which take a portion of greed (*lobha*) as their essential nature, are the direct opposites [of the former two].

*Supplement:* Among the ten minor derivative afflictions, the middle two are directly translated as shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). Only "harm" (*vihiṃsā*) is translated as "non-harming" (*avihiṃsā*).
Since the remaining nine are not translated [into corresponding opposites], they are now shown one by one with their translations.
△ Third, the triad beginning with non-concealment (*anivṛti*).

Non-concealment, non-deception (*amāyā*), and non-flattery (*aśāṭhya*) are each a portion of non-attachment (*alobha*) and non-delusion (*amoha*). (This extends to) the statement that concealment (*mrakṣa*) is also a portion of attachment.
[Commentary on the terms: Non-concealment, non-deception, and non-flattery—these three are all portions of non-attachment and non-delusion.

This is because they correspondingly and correctly have as their essence a portion of greed and delusion, being the three minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*) of concealment (*mrakṣa*), deception (*māyā*), and guile (*śāṭhya*).
The subsequent explanation can be understood accordingly. However, concealment is also generally included within a portion of greed.
△ Fourth, non-conceit (*an-unnati*).
There is one interpretation that it is subsumed under a portion of faith (*śraddhā*), because if one honors another, one does not become conceited toward them.
Regarding the meaning of the term: the essence of non-conceit is appropriate according to all three explanations, as it is the direct antonym of fundamental conceit (*māna*) as the case may be.
△ Five: Non-doubt (*a-vicikitsā*).
There is an interpretation that non-doubt is subsumed under faith (*śraddhā*), because one who possesses right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) has no hesitation.

Regarding the meaning of the term "non-doubt," there are three explanations, each of which accords with reason, as they correspondingly represent the direct antonym of fundamental doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Supplement: Fundamental pride and doubt each have their own distinct substance (*svabhāva*). Since they can be transformed from afflictions into wholesome states, why would they lack an intrinsic nature?

As stated in the subsequent text: "Awakened understanding penetrates the principle, thus it is said that many share the same substance; deluded sentiment is restricted to phenomena, thus it is divided into many according to its manifestations."
△ Six: The four beginning with non-distraction.
The essence of non-distraction is subsumed under right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Up to "not forgetting mindfulness" refers to right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
Supplement: Non-distraction has right concentration as its essence; it is the direct opposite of "distraction" (*auddhatya*) among the great secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

"Distraction" (*vikṣepa*) is the opposite of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), which subverts the fundamental view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). "Lack of clear comprehension" (*asamprajanya*) is the opposite of clear comprehension (*samprajanya*) among the ten universal secondary afflictions (*mahābhūmika-upakleśa*).
Both of these have wholesome wisdom (*kuśala-prajñā*) as their essence. "Non-forgetfulness" (*asmṛti*) has right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) as its essence;

it is the direct opposite of forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) among the ten universal secondary afflictions. The six minor sections from "Self-delight" up to "Non-forgetfulness" together comprise ten [factors].

Regarding the seven wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), there are no distinct counterparts for the two [states] of longing and aversion. As for the other counterparts, they may be understood from the commentary (*vṛtti*).
These are the meanings subsumed by the word "and" (*ca*) in the root verse (*mūla-kārikā*).
△ Next, the non-translation of remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and so forth is briefly indicated.
Remorse, torpor (*middha*), vitarka, and vicāra—whether defiled or non-defiled—are like contact (*sparśa*), desire (*chanda*), and so on; they have no distinct counterparts.

Regarding the meaning of the sounds: these four indeterminate factors (*aniyata-dharma*), like the universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) mental factors, have meanings that span all three moral natures (*tri-śīla*); therefore, there are no distinct [counterparts].

[The term "flipping" (fan)] refers to [states that are] defiled—namely, the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*)—as well as non-defiled—namely, the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

△ Next, the detailed analysis of the distinct establishment [of these categories] (in two parts). First, the analysis based on the principle of establishing or not establishing [the distinction]. (In two parts. First, the question.
For what reason are there distinct establishments among the wholesome states that are the opposites of the various defilements, such that some are so established while others are not?

[The meaning of the term *yinyi* (sound-meaning): The intent of the question is as follows: Among the twenty-six types of wholesome dharmas that are the opposites of the various defilements, there should be...
Regarding the reason why only the eleven beginning with faith are established and the other fifteen are not: what is the intended meaning?
△ Second, the answer (in two parts): first, the answer based on their characteristics and functions.

Regarding the distinction between their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and functions (*vṛtti*): those that differ in these respects are established separately, whereas the remaining wholesome factors are not so;

therefore, one should not hold them all equally accountable. [Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms] The answer intends to say: Among the eleven [factors] beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), because each has distinct characteristics and functions, they are established separately.
As for the others which do not differ in this way, they are not treated thus. Therefore, one should not level these two criticisms against them simultaneously.
△ Next, the answer by way of universal predominance (in two parts). First, the direct explanation:

Furthermore, while all defiled dharmas that pervade the six consciousnesses [are present], pride and so forth, as well as anger and so forth, are associated exclusively with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Commentary on the Terms: Regarding the statement that "defiled dharmas pervade the six consciousnesses," this refers to the two universal [mental factors], the eight great universal [mental factors], and the fundamental afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion.
These pervade the preceding six consciousnesses because their functional activity is predominant; thus, they are contrasted with the establishment of wholesome dharmas.
If the three— pride, doubt, and views— among the root afflictions, as well as the nine minor derivative afflictions such as anger, exist only within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
they are not established separately [as distinct categories].
△ Next, the resolution of objections.

Although *vihiṃsā* (harmfulness) is likewise [a mental factor associated only with the mind], it is not mentioned among the "wholesome" (*kuśala*) factors within the category of "object-specific" (*viṣayaviniyata*) factors because it frequently arises [in opposition to them].

Regarding the meaning of the term, the commentary states: "Harmfulness is also exclusively associated with the mind; why then is 'non-harmfulness' (*avihiṃsā*) established separately? Therefore, the explanation says:

"Although harmfulness is likewise [associated only with the mind], because it frequently causes affliction and distress, and because it obstructs great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), 'non-harmfulness' is established as its opposite in order to recognize its faults."

[The section on] *muṣitasmṛti* (loss of mindfulness) concludes. Again, it is asked: The treatise states that [these factors] pervade the six consciousnesses; because they are predominant, they are the opposites of the [wholesome] excellences.

Since loss of mindfulness, distraction, and lack of clear comprehension already pervade the six consciousnesses, why are they not established as distinct wholesome dharmas by being the opposites of those [unwholesome ones]? The commentary explains:
These three, in turn, enter among the object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*), namely *samyaksamādhi* and so forth. Therefore, they are not mentioned among the wholesome factors.
Next, the distinction is made based on the predominance of defilement and the scarcity of purity. (2) First, the question:
The defiled and the pure are opposites; how could the pure ever be fewer than the defiled?
△ Next, the answer:
Because the pure is superior and the defiled is inferior, and because the former is few while the latter is many, one should not demand parity between the defiled and the pure.
Regarding the meaning of the terms: it is said that pure dharmas are superior while defiled dharmas are inferior; a small amount cannot oppose a great deal, so why must they be equal?

Furthermore, pure dharmas consist of the realization of principles that are universally penetrating, and thus many are said to share the same essence; therefore, they are not established extensively. Defiled dharmas, however, arise from deluded sentiments and are limited in their objective scope;
they are distinguished according to their specific characteristics and are therefore divided into many. Thus, one should not demand parity between the defiled and the pure.
△ III. Analysis by Various Gates (10). First, the gate of the provisional and the real:
Among these eleven dharmas, three are provisionally existent; the remaining eight are substantially existent because their characteristics and functions are distinct.

*Harṣavardhana* (合響) states: Regarding *yoga*, it is said that heedfulness (*apramāda*) is equanimity (*upekṣā*), because it is a constituent part of non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion, as well as diligence (*vīrya*).
Thus, these dharmas are established as equanimity in the sense of being free from defilement (*saṃkleśa*), and established as heedfulness in the sense of counteracting defilement.
Non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) is simply a constituent part of non-hatred; therefore, there is no separate substantial entity [for it] (text).

△ Section Two: The Gate of Pervasiveness and Non-Pervasiveness (2). First, the initial master establishes that four are pervasive and seven are not necessarily pervasive (2). First, the formal establishment:

There is an interpretation that eleven [mental factors] are pervasive of the wholesome mind... (up to) because non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) exists only at times when one feels compassion for sentient beings.

*Yinyi* (Explanatory Notes on Phonology and Meaning): This master asserts that the three roots of diligence (*vīrya*) pervade all wholesome states of mind, whereas the remaining seven are indeterminate.

Regarding the phrase "seeking and examining below," this explains the meaning of the seven indeterminate factors. As for the phrase "the bases are each distinct," the intention is that *hrī* (moral shame) relies upon one's own qualities (*svadharma*).

The sense of shame (*hrī*) relies upon the world; since its basis is distinct, it arises as a single moment and does not arise a second time. This is precisely what is meant by "indefinite" (*aniyata*).
The remaining five [mental factors] may be understood accordingly.
△ Next, the scriptural evidence is cited.
The treatise states that among the eleven stages (ṣaḍ-avasthā), [non-harming] arises [at certain times], because there is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) at the time of gathering sentient beings.
△ Next, the Master establishes that ten [mental factors] are universal while pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is not; first, he refutes the aforementioned error.
There is an interpretation that this explanation is not yet reasonable (up to the point where it contradicts the existence of non-harm as a factor capable of causing harm).

Regarding the meaning of the terms: the first phrase provides a general refutation; the subsequent search and investigation provides a specific clarification. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:

A mind that has not yet reached certainty through the investigation of facts and principles should not be wholesome, because it lacks pure faith, just like defiled minds and the like. If it were admitted to be wholesome, [it would contradict the definition].
It may well be that one lacks faith; however, the distinction between shame (*hrī*) and dread-of-blame (*apatrāpya*) lies in their differing natures of veneration and rejection.

As for their distinct bases, these refer to reliance upon either one's own Dharma or the worldly path. Regarding their identical objects, this means that regardless of whatever object they encounter, both possess the sense of veneration and rejection.
If it is argued that while the worldly path attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) at the time of abandoning afflictions, the supramundane path does not—

Furthermore, since this factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is not included within the untainted (*anāsrava*), if one were to claim that equanimity (*upekṣā*) and heedfulness (*apramāda*) exist during the untainted path but not during the mundane path, then these two factors would not constitute the cultivation of tranquility and restraint.

Moreover, they would fail to subdue restlessness (*auddhatya*) and heedlessness (*pramāda*). How, then, could they be called the mundane path? To address this, [the author] establishes the following inference (*upamāna*) regarding the tainted (*sāsrava*) [path].

The *Mingyouliang* (Treatise on the Illumination of Existence) states: "Wholesome minds with outflows (*sāsrava*) must possess both equanimity (*upekṣā*) and heedfulness (*apramāda*), for they are endowed with four factors, just like the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*).
If one maintains that non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) exists only when one feels compassion for sentient beings, one fails to realize that whenever a wholesome mind arises, it does not damage things;
thus, non-harming must exist [in all such cases]. Since this contradicts the nature of that which causes harm, is it not universal?"
Therefore. △ Next, the general discussion of the intent:
[The treatise states that eleven arise in six stages] (up to) "therefore, what they have said is certainly not reasonable."

Regarding the "Explanation of Terms": "Increasing according to each respective [stage]" means that in the stage of determination (*niyāma*), faith increases, up to the point where, at the time of gathering sentient beings, non-harming increases.
Thus, the statement is made because there is faith in the stage of determination, and so on, up to the presence of non-harming at the time of gathering sentient beings.
Therefore, the following section concludes with a reprimand.
△ III. Stating the Correct Principle (II). First, the general explanation of the eleven factors:
Among the eleven factors beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), [they are included] because pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) increases within the mind of the meditative states (*samāhitabhūmi*).

Commentary on Terms: First, it was clarified that the ten universal wholesome mental states are universal, whereas pliancy is not. Below, in the section on "Decisive Discrimination," a treatise is cited to establish this proof.
"Concentrated stages" refers to the meditative absorption (samādhi) within the realms of form and formlessness; "non-concentrated" refers to the state of distracted mind in the desire realm.
△ Next, the specific exclusion of pliancy (two parts). First, the opinion of the former master:

There is an interpretation that the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of meditative concentration is also designated by the name "concentration" (*samādhi*); thus, the eleven factors beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are present throughout all stages.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: This explanation intends to clarify that when the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states that the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*) is characterized by an increase in pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), it does not necessarily refer only to the fundamental state of concentration (*mauladhyāna*).

Even the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) preceding concentration may receive the designation "stage of concentration," because they also possess, albeit slightly, the quality of being harmonious and supple.
For this reason, pliancy exists even in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Were it otherwise, it would contradict the treatise’s own statement.
△ Next, regarding the Master [Vasubandhu]:

There is an interpretation that *praśrabdhi* (serenity/pliancy) exists only in the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*), because it is said to exist throughout all three stages, including those with applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*).

[The commentary on the meaning of the terms: First, the formal explanation of *praśrabdhi*: It exists only in the stages of concentration and does not extend to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). This is stated because... [all]... exist.

Next, the general discussion of the mental states (*manasikāra*) follows. This refers to what is stated in the *Maulī Bhūmi*: that the eleven [mental states] beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) "pervade all stages" (*sarvabhūmika*).

That statement means they exist in all three stages—namely, those with vitarka and vicāra, those without vitarka but with vicāra, and those with neither vitarka nor vicāra—and does not refer to "all stages" within the context of the nine stages.
The stage with vitarka and vicāra consists of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the two heavens of the Brahma-pāriṣadya and Brahma-purohita within the first dhyāna.

The stage with no vitarka and only vicāra consists of the Mahābrahmā heaven. All stages from the second dhyāna up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) are termed the stage without vitarka and without vicāra.
*He-xiang* (Harmony of Resonance). The fourth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"In this context, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), excluding the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), whether in meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) or as a birth (*upapatti*), are called the stage with vitarka and vicāra (*savitarkā savicārā bhūmiḥ*).

That is to say, the intermediate dhyāna, whether in meditative absorption or as a birth, is called the stage without vitarka and with only vicāra (*avitarkā vicāramātrā bhūmiḥ*). A sentient being, by practicing this [stage],..."

One attains the status of Mahābrahmā. From the second dhyāna upward, the remaining realms of form (rūpadhātu) and the entire realm of formlessness (ārūpyadhātu) are collectively termed the stage devoid of vitarka and vicāra.
△ Third, the section on the association of consciousnesses.

These eleven types have already been explained in detail [up to the point that] they are necessarily accompanied by pliancy (praśrabdhi) when associated with the wisdom of accomplishment (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna).

Regarding the meaning of the terms: these eleven wholesome states are entirely absent in both the seventh and eighth consciousnesses during the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti); however, once the basis has been transformed, they are present.

Both [types of] consciousness possess them. Regarding the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it possesses all eleven in its "fixed states" (as for "possessing all in fixed states": both contaminated meditative goodness and uncontaminated meditative goodness possess all eleven;

contaminated non-fixed goodness lacks *praśrabdhi*). In non-fixed states, it lacks only *praśrabdhi*. Regarding that which is associated with the five sensory consciousnesses, there are two masters' interpretations:
one opinion holds that there are only ten; another opinion holds that all are present. The latter interpretation is correct.
△ Section Four: The Gate of Association with the Various Feelings (vedanā).
With which feelings are these eleven wholesome [factors] associated? [They are associated with all except those that involve] oppression and lack of composure. Glossary:

The ten wholesome [paths of action] are associated with five feelings; [the factor of] pliancy (praśrabdhi) is associated with all except the two feelings of grief (daurmanasya) and suffering (duḥkha).
△ 5. The Section on Association with the Five Particular Objects:
These [mental factors] may all be associated with the particular objects, because faith and so forth, as well as desire and so forth, are not mutually contradictory.
△ 6. The Section on the Subsumption of the Three Natures.
Eleven are exclusively wholesome.
△ Seventh, the gate of affiliation with the three realms:
pliancy does not belong to the desire realm; the others are common to all three realms.
△ Section Eight: The Gate of Mutual Inclusion of the Categories of Learners (*śaikṣa*), etc.

All are comprised within the three categories of learner, non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and neither. Regarding the phonetic meanings: these eleven wholesome factors, among the three positions of learner, non-learner, and neither, are all fully present.
Regarding "because they exist":

the supplementary note states that those subsumed under the category of *śaikṣa* (those in training) refer to the first three fruits [of the śrāvaka path] and the eleven wholesome factors within the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva.
Those subsumed under the category of *aśaikṣa* (those beyond training) refer to the fourth fruit, the pratyekabuddha, and the Tathāgata.

These are the eleven factors. Those not subsumed under either the state of training (*śaikṣa*) or the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) refer to the eleven factors of all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
△ Ninth: The Section on the Mutual Subsumption of the Three Types of Abandonment.

"Not abandoned by insight" (*na-darśana-heya*): The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the six faculties, beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and are not abandoned by insight.

Regarding the meaning of the term "not abandoned by insight": this clarifies that they are comprised within both those abandoned through cultivation and those that are not to be abandoned at all (*aheya*).

In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is cited as proof that [the faculties] are cultivated for abandonment (*prahāṇa*). The six faculties refer to faith (*śraddhā*), diligence (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvyājñendriya*).
Faith is as its name implies; diligence is energetic application. Since these two are thus, the other nine are likewise.
Therefore, they are cultivated for abandonment.
Supplement: These eleven wholesome factors are not associated with the afflictions of conceptual discrimination; therefore, they are not abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

If they are contaminated wholesome factors (*sāsrava-kuśala*) or wholesome factors of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśala*) that are uncontaminated, they belong to what is abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

If they are the truly uncontaminated wholesome factors, they are subsumed under what is not to be abandoned (*aheya*). The five faculties, such as faith (*śraddhā*), are common to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated. If...
Regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*): these are subsumed within the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*). Herein, the five faculties are for the time being referred to as tainted.
Within the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), all nine untainted faculties are termed the faculty of "knowing what is not yet known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

These nine faculties consist of the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) and the four faculties of mind (*manas*), joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and pleasure (*sukha*). [These] are the untainted [faculties] within the stage of training (*śaikṣa-avasthā*).

The nine faculties are called the faculty of "one who has already known" (ājñātendriya). The nine untainted faculties within the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) are called the faculty of "one who possesses complete knowledge" (ājñātāvīndriya).

Although one enters the path of seeing (darśanamārga) by means of the faculty of "one who knows the unknown" (anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya), once the path of seeing has been realized, there is nothing further unknown that remains to be known.
Therefore, after the single moment of the path of seeing, one is subsumed under the stage of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga); thus, it is the path of cultivation.
Within this stage, one immediately abandons the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) as well as the five contaminated faculties (*sāsrava-indriya*).
△ Regarding the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*),
other categories should be analyzed accordingly through reasoning.
△ III. The Three Root Afflictions (2). First, connecting the preceding with the subsequent question:
Having thus already explained the mental factors of the wholesome state and the mental factors that are afflictions, what are their characteristics?
△ Next, the root verse is cited in response. The verse says:
"The afflictions are said to be greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong views.

△ Third, the commentary explains and establishes [the meaning] (in two parts): first, the direct explanation of the verse; second, a brief explanation of the general name. First, the brief explanation of the general name.
The Commentary states: Because these six natures, beginning with greed, are subsumed under the category of root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), they receive the name "affliction" (*kleśa*).
The *Hui-xuan* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), Volume 17, says: "As for 'root,' they are so called because they can give rise to the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);

the remaining secondary afflictions are either their outflows or their functional states, like branches and leaves. "Affliction" (*fan*) means to disturb; "distress" (*nao*) means to confuse. To disturb...
That which disturbs sentient beings and causes them to dwell perpetually in birth and death is called *kleśa* (affliction). Its root is affliction itself;
"affliction" (*fan*) and "disturbance" (*nǎo*) form a *karmadhāraya* compound.
△ Next, the detailed explanation of their individual characteristics (six parts): first, the explanation of greed (*rāga*).
What is craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*) and its requisites? It refers to the arising of the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*) through the power of craving.

Regarding the meaning and terminology: first, the essential nature and function are correctly explained. As for "existence and its requisites," the meaning is seen in the section on wholesome states; that is, by means of the lower [fetters].
This explains the suffering of birth: it is because, through the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādānaskandha*) arise once again.
*Abhidharmasamuccaya*, Volume One, states: "Why are they called 'appropriated aggregates' (*upādānaskandha*)? Because they are conjoined with appropriation, they are named 'appropriated aggregates.
What is appropriation? It refers to all desire and greed (*chandarāga*) within the aggregates. Why is there desire and greed?"
It is called "clinging" (*upādāna*). This refers to the ability to attract and not relinquish the aggregates (*skandha*) of the future and the present;

it is the longing for the future and the defiled attachment to the present. Thus, desire and greed are termed "clinging. (Text). The *Daichao*, Volume 18, cites the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which states:
"There are five kinds of greed: first, the desire for and greed regarding one's own internal body; second, the lust for external bodies..."
1. Desire for lust (*kāma-kāma*). 2. Lust for the objects of desire (*kāma-viṣaya-kāma*). 3. Lust for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-kāma*). 4. Lust for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-kāma*). 5.
Lust for the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-kāma*). The commentary explains: According to Ci'en’s interpretation, the first "lust" has two aspects.

First, it refers to the initial arising of slight desire within one's own internal body; thus it is called "desire for desire" (*kāma-kāma*). Second, it refers to the subsequent arising of heavy greed; thus it is called "desire-greed" (*kāma-rāga*).
The second [interpretation] says: The internal body is the object (dharma) that one desires. Therefore, it is said "desire for the internal body.
Because desire arises upon this desire for the internal body, it is the desiring mind itself; this is called "desire-greed" (*kāmacchanda*).

Thus, the first instance of the word "desire" refers to the desired object, the second refers to the desiring subject, and the third instance of the word "desire" is the name of the fetter (*saṃyojana*) (text).
△ Second, the explanation of hatred (*dveṣa*). What is hatred?
It is that which, regarding suffering and the instruments of suffering... gives rise to various evil karmas because it is of an unwholesome nature.

[Commentary on the Meaning and Phonetics]: First, the correct explanation of its essence and function. Regarding "suffering and the instruments of suffering," the explanation of the meaning is as before. That is to say, below the word "hatred" (*dveṣa*), it is transformed.

Explaining the preceding phrase: "the heat and affliction of body and mind" explains the nature of lack of peace and security; "giving rise to various evil karmas" explains the basis for unwholesome conduct.
Since this is exclusively evil and does not extend to the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), it is termed "unwholesome nature" (*akuśala-svabhāva*).
△ Third, the explanation of delusion (*moha*).
What is delusion? Regarding all principles and phenomena (*dharmas*)... because it can招 (*ākarṣati*) the defiled dharmas of future rebirth. Regarding the meaning of the terms:

Qingliang says that independent (*svatantra*) ignorance (*avidyā*) is mostly deluded regarding the principle of the Truths (*satya*), while associated (*samprayukta*) ignorance is also [deluded regarding the Truths].
Delusion regarding the characteristics of phenomena refers to the arising of doubt concerning the Truths and so forth. To summarize all defilements, they do not exceed three types:
namely, afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and birth. This is explained by way of descending progression;
that is, through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), one gives rise to doubt, wrong views, the root afflictions such as greed, and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as anger.

Afflictions (*kleśa*). This is the defilement of affliction (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), which arises from this cause. Because of afflictions, one performs various types of out-flowing karma (*sāsrava-karma*), both wholesome and unwholesome.
Through the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of such karma, one is able to summon the wholesome and unwholesome fruits of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) in future births.
This is the birth of karma (*karma-jāti*). These two kinds of defilements arise in dependence upon it; therefore, it is said that all [defilements] are...
The basis for defilement.
△ Fourth, the explanation of pride (in two parts): first, the formal explanation of its essence and function.
What is pride? It is to rely upon oneself in relation to others... [up to] ...because one wanders through saṃsāra without end, undergoing all manner of suffering.

**Commentary on the Meaning:** Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of causing the mind to become haughty by relying on one's own learning, skills, and arts, or on one's noble lineage, physical beauty, strength, wealth, or power, thereby excelling over other sentient beings.
Its function (*karma*) is to obstruct the wholesome quality of non-arrogance and to give rise to all forms of suffering.
That is to say, it leads to the production of suffering through the downward turning of one's understanding regarding virtues.

Regarding those with virtue whose minds are not humble: this refers to those who, toward the true and pure virtues of the Triple Gem, as well as toward teachers, friends, and virtuous persons superior to themselves, do not maintain a humble mind but instead competitively give rise to notions of "self" and "other.
Because of this, they transmigrate through birth and death without end, undergoing all manner of suffering.
△ Next, the specific distinctions are explained.
These distinctions of pride (*māna*) consist of seven and nine types; thus, there is no error in the arising of these various categories of pride.
Regarding the meaning of the terms: "seven and nine types" refers to the seven kinds of pride and the nine varieties. As for the seven kinds of pride:

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya*: To regard oneself as superior when one is inferior to others, or to regard oneself as equal when one is equal to others, causing the mind to become uplifted, is called *māna* (pride).

To regard oneself as superior when one is equal [to others], or to regard oneself as equal when one is superior [to others], causing the mind to become uplifted, is called *atimāna* (excessive pride).
To regard oneself as superior when one is actually superior [to others], causing the mind to become uplifted, is called *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride).
To falsely perceive all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as "I" or "mine," thereby causing the mind to become uplifted, is called *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am").
To claim to have attained what has not yet been attained regarding the sublime dharmas realized, thereby causing the mind to become uplifted, is called *abhimāna* (overweening pride).

To claim one is slightly inferior when among many who are superior, thereby causing the mind to become uplifted, is called *ūnamāna* (the pride of inferiority). To claim to possess virtues that one actually lacks...

When one possesses virtues, it causes the mind to become haughty; therefore, it is called "wrong pride" (*mithyāmāna*). The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* explains the meaning in much the same way as this.
Regarding the nine types, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* first sets them forth as follows: (1) the type of pride thinking "I am superior"; (2) the type of pride thinking "I am equal";

(3) the type of pride thinking "I am inferior"; (4) the type of pride thinking "there is someone superior to me"; (5) the type of pride thinking "there is someone equal to me"; (6) ... [text truncated] ... six.

There is the class of inferior *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am inferior"), the seventh, the class of non-superior *asmimāna*, the eighth, the class of "equal to me" *asmimāna*, and the ninth, the class of non-inferior *asmimāna*.
The subsequent commentary states: these nine types arise from three among the previously mentioned seven types of pride (*māna*).
From which three? First, pride (*māna*); second, over-pride (*atimāna*); and third, inferiority-pride (*ūnamāna*). Among these, the first three classes of pride are based on...
The arising of views of cessation corresponds, in order, to *atimāna* (conceit), *māna* (pride), and *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride).

Regarding the next three types of conceit, the first two are *māna*, and the last one is *atimāna*. Regarding the final three types of conceit, they likewise correspond, in order, to *māna*, *atimāna*, and *ūnamāna*, as explained extensively therein.
As for "arising from the three grades of self and qualities," this refers to [arising] based on six matters.
This gives rise to pride (*māna*). First, inferior sentient beings; second, equal sentient beings; third, superior sentient beings—these constitute the three grades.

Fourth, the internal appropriated aggregates (*ādhyātmikopādānaskandha*); fifth, the inversion regarding what has been attained and what has not yet been attained; sixth, the inversion of falsely claiming virtues;
seventh, "pride" (*māna*) arises based on the objects of the two grades of inferior and equal sentient beings. "Excessive pride" (*atimāna*) arises based on the two [grades] of equal and superior.
The pride of superiority (*māna*), the pride of superiority beyond superiority (*atimāna*), and the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*) arise based on the objective basis of superior sentient beings.
The two types of pride—false pride (*mithyāmāna*) and excessive pride (*adhimāna*)—arise from perversion; that is, they arise in relation to objects that possess actual virtues.

The pride of self (*asmimāna*) consists of the false conceptualization of the appropriated aggregates as "I" and "mine"; thus, it arises in relation to the self. [The phrase] "all below" next clarifies the inclusion within the abandonment.
That which arises based on views is called abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). That which arises conditioned by objects is called abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Below, in the stage of the Noble Ones (*ārya*), this establishes that it is abandoned by cultivation. This means that within the stage of the Noble Ones, since innate self-conceit (*asmimāna*) already manifests, by analogy with the other six types of conceit as well as the categories of conceit, there is no fault in its arising.
△ 5. Dispelling Doubts (2): First, the direct explanation of essence and function.
Regarding the doubt as to what constitutes the principle of the various truths... (up to)... it is said that for one who is hesitant, wholesome states do not arise.
**Commentary on the Meaning:** This refers to being hesitant and indecisive as to whether the principles of the various truths exist or do not exist.
Its intrinsic nature is to act as an obstacle to freedom from doubt; its functional activity is to obstruct all categories of wholesome qualities. How does it obstruct the wholesome?
It is because for one who is hesitant, wholesome states do not arise.
△ Next, the specific determination of its essential nature (2): The first master holds that wisdom (*prajñā*) is its essence.
There is an interpretation that this doubt has wisdom as its essence, because there is no difference in meaning between *vicikitsā* and *prajñā*.

*Yinyì* (Explanation of Terms): This master’s interpretation of the meaning is as follows: he asserts that doubt (*vicikitsā*) has defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭa-prajñā*) as its essence and possesses no separate intrinsic nature.

The subsequent passage clarifies the intention: wisdom has discernment (*pravicaya*) as its essence; when one wavers regarding the object under investigation, this wavering discernment is called "doubt.
*Vi* has the sense of "comparison" (*upamāna*), and *saha* means "to assist. *Mati* is a Sanskrit term, or...
*Yunmo ti* (雲摩提) is translated here as "Cloud-Wisdom" (*yunhui*). Its meaning is identical to *prajñā*.

The intent is to clarify that what assists and supports wisdom is precisely the object of doubt; since the method that aids wisdom ought to be wisdom itself, one knows that this doubt takes wisdom as its essence.
△ Next, [the author] states that doubt has a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
One interpretation holds that this doubt has a distinct intrinsic nature (up to the point where it concludes): "Therefore, this doubt does not have wisdom (*prajñā*) as its intrinsic nature.
[The commentary on] the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* clarifies that it possesses a real entity, demonstrating that it is not identical to wisdom. This is established as a factual proof through citation.
"Vī-ju (毗助)" at the bottom: this provides an example to refute the preceding argument. "Nan" (南) here means "wisdom" (*jñāna*).

That is to say, if one suspects that "assistance" refers to wisdom, and thus clings to wisdom as being doubt, then since consciousness assists wisdom, would wisdom also have to be consciousness? [The answer is] no, because... [the passage continues with "fei-you-xia" (非由下)].
The conclusion indicates that [the view] has a substantial entity.
△ Sixth, the explanation of wrong views (in two parts): First, the formal explanation of its essence and function.
"What is a wrong view regarding the principles of the truths... [omitted] ...it is said that those with wrong views undergo much suffering."

Commentary on Terms: "Seeking through inversion" refers to defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭā prajñā*). This means reckoning the pure as impure, the existent as non-existent, suffering as pleasure, and so forth.
Regarding "karmic actions that invite suffering," this refers to those with wrong views who abandon suffering by means of suffering;
because they constantly undergo much suffering in both this world and future worlds.
△ Next, the specific characteristics of its modes of activity are shown (in two parts). First, the heading:
These distinctions in the modes of activity of this view are fivefold.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: although it is essentially nothing but defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭa-prajñā*), it is separately divided into five because their respective functions (*karmaprayoga*) differ.
△ Second, the explanation [of the five views] (2): First, the formal explanation of the five views (5).

First, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). 1. *Satkāyadṛṣṭi* refers to [the view] regarding the five aggregates of clinging... up to... [included in] the sixty-five types of conceptual proliferation.
*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonances): *Huayan Chao*, Scroll 17-2. It quotes the ancient commentary (*Gu shu*), which states: "The view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
its full Sanskrit name is *satkāyadṛṣṭi*. The masters of the Sautrāntika school state that *sat* has the meaning of 'false' (*mṛṣā*)."
*Kāya* means "body. *Dṛṣṭi* means "view. Since "body" (*kāya*) has the meaning of an "aggregation," it is a conventional designation for a collection;

thus, one should say that a view arises with respect to the body as an aggregation, and this is called "satkāyadṛṣṭi" (the view of a real body). According to the Sarvāstivādins, *sat* has the meaning of "existent. *Kāya*, etc., are as explained before.
Although it is a body as an aggregation, it is substantially existent. "Body" (*kāya*) here refers to the distinct self-entity (*ātman*).
[This is] the name. It should be stated as "seeing its own substance. The Dharma Master of the Mahāyāna explains: when the *saṃgha* eats rotten *sā*, it becomes a "transference" (*saṃkrānti*).
Because it is a phenomenon transformed by the mind, it is called a "transference. The view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises based on the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*);
since these serve as its basis, all [other] views are produced. Therefore, it is said that its function is to serve as the basis for the various types of views (*dṛṣṭigata*).
"Qu" (趣) means "to illustrate" or "by way of comparison," or it refers to "the place of resort. Regarding the twenty phrases, the *Abhidharma-prathama* states:

"For example, one conceives that form is the self, the self possesses form, form belongs to the self, or the self is within form. Each of the five aggregates has these four [conceptions], totaling twenty phrases.
Five of these constitute the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*); the remainder are all views of 'mine' (*mamakāra*), specifically the 'mine' associated with [the self]."

(That is, "I have form") follows after what belongs to the self (that is, "form belongs to me"); it does not depart from what belongs to the self (that is, "I am within form"). Thus, there are fifteen instances of "what belongs to the self.
This is precisely the discrimination of the formations that take the aggregates as their object, without discriminating the place where they arise. If one traverses the three periods of time:
There are thus sixty [views]; adding the self as identical to the body makes sixty-one. If the self is again considered distinct from the body, it becomes sixty-two.

Furthermore, calculating based on permanence, impermanence, and so forth, they constitute sixty-two views, as in the *Daśaka-nidāna-parivarta*. As for the statement that there are sixty-five in the treatise, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
"This refers to taking form (*rūpa*) as the self; regarding each of the other four aggregates (*skandha*), there are three ways of conceiving them as the self."
That which is called "mine" consists of my ornaments, my servants, and my vessels—these amount to twelve. Adding the self as one, there are thirteen in total.
Regarding the five aggregates (*skandhas*), there are sixty views of "mine" (*mamakāra-dṛṣṭi*). There are five views of "self" (*ātmadṛṣṭi*); together these make sixty-five.
These are the analytical contemplations upon the aggregates as objects, and they also analyze the bases from which [such views] arise. All of these...
This is the discrimination of the view of self (text).
△ Second, the view of extremes.

The view of adhering to the two extremes refers to those [views] from the seven theories of annihilationism up to the theory of non-existence after death; these are comprised within the category of discrimination.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: This refers to the mind’s clinging and superimposition upon that very "self" grasped by the view of a transitory collection (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

To calculate this self as either annihilated or eternal is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Its function is to obstruct the practice of the Middle Way leading to renunciation and liberation, causing one to fall into partiality and bondage.
This [view] is comprised of both the innate (*sahaja*) and the conceptual (*vikalpita*) types. Below this, it is explained.

Regarding the distinctions and their correspondence: the *Huayan chao* states that in the treatise, the sequence is established based on delusion regarding the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) and the posterior limit (*aparānta*).

Here, following the *Vijñaptimātratā*, they are categorized according to what is perceived: namely, regarding the prior limit, one calculates four types of eternalism and four types of partial eternalism.
Furthermore, based on speculations regarding the future limit (*aparānta*), there are sixteen views involving perception, eight views involving non-perception, and eight views involving neither;
these constitute forty types of distinctions within the eternalist views (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*). There are seven theories of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*) that speculate regarding the future limit.

These forty-seven views all arise from the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and give rise to the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Regarding speculations about the past limit (*pūrvānta*), there are two theories of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*) and four theories of finitude (*antavāda*).

There are four types of evasive equivocation regarding immortality (*amarā-vikkhepa*), as well as those who speculate about the future limit (*aparanta-kappika*) and those who claim present nirvana (*diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna-vāda*);
thus, there are sixty-two. These sixty-two have wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) as their essential nature, while the remaining two views serve as their attendants.
Based on the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), this serves as the root. This also cites the general enumeration. Next, regarding the explanation of their characteristics based on yoga:
first, the four [theories of] universal permanence mean that both the self and the entire world are eternal, existing only through alternation of concealment and manifestation.

Based on the higher and middle *dhyānas*, one gives rise to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) and, through such recollection, produces the four theories of permanence. First, by...
1. One who can recollect twenty eons of formation and destruction; 2. one who can recollect forty eons; 3. one who can recollect eighty eons; and 4.

one who, relying on what is seen by the divine eye, perceives in the present world the death and birth of sentient beings and the continuity of their aggregates, thereby clinging to the view that both the self and the world are eternal.
Regarding "those for whom one part is eternal": this refers to those in all four [categories] who hold that one part [is eternal].

There are three [types of] partialists (*ekāṃśavādin*). First, those who have passed away from the Brahmā world and been reborn here, having attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), hold such views as:
"The Brahmā King is eternal, whereas we are impermanent. Thus they are called partialists. Second, those who hear that the Brahmā King holds such a view:
"The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are eternal, while the mind (*citta*) is impermanent," or conversely. Third, those who previously [lived] out of playfulness...

Having forgotten heaven and perished there, they are born in this realm. Attaining supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), they give rise to attachment: "Those who were not born here are eternal; I, having been born here, am impermanent.
Furthermore, some previously descended from the Heaven of Mental Wrath (*manasikāra-kopa-deva*). One portion is the same as before.
This heavenly abode dwells upon a wondrous high tier, or belongs to the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśa*). The commentary states: according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, herein...
It then states that there are two [types] without cause, because they are alike in their reckoning of the prior limit (*pūrvānta*). Regarding "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*):
immediately following this, it clarifies the sixteen [views] with perception (*saṃjñin*) and so forth. As for the sixteen, there are four sets of four propositions. First:

"I have form (*rūpin*), and after death I possess perception. Taking form as the self is called "having form"; taking up various phenomena to speak of them is called "possessing perception. This refers to the entirety of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

1. A portion of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), excluding the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*). These hold that there is a self after death with perception, and they grasp the formless aggregates (*arūpaskandha*) as the self;
these reside in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), excluding only the Heaven of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

2. A self that is both with form and without form, which after death has perception, grasping the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as the self. 3. A self that is neither with form nor without form, which after death has perception. 4. A self that is neither existent... [text ends]
"Form is not formless; there is perception after death. This excludes the third [view]. Based on the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of vitarka and vicāra, all [of these views] can arise.

The second set of four propositions states: first, one who clings to the self as finite and perceives that there is perception after death, clinging to form as the self, which has limited dimensions, such as a finger joint and so forth.
Second, one who clings to the self as infinite and perceives that there is perception after death, clinging to...
1. That form is not the self, because [the self] pervades all places. 3. Grasping that the self is both finite and infinite, and that after death there is perception;
grasping that the self expands and contracts according to the body, and so forth. 4. Grasping that the self is neither finite nor infinite.
"Having perception after death" excludes the third [alternative]. Alternatively, it arises based on the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of vitarka and vicāra.
Regarding the four phrases of the third [alternative]: first, "I have one perception"; second, "I have various perceptions";
third, "I have limited perception"; and fourth, "I have immeasurable perception. "One perception" refers to those in the first three formless realms (*ārūpya*). "Various perceptions" refers to...

In the desire realm and the form realm—excluding the Heaven of Non-perception—one clings to a small amount of form, or clings to formlessness as the self or as belonging to the self, or as being conjoined with the self; this is called "small perception.

In the desire realm and the form realm—excluding the Heaven of Non-perception—the four immeasurable perceptions consist of clinging to immeasurable forms, or clinging to immeasurable perceptions and forms as the self.
"I am united with that. Regarding the fourth set of four propositions: first, "I possess exclusively pleasure and have perception after death," which refers to the three lower dhyānas;
second, "I possess exclusively suffering and have perception after death," which refers to being within the hells;

third, "I possess both suffering and pleasure and have perception after death," which refers to humans, the desire-realm devas, and the animal realm; fourth, "I possess exclusively... [the text continues].
There is neither suffering nor pleasure; after death, there is perception. In the fourth dhyāna and above, the attainment of vitarka and vicāra can all arise.

Regarding those who maintain that there are eight theories concerning the non-percipient (asaṃjñin) and the neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient (nevasaññānāsaññin), there are two sets of four propositions.
As for the first set of four propositions: first, "I have form; after death, I am non-percipient," which is the attachment to form as the self, attaining the state of non-perception.
Regarding the attainment of the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*): seeing others who have attained this concentration and are reborn there, one forms the following conception:
"I am formless; after death, I shall be without perception. Thus, one clings to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as the self and attains the attainment of non-perception.

Third, one clings to the self as being both with form and without form, such that after death one is without perception; thus, one clings to both form and the life-faculty as the self. Within these two [positions], one gives rise to a single [view].
I think as follows. Regarding the fourth [position], one clings to a self that is neither material nor immaterial, which is non-perceptual after death;
this excludes the third alternative, because both meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) are possible therein. As for the second set of four [positions]:

first, one clings to a self that is finite and non-perceptual after death, clinging to matter as the self and perceiving its dimension as narrow and small, etc., and thereby attaining the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Second, one clings to a self...
Infinite. After death, there is no perception (*asaṃjñin*). One clings to form (*rūpa*) as the self, which pervades all places. The third [view] clings to the self as both finite and infinite;
after death, there is no perception, because one clings to form as the self, which expands and contracts according to the body.
The fourth alternative merely negates the third and has no further distinct meaning. Regarding meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), both vitarka and vicāra are capable of arising.

Regarding the subsequent eightfold discussion on "neither [existence nor non-existence] after death," there are two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). The first states: One clings to the self as having form (*rūpin*), asserting that after death it is neither percipient nor non-percipient (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñin*).
Clinging to form as the self, one observes sentient beings entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*);

because their perception is not clear or sharp, they form such a clinging. This is merely a clinging based on vitarka and vicāra, and does not constitute the attainment of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). The second [proposition] involves clinging... [text truncated].
"I am formless," as before after death; grasping the formless aggregates (*arūpaskandha*) as self, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Because perception is not clear, one forms such a grasping. Third, grasping that "I am both with form and without form," as before after death;
grasping both form and formlessness as self, one views sentient beings as being equal to the aforementioned. Thus it is said.
All arise based on vitarka and vicāra, not by means of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). The fourth phrase serves to exclude the third phrase and has no further distinct meaning.
Regarding the second set of four phrases: first, one clings to the self as being finite; after death, it is neither-perceptual-nor-non-perceptual, and so on up to the fourth phrase.
The text is easy to understand. In all such cases, these are all clingings to the four formless realms (*ārūpya*).
For me, because one has attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), such an adherence may arise:
first, because that meditative absorption is of brief duration, one takes each individual aggregate (*skandha*) as an object and adheres to the self as being finite;
second, because that meditative absorption is of long duration, one takes the four aggregates collectively as an object and adheres to the self as being infinite; third, because of that...

[This constitutes] the third alternative, because [the self] is taken as the object of focus either individually by each aggregate (*skandha*) or collectively as a whole. The fourth alternative excludes the third;
it has no further distinct meaning. Regarding the seven theories of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*):

first, some maintain that the self possesses form (*rūpin*), having the nature of being composed of the coarse four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and that after death it is annihilated and ceases to exist altogether. [Others] see the body as existing after death...
