There is no reason [for this]. Second, "I am a deva of the desire realm; after death, I shall be annihilated. Third, "I am a deva of the form realm;

after death, I shall be annihilated. Fourth, "I am in the sphere of infinite space," and so on up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—all claim that after death they shall be annihilated.
As for the latter four attachments, they hold those respective stages to be the pinnacle of birth and death. The former forty views constitute the eternalist position; the latter...
The seven views are abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*); all of these are abandoned by insight and are termed "arising from discrimination" (*vikalpa-utpanna*).
△ Third, false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).
The three false views refer to the denial of cause and effect (up to) all such categories as these are subsumed under false views.

**Commentary on Terms:** To slander cause, effect, activity, and substantial reality means: to claim that there is no giving and no receiving, and likewise no sacrificial offerings—this is called slandering the cause.
To claim that there are no fruits and no maturations (*vipāka*) resulting from the various karmas of sublime conduct and evil conduct—this is called slandering the effect.

To claim that there is neither sublime conduct nor evil conduct—this is called slandering activity. To claim that there is no father and no mother, and no [spontaneous] transformation—[this is called slandering substantial reality].
Sentient beings are born, yet there are no true Arhats or the like in the world; all such [views] are termed the "destruction of real entities.
A detailed explanation is as found in the section on the view of emptiness in the seventh fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

Furthermore, there are those with various false attachments that are not among the four views, meaning they are not subsumed within the aforementioned four views; these include those who slander the Triple Gem or the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) sūtras, and so forth.

All other false attachments are subsumed within this wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Just as the term "dominant condition" (*adhipatipratyaya*) is so named because its scope is universal, whatever is not subsumed under other conditions is all subsumed under this condition. Below this, the distinctions [of this view] are clarified.

Regarding "Harmonizing Resonance" (*Hexiang*), the *Huayan Chao* states: As for the mention of the two types of causeless theories (*ahetuvāda*) concerning the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), these all arise from false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Because the view is not correct, it is termed "false. Regarding the two types of causeless [theories]: first, there are those who, having passed away from the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), are reborn in this world;
lacking the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), they are unable to remember the state of mind prior to their emergence [from that realm].
All those individuals, perceiving that all phenomena arise having been originally non-existent, think: "I, too, must have arisen having been originally non-existent.
They then give rise to the attachment of claiming that both the self and the world arise without cause.

These two types of people—those who do not recollect their previous lives through the application of vitarka and vicāra—form this attachment that things arise without cause. Such two views [arise] due to the Heaven of Non-perception and...
It arises from two things: false conceptualization and discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). Regarding the four types of those who hold to finitude:
first, by means of recollecting exclusively downward as far as the Avīci Hell and upward as far as the fourth dhyāna, they maintain that the self completely fills all within this interval.
Then he forms this thought: "Beyond this there is a self; I ought to be able to see it. Therefore, he knows there is finitude.
Second, because he can recollect exclusively in the horizontal direction without limit, and clings to the self as being all-pervasive, he clings to infinitude.

Third, because he can recollect [the self] above, below, and across, he clings dualistically to both finitude and infinitude. Fourth, because he can recollect the state of annihilation during the kalpa of destruction.
Thereupon, they give rise to the notion that it is neither finite nor infinite, because no such thing as the receptacle world can be apprehended.

Regarding the fourth type, the "Evasive Eel-Wriggling" (amarā-vikkhepika): first, to explain the name in general according to the intent of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Non-Buddhists reckon that the heavens are eternal, which they call "immortality" (amara);
they further reckon that by answering evasively, one will be reborn in those heavens. Now, the Buddha rebukes them, saying: "Your words are secret."
...and so forth; this constitutes equivocation (*vibhāṣā*). As for the four types: first, out of fear of appearing ignorant, one thinks, "I do not know what is wholesome or unwholesome and so forth.
If others question me, I shall not be able to give a definitive answer. If I were to give a definitive answer, I fear they would perceive my ignorance."
Consequently, he immediately laughed at me lightly, saying, "The secret meaning of that deity should not be explained in its entirety," and so forth.
Second, regarding those who act with deceit: they think to themselves, "It is not my case that all secrets of the Pure Deity are permitted to be prophesied;
this refers only to what one has personally realized and the path of purification. Third, they do not provide a prophecy out of fear, fearing that I am dull-witted.
1. Inferiority: Being known by others, one fails to attain liberation due to these causes and conditions;
taking this as one’s dwelling, one settles therein out of a sense of dread. 2. Foolishness: One exclusively cultivates the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) while lacking true knowledge.

If someone were to question me, I would instead counter-interrogate them; though I follow all their words without contradiction, I merely acquiesce to them. 3. Manifestation... [The text continues with further points.]
Regarding *nirvāṇa*: first, some perceive the various sensual pleasures of the five desires experienced in the present by gods or humans, and they immediately claim this to be *nirvāṇa*.

Second, although they may feel aversion toward the five desires, they currently abide in the first dhyāna and consider this to be *nirvāṇa*; because it is induced within their own bodies, they call it "attaining bliss.

Seeing others currently abiding in dhyāna is also treated in the same way. The following cases are all to be understood according to this principle. Third, [those who] feel aversion toward vitarka and vicāra...

Therefore, one presently attains the second dhyāna and regards it as nirvāṇa; fourth, out of aversion toward all vitarka, vicāra, and prīti, one presently dwells in the third dhyāna and regards it as nirvāṇa;
fifth, out of aversion toward prīti and sukha, up to and including the inhalation and exhalation of breath, one presently dwells in the fourth dhyāna and regards it as nirvāṇa.
Because it awaits the past, it is called the "future limit" (aparānta). Furthermore, this conception of a self [regards] the present...

Since there is happiness now, there will also be happiness later; therefore, it is subsumed under the future limit (*aparānta*). Taking present happiness as a precursor while clinging to future happiness is collectively termed "the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma*).
Because this does not arise based on the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), it is subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). (Text).

Alternatively, regarding those who see [beings such as] Īśvara or Maheśvara, the meaning is seen in the first fascicle. Or, there are those who recklessly calculate various false liberations; these are not [correct views].
To regard what is not a fruit as a fruit is [to hold] the view of a fruit; or to have the false attachment of regarding what is not the path as the path is [to hold] the view of a cause.
All such instances as these are subsumed under wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
△ Fourth, the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

The four types of adherence to views refer to [the act of] grasping at any one of the various views—such as those of extremes or false views—and [taking them to be supreme]. Its function is to serve as the basis for all disputes.
Regarding the meaning of the terms: it means that among the various views, such as those of extremes or falsity, one adheres to a particular view and...
To rely upon the aggregates and grasp them as the supreme cause capable of attaining the fruit of purification and liberation is called the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

All strife arises based upon this; such is its function. As for "strife," it refers to those various views being mutually contradictory, because one grasps one [view] as correct while regarding all others as false.
△ The fifth is the grasping of rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

The grasping of rules and observances refers to [the adherence to] rules such as those of cattle or dogs, as well as practices such as pulling out one's hair or sleeping on needles; its function is to serve as a basis for fruitless exertion and suffering.

*Commentary on the Phonology and Meaning:* "Various views and rules and observances" refers to the precepts of cattle, dogs, and so forth, as well as [practices] such as plucking out one's hair or sleeping on needles.
The precepts such as lying on thorns refer to the ascetic observances maintained in accordance with various views, as well as the aggregates that serve as the basis for those observances;
to grasp these as supreme and capable of bringing about purification is called the "clinging to rules and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa). It is a fruitless exertion of hardship.
This is the functional operation of that [view]. "Without benefit" means that it cannot achieve the sense of escaping from suffering.
△ Next, [the text] generally addresses the objection regarding the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).
However, there are places where it is stated that holding [something] as supreme (up to) being described as false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is not subsumed under the two types of grasping.

*Yinyi* (Explanations of Terms). Question: In other places it is said that clinging [to views] as supreme is called *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views), and clinging [to precepts] as capable of bringing about purification is called *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to precepts and rituals).
What is the meaning of this? Answer: This is an abbreviated or elliptical statement, or it follows a specific pedagogical approach (*anuvartana-mukha*).
Otherwise, below, he explains this as an elliptical statement; that is, if one were to insist that in other places it is not elliptical, then as follows:

Why is it that regarding what is not cessation as cessation, and what is not the path as the path, all treatises state these are subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) rather than the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*)?
This is intended to clarify that reckoning cause and effect individually belongs to wrong view, whereas reckoning both cause and effect together constitutes the two types of grasping.
Thus, one should know that in other passages, this is merely an abbreviated indication.
△ Next, the analysis by way of various categories (11). First, the category of analysis regarding co-arising (2). First, a general judgment on the ten delusions.
Within these ten afflictions, both general and specific, [they arise] only after one has personally examined and deliberated.

Explanation of Terms: Regarding the general and specific categories, the first five are called "general" because they are not divided into sub-types; the latter five are "specific" because they are opened up into distinctions.
As for the "six pervasive [afflictions]," these refer to greed, hatred, delusion, pride, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).

These six are all pervasive in being comprised within both the innate (*sahaja*) and the conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*) categories. The phrase "arising spontaneously" explains their inclusion in the innate category; the phrase "arising from deliberation" explains...

[These are] conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). Doubt, false views, and the two types of grasping—these four arise solely from conceptual construction; their meanings can be understood through the commentary.
△ Next, the specific determination of the view of extremes (in two parts): first, the heading.
Regarding the innate forms of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*):
Next, [the text] explains [the two types]. According to the first master, the innate [view] is severed only [by the path of seeing].
There is an interpretation that it severs only the coarse aspects of eternalism and nihilism; [this is because] all [beings] give rise to terror, fearing that their self will be annihilated.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: Regarding the statement that the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) includes that which is innate (*sahaja*), it is only the [view of] annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) that is so.

Why? Because the characteristic of the view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) is coarse; it is only through the influence of evil friends and the like that it is induced to arise. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Volume below) cites scriptural evidence to prove that it is only [annihilationism] that is innate.
The question, "Which view of extremes is innate? is an inquiry. The answer states: "It is comprised within the view of annihilationism. How is this known to be so? It is said:
Regarding those who practice the realization (abhisamaya) prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*):

although they have already suppressed the manifest afflictions arising from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), they still give rise within their minds to a fear of annihilation (*ucchedabhaya*), thinking, "Now that I am [no longer], where does my self reside? Is this innate view (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*) not itself a form of annihilationism?
Therefore, the text below further cites the innate terror of birds and beasts, which is likewise nothing but [the fear of] annihilation.
△ Next, the Master [Vasubandhu] states that [the view] is both innate (*sahaja*) and acquired (*parikalpita*).
One interpretation holds that this treatise speaks according to coarse characteristics (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*), stating that it is "either innate or conceptually arisen.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: the treatise asserts that the innate [view] is severed only by those who have abandoned the [wrong] views; this is stated according to coarse characteristics. If one were to examine it in detail...
The term "also" (亦) refers to what is commonly observed (*pratyakṣa*). That is to say, regarding animals and below: it explains what is commonly observed.

"Those who construct and accumulate requisites over a long period" refers to beasts constructing burrows, magpies building nests, and so forth; thus, the meaning can be understood from the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (or *Xianyang lun*).
△ II. The Section on Mutual Correspondence within the Same Category (2). First, the inquiry:
Among these ten afflictions, which ones correspond with how many others?
△ Second, the explanation (6). First, taking greed as the primary subject, it is contrasted with the remaining eight.

Greed (*lobha*) and hatred (*dveṣa*), as well as doubt (*vicikitsā*), certainly do not arise simultaneously. (Up to: There is no fault in greed being associated with the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*). Regarding the meaning of the terms:

the first sentence first addresses how [greed] definitely does not arise simultaneously with hatred and doubt. As for "the objects of love and hatred being different": *Note: This passage is an excerpt from a commentary on the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, specifically concerning the section on the non-simultaneous arising of mental factors and the association of afflictions with the views.*

The phrase "greed and hatred do not coexist" explains that they do not arise simultaneously. The phrase "uncertainty regarding an object without attachment" explains that greed and doubt do not coexist.

In the passage "greed, pride, and views," the term "others" refers to the remaining six [afflictions]. The word "or" (*vā*) is an indefinite term intended to indicate that there are also cases where they are not associated.
"That which is loved" refers to what is craved; "that which is despised" refers to what is the object of pride. These two refer to the focal objects (*ālambana*).
Alternatively, it is said that they do not arise simultaneously because they are not identical.

As for the statement that "the objects of defilement and the objects of reliance can be the same," this means that, for example, when someone develops deep attachment to their own prosperity and relies upon that very thing to become arrogant toward others;
thus, it is said that they can be associated because the object is the same. The meaning of the five views that coexist with greed can be understood accordingly.
△ Second, taking hatred as the primary factor in relation to the other seven:
Hatred may arise together with pride or doubt; as stated in sequence, hatred may or may not be present.

Commentary on Terms: First, regarding anger (*dveṣa*) in relation to pride (*māna*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), the subsequent section provides an explanation. There are two senses in which anger may coexist with or not coexist with pride.
Regarding the first point, "hesitation" and so forth, this explains anger in relation to doubt; here too, there are two senses. As for "doubt being either favorable or adverse":
if one hesitates at the outset regarding a favorable object, or if one reflects for a long time without reaching a decision regarding an adverse object, then anger does not arise.

It is said that [hatred] is not associated [with the lower fetters]. If, regarding favorable objects, one reflects for a long time without reaching a decision, or regarding unfavorable objects, at the initial moment of hesitation, hatred arises together with them;
thus it is said to be associated. Hatred has no sense of association with the two [lower fetters] of inferiority (*avarabhāgīya*) and subsequent grasping (*parāmarśa*).

As for its association with the three views—identity view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—regarding the existence of the lower [fetters], this explains the association of hatred with both identity view and view of extremes.

[The text] observes that there is the sense of both being simultaneous and not being simultaneous. Regarding the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), it is explained as the opposite of this. As for the presence or absence of hatred (*dveṣa*), it is the opposite of the aforementioned aggregates of suffering and the aggregates of pleasure;

here too, there is the sense of both being simultaneous and not being simultaneous. Below, under "False View" (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), [the text] explains the sense of both being simultaneous and not being simultaneous regarding hatred and false view.

That is to say, when false view involves slander and the denial of existence—such as the absence of hatred toward evil deeds like the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*)—it is said to be [not simultaneous].
They arise together. [The view of negation] slanders all wholesome things such as giving and morality, asserting that they can be attained through [wrong] association.
△ Third, with pride as the primary factor, it is contrasted with the other six [afflictions].
Pride is fixed toward its object; doubt is not so. (Up to: It is also the same for a portion of bodily misconduct and wrong views.

Commentary on the Meanings and Terms: First, pride (*māna*) is contrasted with doubt (*vicikitsā*); there is no sense of their being associated (*samprayukta*). Pride and the [afflictions] below it are next contrasted with the five views (*dṛṣṭi*);

there is no fault in their arising together. However, pride and those below it do not coexist with the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and the same applies to one portion of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).
This means that the view of a self-identity clings to the inferior aggregates of suffering, while false view denies all things that are wholesome or excellent.
Because there is no mutual disparagement or reliance, they are also not associated.
Fourth, regarding the five views with doubt as the primary factor:
because doubt is indecisive and thus contrary to view, doubt and view certainly do not arise together.
△ The five views are not mutually concomitant within their own class.
The five views are necessarily not concomitant with one another because there cannot be multiple instances of wisdom (*prajñā*) within a single moment of mind.
Regarding the meaning of the term "not in a single moment of mind": this is because all five views have wisdom as their essential nature.
△ 6. With delusion (*moha*) as the primary factor, it is contrasted with the other nine [afflictions].
Delusion is invariably associated with all nine types of afflictions, because the arising of all afflictions necessarily depends upon delusion.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: "invariably associated with the nine types" means that the arising of all afflictions is due to being obscured by ignorance regarding the principles of truth (*satya*).
Only then can they arise.
△ Third, the section on the association of the various consciousnesses:
With which consciousnesses are these ten afflictions associated? (Up to: Because pride and so forth arise through weighing and so on.

Commentary on the Terms: Regarding "non-discriminative," the five consciousnesses possess only *svabhāva-vikalpa* (intrinsic discrimination); they lack the two types of discrimination, namely *anusmaraṇa-vikalpa* (recollection) and *abhinirūpaṇa-vikalpa* (conceptualization).
Regarding "weighing and so forth," "and so forth" refers to hesitation and investigation. Regarding "giving rise to pride and so forth," [the phrase "and so forth"] likewise applies.
This is equivalent to doubt and the five views. That is to say, pride arises from weighing oneself against others, conceiving of oneself as superior, equal, or inferior;

doubt arises from hesitation and deliberation; and the five views arise from investigation. Since these modes of activity do not exist within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), pride and the others do not coexist with them.

Supplement: An ancient commentary states that the five consciousnesses possess only three [mental factors], because they lack discrimination (*avikalpa*). Therefore, pride (*māna*) and the like do not exist therein;
for pride and the others necessarily arise from the presence of recollective (*anusmaraṇa*) and conceptualizing (*abhinirūpaṇa*) discrimination.
△ Section Four: The Gate of Correspondence with the Various Feelings (2). First, the inquiry:
With which feelings (*vedanā*) are these ten afflictions associated?
△ Second, the explanation (2). First, the explanation based on the actual meaning (4). First, greed, hatred, and delusion.
Greed, hatred, and delusion—both innate and discriminative—are associated with all five feelings. Regarding hatred, because it encounters favorable objects, it is accompanied by joy and pleasure.
[Regarding] the meaning of the terms: this means that greed, hatred, and delusion, without distinction between the innate and the discriminative, are all associated with the five feelings.

[The text] says "greed meets the lower [feeling]," fearing there might be a question: "If the object of greed is agreeable to the mind, how can it be associated with sorrow and suffering? As for the object of hatred...
A contrary mind—how could there be joy or pleasure? One should reflect upon this intention.
△ Second, pride (in two parts). First, the first master:

There is an interpretation that both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptually arisen (*vikalpita*) pride [exist]... because it relies on the inferior aggregates (*skandha*) and is associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*).

Commentary on the Terms: *Sahaja* (innate) and *vikalpika* (conceptual). Among the four types of feeling (*vedanā*), suffering (*duḥkha*) is excluded. Question: Pride (*māna*) consists solely of haughtiness;
how can it give rise to sorrow (*daurmanasya*)? Explanation of the meaning follows the text.
△ Next, the Master [Xuanzang]’s Successor.
There is an interpretation that innate (*sahaja*) pride also arises together with suffering (up to: ... because it is only the discriminative (*vikalpita*) [pride] that can give rise to it).

[Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms]: First, explaining the innate: that is, innate pride (*sahaja-māna*). It is not limited to arising with the four [mental factors]; it also extends to association with the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*).
Why is this? It has already been stated that within the realms of pure suffering (*ekānta-duḥkha-gati*), there is suffering on the mental level (*manobhūmika*).

Following the explanation of the "inferior" [type of pride], we shall next clarify the "discriminated" type. Why is it that discriminated pride does not coexist with suffering? It is because discriminated pride does not exist within the realms of pure suffering;
for there, no false teachers, false teachings, or false reflections exist to induce the arising of discriminated pride. Nevertheless, they do not [create it].
Regarding karma leading to the miserable realms (*apāya*): because it can be initiated by non-conceptual pride (*nirvikalpa-māna*) and so forth, it is like an echo.

In the seventy-fourth fascicle of the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the School), it is asked: "Within the three miserable realms, are both conceptual (*vikalpita*) and innate (*sahaja*) [afflictions] still present?
The answer, citing Dharmapāla, states: "Within the three miserable realms, there is generally no conceptual [affliction], yet karma is not initiated."
The afflictions belonging to those such as monkeys are all powerful; they are innate (*sahaja*) rather than discriminative (*vikalpita*).

Even if they perform karma, it results only in individual retribution (*vyaktavipāka*). If there were discriminative [afflictions] that performed collective retribution (*sāmānyavipāka*), there would be no time of escape at all.
Question: Since there are discriminative seeds, why do they not create collective retribution? Answer: Because they lack the primary [affliction] and its associates (*saparivāra*).
Manifest activity is the principal factor; the seeds that assist its arousal are the accompaniments. Question:

If it is said that those in the three miserable realms do not create karma, how is it that a powerful hungry ghost struck Śāriputra on the head and immediately entered hell, while a parrot bird heard the Dharma of the Four Truths and attained rebirth in heaven?
Answer: These beings created distinct retributive karma; this karma was so potent that it was able to assist their past [karma].

This refers to the collective retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*). Once the collective retribution has been assisted, one is then able to fall to earth or ascend to heaven according to the force of one's karma. Furthermore, an ancient master asked:
"Within the realms of humans and devas, is the collective karma that initiates rebirth (*ākṣepaka-karma*) necessarily produced? He replied:

"In the human realm, those in the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*) do not create karma for either collective or individual retribution, because they lack discriminative conceptualization (*vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*). In the other three continents, such karma is indeed initiated; this includes the delusion (*moha*) of this very continent [Jambudvīpa]."

Question: If people do not initiate karma, and as previously stated there is no discrimination within the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*), how is it known that they recognize their parents and so forth?
For example, birds feed their parents in return, and cats and dogs recognize humans and perceive their anger or joy. Answer: This is not discrimination arising from afflictions (*kleśa*).
That is spontaneous discrimination (*svarasavāhin-vikalpa*), not discrimination arising from afflictions. (Text)
△ Regarding the three doubts and the last three views:
it is possible for the three doubts and the last three views to be associated with four feelings (up to the point where they may be associated with sorrow).

[Commentary on the Meaning of the Sound]: Regarding the three doubts and the last three views, these four are associated with all [feelings] except for suffering (*duḥkha*). Question: How can doubt be associated with joy (*prīti*)? Explanation: [It is so] because of desire (*kāma*).
Doubt bound to the realms (*dhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) is associated with joy, because it involves hesitation regarding future matters such as the non-existence of suffering and so forth. Question:

With what [feeling] are the two graspings (*parāmarśa*) associated? Answer: The two graspings, when they take as their object views associated with grief (*daurmanasya*) and the aggregates that serve as their basis—such as practices like smearing oneself with ashes or plucking out one's hair—are able to be associated with grief. False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is associated with both joy and grief; this is its meaning.
This is easy to understand; therefore, it is not explained.
△ Fourth: The Two Views of Self and Extremes (2). First, the initial master:
There is an interpretation that the innate views of self and extremes (up to) the view of nihilism are the opposite of this, as they are associated with sorrow.

Commentary on the Meanings of Terms: First, we shall explain the two innate views—view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi). Why do they coexist only with the three feelings of joy, pleasure, and equanimity, and not with suffering?
Because these two views are not associated with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*). Why do they not coexist with mental distress (*daurmanasya*)?

The two innate views (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*) belong exclusively to the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature; therefore, the treatise states that the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not unspecified.
Next, the two discriminative views (*vikalpita-dṛṣṭi*) are explained: among the four [mental factors], excluding suffering (*duḥkha*), how can there be sorrow? The commentary explains:
when one grasps the aggregates associated with suffering as "self" or "mine," or grasps the aggregates associated with permanence and pleasure as "self" or "mine," at that time, one attains [sorrow].
Because they are associated with *daurmanasya* (sorrow).
△ Next, according to the Master [Vasubandhu]:
There is an interpretation that the two views (*dṛṣṭi*) arise simultaneously with the suffering [truth]... [the details] are explained as before; the rest is as previously stated.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: First, the formal explanation. This refers to the two innate views—view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

They are not associated exclusively with joy, pleasure, or equanimity, but also extend to painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*). Why? Because in places where one experiences purely suffering, they are associated with that suffering. The phrase "The treatise says, below" indicates the subsequent proof;
"as explained extensively before" refers to the passage in the fifth fascicle concerning the explanation of the three types of sensation. The remainder is as previously stated.
Regarding "the speaker": this refers to one who experiences [feelings] associated with the discrimination of the two views. This follows the first interpretation given previously.
△ Next, the explanation according to coarse characteristics (in two parts): first, the discourse on the feelings corresponding to the afflictions.
"This is based on the actual meaning according to the coarse characteristics" (up to) "false views and doubt—these four are all excluded from suffering.
[Commentary on the Meaning of the Words: The first phrase concludes what preceded. "According to the coarse characteristics" and below correctly elucidates the main point.

"According to the coarse characteristics" means, for the time being, clarifying the general outline; it is also the *anuloma-naya* (the method of following the sequence). This may be reflected upon according to the text.
△ Next, regarding the treatise on realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi-viniścaya*):
pleasure associated with both greed and delusion (*lobha-moha*) pervades the four lower stages; it should be understood accordingly that [pleasure] arises together with other sensations as well.
*Yinyi* (Explanation of Terms): This refers to the sensation of pleasure associated with greed and delusion, which, among the nine stages, pervades the four lower stages. That is to say:
This extends from the desire realm up to the third dhyāna. It does not extend further upward because the five higher stages are associated exclusively with equanimity (*upekṣā*).

The remaining seven [mental factors] are associated with pleasure (*sukha*); excluding the desire realm, they extend through the first, second, and third dhyānas. Regarding the exclusion of the desire realm:
these remaining seven exist only in the mental stage (*manobhūmi*), and the pleasure of the mental stage does not exist in the desire realm. As for the non-mention of hatred (*dveṣa*): if...

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), hatred (*dveṣa*) does not coexist with pleasure because it is not pleasurable; furthermore, hatred does not function in the two higher realms. Doubt (*vicikitsā*) and independent ignorance (*moha*) coexist in the desire realm only with mental pain (*daurmanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
In the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), as well as with other afflictions (*kleśa*), they arise together with other feelings (*vedanā*).
The specific realms and stages (*bhūmi*) through which these are accessible may be determined by analogy with the case of volition (*cetanā*).

Appendix: Regarding the remaining seven types of pleasure (*sukha*). Excluding the three—greed, hatred, and delusion—the remaining seven, namely pride, doubt, and the five views, are associated exclusively with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
They are excluded [from the first dhyāna] because there is no pleasure belonging to the mental stage within the desire realm.

Doubt and independent ignorance (*avidyā*) are also associated exclusively with the mental consciousness (*manas*). Since there are no sensations of suffering or pleasure in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it was previously stated that doubt and ignorance are without suffering and are accompanied by the sensation of joy (*saumanasya*).
That this is not mentioned here is because the previous statement was made according to their subtle characteristics, whereas the present one follows their coarse characteristics.

When doubt has not yet reached a resolution, how could there be joy? As for the remaining seven afflictions in the two higher realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*): [they are associated with the mental consciousness].
It should be understood accordingly that it is associated with other forms of joy and suffering.
△ Fifth, the section on association with the object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa-viprayukta-dharma*).

With how many of these object-specific factors is this [mental factor] mutually associated? (Up to: It is not associated with *dṛṣṭi* (view), because [this factor] is not distinct from *prajñā* (wisdom).

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: The first phrase poses a general inquiry. Regarding "greed, hatred," and so forth, this explains greed, hatred, delusion, and pride, which can coexist with the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*).
Question: These four [afflictions] have coarse and agitated modes of activity (*ākāra*); how can they coexist with meditative concentration (*samādhi*)? Answer:

As in the case of the gods of the *Pramadā* (Playful Forgetfulness) heaven, who, while focusing one-pointedly on a single object, give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion; thus, it is possible for them to possess concentration. As for doubt and the five views, each...

It can coexist with four [mental factors]: doubt excludes resolve (*adhimokṣa*) and the five views (*dṛṣṭi*). It does not coexist with wisdom (*prajñā*), because doubt is not a definitive determination, whereas view is itself wisdom.
△ Sixth, the section on the mutual inclusion of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).
To which natures are these ten afflictions subsumed? (Up to: Although they frequently manifest, they do not obstruct the wholesome.
[Commentary on the Meaning and Phonetics: First, the inquiry. Regarding "hatred is exclusively," the following explains: among the ten, hatred is subsumed under the nature of unwholesomeness alone;
the other nine are common to both the unwholesome and the obscured-neutral natures. The phrase "the two above" explains their commonality with the two natures; that is, the two above...
The remaining nine [afflictions] bound to the two higher realms—whether innate (*sahaja*) or discriminative (*vikalpita*)—are always suppressed by the power of meditative concentration;
therefore, they are comprised solely within the nature of obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). As for the remaining nine bound to the desire realm, those that arise discriminatively...

They are categorized exclusively as unwholesome (*akuśala*), because they can give rise to conduct leading to the miserable realms (*apāya*). If they are innate (*sahaja*), they are categorized according to both natures:
those that give rise to evil conduct are categorized as unwholesome, while those that do not give rise to evil conduct are categorized as exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*).

It should be understood that the following provides a detailed explanation: the two innate views are categorized exclusively as neutral and do not extend to the unwholesome, because they certainly do not give rise [to such conduct].
Because of karma; because they arise without obstructing the wholesome.
△ Section Seven: The Gate of Affiliation with the Realms and Present Conditions (2).
First, the inquiry: To which realm do these ten afflictions belong?
△ Next, the explanation [of the three sections]: first, the affiliation with the three realms.
Hatred exists only in the desire realm; the others pertain to all three realms.
△ Next, the manifestation of the three realms (in two parts): first, clarifying that those in lower realms do not give rise to afflictions of higher realms.
For one born in a lower stage who has not yet abandoned the defilements of that lower stage, all co-nascent afflictions are capable of manifesting.
Regarding the meaning of the term "not manifesting": for one born in a lower stage who has not yet abandoned the defilements of that lower stage, the afflictions of the higher stages do not manifest.

This means that as long as one has not abandoned the defilements of the lower stage, the defilements of the higher stages do not appear. For example, one born in the desire realm who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm [does not experience the afflictions of the form realm].

The afflictions (*kleśa*) of the first dhyāna will certainly not manifest; likewise, up until one has not yet abandoned the afflictions of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), the afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) will certainly not manifest.

This is because only when one has abandoned the defilements of a lower stage and attained the fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*) of that stage—from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—can the afflictions of that respective stage potentially manifest. Thus it is for all [stages].
"Leakage" (*āsrava*) refers to the meaning of abandoning the defilements of a lower stage and giving rise to afflictions of a higher stage.
"All contaminated paths" refers to the mundane dhyānas of relish cultivated by ordinary beings and non-Buddhists; that is, the four dhyānas and eight concentrations.

Because they lack the wisdom of the contemplation of the two emptinesses, they cannot subdue the afflictions arising from discrimination, nor the subtle innate afflictions within the seventh consciousness. This is because [they] still harbor aversion toward the suffering of the lower stages.
By means of the six modes of mental application regarding the coarse hindrances and so forth, one is able to suppress and eliminate the innate coarse afflictions within the six consciousnesses.

As for "gradually realizing the fundamental meditative absorptions," this refers to how, by suppressing and eliminating the innate coarse afflictions of the desire realm, one immediately attains the fundamental absorption of the first dhyāna;
and by suppressing the coarse afflictions from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness, one immediately [attains the respective fundamental absorptions].
Because one attains the fundamental dhyāna of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is called "gradual. As for those who are merely deluded regarding phenomena:
within these six consciousnesses, the innate coarse afflictions arise spontaneously; they do not obstruct the principle [of reality]. Regarding their functioning through the external gate:

because they arise by taking the five external sense-objects as their objects, they are distracted, coarse, and agitated, and thus directly obstruct that meditative concentration. Having subdued these... below.

Once one has attained the meditative absorption of a higher stage, the coarse afflictions innate to that [lower] stage, as well as the discriminative and subtle innate afflictions of that higher stage,
are all capable of becoming manifest.
△ Next, the explanation that those in higher realms can give rise to afflictions of lower realms (2). First, the direct explanation:
Those born in a higher realm [give rise to] various afflictions of lower realms because they give rise to the innate craving (*upapatti-tṛṣṇā*) that moistens rebirth in the lower realms.
Commentary on the Phonology and Meaning: When one is born in a higher stage (*bhūmi*), the various afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower stages may all manifest.

Regarding the phrase "born below the fourth," this explains the arising of the lower [afflictions]. As for the "fourth dhyāna," it refers to the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) within the fourth dhyāna.

Regarding "among those in the intermediate state" (*antarābhava*), it means that there are non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who, while in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), cultivate and attain the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Some say they attain *arhat*... [text truncated]
After attaining the fruit of arhatship, he was reborn in that celestial realm.

When his karmic retribution there was exhausted and he was about to descend to be born again, he saw the arising of an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) and slandered it, saying, "There are no true arhats in this world.
Because of this slander, he fell into the Avīci Hell. As the sutra says: "The unlearned bhikṣu, having slandered an arhat, underwent further existence"—this refers to precisely this case.

This is precisely the actual fact of the conceptual discrimination that arises from the higher [level] and engages with the lower. When the body is in the lower state, it explains the arising of the innate (*sahaja*).
Its meaning should be understood through reflection.

Supplement: Regarding "craving for rebirth" (*upapatti-tṛṣṇā*), it refers to the spontaneous defiled attachment toward the place of future existence (*punarbhava*), such as at the time of entering the womb.
This refers, for example, to those who give rise to perverted forms of affection toward their parents.
Next, to resolve potential objections:
the statement that one born in a higher realm does not give rise to [affection] for a lower one is said according to the majority of cases, or as a provisional teaching (*anuvartana-mukha*).
Commentary on the Phonology and Meaning: In some places it is stated that "one born in a higher realm does not give rise to [afflictions] of a lower realm. This is based on the majority of cases;
it is not that there are no instances whatsoever where one does not give rise to [afflictions] of a lower realm.
△ Third, the mutual conditioning of the three realms (in two parts): First, afflictions of a lower realm conditioning those of a higher realm (in two parts): First, the direct explanation.
The afflictions of the lower stages also take the higher stages as their objects; that the remaining five [afflictions] take the higher as their objects is a principle fully established.
Regarding the meaning of the terms: the first phrase provides a general heading—that lower delusions take the higher as their objects. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* cites this as proof.

Since it is stated that craving takes the higher stages as its object, one may infer by analogy that hatred likewise takes the higher as its object. "The stage of being free from desire" refers to the two upper realms (*dhātu*).

"Taking [them] collectively as objects" and below: next, it clarifies that the three—view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and pride (*māna*)—can take the higher stages as their objects. Regarding "taking all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) collectively as objects":

this refers to certain non-Buddhists who take all conditioned phenomena—the matter and mind of the three realms—collectively as objects, grasping them as "self" and "mine," reckoning the self as either annihilated or eternal, and exalting themselves above others.

Therefore, the view of self, the view of extremes, and pride can also take the higher stages as their objects. The remaining five [defilements] are to be understood by analogy with those of the lower stages.

As for the remaining five afflictions—namely, the five beginning with greed—once they have obtained an object in a higher realm, the other five, beginning with delusion, can likewise take a higher stage as their object;
this principle is fully established. (The "other five" beginning with delusion refer to delusion, doubt, view-grasping, precept-and-vow-grasping, and false view.)
△ Next, the general rebuttal of objections.
There are places where it is stated that greed, hatred, pride, and so forth—up to the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—necessarily arise based on the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the meaning of the words: "Or, depending on distinct conditions" means that this is said with reference to those [afflictions] that take only their own level as an object; therefore, it is said that greed and the others do not [arise based on the view of a self-identity].

Regarding the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhūmi*): one does not perceive the phenomena of other realms as "self" or "belonging to self. Therefore, it is said that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not take the higher realms as its object.
Furthermore, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arises based on the view of a self-identity;

since one does not perceive the "self" of another realm while giving rise to the notions of annihilation or permanence, it is said that the view of extremes does not take the higher realms as its object. Those who provide this explanation all rely upon [this principle].
This is a rough description stated for the time being. In reality, greed and other afflictions can take the higher stages as their objects; this point is explained in the preceding text.
△ Next, the higher afflictions taking the lower stages as objects (2): first, the formal explanation.
The afflictions of the higher stages also take the lower stages as their objects; this applies up to the three views following doubt, which should be reflected upon according to principle.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: the first phrase provides a general heading. It states that the defilements of the upper [stages] take the lower as their objects, and it cites the arising of these [afflictions] as proof.

Pride takes the lower stages as its object; this is explained by taking the lower stages as a whole. As for the three—view of self, view of extremes, and craving—they obtain their objects by taking the lower stages as a whole, such as all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and so forth.
The preceding discussion concerned the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); this statement refers to the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*).

That is to say, there are non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) born in the higher realms who, taking all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as their general object, grasp them as "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*), thereby giving rise to views of annihilationism (*uccheda*) or eternalism (*śāśvata*) and developing deep attachment.

For this reason, these three [afflictions] can also take the lower realms as their objects. Regarding doubt (*vicikitsā*), the subsequent cases follow the same principle as the other four types. As for why hatred (*dveṣa*) and delusion (*moha*) are not mentioned, it is because in the higher realms...
Because hatred is practiced [only in higher realms], and because delusion universally defiles [all levels].
△ Next, [the author] addresses potential objections:
as for the statement that the higher afflictions do not take lower levels as objects, that too is mostly stated in reference to specific instances of such objects.
△ Section Eight: The Gate of the Mutual Inclusion of the Categories of Learners (*śaikṣa*) and Others.

Regarding these ten afflictions, under which category—learner (*śaikṣa*), non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), or neither—are they subsumed? They are not subsumed under the learner, nor are they subsumed under the non-learner, because they are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*).
[The commentary] first poses the question and then provides the explanation: "They are not included in the stage of the learner, nor are they included in the stage of the non-learner. Why is this?"

Within those two categories, because they are associated exclusively with the wholesome (*kuśala*), they are subsumed under the category of "neither" (i.e., neither-defiled-nor-undefiled). This is because the ten [mental factors] are exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
9. The Section on the Mutual Subsumption of the Three Types of Abandonment (2): First, the Inquiry.
What do these ten afflictions abandon?
Next, the explanation [of the two categories] begins with the exclusion of what is not to be abandoned:
they are not "not-to-be-abandoned," because those are not defiled.
△ Next, the abandonment through seeing and cultivation is explained (in two parts). First, the general explanation:
those [afflictions] that arise through discrimination are abandoned only by seeing; those that are subtle and difficult to sever are abandoned only by cultivation.

△ Second, the detailed explanation (in two parts): First, explaining that [the afflictions] are abandoned solely by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) based on their coarse characteristics (in two parts). First, clarifying that all ten are abandoned simultaneously:
The ten [afflictions] abandoned by seeing are in fact all abandoned simultaneously, because the true path of seeing (*tattva-darśana-mārga*) takes the [four] truths as its collective object.
Appendix: By means of the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*), one takes the four truths of the three realms as a collective object.

Since the truths are realized instantaneously, the delusions regarding those truths should likewise be severed instantaneously. This is explained by contrasting the objects of delusion with the subject that deludes.
△ Next, the detailed explanation of the characteristics of delusion regarding the truths (in three parts). First, the heading:
Now, the characteristics of delusion regarding the truths are both general and specific.
△ Second, the explanation (in two parts). First, general delusion.
In summary, it is said that all ten types [of beings] are deluded regarding the Four Noble Truths; this is because cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are objects of their fear.

Regarding the phrase "Suffering (*duḥkha*) and Accumulation (*samudaya*) are its causes and bases": "Accumulation" refers to the seeds and manifest forms of afflictions (*kleśa*), which constitute its cause.
"Suffering" refers to the resultant body and mind, which constitute its basis. Cessation and the path are the objects of their fear.

"Cessation" refers to the fruit of abandonment; "the path" refers to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). Because the obstacles and their remedies are mutually contradictory, it is said that these [afflictions] are the objects of fear for them.
Due to these ten delusions regarding the principles of the Four Noble Truths, sentient beings are unable to know suffering and abandon its origin.
They aspire to the path that leads to cessation.
△ Next, the specific delusions (2): first, the general explanation;

"specific" refers to the distinct delusions regarding the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths, which give rise to two types: those that exclusively delude regarding suffering (*duḥkha*), and those that pervasively delude regarding all four.

Commentary on the Terms: Two [of the afflictions] delude only regarding suffering, because the three [truths] of origin, cessation, and the path do not give rise to the two views of self-identity and extremes;
these two views delude only regarding the truth of suffering. Eight [afflictions] delude all four [truths], because the remaining eight all delude the principle of the four truths.
△ Second, the detailed explanation (in two parts): The first two [views] are exclusively deluded regarding suffering.

The two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arise only with respect to the locus of the fruit, because their specific objects—emptiness and non-self—belong to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: As stated previously, the two [views] that are exclusively deluded regarding suffering are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

These two arise only with respect to the locus of the fruit; for "suffering" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), which are the karmic retribution of the world, and these two views arise only through being deluded about this fruit.

How is this known? Because the specific [notions of] emptiness and non-self pertain to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). This is because, within the stage of the Path of True Insight (*darśanamārga*):
One separately cultivates the contemplation of emptiness and the contemplation of non-self as antidotes to the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes;
for these two contemplations observe only the objective sphere of the Truth of Suffering.
△ Next, eight [afflictions] are generally deluded regarding the four [truths]. (2) First, it clarifies that the ten [afflictions] are generally deluded regarding suffering:

namely, doubt and the three views are directly deluded regarding the principle of suffering, up to non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*), which is directly deluded regarding the principles of the truths.

**Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms:** This explains the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Since it combines both the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the views of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), there are ten [factors].

In the text, first the four types of direct delusion are clarified: namely, doubt (*vicikitsā*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).

According to the explanation in the fifty-eighth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it asks: "What are the ten latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that delude one regarding suffering? Briefly stated, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are collectively termed [suffering].
It is suffering. Within these five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), the fool gives rise to twenty types of views of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
Five of these views perceive a self; the remaining views perceive what belongs to a self. This is called the view of a self-identity that is deluded regarding suffering.

Taking such a view of a self-identity as its basis, one perceives the five aggregates of clinging as being subject to annihilation or permanence; therefore, it is the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).

They are also deluded regarding suffering. Furthermore, there are various wrong views, such as the claim that there is no giving and so forth, up to the absence of the results of wholesome and unwholesome actions, as well as their maturation (*vipāka*). These are called wrong views that are deluded regarding suffering.

If there are non-Buddhists who, with respect to these views, neither definitively accept them nor categorically disparage the Truth of Suffering established by the Tathāgata, [they are not included among those deluded].

However, one harbors hesitation regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). This, along with what follows, constitutes doubt regarding suffering; this is the "doubt that is delusion concerning suffering. Second, below, the five types of remote delusions are explained:
namely, the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), the adherence to precepts and vows (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*), as well as greed, hatred, and pride.
The treatise states: "If there is the adherence to views, one falsely grasps at any views that are deluded regarding suffering, taking them to be supreme, [thinking] they are able to..."
"Purity, liberation, and transcendence"—this is called the adherence to views regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

If one falsely grasps at anything that accords with this view, or regards the observance of prohibitions and precepts associated with this view as supreme, thinking they can bring about purity, liberation, and transcendence—this is the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
This is delusion regarding the Truth of Suffering. If, in such a manner, one gives rise to [these views] for oneself...

Seeing [it] as precious and cherishing it with firm attachment—such a view and craving are delusion regarding suffering that is craving. If, toward another’s divergent views, one harbors resentment and hostility, this is delusion regarding suffering that is hatred.
If one relies on such a view and the mind becomes puffed up with pride, this is delusion regarding suffering that is conceit.
Following the associated [afflictions], the text next clarifies that ignorance possesses both the meanings of being "intimate" and "distant. The treatise says: "If there is..."
Ignorance (ajñāna) is associated with these various views, doubt, craving, and other afflictions.
When ignorance functions alone regarding suffering, both are termed "ignorance deluded regarding suffering. These ten afflictions are all delusions regarding the Truth of Suffering.
[These] are abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Supplement: Greed for one’s own views; hatred toward other views; pride associated with those [views] and their retinues;

and the ignorance that is co-mistaken with the nine—meaning that which is co-mistaken with doubt, the three views, and the four [afflictions]. These are the primary delusions regarding the principle of suffering. Co-mistaken with the two graspings [of views and precepts], greed, hatred, and pride are likewise included.
5. Fifth: Being vaguely deluded regarding the principle of suffering.
△ Next, explaining the eight [afflictions] that generally delude regarding the three [truths]:
doubt and false view directly delude regarding origination and so forth (up to: because one gives rise to hatred and jealousy out of fear of them).

Commentary on Terms: Regarding "doubt," "wrong views," "direct delusion regarding the origin [of suffering]," and so forth—[the phrase] "the two types of grasping, craving, and so forth should be understood by analogy with suffering" refers to the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), as well as craving, hatred, and pride;

these are also indirect delusions regarding the three truths of origin, cessation, and the path, no different from the preceding truth of suffering. The treatise asks: "What is delusion regarding the origin?"

There are eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). That is to say, when certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas slander the cause through wrong views, or conceive of Īśvara and so forth as the progenitor, transformer, and creator of all things—such wrong views regarding the doctrine of evil causes are the wrong views arising from delusion concerning the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).
Furthermore, if there is the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), one clings to those [views].

To regard [a view] as supreme, thinking it can bring about purity, liberation, and deliverance—this is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) arising from delusion regarding the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).

If one regards the precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) associated with such views, as well as the dharmas accepted along with them, as supreme and capable of bringing about purity—as explained at length above—this is the adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arising from delusion regarding the truth of origination. Other factors, such as doubt and craving, are as previously described.

It should be understood as previously explained. Thus, these eight types of afflictive latent tendencies (*kleśānuśaya*)—namely, the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), which arise from delusion regarding suffering as before, plus those arising from delusion regarding the truths of origin, cessation, and the path—constitute the eight types abandoned through the vision of the truth of origin.
How is it that there are eight latent tendencies deluded regarding the truth of cessation?
They refer to certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who hold views concerning finitude and infinitude, the "evasive" (*amarāvikṣepa*) views, and a portion of other views.

...up to the point of denying the true Arhats of the world and all their qualities of abandonment, and slandering the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) and so forth—such views as these are wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) arising from delusion regarding the Truth of Cessation.

If there is the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) that takes those various views and regards them as supreme, as explained at length previously, this is the clinging to views arising from delusion regarding the Truth of Cessation. If, regarding...
In accordance with those views, one adopts the various precepts and observances regarding all phenomena and grasps them as supreme. This is explained in detail as before;

this is the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) that is deluded regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*). As for the remaining afflictions such as craving and so forth, they should be understood as previously described.

Thus, these eight types of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are deluded regarding the Truth of Cessation and are abandoned through the vision of cessation. How is it that there are eight underlying tendencies deluded regarding the Path (*mārga*)?
This refers to the denial that there are true arhats in the world, and so forth, as explained at length.

Among these, one should know that all such views, foremost of which is the slander of the Omniscient One, as well as those regarding conditioned and untainted phenomena, are wrong views arising from delusion concerning the Truth of the Path.
Furthermore, the wrong views of non-Buddhist outsiders who slander the Path maintain that the Śramaṇa Gautama’s lineage...
O disciples, the paths of renunciation taught by those [non-Buddhists] are not actually paths of renunciation, because by means of them one cannot fully transcend [suffering].
The view of selflessness as established by the Buddha, as well as the observance of precepts in accordance with the Dharma, is a path of evil and heterodoxy, not the true and sublime path.
This is also called the "deluded-path wrong view. Furthermore, those non-Buddhists act as follows:
"This is our calculation; this is what we practice; whether it be our conduct or our path, this is the true practice of the path that can exhaust and transcend all suffering.
Such a view is also called the "perverted view of being lost in the path" (*mārga-vibhrama-mithyādṛṣṭi*). If one holds to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), one grasps those very perverted views.
To regard [such views] as supreme, capable of attaining purity, liberation, and transcendence—this is called the "clinging to views regarding the path.

If one regards the various dharmas and observed precepts that accord with those views as supreme, capable of attaining purity, liberation, and transcendence—this is called the "clinging to precepts and observances regarding the path.
The remaining factors, such as craving and so forth, constitute delusion regarding the path.
Regarding the afflictions: as with delusion regarding the Truth of Cessation, the principle should be understood accordingly.

Thus, these eight kinds of latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) are deluded regarding the Truth of the Path and are abandoned through the vision of the Path. However, below [the section on] hatred, there is a further detailed explanation that hatred also directly deludes [one] regarding cessation and the path.
The treatise states: "That is to say, regarding the Truth of Cessation, one gives rise to a mind of fear, a mind of harm, and a mind of resentment. Thus.

Hatred (*dveṣa*) is deluded regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); by analogy, it should be understood that it is likewise deluded regarding the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). Thus far, we have discussed both general and specific delusions regarding the Truths.
If speaking in terms of general delusion, there are forty types of afflictions regarding the Four Truths of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

In each Truth of the two upper realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*), hatred is excluded; thus, there are seventy-two types in total. Consequently, there are one hundred and twelve types of afflictive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) across the two upper realms.

If we speak according to specific delusions, there are thirty-four categories within the Four Truths of the Desire Realm (because the three truths of Origin, Cessation, and the Path do not give rise to the two views of self-identity and extremes).
Combined with those of the two upper realms, there are sixty categories; thus, the afflictions and latent tendencies throughout the Three Realms total ninety-four categories.
These are precisely what the Sūtra refers to as the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through insight.

This refers to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the two graspings (*parāmarśa*), as well as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), together with those associated with doubt (*vicikitsā*).

The two innate views (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*) and their associated [factors] are abandoned only through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because they are subtle and difficult to sever.
"Resonance" refers to the following: the two innate views of self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*). (The two innate views refer to that portion which arises spontaneously.)

△ Next, the four [afflictions] that delude one regarding the Four Truths:

hatred and the remaining forms of craving arise from delusion regarding specific objects; because they do not contradict the contemplation of the Truths, they are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "What are the outflows (*āsrava*) to be abandoned by the path of cultivation? They are the anger of the desire realm."
The three types of greed, pride, and ignorance within the three realms can only be severed through long-term cultivation of the right path;

therefore, they should be understood as abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). The remaining [afflictions] are explained in contrast to those associated with the two views (*dṛṣṭi*), namely craving and so forth.

That is to say, these four afflictions arise only from a specific delusion regarding phenomena (*vastu*) and do not [conflict] with the wisdom that contemplates the principles of the truths (*satya*).

Because they are contradictory [to the path], they are also abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). The above are the subtle innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) abandoned through the path of cultivation.
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are six: namely, the two views (*dṛṣṭi*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and anger (*pratigha*) which is deluded regarding objects.

In the two upper realms, anger is excluded. Combined across the three realms, there are sixteen categories of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), which constitute the eighty-one categories of afflictions to be abandoned through reflection (*vicikitsā-heya*).
△ Section Three: The Gate of Establishing Names According to the Object (3). First, regarding afflictions with and without objects:

although all afflictions possess objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*), [those that take] existing things as their objects are termed "afflictions with objects," and [those that take] non-existent things as their objects are termed "afflictions without objects."
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: Regarding the statement that "all afflictions possess objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*)," this refers to what was said in the first fascicle:

"The internal aggregates of one's own mind all exist as the objective basis (*ālambana-vastu*) upon which they rely. Regarding the statement that "some exist and some do not," this refers to what was said previously:

"The external aggregates of one's own mind may exist or may not exist. This means that if the various afflictions take an existing, real object as their condition, then the objective basis upon which they rely [exists].

There are some called "afflictions that take existent things as their objects. If they take as their objects mere mental images (pratibimba) that lack substantial reality—such as past or future phenomena, or objects like flowers in the sky—then the substance upon which they rely may be non-existent;
these are called "afflictions that take non-existent things as their objects."
△ Next, regarding tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) afflictions:
although their direct objects of perception (*ālambana*) are all tainted, they are termed "afflictions that take tainted and untainted things as objects.

[Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: As for the statement that "their direct objects of perception are all tainted," this is because the mind that undergoes transformation consists solely of afflictions.

As for those that rely on the substance [of the object] and pertain to the untainted (*anāsrava*), they take suffering (*duḥkha*) and origination (*samudaya*) as their objects; these are called "afflictions that take the tainted (*sāsrava*) as their object. Since the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*) belong to the untainted, they are excluded.
△ Third, the afflictions of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-viṣaya-nāman*).
Regarding those that take their own level as an object, the aspect (nimitta-bhāga) resembles the substance (vastu); this is called an "object arising from conceptualization" (*vikalpa-utpanna*).

[Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms]: Because the aspect and the substance of the objects of one's own level are similar to each other and both possess substantial reality (*dravya*), they are termed "objective objects" (*vastu-viṣaya*).

Regarding the path and the truth of cessation as objects: because they have never previously been cultivated or realized, and because they are merely seen or heard, they are termed "objects consisting of names" (*nāmālambana*).

This indicates that they exist only as names and lack substantial reality. There are twenty such objects, which are fully detailed in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Exposition of the Noble Teachings).
These consist of only six.

△ IV. The Secondary Afflictions (3): First, connecting the preceding with the subsequent question.
Having already explained the characteristics of the six root afflictions, what are the characteristics of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)?
△ Next, the root verse is cited in response.
The verse says: "The secondary afflictions are anger... [omitted] ...heedlessness, forgetfulness, distraction, and lack of correct awareness.

△ Third, the commentary explains and establishes the meaning (in two parts): first, the direct explanation of the verse text (in three parts); first, a brief explanation of the general name (in two parts).
First, the formal explanation of the name.

The treatise states: "Because they are of the nature of an outflow (*niṣyanda*) from specific states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*), they are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). [Commentary:
*Kaimō* (Opening the Ignorant) asks for the name and answers: "In accordance with the specific states of the afflictions, they are of the nature of an outflow."

Therefore, they are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Regarding the differentiation of their states: these refer to the ten [afflictions] beginning with anger (*krodha*), along with forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), and heedlessness (*pramāda*).

These thirteen dharmas (as Qingliang says: "These thirteen dharmas are nominal defiled mental factors; they are the differentiated states of greed and the others") are the differentiated states belonging to the primary afflictions.
Regarding their nature as outflows (*niṣyanda*): the answer is that they are shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
Lethargy, distraction, lack of faith, and laziness—these seven factors, although possessing distinct essential natures, are of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*) from their respective roots.
Question: Since these seven factors possess distinct essential natures, why are they called "outflows"? Answer:
Because they arise with the root as their cause, they are termed "outflows" (text).

Supplement: Regarding the distinction of stages (*avasthā-viśeṣa*), this refers to that which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Regarding the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*), this refers to that which possesses intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*).
△ Next, the classification.
These twenty types are divided into three categories; because they universally defile the mind, they are called the "great secondary afflictions" (*mahā-kleśa-mahābhūmika*).
[From] *Kai-meng* (Opening the Ignorant). Question: Do these secondary afflictions have further distinctions? Answer: Their categories are threefold.

This refers to the small, medium, and great [secondary afflictions]. Question: Who are the "small" and so forth? Answer: The first ten, beginning with anger (*krodha*), are called the small secondary afflictions (*parīttakleśabhūmika*).

The two, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), are the medium secondary afflictions. The final eight, beginning with restlessness (*auddhatya*), are the great secondary afflictions. Question: Based on what criteria are they designated as small, medium, and great?

Answer: They are based on three meanings. Those that possess none [of these meanings] are called small; those that possess one are called medium; those that possess all three meanings are called great.

"Great. [The interlocutor] asks: "What are these three meanings? [The Master] answers: "First, they do not arise simultaneously with their own kind; second, they pervade both types of defiled [minds];

third, they pervade all defiled minds. [The interlocutor] asks: "Please provide a general demonstration regarding the dharmas' non-arising with their own kind and so forth. [The Master] answers: "The ten dharmas such as anger (*krodha*) and the rest arise individually;
therefore, they do not coexist with their own kind. Thus, they lack the first meaning. Being exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*), they lack the second meaning. They pervade only the defiled."

Regarding the two natures: as for the "defiled" nature, it consists of the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured (*nivṛta*). Since the obscured is absent [in this context], we know that these do not pervade all defiled minds;
thus, they lack the third criterion. Among these ten factors, those that lack all three criteria are termed "minor.

Regarding the question of "concomitance," the answer is that the two—lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*)—arise together with their own kind, thereby possessing the first criterion. Since they are exclusively unwholesome...

The ten minor derivative [mental factors] also lack the latter two [of the three characteristics]. As stated previously, possessing one [of these characteristics] is termed "intermediate derivative. Question: What are the major [derivative mental factors]? Answer:

The eight factors, such as restlessness (*auddhatya*) and so forth, possess the first characteristic because they arise simultaneously within their own class. They possess the second characteristic because they are both unwholesome (*akuśala*) and obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Since they possess both of these natures, they pervade both types of defiled natures and thus possess the third characteristic, which applies to all defiled minds.
Since it possesses these three meanings, it is termed "great. The verse summarizes this: "Arising together with its own class, having two natures, and pervading all defiled minds;
The 'small' lacks these in the intermediate state and at the beginning [of rebirth], whereas the 'great' accompanies [the mind] and possesses all three meanings. (Text)
Supplement: The ancient commentary states: "However, the ten [root afflictions] such as anger (*krodha*) arise individually when compared to their own kind; they are not non-common to others.
