Regarding the meaning of the terms: when first practicing this concentration, one must take the meditative attainment of the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) at the Peak of Existence as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), traversing and examining it while taking the true, untainted principle (*anāsrava-tattva*) as the object; only then can one enter [the concentration]. Why is this so? Because there are nine...
Within the sequence, this is the final one; that is to say, from the first dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one enters them in immediate succession without disorder.
Since this concentration follows the concentration of the Peak of Existence, it is entered by taking the Peak of Existence as its preparatory application (*prayoga*).
As there is no other distinct level above the Peak of Existence, this concentration also belongs to the Peak of Existence. Question: If...
If it belongs to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it would apply to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*). Why then is it said that only noble ones cultivate it? Answer:
Although it belongs to the Peak of Existence, it is subsumed under the untainted (*anāsrava*). Question: Can this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) also arise after the other seven stages?

If one has cultivated this absorption until it is fully matured and has attained mastery over its entry and exit, can it manifest even after the minds of the other stages? Question: Does this belong to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*)?
By what are the trainings (śaikṣa) and so forth subsumed? Answer: Although they belong to the Truth of the Path, they are not subsumed under either of the two [categories].

Why are they not subsumed under the two? Because they resemble nirvāṇa. The meaning is that, because they are tranquil and subtle, they resemble nirvāṇa; thus, they are not subsumed under the category of the trainings.
Since they are not true nirvāṇa, they are also not subsumed under the category of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
△ Section Four: The Locus of the Initial Arising of the Four Dhyānas (2). First, the locus of initial arising:
this dhyāna first arises only among human beings (up to) because one knows that the ālayavijñāna exists and is not interrupted.

Regarding the explanation of the terminology: this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) necessarily arises among human beings within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because it arises through the power of the Buddha and his disciples preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, among the five destinies (*pañcagati*), the wisdom and understanding of humans are extremely sharp and acute.
Once one has cultivated this absorption and attained mastery over it, even if one is later reborn in the form or formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), it can still manifest before them.
Question: It may be granted that this [attainment] can arise for one who possesses a body in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

However, since there is no physical body in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), how can this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) manifest there as well? Answer: The *Udāyi-sūtra* provides the very proof for this; it speaks of the formless realm.

It is also called the "mind-made god" (*manomaya-deva*). This indicates that although those gods lack the fruits of karma, since they are designated as "mind-made," they are not excluded from the scope of names.
Furthermore, because the four formless aggregates (*arūpa-skandha*) can also give rise to this meditative absorption, it is so named; yet, even though it can arise, [it is distinct].

There are two categories of people. Among those born as humans, if one hears the name of the eighth consciousness as taught in the Mahāyāna teachings but does not believe or accept it, although [the consciousness] may arise [at birth], it will not manifest.
Why? Because they fear that both form and mind would be non-existent, resulting in the error of nihilism.

If, however, one hears of it and believes that the eighth consciousness exists, then even when born there [in the formless realm], it can manifest before them. Why? Because they know that the *ālayavijñāna* exists.
Because consciousness is neither interrupted nor extinguished.

△ Next, the arising [of the path] following the abandonment of afflictions (2). First, a general clarification of the three vehicles (2). First, the arising [of the path] upon the complete abandonment of the views:
one must abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing within the three realms (up to) because they are subsequently induced by the subsequently attained wisdom as appropriate.

Commentary on the Phonology and Meaning: When first cultivating this meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one must necessarily rely upon the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), because it involves the contemplation of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
For this absorption to first arise, one must have severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*). If these have not been severed, one remains an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*);

as an ordinary being, one is incapable of either suppressing or extinguishing the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the Peak of Existence. Furthermore, this absorption is subtle and profound; it requires the realization of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*). Accordingly...

It should be understood as subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), because it is induced by that [wisdom]. Regarding the phrase "subsequently attained in accordance with [the fundamental]," this refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Having first realized the two kinds of emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) through fundamental wisdom, one subsequently practices further application within subsequently attained wisdom; only then can one enter this meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Even if one has not yet abandoned the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), because subsequently attained wisdom is absent, one must completely abandon the afflictions of view regarding both the emptiness of persons and phenomena before subsequently attained wisdom exists in relation to them.

It is attained. For the two vehicles, it may be either single or multiple; for Bodhisattvas, it may be either combined or separate, and is not fixed. Therefore, it is said to be "according to what is appropriate.

△ Next, the division of abandonment, cultivation, and arising (2). First, the formal explanation (2). First, according to the Master [Vasubandhu], from the eighth stage downward, one suppresses the seven [categories of afflictions] and abandons those of the desire realm.

There is an interpretation that [the afflictions] to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the lower eight stages—up to those arising when one is born in the upper eight stages—all arise subsequently.

Regarding the meaning of this: this explanation refers specifically to the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the lower eight stages, excluding those of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
One must completely sever the afflictions of the single stage of the desire realm; the others are merely suppressed and eliminated. Only then can this meditative absorption (samādhi) first arise.

Why must the desire realm be completely severed? It is because the seeds of the afflictions of the desire realm—consisting of both the unwholesome and the obscured-unwholesome natures—are manifold and complex, and they strongly obstruct meditative concentration.

Furthermore, the sacred teachings state that only those who have attained the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and so forth can obtain this absorption. Thus, one must sever the nine [categories of] afflictions of the desire realm.
Only when the afflictions of that stage are exhausted can one be designated as having attained the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
As for the statement that "he gives rise to [the meditative attainments] in all eight higher stages as appropriate," this refers to those who have attained the fruit of Non-returner and the like.

"As appropriate" means that whether by "complete skipping" (*atyantātyaya*), "half-skipping" (*ardhapluta*), or "falling back through all stages" (*sarvasthānacyuta*), those who are born in the higher stages are all able to give rise to these [attainments]; therefore, it is said "as appropriate."
It is so. △ Next, regarding the Master’s [view] that on the ninth stage one suppresses five [categories of afflictions] and abandons four:
there is an interpretation that one must abandon the four lower stages; [only after this] can one be born in the five higher stages and give rise to subsequent [attainments].

Commentary on the Phonology and Meaning: This explanation states that among the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), one must first abandon those of the lower four stages and suppress those of the remaining five;

only then can this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) initially arise. Why is this? Because within the lower four stages, the seeds of affliction associated with the sensation of change (*vipariṇāma-vedanā*) constitute a powerful obstruction to concentration. The final phrase follows the preceding logic.
△ Next, resolving the objections (2): First, the objection.

At the time of their falling back and giving rise to the afflictions not yet severed which moisten rebirth, would it not be so?
Is there not the fault of abandoning the afflictions of a lower stage while having been born in a higher one?

Supplement: For example, when one who has attained the state of an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*) is born in a higher realm, they simultaneously and instantaneously sever the innate (*sahaja*) afflictions associated with the manas (*manas*) belonging to the nine lower stages.

△ Next, the Bodhisattvas are explained individually (2). First, regarding the turning of the mind:
if Bodhisattvas were previously in the stage of the two vehicles (up to) all stages, they are able to give rise to this meditative absorption.

Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: If one has already attained this samādhi while previously in the stage of the Two Vehicles and later turns the mind toward the Mahāyāna, since it was already obtained previously and can arise wherever one is, there is no longer any need to discuss the relative high or low status of one's position;
thus, one is able to give rise to this samādhi in both the stage of the Ordinary Person (pṛthagjana) and the stage of the Noble One (ārya).

△ Third, the explanation of sleep and fainting (in three parts). First, the general statement:
Regarding those who are mindless in sleep or fainting, it causes the first six consciousnesses to all cease to manifest.

therefore, these two types also receive the designation "mindless" (*acittaka*).
△ Next, the specific explanation (three parts): first, sleep.
The state of the body induced by conditions such as extreme exhaustion is designated by that name because it resembles it. Regarding the meaning of the term:
first, the formal explanation. This refers to a state of the body induced by conditions such as extremely heavy fatigue;
because the body is suddenly exhausted, the six sense faculties become dull and obtuse, causing the first six consciousnesses to all cease their activity. Therefore, it is called "extremely heavy."
Sleep. This follows the previous discussion on the obstruction of the "sleep" state. An objection is raised: sleep is indeterminate;
as a mental factor (*caitta*), it must be associated with the mind (*citta*). Since this state is without mind, how can there be a mental factor? The explanation states:

Although the substantial entity (*svabhāva*) of that mental factor of sleep does not exist at the time of sleep, it is nevertheless similar to it because it is induced by that mental factor of sleep. Therefore...

△ Next, regarding "fainting" (mūrchana):

therefore, it is called "fainting" (mùn jué).

Alternatively, both of these are portions of the sense-base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).

excluding these five states, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises constantly.

This clarifies that after the six consciousnesses have been severed, [at that subsequent time]—for this reason, it does not say one enters the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

The explanation says: This section elucidates the gate of the states of arising and ceasing; therefore, it reveals what occurs after the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

the noble ones (*ārya*) possess only the latter three, because the cause and fruit of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) belong exclusively to ordinary beings.
As for the sovereign Bodhisattvas—referring to those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward—they possess only one, as they likewise lack extremely heavy sleep and fainting.

Therefore, as a supplement: ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are both termed "ordinary beings" (*visabhāga-jana*), because they have not yet realized the noble Dharma and are unable to enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Noble ones of the three vehicles do not enter the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), nor are they born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-deva*). [This applies up to] the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).

The above [passage] is because they have attained mastery over the Dharma; thus, there is no extreme heavy sleep or fainting, but only the entry into the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Supplement: Introduction for Beginners. Question: Regarding the eight consciousnesses within a single body, do they always evolve simultaneously? Or are there times when they do not evolve simultaneously?

△ Next, the analysis of the meaning of simultaneous occurrence (6). First, the analysis showing that although multiple consciousnesses occur simultaneously, there is only one sentient being (2).
First, the question:
If multiple consciousnesses occur simultaneously in a single sentient being, how can it be said that they constitute one sentient being?

*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance) and *Kaimeng* (Opening the Ignorant) state: When a follower of the Hīnayāna asks, "If multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously within a single body, how can it be said that this constitutes a single sentient being? (Text).
△ Second, the response (in two parts): first, the counter-interrogation.
If one posits that sentient beings depend on the number of their consciousnesses [and so forth], how can one speak of "sentient beings of one's own kind"?

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: If you claim that the number of sentient beings is established based on the presence or absence of consciousness, then you must consider those in a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*):
since they lack consciousness at that time, would they not then cease to be counted as sentient beings?

Furthermore, if the status of a sentient being were established solely by means of consciousness, then at the moment when the sixth consciousness arises in association with the virtue of ethical discipline (*śīla*), one could only then say that one belongs to the human realm.
Sentient beings, even when they give rise to a mind belonging to another realm of existence, should not cease to be of their own human category. Why?
Because you maintain that a single consciousness constitutes a single sentient being; this would logically entail such a consequence.
△ Next, the correct position is revealed.
However, a sentient being is established based on the number of life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*), because those [life-faculties] are always present as only one at a time.
Supplement: That is to say, based on the single number of the life-faculty—which rests upon the eighth seed-consciousness—one sentient being is established.

Alternatively, one sentient being is established based on the single number of the eighth resultant consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) in its active state, and not based on the number of consciousnesses.
Why? Because within a single sentient body, there is always only one [such consciousness].
△ Second, distinguishing and demonstrating that when multiple consciousnesses arise, there are many equal-and-immediate conditions (II). First, the question:
If a single body has only one equal-and-immediate condition, how can multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously?
Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: The objector’s intention is as follows. All minds and mental factors arise in dependence upon four conditions.
While the other three conditions may admit of multiplicity, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is singular within a single body.
Since it is strictly singular, how can it at one time open the way for multiple consciousnesses and cause them to arise simultaneously?
Supplement: Regarding the seventy-five dharmas maintained by the Hīnayāna, mental factors are singular.
Because a preceding extinguished mind induces the arising of a subsequent mind, it is said that within a single continuum there is only one immediately antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
△ Second, the response (in two parts): First, the response concerning the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). (1) First, the response that accords with the intent of the question:
Since you already admit that this single [mental factor] induces multiple mental concomitants (*caitta*), why do you not admit that it can also induce multiple minds (*citta*)?
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: This refers to the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Regarding the phrase "drawing forth many mental factors" (*citta-caittas*):

it means that when a preceding moment of visual consciousness draws forth a subsequent moment of visual consciousness as it takes objects such as form as its conditions, there must necessarily be wholesome or defiled mental factors present;

this is precisely the meaning of one equal-and-immediate condition drawing forth many mental factors. Since it is so for what is drawn forth (the mental factors), it is likewise for what draws them forth (the primary mind). This is [the case].
Therefore, there is no fault in the simultaneous arising of all consciousnesses.
Next, [the opponent’s claim that] there is only one [object] is refuted:
Furthermore, who has definitively stated that this object-condition is only one? For we admit that this object-condition is manifold, even when multiple consciousnesses arise together.

△ Next, the response to the meaning of the transformation of multiple consciousnesses (4). First, it is shown that all consciousnesses arise simultaneously through the power of the conditions for birth;
furthermore, for one who wishes to apprehend multiple objects at once, it would be illogical for consciousnesses to arise sequentially.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: The preceding question asked, "How can multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously? This explanation states:
when many objects appear before one and various conditions converge with equal force, it is not possible for consciousnesses to arise sequentially;
therefore, they may indeed arise together.
△ Second, citing mental factors (*caitta*) as an analogy to clarify that different categories arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, although there is no difference in their nature as mental factors, how could one not allow for the simultaneous arising of different categories of mind?

Regarding the meaning of the terms: although there is no difference in the essential nature of the various mental concomitants (*caitta*) and mental factors (*cittadharma*), those belonging to the six distinct categories—such as the wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth—arise simultaneously within a single continuum without mutual contradiction.
Since this is the case for the mental concomitants, why should one not likewise allow for the simultaneous arising of different types of the primary mind (*cittarāja*)?
△ Third, again using analogies to clarify that multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, just as waves and reflections arise in multiplicity based on a single [source], so too do multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously based on a single mind.
Regarding the meaning of the words: it is like a single torrent of water; when it encounters many conditions such as the wind, many waves arise together, yet they do not interfere with one another.

There is no contradiction. Just as a single clean mirror reflects many external objects with multiple images arising simultaneously without mutual conflict, so too, within a single ālayavijñāna, when it encounters various conditions such as multiple objects, multiple consciousnesses arise.

Commentary on the Meaning: The reason the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) are associated (*samprayukta*) is that they possess five common characteristics: namely, they exist at the same moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).
They appear as one through their conjunction; they arise and perish simultaneously; they share the same supporting faculty (*indriya*); and they have a common object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Now, although these various consciousnesses possess the principle of arising together momentarily, they do not correspond with one another because they do not share the same object. Question:

Is it not the case that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) accompanying the five [sensory consciousnesses] shares the same object? Answer: Even if they were to share the same object, the substance and number of their respective supports (*āśraya*) would differ.

Therefore, they are not mutually associated (*asaṃprayukta*). As for their having different bases (*āśraya*), it is because they do not share the same sense faculty as their common basis, unlike the mind and its mental factors.
As for their having different substances and numbers (*dravya-saṃkhyā*), it is because they do not merge into a single entity through combination like the mind and its mental factors.
For example, although visual consciousness and other such cognitions arise simultaneously with their respective faculties such as the eye, they are not associated; this case is likewise.
△ Section Three: A Summary Presentation of the Two Truths (3). First, the formal presentation.
The intrinsic nature of the eight consciousnesses cannot be said to be fixed, because—down to—the point that they lack a fixed nature, being like illusory phenomena and the like.

Commentary on the Terms: This concludes the demonstration of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). First, it is shown through four meanings that [the mind] is not fixed as a single entity: (1) aspect (*ākāra*), which refers to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*);

(2) basis (*āśraya*), which refers to the sense faculties; (3) object-condition (*ālambana*), which refers to the objective support; and (4) association (*samprayoga*), which refers to the mental factors (*caitta*).
Because these four meanings are each distinct; and because when one consciousness ceases, the other seven and so forth do not necessarily cease;

and because the seventh is the perfumer (*vāsaka*) while the eighth is the perfumed (*vāsyatva*), their characteristics are different; and furthermore, the seventh is the cause while the eighth is the fruit.
Next, it clarifies that they are not definitively distinct: the eighth and the preceding seven are like water and its waves; they are not [separate].
Because they possess distinct characteristics. If they were definitively distinct, they could not be mutually related as cause and effect, just as barley does not produce the sprouts of beans.
One understands this through wisdom that [all things] are like illusions and the like, because they lack a fixed nature. As a sutra says:
For example, like the great waves of the ocean, they possess no distinct characteristics; so it is with the various consciousnesses—no difference can be found between them.

It does not exist. Why? Because there is no separate entity apart from the grasping subject and the grasped object; nor is there a grasping subject that exists apart from its basis.

among the previously mentioned transformations, the transformed *darśana-bhāga* is termed "discrimination.

"Alternatively, 'transformation' refers to the various internal consciousnesses (up to) the establishment of the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), which accords with the Middle Way.

Regarding the distancing from the two extremes of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*): because there are no phenomena external to the mind, the extreme of superimposition is eliminated;

The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, it is taught that objects of perception are manifestations of consciousness-only; that is, all objects of perception."
This realm is solely a transformation of consciousness; there are no external phenomena whatsoever. Therefore, the Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"There is not even the slightest phenomenon that can apprehend another phenomenon, because there is no functional activity. The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra also states:
All phenomena do not depart from the mind. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* further states: "Sentient beings follow the defilement or purity of their minds.
△ Next, the four wisdoms are cited (3): first, the heading.
Furthermore, it is said that a bodhisattva who has attained the four wisdoms is able to realize, in accordance with reality, that there is only consciousness and no external objects.
This is stated in the *Abhidharma-sūtra*. The *Zongjing lu*, fascicle 62, says:

This refers to a small bodhisattva prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). Although they have not yet realized the principle of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), by relying on the Buddha’s teachings and by observing the bodhisattvas of the [ten] stages who have attained the fourfold wisdom of consciousness-only, they subsequently enter into contaminated contemplation (*sāsrava-bhāvanā*).
In this contemplation, they perceive that the great earth transformed by those bodhisattvas of the ten stages becomes gold, and that the long river is stirred into curd and butter. They transform...
Regarding matters such as mountains of meat and seas of rice, when this minor bodhisattva enters into contemplation and has observed them, he immediately says:
"These transformed things, such as actual gold and silver, do not exist apart from the transforming mind of a Bodhisattva of the Tenth Stage; there is no external object.
Having performed this contemplation, he is also able to accordingly awaken to and enter into the principle of True Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātratā*). This is also like the Vaiśeṣika school.
The Master [Vasubandhu] transformed his body into a great stone in order to uphold the meaning of the six propositions; this has practical utility.
If one were to maintain that objects are real entities, then it would not be possible for him to transform his body and its environment into a stone according to his will (text).
△ Next, the explanation of the four [reasons]: first, the cognition of contradictory perceptions.
Regarding the cognition of contradictory perceptions: if the object were real, how could this [contradiction] be established?

*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance). The *Zongjing* says: Regarding the first type, "knowledge of the characteristics of mutually contradictory cognitions," this refers to the four classes of sentient beings, each possessing their own distinct perceiving consciousnesses.
Since these consciousnesses are mutually contradictory, the objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*) they transform are likewise contradictory.
Thus, the devas see it as a pond adorned with jewels; the fish see it as their dwelling place; and humans see it as clear, cool water.

Ghosts perceive this as a river of pus and fierce flames. Because the transforming consciousnesses of these four classes of sentient beings are each mutually distinct, the objects they transform also become mutually distinct.
As for what is called "aspect," it is not the aspect of the parikalpita (imagined nature), but rather the aspect of the nimittabhāga (the objective division).
By the power of the prior karma of these four classes of sentient beings, [they] rely together upon...
In a single location, the various transformed *nimitta-bhāga* (objective parts) differ; therefore, they are said to be "contradictory.

When it says "the wisdom that cognizes the *nimitta* of consciousness," this refers to the wisdom of the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) who are able to perceive as objects the different *nimitta-bhāgas* transformed by the consciousnesses of the four classes of sentient beings through their own karma.
There are no separate four external objects apart from the mind. What was formerly called "one object corresponding to four" [is thus explained].
The mind is not [fixed upon] a single object. Question: Why is it not fixed? Answer: If one says it is a single object, it is not yet determined what that object is.
If there were a separate object existing apart from the manifestations transformed by the four classes of sentient beings, [it would be so]; but there is none.

This means that there are dharmas external to the mind. If one asks whether the four classes of sentient beings each transform their own *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) or whether their *ālambanavastu* (underlying essence) is also distinct, the answer is:
due to the predominant power of karma, the *nimittabhāga* transformed by the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is also distinct for these four classes of sentient beings.
If one regards this *nimittabhāga* of the eighth consciousness in relation to the six consciousnesses of the four classes of sentient beings...

[The opponent] says: "Because [the object] is the very essence [of the cognition], and because the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) and the essence (svabhāva) are distinct, we know that there are no external objects;

there is only consciousness. The Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty said: "The object is not fixed as one; therefore, it is the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by four classes of sentient beings."
In accordance with the transformative minds of the four classes of sentient beings, objects also become fourfold. First, there is the difference in perception regarding a single location.
This proves that there is only consciousness. As the treatise says: "For example, where humans see a place full of filth and excrement, animals see it as pure and excellent food;
and what humans see as pure and excellent food, the gods see as foul-smelling, impure, and unclean. Therefore...

Knowing that the differences in what is seen follow from karma and merit, one realizes that defilement and purity are solely mind; karma itself varies, and food has neither coarseness nor subtlety (text).
△ Second, the wisdom of consciousness that has no objective referent.
2. The Knowledge that Consciousness Has No Object (up to): "Since that object does not exist, the rest should likewise be so.
*Heqiang* (Combined Resonance). The *Zongjing* says: Regarding the second, the knowledge that consciousness has no object—what is meant by "consciousness having no object"?

This refers to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). When they take their own sixth, solitary, and distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as the object-condition for things such as past and future phenomena, water-moons, or mirror-images, it transforms and gives rise to these provisional *nimitta-bhāga* (objective portions).

These *nimitta-bhāgas* are merely the false constructions and pervasive conceptualizations (*parikalpa*) of the sixth consciousness of sentient beings; they arise as transformations according to the mind's state and do not exist at all as real objects external to the mind.
This is called "consciousness without an objective referent. As for the term "the wise," this refers to the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages; it is their cognizing mind. The Bodhisattva says:
"These provisional *nimitta-bhāga* (objective images) transformed by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not exist apart from the transforming minds of all ordinary beings;
they are their very *vijñapti-mātra* (representation-only). By this same analogy, even with respect to all real objects, they likewise do not exist apart [from the perceiving mind].

The cognizing mind of all sentient beings exists such that, apart from the mind itself, there is not a single thing else. The old saying, "That which is non-existent cannot be an object of cognition," is incorrect.
Question: Why is it incorrect? Answer: For instance, when one takes as an object a flower in the sky or other such purely imaginary objects, the mind nevertheless arises.
How, then, can you say that "that which is non-existent cannot be an object of cognition"? Thus, it is known [that the old view is wrong].

When taking a non-substantial, provisional object as a condition, it is not that the internal aspect of the true nature (*dharmatā*) is absent; this [internal aspect] is capable of inducing the arising of the mind.

In relation to the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), it also fulfills the definition of being an *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition). There has never been a state of mind devoid of objects, nor has there ever been a mind devoid of its objective field.

Furthermore, this does not contradict the meaning of the fourfold division of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) established by Dharmapāla. Apart from the internal aspect of the true nature, its...
The objects of the mind that constructs and imaginatively clings to them are simply non-existent. The Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty said:
"One should say that the object is not real, yet mental deliberation arises; this proves that there is only consciousness" (text).
△ Third, the wisdom that should naturally be non-erroneous for oneself.
Regarding "the wisdom that should naturally be non-erroneous for oneself" (up to) "liberation should be attained without effort":
the *Zongjing* says, "The third, the wisdom that should naturally be non-erroneous for oneself, refers to the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages."
Arising wisdom, one observes all sentient beings who falsely cling to themselves as being permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
The Bodhisattva says: "This is merely the inverted view of the clinging mind of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Apart from this falsely clinging mind, within the bodies of these ordinary worldlings, there is truly no state of permanence, bliss, self, or purity. If such a state did exist, it would be distinct [from the mind] and ordinary beings would not need to [cling to it]."
Through cultivation, one attains liberation. Since this is not the case [otherwise], it is clearly known that there is only deluded consciousness (text).
△ Fourth, the wisdom that functions in accordance with the three wisdoms.
Fourth, the cognition that evolves in accordance with the three cognitions (*anuvartaka-jñāna*). [Question: If the object were real, how could it fail to appear?
[Answer: It is like an echo. The *Zongjing* says: "Regarding the fourth, the cognition that evolves in accordance with the three cognitions:

first is the cognition that evolves in accordance with the cognition of the Sovereign (*vaśavartin*), which is the wisdom arising from the Bodhisattva observing that all objects transformed by himself do not depart from the self."
The mind capable of transformation is precisely this *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

For Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, they are able to spontaneously transform the great earth into gold and churn the long rivers into ghee and curd. This is the transformation of the objective realm in accordance with true wisdom, whereby all transformed phenomena are accomplished.
"Transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) carries the meaning of changing and replacing the original substance; that is, it follows and replaces the original nature of the great earth, mountains, and rivers.
Substance: gold, silver, and so forth. Sentient beings truly obtain and enjoy them; they can all be forged and fashioned into various utensils.
If there were external real objects apart from the mind, how could mountains, rivers, and the like transform into gold, silver, and other such things in accordance with the mind of a Bodhisattva?
This is because the objective counterparts (*nimitta-bhāga*) and their underlying substances (*vastu*) are entirely transformed. Therefore, one knows that all [phenomena]...
All objects do not exist apart from the Bodhisattva’s mind capable of transformation.

Even ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) can transform fire into water, turn day into night, and transmute iron into gold; all such instances are cases where objects follow the shifting of the wisdom of the situation.
All transformed objects are established as being merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).

If it were the case that the palaces, gold, silver, and so forth transformed by Kātyāyana were not established, then one would know that there are no real external objects apart from the mind. The treatise states:

"Generally, those who transform gold, silver, palaces, and so forth, are manifesting the color of the actual fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*); this can only be accomplished from the first bhūmi onward. If...
Regarding the Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above who possess mastery: they attain mastery over both signs and lands.
Because their superior meditative minds possess great power, the transformed palaces of gold and silver and so forth are all successfully accomplished.
Just as when gold and silver are smelted and forged into various utensils, they can actually be used; the gold and silver thus transformed is [real].
The truly established resultant forms are all inseparable from the bodhisattva’s internal mind; they are his *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). There is no object external to the mind.

When the śrāvakas and the lesser bodhisattvas prior to the [first] bhūmi transform gold, silver, palaces, or halls, they rely upon the gold, silver, palaces, and halls transformed by the bodhisattva as their objective basis (*bimba*). It is the sixth consciousness that transforms [these appearances].
Silver and the like are all unestablished and lack any real function. However, the gold and silver that are transformed are merely the color-form (rūpa) of a provisional fruit;
they do not exist apart from the internal minds of śrāvakas and lesser bodhisattvas, and are thus consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra). There is no object external to the mind.
Now, because Kātyāyana was a śrāvaka who had not yet attained the superior grades of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the gold and silver he transformed lacked actual functional efficacy;
nevertheless, they did not exist apart from internal consciousness. Thus, there are no objects external to the mind. Furthermore, the ancient masters said:
"Because form arises from the sovereign power of the mind, the mind can transform form. Therefore, one may move mountains, cover the seas, overturn the earth, and turn over the heavens.
To churn the great river into butter and curd, or to transform the great earth into gold—none of these would be difficult tasks.
Second, regarding those whose wisdom turns according to the wisdom of the observer:

the Bodhisattva Wuxing (No-Nature) stated that when Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas cultivate contemplations such as suffering and emptiness and attain correspondence with them, or when they perform the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, their observation follows accordingly.
Upon a single phenomenon (*dharma*), there are only such characteristics as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, which are clearly manifest.

It is not that these numerous meanings of suffering, emptiness, and so forth exist within the substance (*svabhāva*) of the phenomena; rather, they are merely the various characteristics of suffering, emptiness, and the like.

This is the very essence of all phenomena (*dharmas*). Since they possess the characteristic of impermanence, and because they exist upon the mind as perceived by the contemplation of the sages, one knows that all phenomena do not exist apart from the mind of contemplation.
Third, regarding the wisdom that accords with the revolution of non-conceptual wisdom:
this refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the Bodhisattva. When realizing *tathatā* (suchness), the object of suchness and the wisdom merge into one.
[They] merge; subject and object are of one essence, with no further differentiation. Apart from fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*), there is no separate object.
Thus, the object itself turns in accordance with true wisdom. For this reason, it is said that "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) exists.

If you followers of the Hīnayāna cling to the notion that there are real objects external to the mind, then at the moment of realizing *tathatā*, why would all objective appearances not manifest before you? (Text)
△ Third, the summary:
Bodhisattvas who have accomplished the four knowledges definitively awaken to and enter the principle of *vijñapti-mātra*.
△ Third, the citation of one verse.
Furthermore, a verse from the *Gāthā* states: "Because the objects of mind, intellect, and consciousness [are not separate from them], I say that all is merely consciousness and nothing else.
Commentary on the Meaning: The objects of all consciousnesses do not exist apart from consciousness itself. Therefore, the Buddha taught that "all is but mind."
△ Next, the summary:
These scriptural authorities providing authentic proof are not limited to one.

△ Next, the revelation of the principle (in two parts). First, the actual revelation (in two parts). First, revealing the direct image-part (*nimittabhāga*) by way of the perceiving subject (*ālambaka*). (First part:)
The first five [consciousnesses].

Because each is one of the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, which are universally established, they do not directly perceive objects separate from their own forms and so on, just like the others.

Regarding the meaning of the term "sound" (*śabda*): the *Zongjing* says, "First, it is established that the *parabhāga* (objective images) of the five sensory objects are all not separate from the five consciousnesses."

Now, it is established that the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of a single consciousness does not exist apart from that consciousness itself; the remaining four consciousnesses are to be treated accordingly. The formal inference (*prayoga*) is as follows:

"The subject (*dharmin*), which is the universally established visual consciousness, definitely does not directly perceive objects (*rūpa*) that are separate from its own consciousness—this is the thesis (*pakṣa*).

The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is included within one of the universally established five sense-consciousnesses, just like the other universally established four consciousnesses. To explain this further:
The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is divided into two parts: first, explaining the name and eliminating errors; second, briefly presenting questions and answers.

Regarding the first, concerning the thesis (*pakṣa*), what was previously stated as "universally established" (*prasiddha*) serves to exclude eye-consciousness that is not universally established by both schools. For instance, within the Mahāyāna school...
It is accepted that there is the Buddha’s eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) belonging to other realms, as well as the Buddha’s untainted (*anāsrava*) eye-consciousness;

however, since these are not accepted by the Hīnayāna, they are likewise excluded and not taken up. If, within the Hīnayāna school, one maintains that the Buddha possesses tainted eye-consciousness or that the Bodhisattva in his final body possesses defiled eye-consciousness, this is not accepted by the Mahāyāna and must also be excluded. Thus, it is between these two schools...

That which is not mutually accepted is not a "thoroughly established" (*prasiddha*) phenomenon. Now, we only take that eye-consciousness which is thoroughly established and mutually accepted by both schools as the subject of the thesis;
therefore, the preceding statement specifies "thoroughly established eye-consciousness. Question: If one does not specify the two schools' mutual consensus, what fault would there be? Answer:
The preceding statement would then possess a portion of the object of qualification (*viśeṣya*) that is not accepted by either oneself or the other.

There is no fault of non-establishment (*asiddha*). Within the reason (*hetu*), there is likewise the fault of partial non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for both oneself and others, because the subject (*pakṣa*)—the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*)—is not established [for the opponent].
Therefore, the two characters "established" (*prasiddha*) are placed [in the definition] to exclude such cases.

Regarding the thesis (*sādhya*) that it "definitely does not directly perceive" [objects], the phrase "apart from its own consciousness" refers only to being apart from the *nimittabhāga* (objective image part) of the visual consciousness.
Externally, all essential forms (*dravya-rūpa*) and the other four objects (*viṣaya*), provided they are dissociated from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), are not directly perceived.
If opponents and proponents debate, they debate only regarding these essential forms. This is how the Mahāyāna’s own school establishes visual consciousness.

[The text] refers to the form that is the immediate objective aspect (*sākṣāt-svabhāga-rūpa*). Question: Why does [the author] not state that it is necessarily the immediate condition (*sākṣāt-pratyaya*)—namely, the form that is not separate from its own consciousness? Answer:

For fear of committing the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the qualifier (*asiddha-viśeṣaṇa*). That is to say, the Hīnayāna schools do not admit that form is not separate from visual consciousness.

Next, regarding the reason (*hetu*) which states, "because it is included within any one of the five universally established (*prasiddha*) consciousnesses," the term "universally established" is used for the reason.
This also excludes the non-universally established (*aprasiddha*) five consciousnesses.

If the term "universally established" were not used for exclusion, and one were to merely state that [the subject] is included within any one of the five consciousnesses, this reason would incur the fault of being unestablished for either one or both parties (*anyatarāśrayāsiddhi*).

Therefore, the word "universally established" is added to the reason to exclude them. The example states, "like the other universally established four consciousnesses," where the word "universally established" is likewise used in the example.

This also excludes those dharmas that are not universally established (*aprasiddha*). If one does not establish what is universally accepted, one commits the fault of the "unestablishedness" (*aprasiddhatva*) of either the probans (*sādhana*) or the probandum (*sādhya*) in part.
Therefore, the term "universally established" is included for the sake of exclusion.

Since it has been established that the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of form is not separate from visual consciousness, the same principle applies to the remaining [objects]—sound, odor, taste, and tangibles—all of which are established as not being separate from their respective other four [consciousnesses].
Because it is consciousness. Next, the question and answer are presented. First, the basis of the thesis must be mutually accepted by both parties.

Now, regarding the proponent’s statement that [consciousness] does not directly perceive form apart from its own consciousness, while the opponent accepts that it directly perceives form apart from its own substantial essence—how can this be said to be "universally established" (*prasiddha*)?
Answer: Even the Hīnayāna schools accept that visual consciousness does not directly perceive the other four sense-objects, because they are distinct from the eye.
Because it is consciousness. It merely requires that the opposing school admit the existence of form (*rūpa*) that is not directly perceived and is distinct from its own consciousness;

this is simply the basis of the thesis (*pakṣāśraya*) as established by common consensus. Second, [the opponent asks]: "Since the opposing school already admits that the other four objects (*viṣaya*) are not directly perceived by visual consciousness, if these are later combined into a single thesis, they would be mutually supportive.
How could this constitute a point of contention? [The respondent] answers: "What is currently being contested concerns only the object of form (*rūpaviṣaya*)."

The essential nature [of the object]. The eye does not directly perceive it; they are mutually distinct. What is favorable to oneself is contrary to others, thus correctly establishing the body of the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Although the Hīnayāna school admits that the essential nature of form is separate from visual consciousness and yet constitutes a direct condition (*ālambana*), you now state that it is not a direct condition.

Is this not a point of contention regarding the thesis? Third question: Regarding the point of contention within the thesis, is it that visual consciousness does not directly perceive the essential nature?
"Form (rūpa). It is analogous to the other four consciousnesses. [Objection: "The other four consciousnesses do not directly perceive their respective objects; how can there be similarity? [Response:
"The other four consciousnesses serve as the basis for the analogy (dṛṣṭāntāśraya). Each has that which does not directly perceive phenomena apart from its own consciousness;

this is the body of the analogy (dṛṣṭāntasvabhāva). Now, we take the body of the analogy, not the basis of the analogy. It is also like the thesis that sound is impermanent, where the analogous example is like..."

Regarding the jar: one should not differentiate between the sound and the jar as being distinct entities. Rather, one takes the fact that both the sound and the jar possess the property of impermanence as the basis for their similarity, and so forth (as stated in the text).
△ Next, the latter three [consciousnesses].
Because they are cognized by other consciousnesses, like visual consciousness and so forth, they also do not directly perceive phenomena other than themselves.
[This is] the "Concordant Resonance" (Hesyang). The *Zongjing* says: "The second establishes the sixth by means of reasoning, while also implicitly establishing the seventh."

Regarding the eighth [point], the second consciousness: the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states: "The remaining consciousnesses, which are universally established (*prasiddha*), are the subject (*dharmin*).

They do not directly perceive objects that are separate from their own consciousness; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: 'because they possess the nature of consciousness. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is: 'like the five universally established consciousnesses. The commentary explains:

the term "universally established" is placed at the beginning of the thesis (*pakṣa-pūrvacana*) to exclude what is not universally established. If one did not say "universally established," one would commit the fault of contradicting oneself or others.

There is the fault that the subject (*dharmin*) is not established for one party. If one says that the six, seven, or eight consciousnesses constitute the subject, the opponent does not accept the seventh and eighth consciousnesses;
thus, one commits the fault of the subject being unestablished for one party.

If, however, one establishes only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as the subject, then within the reason (*hetu*), one commits the fault of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), as it could be countered by the opponent using the seventh and eighth consciousnesses [as counter-examples].

The dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) commits the fallacy of being "uncertain" (*anaikāntika*) within the common [category], specifically the "self-uncertainty" (*svato 'naikāntika*). (That is to say: the six, seven, and eight consciousnesses all share the nature of consciousness; thus, the reason—"the nature of consciousness"—is too broad.

It applies to the dissimilar examples of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, and is therefore uncertain. The Hīnayāna raises this objection: "Is it like the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness? Because they are of the nature of consciousness, does this prove that your sixth consciousness does not directly perceive objects separate from itself? Or is it like the seventh and eighth consciousnesses?

Because they are of the nature of consciousness, does this prove that your sixth consciousness is one that directly perceives objects separate from itself? [The Mahāyāna responds: Since the Hīnayāna accepts that substantial form (*dravya-rūpa*) is separate from the visual consciousness and yet is directly perceived by it, [your argument fails]. Furthermore, if the Mahāyāna [position] were not to establish [this direct perception]...

[The opponent] posits the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses]. That is, from the perspective of those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) who rely on their own calculations, they claim that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses directly perceive form (*rūpa*) that is distinct from their own essential nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, they employ the seventh and eighth consciousnesses as counter-examples (*vipakṣa*).

Now, [the author] simply uses the general term "the rest" (*śeṣa*), yet specifically selects the sixth [consciousness], while the intention includes both the seventh and eighth. Thus, it is implicitly established that the seventh and eighth are included within "the rest" of the consciousnesses.
The subsequent statement, "nor do they directly perceive phenomena (*dharma*) distinct from their own consciousness," uses the word "also" (*api*) to indicate similarity [to the preceding case].

It is the same as before. [The opponent’s] proof that the five consciousnesses do not directly perceive phenomena external to their own consciousness—citing the reason "because they are of the nature of consciousness"—is identical to [the reason] "because the five consciousnesses are of the nature of consciousness.

As for the example "just like the established five consciousnesses," this is identical to [the fact that] the five consciousnesses likewise do not directly perceive what is external to their own [consciousness].
Thus, it is clearly understood that [the five consciousnesses] directly perceive what is not external to themselves.

Once the doctrine of consciousness has been established, it is therefore known that all objects which serve as the directly perceived conditions (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*) do not exist apart from the mind;
this is the meaning of "Cognition-Only" (*vijñapti-mātra*). (Text)
△ Next, it is explained that the object of cognition does not exist apart from the essence of mind (3). First, regarding the direct object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
The objects of this consciousness are certainly not separate from either of these two [aspects], because they are like their respective subjects (*grāhaka*).

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: The *Zongjing* states that the third [point] establishes this through reasoning. The objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*) directly perceived by the first six consciousnesses all revert to the substance of the mind (*citta-tattva*).

What is called the "substance of the mind" is precisely the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*). Although the seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) also functions in dependence upon the self-verifying portion, we establish only the objective image here because the seeing portion is universally accepted [as existing].

The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: *(The objective image of the sixth consciousness is not separate from the substance of the mind, because it is the object of direct perception by that consciousness, just like the self-verifying portion.)*

It is said: "The immediate objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the six consciousnesses is a functional entity (*dharmin*). It is necessarily not separate from the substance of the six consciousnesses; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is:

because it is subsumed under either of the two parts, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) or the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), just like the aforementioned seeing-part which acts as the subjective cognizer (*grāhaka*).
This is taken as the concordant example (*sapakṣa-dṛṣṭānta*), for the Hīnayāna schools admit that the seeing-part is not separate from the substance of the mind. (Text)
△ Next is the remote object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Because it is an object-condition (*ālambana-dharma*), like associated mental states (*samprayukta-dharma*), it is definitively not separate from the mind and mental factors.
Regarding the meaning of the term: *Zongjing* says, "The fourth principle establishes that all objects of the remote object-condition exist."
All [objects] are not separate from the mind; this is their nature as *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). Specifically, they are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness.

In relation to the first six consciousnesses, they are called the "distant objective condition" (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*), because the Hīnayāna schools do not admit the existence of an eighth consciousness; thus, it is simply termed the "distant objective condition. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
All objects perceived by their respective cognitions are the subject of the proposition (*dharmin*); they are necessarily not separate from my own subjective cognition (*ālambaka*).

Commentary on the Phonology and Meaning: According to the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*, "false discrimination exists" means that there is the discrimination of the grasped object (*grāhya*) and the grasping subject (*grāhaka*).
"In this, both are entirely non-existent" means that within this very false discrimination, the two natures of the grasped and the grasper are forever absent.
"In this, only emptiness exists" means that within false discrimination...

"Merely the emptiness of the apprehended and the apprehender": this means that even within that [emptiness], there is still this [element], namely, this very false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*) within those two types of emptiness.
"All phenomena" refers to both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
False conceptualization is called "conditioned," while the emptiness of the two types of grasping is called "unconditioned."
This is because of the aforementioned principle. It is said that all these phenomena are neither empty nor non-empty:

they are said to be "not empty" because of the existence of the emptiness-nature (*śūnyatā*) of false conceptualization; they are said to be "not non-empty" because of the absence of the nature of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).
"Because of existence" means because of the existence of the emptiness-nature of false conceptualization; "because of non-existence" means because of the non-existence of the [grasped and grasper].

"Because of the two natures of the grasped and the grasper," and "because they exist," means that within unreal conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*) there is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and within emptiness there is unreal conceptualization. This is what accords with the Middle Way:
namely, that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are neither exclusively empty nor exclusively non-empty. Such a principle perfectly accords with the Middle.
This Way also perfectly accords with the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras, which state that all phenomena are neither empty nor existent.
Supplementary Note: The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states: "That which exists as false discrimination" refers to the mind of false discrimination within the three realms.
"That which is utterly non-existent in these two" refers to the absence of the dual attachments to self and phenomena, namely the grasping subject and the grasped object.
These characteristics do not exist at all within the mind of *tathatā*.
That which exists here solely as emptiness means that within this deluded mind, there is only this delusion; this is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because it is manifested based upon emptiness.
"In that, too, this exists" means that within that emptiness, this also exists—namely, this deluded conceptualizing consciousness.
False conceptualization is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Within this conventional truth, there is also the emptiness that is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Therefore, when it says "all phenomena," it refers to the two categories of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena; these constitute all phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "neither empty nor non-empty": "not empty" refers to false conceptualization and its emptiness.
That which is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) exists; therefore, it is called "not empty. Because both truths exist, it is not "not non-empty.

This means that the characteristics of the dual grasping at self and phenomena—the grasper and the grasped—are empty; this refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Regarding the phrase "because of existence, non-existence, and existence":
"existence" refers to the existence of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*); "non-existence" refers to the absence of the two graspings of self and phenomena.

Therefore, regarding "because of existence and because of non-existence": this means that within false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), there is true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and within true emptiness, there is also false conceptualization.
This is what accords with the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*): it is not exclusively empty, as [the view of] Bhāviveka and others;
nor is it exclusively existent, as [the view of] the Hīnayāna and others. Thus it is called the Middle Way, meaning that the two truths exist.
This is the same as Bhāviveka [in asserting that] the grasping at self and phenomena does not exist; it differs from the Hīnayāna, and is therefore called the Middle Way.
