△ Fifth, the four parts of the same substance (*ekasvabhāva*) function as conditions for one another in turn.

The aspect of being of the same substance (tongti) is divided into seeing and its object-conditions (yuan), because it is taught that only those that actually arise serve as mutual conditions for one another.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: although all minds and mental factors (citta-caitta) possess four aspects, they are called "of the same substance" because they are transformations of a single consciousness.

Among the four parts, the *nimittabhāga* (objective part) serves as two conditions for the *darśanabhāga* (perceiving part), namely, the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

For the *darśanabhāga*, the *nimittabhāga* serves only as the dominant condition, because logically the *nimittabhāga* lacks the functional capacity to act as a cognizer. The *darśanabhāga* may serve as two conditions for the *svasaṃvedana* (self-cognition).

For the *darśanabhāga*, the *svasaṃvedana* serves only as the dominant condition; this is because the *darśanabhāga*—which can be either non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*) or not—is not internally directed toward itself.
The other two [aspects] function as the two conditions for one another, because they mutually serve as the objects of self-cognition and its cognition.
Herein, it is only the manifesting aspect (nimitta-bhāga) that is said to act as a mutual condition; it is not spoken of as a seed-aspect (bīja-nimitta).
△ Next, as an illustration, it is shown that pure [cognition] arises through mutual transformation.

Within the assembly of the eight pure consciousnesses, because there is no principle for the appearance-aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of self and other to function as objects of cognition (*ālambana*), they lack the capacity to act as subjects of cognition (*grāhaka*).
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: This refers to the manifest discrimination of the purified eight consciousnesses.

Whether regarding oneself or others, preceding or succeeding moments of the same category, or distinct or identical entities, when viewed in relation to one another, they all possess an object of cognition (*ālambana*). This is because, within the state of Buddhahood, all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are capable of universally cognizing all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).
The only exception is the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), which lacks the capacity for cognition. [The term] "uninterrupted" (*anantara*)...
The predominance [condition] may be understood by analogy with the preceding discussion on volition.
△ Next, the production of seeds from present manifestations and seeds (2): First, the question.
Since present conceptualization arises from conditions consisting of seeds and manifestations, [how many conditions do] present manifestations and seeds act as toward seeds?

Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: The first phrase provides the analogy; the second phrase provides the subject of the analogy; the final phrase properly asks how many conditions [are involved].
Supplementary Note: Since manifesting discrimination arises from seeds through four conditions, it stands to reason that seeds should likewise arise from manifesting seeds as their condition.
How many conditions can manifest seeds and seeds act as toward one another?
△ Next, the response:
The seeds do not necessarily arise from the two intermediate conditions (up to: even for non-intimate seeds, they function merely as dominant conditions).

[Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms]: First, it is clarified that seeds are not the two intermediate conditions; rather, they must necessarily bring about the manifestation of the mind and mental factors.

Because two kinds of conditions are established therein, it next clarifies that seeds possess only the first and last two conditions. First, one should consider the relationship from the present [dharma] to the seed;
second, one should consider the relationship from seed to seed. Both may be reflected upon accordingly.
Supplement: "Direct seeds" refers to those that are causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*); "indirect seeds" refers to those that are dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
△ Next, the conclusion, the critique, and the reference to the extensive [treatise] (2): first, the conclusion and critique.

Based on this, internal consciousnesses arise through mutual conditioning (*anyonya-pratyaya*). (Up to: How much more so when it contradicts both reason and scripture—why persist in such dogmatic attachment?

*Yinyi* (Explanatory Notes): The preceding question asked: "If there are only internal consciousnesses and no external conditions at all, from what do the various types of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) arise?
This concluding refutation states: "Internal consciousness serves as the condition for the arising of discrimination," which is precisely what is meant by the verse.
All-seed consciousness, through its reciprocal power, gives rise to various forms of discrimination.
Next, to indicate the detailed exposition:
although the term "discrimination" generally manifests the three realms, [the details] are fully and extensively analyzed as in other treatises.
Regarding the definitions of the terms: some speak of two, namely the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*) and the manifesting consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*).

Some speak of three, namely the karma-consciousness, the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), and the manifesting consciousness. Some speak of four, adding the wisdom-consciousness (*jñāna-vijñāna*). Some speak of five, adding the continuity-consciousness (*prabandha-vijñāna*).
Or it may be explained in detail, as fully set forth in treatises such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and in the fifty-sixth fascicle of the *Zhengjijing* (Mirror of the Ultimate Doctrine).
△ Third, the explanation of the difficulty regarding birth and death (in three parts): First, the opponent presents the objection.
Although internal consciousness exists while external conditions do not, by what means does the continuity of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) of sentient beings proceed?
Next, the root verse provides the answer:
"By the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of various karmas, once the previous maturation (*vipāka*) has been exhausted, another maturation arises again."
△ Commentary on the *Triṃśikā* (2): First, the direct explanation (4); first, the first master’s [view] on the continuity of the appropriation of karma (3);
first, the direct explanation of the verse (2); first, the explanation of the first two lines (2); first, the explanation of the latencies (*vāsanā*) (2); first, the latencies of various karmas.

The Treatise says: "All karma" refers to merit (*puṇya*), non-merit (*apuṇya*), and immovability (*āniñjya*). [This] reveals that these are the superior dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for their respective results.

[Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: First, the various types of karma are explained. Karma of merit refers to that which brings about the maturation (*vipāka*) of the happy realms, as well as wholesome karma conducive to experience within the five destinies.
Karma of non-merit refers to that which brings about the maturation of the miserable realms, as well as [unwholesome karma] conducive to experience within the five destinies.

Unwholesome karma and immovable karma refer to that which brings about maturation in the form and formless realms, as well as the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) conducive to the form and formless realms.
These receive the name "immovable" in contrast to the distracted states of the desire realm. These are the three types of karma.

All of these have volition (*cetanā*) as their essential nature. The other mental factors (*caitta*), such as contact (*sparśa*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and feeling (*vedanā*), are the retinue of that karma;

because they collectively induce the same maturation (*vipāka*), they are all termed "karma. As for the actual fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), it is the retribution for the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*); those [factors] produced by maturation (*vipākaja*) are [the result].

It recompenses only the *pūrṇa-karman* (fulfilling karma). Although this [karma] is inferior, we shall next explain *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies). Suppose it is asked: "Karma arises and immediately perishes;

how can it induce a fruit? The explanation is as follows: Although karma perishes immediately and thus lacks the capacity to directly summon a fruit, it nevertheless perfumes the *mūla-vijñāna* (root consciousness), giving rise to its own specific functional capacity, which is termed *vāsanā*.
What is meant by *vāsanā*? It is a portion of the karma's energy, so called because it is formed through perfuming.

To distinguish it from past and present karma: because it is produced through habituation (*vāsanā*), it is not past karma; because it is a residual force (*bhāga*) of that karma, it is not present karma.
Thus, the term "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*) is established to distinguish it from these two types of karma—past and present. The following passage clarifies this habitual tendency of karma.
This is the predominant and superior condition for the realization of future results (*vipāka-phala*), rather than being a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Regarding the "three types of action, such as merit" (*puṇya-ādi-karman*): the *Kaīmōng* (Opening the Ignorant) asks about meritorious action (*puṇya-karman*) and answers that its essence is impure wholesome volition (*sāsrava-kuśala-cetanā*).
The commentary explains: "Merit" (*puṇya*) has the meaning of excellence; both its intrinsic nature and its fruit are objects of delight. Its characteristic is...

Because it is sublime, it is called meritorious action (*puṇyakarman*). Question: What is non-meritorious action? Answer: It is called non-meritorious action because both its intrinsic nature and its fruit are undesirable and its characteristics are base and inferior.
Question: What is immovable action (*āniñjyakarman*)? Answer: It is so called in the sense that it cannot be altered or shifted.
Because that action, whether great or small, abides in one-pointedness of mind and does not waver, it is called immovable action. This refers to the aforementioned...

The karma of the stages of the two dhyānas. Question: What is the meaning of the term "immovable" (*āniñjya*)? Answer: Because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can cause the mind to abide in a single object. Question:
Since these belong to the two upper realms, they should be "meritorious karma" (*puṇyakarman*); why are they called "immovable"? Answer:

The name "immovable" is established based on their superiority relative to the preceding [realm] (text). Regarding "volitional karma" (*cetanākarma*) and so forth, the *Qingliang Chao*, Volume 17, Part 1, states: "Volition..."
There are two meanings. First, regarding its essence (*tattva*): it assists the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) so that they together function as instruments of karma.

Second, regarding its function (*vṛtti*): it is associated with the king so that they together perform karma (text). The *Zhengjing* (Mirror of the Source), fascicle 73, states: "Although this [mental consciousness] arises for but a moment..."
It ceases immediately without interval. There is no object capable of producing a future maturation fruit that exists in the present;

yet, while it lacks present function, it possesses a past substance capable of producing a true future maturation fruit. At the very moment when the karma currently being enacted was performed, [it already existed as a past entity].
It perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), giving rise to the functional capacity for one's own karma. This capacity is precisely the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*).
These habitual tendencies continue in a successive series until they reach maturity, at which point they bring about the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*). (Text)
△ Next, the two [grasping consciousnesses] take up the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

These consist of the seeds of the causes and conditions associated with the characteristics (*nimitta*) and the perceiving subject (*darśana*), as well as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), mind (*citta*), and mental factors (*caitasika*), together with their corresponding [associates].
(From) *Zongjing* Scroll 73. The commentary states: "The characteristics, the perceiving subject, name-and-form, mind, and mental factors..."

Regarding the statement that "whatever is fundamental or derivative is all subsumed under the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*)," there are two: first, the grasping of characteristics (*nimitta*), which refers to grasping those very things as a real grasper (*grāhaka*) and a real grasped (*grāhya*);

this is called the two types of grasping. Second, the grasping of name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*): "form" (*rūpa*) refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and "name" (*nāma*) refers to the four [mental] aggregates;
thus, it means the grasping of the five aggregates. As for what was previously mentioned regarding characteristics, that also includes the grasping of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).

Because it is taken as the essential nature. Now, this [passage] merely reveals the grasping of the immediate object-condition (*sākṣātālambana*), because [the mind] cannot cognize phenomena external to itself.
Furthermore, the image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) that transforms from non-existence is also termed "included," because it is not separate from the mind and so forth.
Third, it grasps the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*); this is because all phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are not separate from these two.
Fourth, it refers to the primary and the derivative: that is, the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*) is grasped as the "primary" because it is the root of all maturation (*vipāka*).

Furthermore, the category of collective grasping is called the "primary," while the other consciousnesses and so forth, which constitute the category of individual retributive maturation, are called the "derivative. Thus, it grasps a single instance of maturation.
"Furthermore, 'those graspings' refers to the four graspings mentioned above. All these graspings are subsumed within the two graspings;

that is, they are graspings in their active manifestation (*samudācāra*). Qingliang says: 'The four kinds of the two graspings can all permeate and stimulate [the consciousness], directly producing functional capacities upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*);
these are called the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the two graspings. This refers to these very habit-energies."

The "predisposition" (*vāsanā*) refers to the seeds of the mind that will arise as the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) in a future life, as well as the seeds of the various causes and conditions associated with it.
Next, the meaning of "simultaneous" (*saha*) is explained.

"Simultaneous" means that the seeds of karma and the seeds of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) exist together; however, because karma gives rise to birth and manifestation, the verse mentions it first.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: This means that the seeds of karma are the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and thus they are called "remote assistance.

The seeds of the two graspings (*dvaya-grāha*) are the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), and therefore they receive the designation of being "proximate. Although the seeds of karma are remote, their role in summoning retribution is actually manifest; for this reason, the verse mentions them first.
△ Next, the final two phrases are explained.
Regarding "the maturation of previous [lives]": this refers to the karmic maturations of various prior births (up to) being able to separately produce further maturational fruits.
[Combined resonance: First, the two characters "previous" (*qian*) and "remainder" (*yu*) are explained. "The karmic maturational fruits of various prior births" means that if...
This is the fruit of karma induced by a single lifetime in the distant past, which is termed "the previous life" (*pūrvajanman*).

If it is induced by the karma of two lifetimes, or even up to hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, this is "the previous-of-the-previous. Because it possesses these two meanings, it is called "the maturation fruit of the karma of the previous-of-the-previous life" (*pūrvapūrvajanmakarmavipākaphala*).
The subsequent [lives] are the reverse of this. Although the two [terms] are taken together, this concludes the explanation of the meaning of the verse.

The *Zhongjing* (Mirror of the School) says: "Although the seeds of the two-grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) result in inexhaustible fruition, the karmic latencies (*karma-vāsanā*) have an end to their fruition.

This is because it is difficult to summon a fruition that differs in nature from its cause, whereas it is easy to evoke one whose nature is concordant—namely, the fruition of equal outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the sovereign fruition (*adhipati-phala*).
Thus, while the seeds of the two-graspings result in inexhaustible fruition, the *Saṃgrahaṇī* states that the karmic latencies have an end. Why is this? Because..."
Regarding the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*): first, its nature is distinct, as it differs from the nature of the karma and does not correspond with it extensively. Second, it is difficult to summon;

although karma may bring it forth, the fruit only ripens when necessarily separated by another lifetime. Furthermore, the karmic latencies (*vāsanā*) are subject to exhaustion, just as the scent of musk or the odor of foul grass wither and cease.
As for the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*): first, their nature is identical [to the cause].
Their essential natures are mutually compatible. Second, they are easily induced because they arise simultaneously. Once this mindfulness has been perfumed, it is able to produce its fruit;

therefore, the seeds of the two types of grasping are easily induced to produce their results. Which of these are outflowing results (*niṣyanda-phala*), and which are dominant results (*adhipati-phala*)?
The predominant [cause] is broad; however, the outflowing [cause] must necessarily be predominant. Regarding "outflowing":

this refers to the fact that seeds, as well as manifest activities and their own seeds, serve as simultaneous and homogeneous causes (*sahabhū-sabhāga-hetu*) for one another. In the case of the predominant [cause], there is no separate essence, because it is of the same nature as the outflowing [cause].
Furthermore, since it is an outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), its nature is identical; and since it is a predominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), it is easily induced. Moreover, regarding the seed...

In relation to its manifest activity (*samudācāra*), it is a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*); in relation to its own homogeneous seeds (*sabhāgavīja*), it is a flow-on result (*niṣyandaphala*).

This is because the seeds of karma, when compared to those [results]—both manifest and seeds—are of a different nature; thus they are merely results of maturation (*vipākaphala*). By the phrase "because it induces the lower," the meaning of "re-arising" in the verse is explained.
The *Zongjing* commentary explains: When the previous karmic maturation (*vipāka*) is exhausted through experience, it is further able to produce other resultant maturations.
This is because the seeds—namely, the karma that brings about future lives—have ripened.

Thus, when the previous karmic maturation within the present body is exhausted through experience, this is precisely the stage of the final moment of this life. At that point, there remains karma whose maturation is yet to come. Furthermore...
A separate capacity arises to produce other subsequent fruits;
that is, when previous karma is exhausted and the seeds for future fruits ripen, the maturation fruit (vipākaphala) is further produced. This is why birth and death are never severed. (Text)
△ Second, the conclusion showing that [the cycle] is not external:
Because of this, the wheel of birth and death revolves without end; why rely on external conditions for its continuity?
*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Echoes) states: "Because of this, karma and its fruits are uninterrupted, and birth and death continue in an endless cycle."
How could it be that one must rely upon conditions external to the mind for birth and death to continue? This consciousness of continuity has no time of interruption.

If one has not yet encountered the path and achieved contemplation, nor clearly realized one’s own mind, then in all cases one will give rise to doubt when facing objects and cling to the existence of external phenomena.
All instances of birth and death are entirely due to this state of doubt; simply by realizing that there is only mind, naturally there will be no fault.
(Text). △ Third, a general statement of the intent of the verse.
The meaning of this verse states that by virtue of karma and the two graspings... [up to] ...because the mind and mental factors constitute their nature.
Commentary on Terms: Karma has volition as its essence. The two types of grasping are the mind and mental factors. Because of the latencies of these two, there is saṃsāra;
therefore, it is said that birth and death do not exist apart from consciousness.
△ II. The Continuity of the Latent Dispositions (*vāsanā*) of the Two Masters (III). First, the general statement:
Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from various latent dispositions; moreover, these latent dispositions are generally of three kinds.
*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance), *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source), Fascicle 76. Question: The continuity of birth and death arises from various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

How many types of habitual tendencies are there that can bring about the cycle of transmigration? Answer: Regarding the essential nature of habitual tendencies, ancient exegesis establishes three general meanings.
Regarding "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*): they differ in name but are identical in substance to "seeds" (*bīja*).

"Habitual tendency" is discussed in terms of the time of perfuming (*vāsanā*), whereas "seed" is a designation established in contrast to active manifestation (*pravṛtti*). There are three meanings in total: first, the seed is called a "habitual tendency.

"Tendency" (*vāsa*) refers to a portion of energy; "habitual" (*vāsanā*) refers to perfuming. Because one acquires this portion of energy through the perfuming by that active manifestation, it is so named. Second...
Manifest activity is also called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*). This means that all manifest activities are produced by seeds;

they are the residual influence (*vāsanā*) belonging to the category of seeds. The term "three habitual tendencies" refers to "habitual tendencies" themselves, like scented paper which possesses a residual fragrance (text).
△ Second, the detailed explanation (in two parts). First, the habitual tendencies of names and speech (*nāma-vikalpa-vāsanā*).
Regarding "habitual tendencies of names and speech": it refers to the distinct causes and conditions for each conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that bring about conditioned phenomena.
*Yinyì* (Explanation of Terms): Qingliang cites an ancient commentary which explains: "The distinct individual seeds" refers to the fact that the seeds of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) differ.

"Sounds that express meaning" excludes sounds that lack expression, for the latter are not names (*nāman*). A name is a particular modification (*kuṭilaka*) upon sound and is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) in nature;
it cannot, by itself, permeate (*vāsanā*) and form the seeds of matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth. Nevertheless, seeds arise because of the name; thus, it is called a "name."

The seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*). That which manifests objects through names and phrases refers to the cognitive portions (*darśana-bhāga*) of the seven consciousnesses and so forth;
it does not refer to the objective-image portions (*nimitta-bhāga*). This is because the objective-image portions cannot manifest objects.

Although these cognitive portions and so forth are in reality not themselves "names and phrases," just as spoken names manifest the meanings they signify, these mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharma*) can manifest the objects they cognize, resembling those very names.
Because they can express meaning, both types of verbal expression (nāma-kāya) accordingly perfume seeds [in the ālayavijñāna].

Regarding the term "harmonious resonance" (*hexiang*), the *Zongjing* commentary explains: "As for verbal expressions that signify meaning, only the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to take its name as an object and is able to produce it;
the others do not take it as an object and cannot produce it either. Thus, it refers exclusively to the sounds that express meaning."
This is the distinction. It excludes those sounds that do not function as expressive designations, for they are not "names" (*nāman*). Names are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Furthermore, names are specific modifications (*vaikṛtya*) upon sound; being exclusively of an indeterminate nature, they cannot perfuse (*vāsanā*) seeds such as those of form (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*).

However, because of names, the mind follows those names and transforms into appearances resembling the five aggregates and the dharmas of the three natures, thereby perfuming and forming corresponding seeds.
Because these arise due to names, they are termed "name-and-phrase seeds. All perfumed seeds are produced by the mind and mental factors.

The seeds of mind and mental factors are of two kinds: those that depend on external conditions and those that do not depend on external conditions. Those that do not depend on external conditions are called "expressive linguistic conventions regarding objects" (*viṣayābhilāpavikalpa*).

Those that do depend on external conditions are called "expressive linguistic conventions regarding meanings" (*arthābhilāpavikalpa*). Thus they are divided into two types; however, this refers to the intrinsic nature of names (*nāmasvabhāva*).
Regarding the phrase "cannot perfume seeds" and "the mind and mental factors that manifest objects through names and phrases":

this refers to the cognitive portions (*darśana-bhāga*) of all seven consciousnesses and their associated mental factors, which are capable of cognizing objects; it does not refer to the objective-image portions (*nimitta-bhāga*), because these cannot manifest objects. (Text)
△ Next, the branch of the existence of self-grasping (2): Part One, the explanation of the two types of habitual tendencies (2). First, the habitual tendency of self-grasping.
Second, the habitual tendency of self-grasping refers to false attachment (up to) that which causes the distinction between self and other among sentient beings and so forth.

Commentary on the Terms: Innate self-clinging (*sahaja-ātmagrāha*) pervades both the sixth and seventh consciousnesses; discriminative self-clinging (*vikalpita-ātmagrāha*) belongs exclusively to the sixth consciousness.
The seeds of these two are precisely the perfuming of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vāsanā*), which cause the differentiation between self and others; therefore, they are established separately.

*Hexiang Kaimeng* (Harmonizing Resonances, Opening the Ignorant). Question: What is the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) of self-grasping? Answer: It refers to the seeds (*bīja*) of the false attachment to "self" and "mine. Question:

Since this "self" is a mere parikalpita (imagined construction), how can it have seeds? Answer: When one grasps the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth as being the self, one perfumes the seeds within those aggregates;
this is termed the habitual tendency of self-grasping. Question: For what purpose is the habitual tendency of self-grasping established separately? Answer: Because...
The seed of self-grasping (*ātmagrāha-bīja*) is established separately because it brings about the distinction between self and others (text).
Next is the habitual tendency of the members of existence (*bhavāṅga-vāsanā*).

The habitual tendency of the three members of existence refers to that which summons the three realms and causes the distinctions between the various destinies (*gati*) within the resultant maturation (*vipākaphala*), whether virtuous or non-virtuous.

Commentary on the Terms: Regarding "the members of existence" (*bhavāṅga*), among the twelve members of existence, the two members of formative action (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*) constitute "karmic existence.
"Desirable" refers to the fruits of the human and celestial realms, which are the good destinies; "undesirable" refers to the fruits of the three miserable paths, which are the evil destinies.

*Hexiang Kaimeng*. Question: What is the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) of the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*)? Answer: It refers to the seeds of karma that summon the maturation (*vipāka*) within the three realms.

Question: What is the name of the members of existence? Answer: Following [the influence of] good or evil, there are seeds perfumed and formed, which cause the fruits of maturation to distinguish between the various good and evil destinies;
this is called the habitual tendency of the members of existence (text).
△ Next, the general conclusion regarding the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

It should be understood that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the members of dependent origination (*aṅga*) associated with the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*) serve as the predominant condition for the differentiated fruits (*viśeṣa-phala*).

*He-xiang* (Harmonizing the Resonance) / *Kai-meng* (Opening the Ignorant): Question: Among the four conditions, what kind of condition are these three types of habitual tendencies? Answer: [As stated above.]

The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of names and words are the direct causal condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). The grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), which is a member of existence (*bhavāṅga*), is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

Question: Since the karma that draws forth the members of existence is a dominant condition, it is understandable; however, the seeds of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the grasping at a self directly produce the seeing aspect (*darśanabhāga*) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

These should therefore be the direct causal conditions. Why, then, are they also called dominant conditions? Answer: Because they cause the distinction between self and others, they constitute dominant conditions. Question: [Why is this so?]
It is asked: To what are the pervasive dissemination of names and phrases (*nāma-pada*) and the seeds of karma (*karma-bīja*) comparable?

The answer is: Names and phrases are like scattered soil; the seeds of karma are like a lump of clay. It is asked: What is the principle underlying this analogy? The answer is: When water mixes with scattered soil, it forms a lump of clay;
likewise, karma brings forth names and phrases, which then become the seeds of karma. It is asked: What is the verification of this analogy? The answer is: A lump of clay does not disperse.
At that juncture, it is the power of water that effects this; until the maturation has withered, the power of karma is likewise [as described in the text]. (Text).
△ Third, the connection to the verse (in two parts): first, the summary of the connection.
Regarding the "karmic latencies" mentioned in this verse (up to the point where they are "perfumed and thus established"), all are designated as "grasping" (*upādāna*).
[From] *Hexiang* and *Kaimeng*: Question: To which of the three types of karma do these correspond as latencies? Answer: They are the latencies of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).

Question: The verse speaks of the "latencies of the two graspings. Which of the three [types of karma] does this refer to? Answer: It refers to the two latencies of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) and linguistic designation (*nāma-kāya*).

Question: What is meant by the "two graspings"? Answer: They are called graspings because they grasp at a self and what belongs to a self (*ātman-ātmīya*), as well as grasping at names and conventions (*nāma-vyavahāra*), thereby perfuming [the mind] and forming [impressions].
Question: What is the meaning of "grasping"? Answer: Grasping means the sense of attachment (*abhiniveśa*). (Text)
△ Next, the reference to the same [text].
The meaning of the remaining passages, such as "both," etc., is explained as before.

△ Third, the continuity of the factors of the hindrances (three parts). First, the direct explanation based on the three hindrances (three parts). First, the habitual tendencies of the three hindrances.
*Qi* (vital energy).

Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering; [this continues] until it is stated that the seeds of afflictions, karma, and suffering are all termed *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies).

Regarding the phonology and meaning: the "initiation of karma" is ignorance (*avidyā*); the "moistening of birth" is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). However, other factors such as hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth are not excluded.
[This refers to] "generating moisture. For now, I shall mention only the most prominent among them. Supplement: The *Zongjing* states:
"Among the six innate afflictions (*kleśa*), greed alone is the primary factor that moistens birth;
the other five can also assist in moistening it. The affliction that generates karma is the link of ignorance (*avidyā*); the affliction that moistens birth is craving (*tṛṣṇā*)."

Two members are taken up: the karma that brings about future existence consists of the two members of *saṃskāra* (volitional formations) and *vijñāna* (consciousness); the various sufferings thus projected consist of the seven members beginning with *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form).
Next, these are categorized according to their two conditions.

**Commentary on Terms:** Someone asks: Since the five factors, beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), are simultaneously produced through the impregnation of karma (*karmavāsanā*), how can they be distinguished as having a sequential order?

The explanation states: Although these factors are in fact simultaneous due to the impregnation of karma, within the various sacred teachings (*āgama*) they are said to have a sequence based upon four meanings.
First is the meaning of "principal and attendant" (*pramukha-parivāra*): the member of consciousness (*vijñānāṅga*) is the principal, while the others...
Fourth is the sense of "companion. The primary comes first and the companions follow; consciousness occupies the first position. Second is the sense of "general and specific.

Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the general, while the remaining three are the specific; the general comes before the specific, and the other three follow it. Third is the sense of "superior and inferior.

The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are superior, while the latter two are inferior; the superior comes before the inferior. Therefore, the six sense bases occupy the positions prior to sensation (*vedanā*) and contact (*sparśa*).

Fourth is the meaning of cause and effect. The six contacts are the cause; the six feelings are the effect. One should understand that the sequence follows the principle that the cause precedes and the effect follows.

The Gate of Distinguishing the Two Types of Abandonment (2). Regarding the first master’s view, there is both commonality and distinction between the two types of abandonment.

There is an interpretation that ignorance (*avidyā*) is abandoned solely through the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*), while the remaining nine [links] are common to both abandonment through seeing and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Regarding the commentary on the meaning: this master asserts that the link of ignorance is abandoned solely through the path of seeing and does not extend to abandonment through cultivation.

His statement, "Because it must delude one regarding the principles of the truths (*satya*) in order to be able to initiate [the karmic process]," intends to clarify that the afflictions which delude one regarding the principles of the truths are abandoned through the path of seeing; thus, for a noble one (*ārya*), [ignorance] necessarily...
Those who do not create karma for future existence are the noble ones (*ārya*), because they certainly lack the capacity to give rise to afflictions and delusions.

By these two points, it is shown that the two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); they do not extend to being abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*).
Those who crave for future existence (*bhava*) and thereby moisten rebirth are the noble learners (*śaikṣa*), such as the *srotāpanna*.
This includes seven births [for the first fruit], two births above and below for the second fruit, and one birth in the higher realms for the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Because they crave for future existence and moisten rebirth through craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*), there are nine types of death-minds. As stated in the fifth volume of the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*: "That is to say, from..."

One who passes away from the desire realm and is reborn again in the desire realm links the continuity of rebirth with a death-moment consciousness associated with craving for the self-existence of the desire realm.

If one is reborn in the form or formless realms, one links the continuity of rebirth with a death-moment consciousness associated with craving for the self-existence of the form or formless realms. It is the same when passing away from the form or formless realms.
Whether one is born in that very realm or is born in another place, there are six types of minds; all of these should be understood according to their respective applications.
Furthermore, this [first type] is shown to be abandoned through cultivation alone by means of two meanings, while the remaining nine are common to both meanings, as explained previously.
△ Next, the Master [asserts that] all are common to both types of abandonment. (2) First, the thesis.
There is an interpretation that all are common to both types of abandonment.
△ Next, the explanation. (2) First, raising an objection against the previous master.

The treatise states that for one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), all [factors] up to the three branches are abandoned; these are also common to both those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
[Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms]: First, the treatise is cited. Regarding the passage beginning with "If ignorance... and below, the argument is raised based on the intent of the treatise:

if it is the case that each branch is abandoned as a single portion, then the branch of ignorance (*avidyā*) would not be abandoned solely by seeing, because a portion of ignorance would still remain. This applies likewise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*).
Regarding the two branches: they are not abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because a portion of them is abandoned upon entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Furthermore, the text below cites a scriptural argument to refute the notion that [afflictions] pertain to the entire realm; "entire realm" refers to one complete realm. For example, when taking rebirth (*pratisandhi*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the entire desire realm [function];
by analogy, it should be understood that when taking rebirth in the two higher realms, the same applies. That treatise states:

It is taught that all afflictions (*kleśa*) throughout the entire realm (*dhātu*) are capable of linking birth (*pratisandhi-bandhana*); it does not say that the afflictions which moisten birth (*upapatti-sneha*) are exclusively abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

How then could the members of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) be abandoned by cultivation alone? Furthermore, it is taught that actions leading to evil destinies (*durgati-gamana-karman*) are incited only by afflictions arising from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-ja*);
it does not mean that all actions which summon a future existence (*punar-bhava*) are [incited] solely by afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).

Is it not the case that the factor of ignorance (*avidyā*) among those produced is exclusively abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)? For this reason, these three factors all pertain to both types of abandonment.

However, regarding the factor of ignorance (*avidyā*), that which acts as the primary initiator is [only] abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); those that assist it are not fixed.
Regarding the primary and assisting factors that initiate karma, the *Zhongjing* (Zhengfa nianchu jing), Scroll 74, states:

"If one distinguishes the afflictions, the innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) assists the primary ignorance in initiating karma. 'Initiating' (*fa*) means the sense of movement; 'karma' (*karman*)..."
Regarding the sense of "inducing [rebirth]": innate [afflictions] can moisten birth, while discriminative [afflictions] can create karma that induces birth with heavy consequences;

innate [afflictions] moisten birth with light consequences. If discriminative [afflictions] give rise to karma for humans or devas, then innate [afflictions] assist in its manifestation, because karma for humans and devas is difficult to produce and requires the assistance of the innate.
If discriminative [afflictions] give rise to karma for the three miserable realms, they do not require the innate.
The "arousing assistance" (janaka-sahakārin) refers to the fact that discrimination is sharp and intense; it does not require further assistance [as a separate category].

Regarding the "moistening of birth" (janma-paripuṣṭi), which consists of both primary and auxiliary factors, it is as previously explained in the section on the arousal and moistening of karma; it is not cited here as a separate heading.

△ Next, a general exposition of the different meanings of the abandonment (*prahāṇa*) of the twelve links (2). First, it is explained that those which are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) should be abandoned by their very nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, because defiled phenomena (*dharma*) should be abandoned by their very nature, they are permanently severed when their antidote (*pratipakṣa*) arises.
Exegesis on Terms: Defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) refer to the three links of ignorance, craving, and grasping, as well as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

They possess a portion of the nature of affliction because they are defiled by the afflictions; therefore, it is said they "should be abandoned. Counteractive phenomena (*pratipakṣa-dharma*) refer to the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*).
Because the obstacles and their remedies are mutually contradictory, it is said that they are "permanently severed.
Next, it is explained that what is not defiled is not something that should be severed by nature. First, the formal explanation that it is not something that should be severed by nature.
All contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena that are non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*) are not by nature to be abandoned, because they do not contradict the Path.
Regarding the meaning of the terms: "all contaminated" refers to one portion of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-bhava*), namely, contaminated wholesome states.

"Non-defiled phenomena" refers to the five [aggregates] beginning with consciousness, as well as the two fruits of birth and old age/death; their essential nature is exclusively maturation (*vipāka*). This...
Since all these do not contradict the *mārga-pakṣya* (factors conducive to the path), it is said that they are not by nature to be abandoned (*na-prakṛti-heya*).
△ Next, there are two senses in which they are said to be abandoned.

However, there are two senses in which they are described as abandonment: [up to] the non-ideational attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and so forth, which are abandoned solely through insight (*darśana-heya*).

**Exegesis on Phonology** Question: Since wholesome states with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and non-defiled phenomena (*akliṣṭa-dharma*) do not contradict the Path, and thus are not by nature to be abandoned (*prahātavya*), why is it said that they all pertain to both types of abandonment?
Explanation: It is said that they pertain to both types of abandonment for two reasons.

First, in the sense of being "freed from bondage" (*bandhana-vigama*). This means they are freed from the bondage of the various defilements (*kleśa*) that take them as objects. Regarding those [objects], the defilements...

"Defilement" (*kliṣṭa*) refers to the innate self-grasping and so forth within the first seven consciousnesses. Because these can take that ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) as their object, they are "mixed" with those afflictions;
that is, the views of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and so forth within the seventh consciousness.

Due to the view of self, the acts of giving and so forth arising within the six consciousnesses are unable to forget their objective signs (*nimitta*); therefore, it is called "mixed. These [afflictions] depend on the abandonment of these two types of defilement.

Regarding the meaning of affliction (*kleśa*): among the two branches of the process of becoming (*bhava*), one portion consists of contaminated wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*);
together with birth, aging, and death (*jāti-jarā-maraṇa*), these constitute nine branches that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Second, regarding the meaning of non-arising: based upon the discrimination of afflictions, those [branches] arise; by abandoning these afflictions, they will never arise again.

Based on the meaning of non-arising, the dharmas that are the fruits of the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) are said to be abandoned solely by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*). [The *Kaīmōng* states: "The dharmas that are the fruits of the eight difficult conditions enter the path of seeing;

thereafter they never arise again. This is because the causes of the eight difficult conditions arise based on ignorance, false views, and so forth. At the time of the path of seeing, one abandons their basis, causing those eight difficult conditions to never arise again. Based on this abandonment, the various evil destinies (*durgati*) and so forth are spoken of."]
[This is] only abandoned through vision). *He-yang* (合響):

furthermore, the seeds for being born among humans as those without sense organs, those with dual sexual organs, those in the northern continent (Uttarakuru), or those in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva) will not produce future results—this is called "severing non-arising.
Regarding "severing the bonds of the three conditions," this refers solely to severing the delusions within the mind. At...

Among the three types of abandonment, the self-nature does not produce these two [afflictions], and they are spontaneously severed.

The actual meaning is concluded below, clarifying that what is elucidated herein is based on the actual meaning (*bhūtārtha*). If one were to speak according to the predominance of their respective characteristics, as found in various holy teachings...

△ Fifteen: The Section on Subsumption by the Four Noble Truths.

All are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering because their nature as aggregates (*skandha*) is grasped by the Truth of Suffering; and all five are also subsumed under the Truth of Origination because their nature as karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) is grasped by the Truth of Origination.

Commentary on the Terms: In terms of the Four Noble Truths, these twelve links are all subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), because they possess the nature of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

Furthermore, five branches—ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and existence (*bhava*)—are also subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), because they possess the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma (*karman*).
△ Section 16: Analysis of the Four Conditions (2). First, a general demonstration of their presence or absence.
While the predominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*) certainly exists when the various members are viewed in relation to one another, the sūtras, based on certainty, state that there is only one [condition].

Commentary on the Terms: Because the nature of the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is broad, it is invariably present; because the other three conditions are restricted, their presence or absence is not fixed.
The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* speaks of there being only the predominant condition based on the definition [of that specific context].

△ Next, the specific explanation of existence and non-existence (three parts). First, the explanation of the existence of causal conditions (two parts). First, the direct explanation of the actual meaning:
"Craving in relation to grasping, and existence in relation to birth" (up to) "the other members in their mutual relations lack the sense of causal conditions."

Commentary on the Meanings of the Terms: Regarding the sense that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) serves as the causal condition for grasping (*upādāna*): because craving, when intensified, is termed grasping, craving is the seed of grasping;

since it can produce manifest grasping, it constitutes its causal condition. Regarding the sense that hope (*bhava*) serves as the causal condition for becoming (*bhava*): consciousness, when intensified, becomes becoming.
Since becoming has no separate essence apart from these, the five aggregates, moistened by craving and grasping, constitute becoming. Thus, hope is the causal condition for becoming.

This refers to the five factors beginning with consciousness, which constitute the branch of arising (*jāti-aṅga*). Since these manifest factors, such as consciousness, arise from seeds, they possess the causal conditions for this arising.

If one speaks of the "lower" [explanation], it accords with the intent of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. If consciousness-seeds are taken as the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*), [then the manifest consciousness is the arising].

Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are not the direct cause of consciousness. If the seed of karma is designated as the limb of consciousness, then volitional formations can serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for consciousness;

this is because the present formations act as seeds, and the seeds perfumed by karmic causes are themselves the seeds of consciousness. Regarding the other limbs, there are no mutual causal conditions.
Furthermore, among the remaining limbs, there are eight positions: namely, ignorance (*avidyā*) in relation to formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) in relation to...

Regarding name-and-form (nāmarūpa), in relation to the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana); the six sense bases in relation to contact (sparśa); contact in relation to feeling (vedanā); feeling in relation to the link of craving (tṛṣṇā);
grasping (upādāna) in relation to the link of becoming (bhava); and birth (jāti) in relation to the link of aging-and-death (jarāmaraṇa):
these eight stages lack [direct] causal conditions because ignorance and the other factors do not directly produce their own specific effects.
*Hexiang* (Harmonious Resonance): *Huayan Chao*, Fascicle 37, Part 1, states: "The initial arising of the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is its manifestation in the present moment;
it immediately perfumes consciousness to form a seed. Based on this seed of craving, grasping (*upādāna*) arises.
Grasping is itself a manifestation. Therefore, the Sūtra says: 'The increase of craving constitutes grasping,' and further: 'Craving serves as the cause and condition for grasping.'"
This is because the seed of craving increases and becomes grasping (*upādāna*), as it is the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the seed of craving;
therefore, the initial stage of greed is termed "craving," while its further intensification is termed "grasping. Thus, this very seed of craving is itself the seed of grasping.

Consequently, both of these two links (*aṅga*) encompass both the state of seed and the state of manifestation (text). Herein, for the time being, we rely on the aspect of craving being the seed of grasping.
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) have the sense of being the conditions for existence (*bhava*).
Next, reconciling with other treatises (2): first, reconciling with the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

The *Samuccaya* states that regarding ignorance (*avidyā*) in relation to formative forces (*saṃskāra*)—[it is] metaphorically designated as ignorance, while in reality it is the seed of formative forces.

Commentary on the Terms: The first phrase first indicates that those [factors] have a basis. From "ignorance" (*avidyā*) downward, it clarifies the meaning of their existence, showing that they are conventional designations.

That is to say, based on the habitual tendencies of volitional karma (*saṃskāra*) that arise simultaneously with ignorance, and which coexist with ignorance, one conventionally designates the seeds of karma as "ignorance.
In reality, however, it is simply the seeds of formative action (*saṃskāra*) that give rise to the actual manifestation of formative action.
△ Next, we shall reconcile this with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

The *Yogācārabhūmi* states that when the various links are considered in relation to one another, there are no causes or conditions; this is based on the teaching that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) depend on the present, while existence (*bhava*) depends solely on karma.

[Commentary on the Meaning]: One might fear an objection being raised: "In the tenth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is stated that when the various links are considered in relation to one another, they possess three types of conditions."

Regarding the meaning of "lack of causal conditions": why, in this context, is it said that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) has a causal condition for grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) has a causal condition for birth (*jāti*)?
In the commentary, the text first restates that passage: "Based on those who currently possess craving and grasping" establishes the sense of craving having a causal condition for grasping.
This is because craving, when intensified, becomes grasping; since the seed produces the manifest, it can function as a causal condition. That [text]...
The craving currently manifesting seeks the grasping currently manifesting; it does not arise from its own seeds. How then could it obtain the conditions?
Those who maintain that "existence" (*bhava*) consists solely of karma explain that the preceding craving serves as the causal condition for birth.

Previously, consciousness arising from its seeds served as the causal condition for birth; now, that [craving] takes the seeds of karma as existence and gives rise to birth. Karma is not the substance of consciousness.
It serves merely as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). How could there be a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*)? Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* asks:

"Why, when compared with one another, do they all lack a causal condition? It answers: "A causal condition is that which is manifested by its own essential seed-cause (*svabhāva-bīja-hetu*). Now, the currently manifesting craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*) are not seeds;
for karma, in relation to birth, is not their own essential nature.
△ Next, the remaining two conditions are explained.

Regarding ignorance in relation to formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in relation to grasping (*upādāna*), [the other links] lack both types of conditions when compared to one another.
(Regarding the phrase "ignorance in relation to formative forces... According to the commentary by Qingliang, it says: "Self..."

There are three meanings. In the first three positions, two conditions are present. Both are explained as having two conditions—namely, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)—by way of mutual observation among manifest states.
This is because they must be manifest mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*); when the preceding moment ceases, it induces the arising of the succeeding moment.
Thus, the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) induces the formations (*saṃskāra*), and the cessation of the mental state of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) induces the grasping (*upādāna*).
Regarding the mind (*citta*): herein, the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) also pertains to the arising of the present [existence] as well as birth and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

It is merely that consciousness (*vijñāna*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) undergo growth and decay; because the growth of the mind ceases and induces decay, these three stages possess immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Since volition (*cetanā*) and the other formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are obtainable only within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they can reflexively take the preceding link of ignorance (*avidyā*) as their object. Thus, there is no contradiction.

The limb of clinging (*upādāna*) is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the limb of becoming (*bhava*). Grasping (*parigraha*) likewise takes as its object the craving (*tṛṣṇā*) that preceded it; thus, craving is the object-condition for clinging.
Within the stage of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), the various minds and mental factors can take as their objects the form and mind produced in the stage of birth (*jāti*);
this is the object-condition for old age and death. This explains the object-condition by way of how a subsequent limb conditions a preceding one.

Regarding the conditions (*pratyaya*): when the two subsequent stages are compared with each other, they possess only one condition. When viewed in relation to arising (*jāti*) and feeling (*vedanā*), and when viewed in relation to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), there is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

There is no equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), because an equal-and-immediate condition must consist of preceding and succeeding mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that mutually induce one another’s arising;
since what exists here is a seed giving rise to [a state], how could there be an actual manifestation (*samudācāra*)?

Feeling (*vedanā*) is also a seed, because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is an active manifestation (*samudācāra*). Regarding the point that there is no sense of being an "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) without immediate succession:
birth (*jāti*) is an active manifestation that can take the seeds of existence (*bhava*) as its object; craving is an active manifestation that can take the seeds of feeling as its object.
Thus, existence and craving serve as object-conditions. In the subsequent branches, three [aspects] are entirely absent, while two remain. For the remaining branches, there are further six [points].

Regarding the stages: this refers to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) in relation to consciousness (*vijñāna*); consciousness in relation to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); name-and-form in relation to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the six sense bases in relation to contact (*sparśa*); contact in relation to the factor of feeling (*vedanā*);
and grasping (*upādāna*) in relation to the factor of existence (*bhava*).

The reason there is no "equal and immediate" (*samanantara-pratyaya*) relationship between them is that their results are not all manifest mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), but rather are produced through mutual induction as seeds. That is to say, from consciousness up to feeling, these are all seeds; existence (*bhava*) is likewise a seed.

Sons, action (*karman*) is the cause of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and grasping (*upādāna*) is the cause of existence (*bhava*). Although these are produced from active manifestations (*samudācāra*), since consciousness and existence are themselves seeds, they are not [simply] immediate antecedent conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*).

As for why they are not object-conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*): since they are neither active mental states nor mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), how could there be any cognitive engagement (*ālambana*)?
△ The three examples of connection have no fixed rule.
Herein, for the time being, one should rely on what is proximate and sequential; those who are wise should reflect upon this according to reason.
Regarding the meaning of the terms: there are four levels. First, based on proximity, which differs from being separated by an interval, or skipping over only one.
First, regarding the greater number: the second [explanation] follows the sequential order, whereas this differs from the reverse order;

it takes only ignorance as the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), rather than taking volitional formations as the condition for ignorance, and so forth. Third, regarding the absence of confusion: this differs from the confused [explanation].

If, as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, ignorance (*avidyā*) is considered in relation to formative forces (*saṃskāra*), one takes that which is the seed of the formative forces within it to be ignorance;
therefore, this is confused. Those who explain dependent origination according to its actual reality differ from those who speak of it figuratively.

For example, the karmic latencies (*vāsanā*) that exist simultaneously with ignorance are actually the seeds of the formative forces, yet they are figuratively called "ignorance. This differs from the perspective of mutual correlation.

This refers to something distinct from the four meanings mentioned above. The preceding analysis of the single gate of the four conditions is entirely based on the commentary in the *Huayan jing shuchao*.

Regarding the "resonance" (*heyang*) that differs from these when viewed in relation to one another, the *Huayan shu* states: "Because there are respective sequences for both the inverse and the direct [order]."

Furthermore, because they are separated by an interval, let us first consider those separated by one stage. For example, ignorance (*avidyā*) has only one predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) with respect to consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the other five [links], as it can only produce their seeds.
Ignorance and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) serve as two conditions for grasping (*upādāna*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*);
namely, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the predominant condition. All other conditions should be understood according to this principle.
[This is] known. Second, regarding the reverse order (*pratiloma*), there are both immediate (*anantara*) and non-immediate (*vyavahita*) sequences; these shall now be explained together.

Old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) have two conditions in relation to birth (*jāti*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and ignorance (*avidyā*): namely, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

For the others, there is only the dominant condition. Third, if they are mixed and disordered, there are two types: first, the forward order (*anuloma*); second, the reverse order (*pratiloma*). Within the forward order, there are immediate and non-immediate sequences, as [explained] in the *Abhidharmapada*.
Regarding the Dharma: the preceding ignorance in relation to the formations (*saṃskāra*) is "remote" (*vyavahita*), yet it is no different from the aforementioned direct conditions (*pratyaya*).

This is also explained with reference to the five types beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*). If one considers them in terms of future rebirth, according to their respective applications within the reverse order, there are both immediate (*sāmantaka*) and remote (*antara*) [conditions].

This should be understood by analogy with the above explanation regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This is explained in terms of predominant influence (*adhipati-pratyaya*), yet there remains a distinction between the distant and the near.

This applies even to the individual members [of dependent origination]. Each should be understood in this manner. Herein, the five members beginning with consciousness, based on their state at the time of arising, are separated by intervals;

they function as conditions for one another by skipping and leaping over them in reverse order, intermingling as conditions. This serves as the standard for each and every volition (*cetanā*). (Textual note)
△ Section on the Subsumption of the Seventeen Defilements and Sufferings. Regarding the subsumption of the twelve [links] within the three categories of defilement (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering:

[the links from ignorance through feeling] are subsumed under the truth of suffering; [the links from craving through becoming] are subsumed under the truth of origin; and [the link of birth] is subsumed solely under the truth of suffering for the purpose of engendering world-weariness.

*Commentary on the Terms:* The three branches of ignorance, craving, and grasping are subsumed under the category of defilement (*kleśa*). The branch of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and the branch of existence (*bhava*) are [subsumed under the category of karma]. One [link, birth, is subsumed under suffering].
[The portion] "is comprised of karma" refers to one part of the seed of karma within the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).

The seven links—namely, the five beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the two consisting of birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—as well as one part of the link of existence, are comprised of the path of suffering (i.e., the five kinds beginning with consciousness within the links of existence).

Below this, [the text] next reconciles other treatises; that is to say, there is a treatise which states that karma fully comprises existence (*bhava*), and it should be understood that this is based on karma.
Some say that [the link of existence] does not depend on the seeds of existence (*bhava-bīja*). Others say that the link of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*) is subsumed under karma.

This is because they explain the link of consciousness by referring to the seeds of karma, rather than explaining the link of consciousness by referring to the seeds of consciousness itself. Question:

Since all twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) should be suffering (*duḥkha*), how can it be said that only the seven links beginning with consciousness are subsumed solely under suffering as being summoned by afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma? Explanation: [The answer is as follows:]...

It is subsumed solely under the Truth of Suffering, as it does not extend to the Truth of Origination. Because it is intended to produce weariness and detachment in sentient beings, consciousness and the other aggregates are subsumed solely under the Truths of Suffering and the Path.
△ 3. The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) correspond to the meaning of the verse.
Since afflictions, karma, and suffering constitute the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*), these are able to cause the continuity of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
△ 4. The succession of defilement and purity according to the masters (2). First, the explicit explanation of the succession of defilement and purity (3). First, the general explanation.
Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from internal causes and conditions; because they assist in the production of birth and death, they are called "conditions" (*pratyaya*).

Regarding the statement that "the two karmas are the cause and the two hindrances are the condition": these two sets of two refer to the fact that while the conditions are merely dominant, karma is also called a "cause" because it brings about the manifestation of rebirth.
In this context, the distinction is not made based on directness or indirectness, but rather based on what is primary and what is auxiliary.
This is called the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*), which is distinct from the "causal condition" among the four conditions.
Next, the reason for this is questioned:
Why is it that birth and death are of two kinds?
△ Third, the detailed explanation (three parts). First, the direct explanation (two parts). First, the classification of births.
"Birth by classification" refers to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) states; because they have fixed limits and boundaries, it is called "classification."
Commentary on the Terms: Wholesome and unwholesome karma acts as the cause for the arising [of rebirth]. The afflictions that provide moisture act as the auxiliary condition.

The resultant maturation (*vipāka*) within the three realms is the fruit produced. Depending on the power of these causes and conditions, the duration of the resulting body and life has a fixed limit;
it cannot be altered or extended forward or backward. Therefore, it is called "segmented" (*paricchinna*).
△ Next, the Transformation of Rebirth (3): First, the formal explanation;
second, the inconceivable transformation-death (upapatti-saṃskāra-maraṇa). [From here until] its wondrous functioning is difficult to fathom, it is called "inconceivable."

Commentary on the Terms: Taking various uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) conditioned karmas as the cause, and with the assistance of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) acting as the condition, a preeminent maturation (*vipāka*) is produced as the resulting fruit.
This uncontaminated sustenance brings about a transformation through the power of compassion and vows;

its wondrous function is unfathomable, lacking fixed limits, and is thus termed "inconceivable transformative birth-and-death" (*acintya-nairmāṇika-saṃsāra*). An ancient questioner asked: "If [this is so]..."

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) varies according to the body it depends upon; thus, one may speak of it as being short or long. However, like the flame of a lamp, it arises and ceases from moment to moment.
It is not like a "segmented" entity, such as a single lifetime, which has a fixed duration. Based on what, then, can one say that it lacks a definite limit? Master Xuanzang explained:
"In truth, the life-faculty has no distinct boundaries of its own; it is only metaphorically said to have limits in accordance with the body upon which it relies."
*Hexiang Kai Meng* states: "To transform the coarse body into a subtle essence, and to change a short lifespan into a long one. Question:
Since the coarse is changed for the subtle and the short is made long, why is this called birth and death? Answer: When the momentum of conscious awareness is exhausted, it is called death;
when one enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to provide further sustenance, it is called birth. (Text) *Hui Xuan*, fascicle nine, states: "That is to say, by means of the non-..."

Its essential nature consists of the outflows (*āsrava*), karma, the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and the five aggregates of maturation (*vipākaskandha*) within the realms of desire and form.

This is because the noble ones cultivate their minds through both compassion and wisdom: they possess compassion because they wish to transform sentient beings below, and they possess wisdom because they intend to seek the fruit of Buddhahood above.
Considering these fragmented existences to be short-lived and incapable of enduring for long periods, they are unable to undertake a distant journey over a great duration of time.

Throughout kalpas, one cultivates sublime practices. Consequently, taking the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as the condition and untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) as the cause, and because these provide secret support to past karma, that karma—being thus supported—is able to permeate (*vāsana*) the seeds of the five branches beginning with consciousness.
