"The nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) refers to the real self and real dharmas imputed by the deluded as being inherent in the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, which they universally conceptualize; this is called the nature of pervasive conceptualization. There is [this teaching].

Second, there are two types: first, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which is the general apprehension that all phenomena possess a real intrinsic nature; second, the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*), which is the distinct apprehension that [phenomena] such as permanence or impermanence possess a real essence.
Alternatively, it refers to the pervasive conceptualization of an object based on a name, such as when one who does not yet know a cow hears the word "cow" and then speculates:
"By what reasoning is it called a 'cow'? Or, it refers to the pervasive conceptualization of a name based on an object. Or...

When one perceives an object but does not know its true name, one falsely conjectures: "What is the name of this thing? This is like someone who has never seen an ox and, upon seeing one, speculates together with others:
"Is it a ghost? Or is it a beast? All such forms of pervasive conceptualization (parikalpa), in terms of their substance, do not transcend the two substances of person and phenomena;
in terms of their grasping, they do not transcend the two types of name and referent. (Text)
△ Second, the detailed explanation (in two parts): First, the general classification.

From "Alternatively, the first phrase reveals the consciousness that performs the pervasive conceptualization" up to "because it has already been extensively shown that such [an object] is unobtainable."
△ Next, the detailed explanation (in three parts). First, the nature of the universal constructor (*parikalpa-svabhāva*). (1) First, the heading and inquiry.
What is the nature of the universal constructor?

△ Second, the explanation of its characteristics (in two parts). First, according to Sthiramati, both the kings [the eight consciousnesses] and their attendants (*caitta*) are capable of universal construction.
There is an interpretation that the eight consciousnesses and their associated mental factors (up to the point of) taking the seeds of self-nature and false attachment as their objects.

Regarding the meaning of the sounds: this explanation refers to the eight kinds of consciousness and their corresponding mental factors; if they are subsumed under the category of *sāsrava* (with-outflows), [they take those seeds as their objects].

All [eight consciousnesses] are the mind of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpaka-citta*). Why is this so? Because all eight consciousnesses, together with their associated mental factors, have false discrimination as their intrinsic nature;

and because they all manifest as if they were the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*). These manifestations as grasper and grasped refer to the object of cognition (*ālambana*) and the subject of cognition (*ālambaka*), which are the two parts of the image (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing (*darśana-bhāga*).
Since these two [parts] serve as the common evidence for all eight consciousnesses, it is established that all are the mind of conceptualization.
Furthermore, regarding the section below on the *ālayavijñāna*, which provides a specific proof for the eighth consciousness as the locus of false conceptualization seeds:
it refers to the seeds of the mind capable of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), namely, the habitual tendencies of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha-vāsanā*).

This clarifies that since the sacred teachings state that the *ālayavijñāna* takes the seeds of pervasive conceptualization as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), one knows that the eighth consciousness is also capable of pervasive conceptualization.
△ Next, regarding the protection of the Dharma, only the six and seventh mental categories (*citta-varga*) are capable of universal conceptualization (*parikalpa*). (2) First, the formal explanation:

There is an interpretation that the sixth and seventh mental categories [are the universal conceptualizers] because they have never lacked grasping (*grāha*), and thus they are capable of perfuming (*vāsana*).

Regarding the "Exegesis of Terms" (*Yinyi*): it is said that only the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, along with the afflicted wisdom (*kliṣṭa-prajñā*) mental factor that grasps at a self and phenomena, are capable of universal imagination (*parikalpa*).
It is not the eighth consciousness, the first five consciousnesses, nor other mental factors. The phrase "only [the sixth and seventh]" below expresses this intent;

the first three lines prove that only the sixth and seventh are capable of universal imagination, while simultaneously excluding the first five, as they lack discursive conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*). Not... [text ends].

The fourth and fifth phrases clarify that the two types of grasping—grasping at a self and grasping at phenomena—are necessarily associated with the wisdom of the "distinctive mental state" (viśeṣa-viṣaya) and with ignorance (avidyā).
This also excludes the eighth consciousness, as it lacks both wisdom and delusion, and thus is not a pervasive conceptualizer (parikalpaka).

The sixth phrase clarifies that these two types of grasping do not extend to a wholesome nature, as they are exclusively defiled. The seventh phrase explains why these two types of grasping do not coexist with a wholesome mind.
This also refutes the previous masters, asserting that all mental factors (*caitta*) are capable of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*).

The eighth phrase excludes only defiled wisdom (*prajñā*); if it were wholesome wisdom, it would lead toward the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*) and thus would not involve grasping at existence.

The ninth phrase cites the two views of eternalism and nihilism as not coexisting, illustrating by analogy that grasping at existence is not the knowledge of emptiness. The intent is that grasping at existence and grasping at non-existence [are mutually exclusive].
Since they cannot even arise simultaneously, how much less could there be a grasping that leads the wisdom realizing emptiness?

The tenth phrase also proves that it is only the sixth and seventh consciousnesses that are the pervasive conceptualizers (*parikalpa*), while also excluding the first five from being graspers, as the eighth consciousness is not a perfuming agent (*vāsana*).

It is not the mind of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), which simultaneously excludes the first six consciousnesses and those neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds and mental factors born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
as these cannot perform pervasive conceptualization nor act as perfumers (*vāsana*).
*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance). The *Zongjing* says: "The first [category] is 'pervasive yet non-apprehensive' (*fei ji*).

This refers to uncontaminated minds (*anāsrava-citta*) and contaminated wholesome consciousnesses (*sāsrava-kuśala-vijñāna*) that are able to pervasively and extensively take objects as conditions, yet do not involve apprehension or grasping (*parikalpa*). Uncontaminated minds refer to the uncontaminated wisdom of the various sages, which realizes the emptiness of all phenomena;
there is no phenomenon that is not pervaded by it, and it is entirely devoid of apprehension and grasping, thus being termed 'non-apprehensive. Only..."

Subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) consists of contaminated wholesome consciousness. This refers to bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), who, even within a contaminated state of mind, are able to perform the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*).
Thus, they are also able to contemplate that all things are devoid of self; this is both universal and free from conceptual construction (*parikalpa*).

Second, there are those that are conceptualizing but not pervasive, such as the seventh *kliṣṭa-manas* consciousness. This consciousness constantly takes the objective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its object, giving rise to the two types of grasping—of self and of phenomena.

Even when one enters the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) from the sixth consciousness, the seventh consciousness still takes the objective aspect of the eighth consciousness as its object and gives rise to the grasping of phenomena.
Therefore, it is known to be conceptualizing but not pervasive. Third, there are those that are both pervasive and conceptualizing.

That is, the defiled mind of sentient beings. Four are neither pervasive nor conceptualizing: namely, the five contaminated sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) and the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*.

Each cognizes only its own respective sphere and is thus not pervasive; furthermore, because they lack the conceptualizing and recollective types of discrimination (*vikalpa*), they are not conceptualizing.

The *ālaya* [consciousness] takes only three kinds of objects—seeds, the body with its faculties (*indriya-śarīra*), and the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*)—and therefore it is still unable [to be pervasive].

Because it takes the seven preceding [consciousnesses] as its active manifestations (*pravṛtti*), it is neither universal (*sarvatraga*) nor a conceptualizer (*parikalpaka*). It can maintain and take as objects the contaminated seeds (*sāsrava-bīja*);
however, regarding uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), it only maintains them and does not take them as objects—how much less so other objects?
Supplement: *Hui xuan* states: "If one is able to grasp at self and dharmas, one immediately attains parikalpita (imagined nature).

If one is unable to grasp at self and dharmas, one cannot engage in parikalpa (imagination). Among the eight consciousnesses, the first five and the eighth are unable to grasp at self and dharmas and thus cannot engage in parikalpa.
The sixth and seventh consciousnesses both grasp at self and dharmas and are both capable of parikalpa" (text).
△ Next, the preceding [position] is refuted:
Because impure minds and so forth do not realize the true reality, they are not stated to be "only" [such], and thus they do not constitute valid proof.
(Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms): This means that if various impure minds and mental factors have not yet realized the true principle, they are all termed "false and illusory."

[Objection: Is it not the case that all minds that have not yet realized reality are necessarily subsumed under "universal conceptualization" (*parikalpa*), and thus you claim that all eight consciousnesses, both kings and their attendants, are capable of universal conceptualization?
Furthermore, although various minds and mental factors manifest images that appear as if they were the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*), [how can they be said to conceptualize?]

This refers specifically to the two parts of the appearance (nimitta-bhāga) and the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga). How could it be that all instances of the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka) are necessarily included within the parikalpita?

If you claim that anything resembling the grasped and the grasper is thereby subsumed under the parikalpita, then would not the Tathāgata’s subsequent non-outflowing (anāsrava) wisdom mind—which also possesses aspects resembling the grasped and the grasper—likewise be subsumed under the parikalpita? The mirror and other metaphors represent the Tathāgata’s wisdom that takes as its object; the image represents the manifestation of the body and the buddha-field (*kṣetra*). If these functions of the grasped and the grasper were absent, how could they be called the body and field manifested by the Buddha’s wisdom?

△ Third, the summary and indication.
Because this principle applies only to the sixth [consciousness] through its various modes of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), it is said to be "this and that" (*tattat*).

Regarding the phonology and meaning: first, the formal summary; below, in the section on consciousness (*vijñāna-kāya*), the obstacles are addressed. Fearing there might be a question: "If it is only the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses]..."
The category of the two consciousnesses is called the "universal imputer" (*parikalpa*). Why, then, is it referred to as "this and that" (*tattat*) in the verse? The intent of the commentary is this:

although the category of consciousness consists of only two types, there are many instances where one gives rise to universal imagination (*parikalpa*) with respect to two phenomena, three phenomena, or even up to ten phenomena; therefore, it is said to be "this and that."

Supplement: The fifth fascicle of the *Xuántán* (Profound Discourse) states: Regarding the capacity for pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), there are many objects conceptualized by the sixth and seventh consciousnesses;

first, conditioned; second, unconditioned; third, permanent; fourth, impermanent; fifth, wholesome; sixth, unwholesome; seventh, indeterminate. The eighth consists of: first, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); second, differentiation (*viśeṣa*);

The pleasant and the unpleasant. The ninth [category] is also included within the previously mentioned sixth, termed "that which is subsumed under conceptual construction" (*parikalpita*).

First, what is this thing? Second, how is this thing? Third, what is this? Fourth, how is this? Fifth, it may be the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); Sixth, it may be the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*);
Seventh, it may be the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); Eighth, it may be the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); Ninth, or...
As for the essence of consciousness, there are ten types: that is, based on the five previously mentioned modes of active conceptualization (*parikalpa*), there are further five kinds:

△ Next, the object of pervasive conceptualization (2): first, the heading and inquiry;
next, what is the nature of the object of pervasive conceptualization?
△ Next, the explanation of its characteristics.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)—up to [the point where it is said] because it is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)—is therefore not the object of universal imagination (*parikalpita*).

**Commentary on the Meaning:** This refers to what the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* teaches: the dependent nature is called the "object of universal imagination" because it serves as the object-condition for the mind and other factors of universal imagination.
Question: How can the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) not be the object of that universal imagination?

Regarding "mind and objects": the answer is that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is exclusively real, because it is not the falsely grasped object of the imagined mind (*parikalpita-citta*). As for the explanation based on successive dependence:
this means that the imagined exists by virtue of the dependent nature (*paratantra*), and the actual nature of the dependent is itself the perfected;

therefore, it is said to be based on the sense of successive dependence. It is also that which is the object of the imagined. Question: Since that which is grasped by the imagined is already the imagined mind and so forth...

...the object of that [consciousness]. Why, then, is it not called the "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*)? The commentary states: Although it is the object of that [consciousness], it lacks the status of being an "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*);
therefore, it is not the thoroughly imagined. One should understand that the meaning of an "object-condition" must involve a real, dependently originated phenomenon (*dharmas*).
Now, the self and phenomena as grasped by the parikalpita (imagined) nature—whether they are existent or non-existent, identical or different, both or neither, and so forth—are merely empty flowers;

they possess no distinct, real nature. Because they lack a real nature, they are not objects-of-conditioning (ālambana-pratyaya). Because they are not objects-of-conditioning, they are not that which is imagined.

*Hexiang* (Harmonious Resonance), *Xuantan* (Profound Discourse), Fascicle Five, states: "That which is the object of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) is, in its primary sense, exclusively the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as its direct objective support (*ālambana*).

By way of indirect explanation, it also extends to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because [the latter] serves as its remote objective support. This is not an object within the sphere of ordinary beings."
Therefore, it is not a direct object-condition (*pratyaya*) (text). The *Zongjing* quotes Ci'en as saying: "Among the three natures, this is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

That which is called an 'object-condition' must necessarily be an existent phenomenon (*dharma*). The mind of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) takes this as its condition; that which is the direct image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) is [the dependent nature]."
Because it must depend on the other-dependent nature (*paratantra*), it does not take the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) as its object; this is because they are dissimilar (text).
Regarding the statement that "it is also the object of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) by way of indirect succession," the *Huìxuánjì*, fascicle ten, states:
"Since the perfected nature serves as the basis for the other-dependent nature, when one directly conditions the other-dependent, one also indirectly conditions the perfected nature" (text).
△ Third, clarifying the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) in contrast to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). (2) First, the inquiry:
What are the characteristics of the thoroughly imagined nature, and how does it differ from the dependent nature?

△ Second, the explanation [of the two parts]: First, Sthiramati establishes self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perceived aspect (*grāhyākāra*) as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

According to one interpretation, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the three realms—up to the point where both the grasping subject and the grasped object are termed the imagined nature—are so designated.

Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: This master’s interpretation of the intent is as follows. The contaminated mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) subsumed within the three realms, along with their two aspects—the objective (nimitta-bhāga) and the subjective (darśana-bhāga)—are the parikalpita-svabhāva (the nature of universal imagination).

The essence of the svasaṃvedana-bhāga (the self-verifying aspect), which serves as the substratum for the objective and subjective aspects, is termed the paratantra-svabhāva (the nature of dependence).
Regarding the phrase "How so? and below, he cites scriptural evidence as in the text.

*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance): The *Huixuan ji* (Record of Meeting the Profundity) states that An-hui’s position holds that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) and mental factors (*caitta*) each possess only a single self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), which is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Due to beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), these [minds and factors] arise appearing as if they were the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*) and the object portion (*nimittabhāga*);
however, these exist only according to deluded sentiment and do not exist in reality, for they are all the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Although each of the grasped [objects] is a single entity, the king and his subjects are not one; therefore, it is said they are "respective.
Only the single self-cognizing division (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) is established as the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva); therefore, it is said that its substance is one. (Text)
△ Next, regarding Dharmapāla’s establishment of the four parts of the "king's place," all four rely on the other-dependent nature as the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
(2) First, the formal explanation. (2) First, the dual explanation of the other-dependent and the imagined.
There is an interpretation that all minds and mental factors (up to this point) are what are termed "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Regarding the meaning of the terms:
in the section on the correct meaning, first the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is addressed.

This means that without distinction between the contaminated and the uncontaminated, the defiled and the undefiled, or the mundane and the supramundane—whatever minds and mental factors there may be, whether they are the basis itself or...

The objective and subjective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*) are all dependently originated (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because they arise from conditions through the power of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Regarding the "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*) below: next, the answer concerning the thoroughly imagined nature is as follows.

That is to say, based upon these dependently originated objective and subjective aspects, the mind and its associates falsely cling to a real self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*) as having existence, non-existence, identity, difference, and so forth; only then are they termed the thoroughly imagined nature.
Regarding the phrase "The pervasive conceptualization depends upon this resonance," the *Huìxuánjì* states:

Based on these two divisions of the perceived (*nimitta*) and the perceiving (*darśana*), one falsely and stubbornly clings to them as being definitively real—asserting they are existent, non-existent, both existent and non-existent, neither existent nor non-existent;
or that they are identical, different, both identical and different, or neither identical nor different. It is through these two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) that...

The name is called the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the nature of universal imagination). Supplement: The *Ghanavyūha Sūtra* states: "The name is the *parikalpita-nature*; the characteristic is the *paratantra-origination*.
When both name and characteristic are discarded, this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)."
△ Next, the specific proof for the dependent nature (in two parts). First, the citation of scriptural authority as proof:
All the holy teachings state that "only consciousness" and "only the two [natures]" (up to the point where they) all explain these as being subsumed within the dependent nature.

Commentary on Terms: "Only-cognition" (*vijñapti-mātra*): The *Liang* commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that there is only the measure of consciousness, because external objects do not exist.

"Only-two": This refers to the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), as they are both subsumed within consciousness. "Various kinds": This refers to the various aspects of the seeing-part and so forth belonging to the different consciousnesses.
"The four factors beginning with 'aspect' (*nimitta-ādi-catur-dharma*)": "Aspect" (*nimitta*) is equivalent to the [remaining] three parts. The eleven consciousnesses.

Regarding this, the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states: "Namely, the body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*), the consciousness of the one who possesses the body (*dehavat-vijñāna*), the consciousness of the experiencer (*bhoktṛ-vijñāna*), the consciousness of what is to be experienced (*bhojya-vijñāna*), the consciousness of actual experience (*bhoga-vijñāna*), the consciousness of time (*kāla-vijñāna*), the consciousness of number (*saṃkhyā-vijñāna*), the consciousness of location (*sthāna-vijñāna*), the consciousness of speech (*abhilāpa-vijñāna*), the consciousness of the distinction between self and other (*sva-para-bheda-vijñāna*), and the consciousness of birth and death within the two paths of good and evil (*śubhāśubha-dvayagati-saṃsāra-vijñāna*).
Among these, the nine consciousnesses beginning with 'body' arise from the seeds of the habitual perfuming of names and expressions (*nāma-vyavahāra-vāsanā-bīja*). Self and other...

Regarding the "discriminating consciousness": it arises from the seeds of the habitual tendencies of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). The latter [consciousness] arises from the seeds of the habitual tendencies of the existence-constituent (*bhava-aṅga*).
That treatise explains: "The body-consciousness refers to the five elements beginning with the eye. The 'body' consciousness refers to the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*).
The 'experiencer' consciousness refers to the mind-element (*mano-dhātu*). The 'object-to-be-experienced' consciousness refers to the six external objects, such as form. The 'actual experience'..."
Cognition (*vijñāna*) refers to the six consciousness-elements (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu*). Worldly cognition refers to the continuous succession of births without interruption.

Numerical cognition refers to calculation from one up to the infinite. Spatial cognition refers to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*). Verbal cognition refers to the four kinds of verbal expression: seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
Cognition of the distinction between self and others refers to the arising [of beings] in the two paths of good and evil based on the distinctions of their physical bodies.

The consciousness of death refers to the immeasurable varieties of rebirth destinies. Such consciousnesses are all explained in the treatises as being subsumed under false conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*);
they are termed the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance), *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source), Fascicle 78. Question: If both the internal and external are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and both mind and objects are empty, why does the teaching further establish the existence of external forms?

Answer: It is because one realizes the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) that one then discusses consciousness-only. If one clings to the existence of characteristics, the meaning of consciousness-only is not established;
if one clings to the absence of characteristics, the principle of true emptiness (*tathatā*) is not revealed. By means of the absence of characteristics...

When characteristics are realized as such, one then attains the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*); when characteristics are realized as being without characteristics, one finally clarifies consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the principle of consciousness-only must clarify three aspects: first, the thorough realization that external objects do not truly exist, and are merely mental representations;
second, the thorough realization that both the grasped aspect (*nimitta*) and the grasping aspect (*darśana*) are consciousness-only; and third, the thorough realization of the various [aspects].
Form arises; it possesses various appearances, yet lacks intrinsic substance (text).
△ Next, the proof by establishing the principle:

[If it were] not so, then regarding the category of post-attainment uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*)... [up to] ...one must understand that the contaminated (*sāsrava*) is likewise not admitted [to be non-existent].

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: If it is asserted that the two aspects—the objective (nimitta) and the subjective (darśana)—are not the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) but definitely belong to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), then the two aspects of the objective and subjective within the category of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) would also have to be called the imagined nature.
If this were admitted as being of the imagined nature, it would follow that it is not an object of noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*), because noble wisdom is not a mind of imagination.

Therefore, since that which takes those [aspects] as its object belongs to the category of wisdom, it should be the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) and not the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

One must understand that while the two untainted (*anāsrava*) portions are not admitted to be the imaginatively constructed (*parikalpita*), the two tainted (*sāsrava*) portions likewise are not the imaginatively constructed.

*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance) states: **Inference 1:** The category of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is the subject (*dharmin*). It should not be the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), according to our thesis. The reason (*hetu*) is:

because it is admitted to take the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as its object. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: like the category of tainted minds (*sāsrava-citta*). **[Response:]** This is not accepted [by us].
**Inference 2:** The two parts of the category of tainted minds are not of the imputed nature, because they are dependently originated (*paratantra-svabhāva*). The example is: like untainted wisdom.

△ Next, the refutation of the preceding [position]:
Furthermore, if these two parts were the parikalpita-svabhāva (the imagined nature), then by extension it should also be so for [the other two natures], because there is no reason for distinction.

When spoken of according to their phenomenal characteristics, the three *tathatās* associated with the suffering and origin [of the *saṃkleśa*] belong to the former two natures [the imagined and dependent], while the remaining four *tathatās* belong to the perfected nature.
△ III. The Mutual Inclusion of the Three Natures and the Six Dharmas (II) 1. First, the Question:
How do the three natures and the six dharmas mutually include one another?
△ Next, the Answer:
Within those six dharmas, all three natures (trisvabhāva) are fully present (up to: because they all possess the nature of being produced from conditions through the mechanism of false attachment).

Regarding the gloss on the meaning: "all possess false attachment," etc., means that, for example, within form (rūpa), to conceive of a real self (ātman) or to conceive of real dharmas is the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva);
that form arises from conditions is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva); and that the nature of form is itself empty is the... [perfected nature].

The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is as explained regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); the same applies to the meaning of the four aggregates beginning with sensation (*vedanā*). The meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is seen in the preceding text.
△ Fourth, the inclusion of the five categories (*pañcavastu*): (2) First, the question.
How are the three natures and the five categories mutually inclusive?
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 72: "What are the five categories? First, the characteristic; second, the name."
Third, discrimination; fourth, suchness; fifth, correct wisdom. What is the characteristic? It refers, in brief, to all things that serve as the basis for conventional discourse.
What is the name? It refers to the designations applied to those very characteristics. What is discrimination?
It refers to all minds and mental factors within the activities of the three realms. What is suchness?
It refers to that which is manifested by the non-existence of "mine" (*anātman*), the domain of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), and not an object that serves as a basis for any conventional discourse.
What is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)? Briefly, there are two kinds: first, exclusively supramundane right knowledge;
second, mundane-supramundane right knowledge. What is called exclusively supramundane right knowledge? It is that by which—
Therefore, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas alike penetrate suchness.

Furthermore, because of this, those Bodhisattvas skillfully cultivate the means within the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and frequently abide in the wisdom of the all-pervading suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatājñāna*).
Consequently, they swiftly realize the complete purification of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). What are called the mundane and supramundane [phenomena]?

Right Knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). This refers to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who, having first realized *tathatā* (suchness) through initial right knowledge, subsequently employ both mundane and supramundane right knowledge regarding the established truths (*vyavasthita-satya*) to cause the mind to feel revulsion toward the faults of the three realms and to find delight in the tranquility of the three realms.
Furthermore, by dwelling predominantly in this state, they swiftly realize [the fruit].

It brings to perfection the purification of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, this very wisdom is called "supramundane" (*lokottara*) because its object is a meaning never before attained.
It is also called "mundane" (*laukika*) because it takes the characteristics of verbal expression as its objective domain. Therefore, it is described as both mundane and supramundane. (Text)
△ Next, the response (in three parts): first, the general indication.
The various sacred teachings state that the mutual inclusion [of categories] is not fixed.
△ Next, the detailed explanation (in four parts): the first two explain how the two natures include the five [aggregates].

This means that in certain places it is taught that from the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature) up to the four types of things produced from conditions, all are subsumed under the *paratantra*.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: first, the text is cited; below that, the underlying intent is explained. Initially, it clarifies that the first three items are subsumed under the defiled *paratantra*.
"Transforming into what is signified" refers to the meaning of what is spoken; "transforming into what signifies" refers to the various forms of language.

The "outflow-free" (anāsrava) refers to the lower level of luminous purity within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which collectively clarifies correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*). Therefore, it is summarized by stating that "the four [factors] arising from conditions are all subsumed under the dependent nature.
As for why the imagined nature (*parikalpita*) does not include the five categories: it is because they are like flowers in the sky, and because they lack substantial reality.

The *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Manifestation of the Teachings) states: "The self-characteristic of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita*) is non-existent, because it is not subsumed within the five categories (*pañcavastu*).
△ Second, the three natures subsume the five;

alternatively, there are places where it is said that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)—up to [the inclusion of] the two types of non-perversion—is subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)."
*Yinyi* (Explanations of Terms): First, the cited text; "That which is taught below" indicates the underlying intent. *Buyi* (Supplement):
Regarding the "thoroughly imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it encompasses only those names. The *Xianyang lun* (Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra-śāstra) asks:
"If the thoroughly imagined characteristic has no intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*), how can it give rise to thorough imagining? The answer is: "It is because the name [relates] to the object."
Because it revolves; that is to say, it flows toward objects according to those conventional designations.
Worldly fools grasp at names and meanings as having a fixed correspondence with a truly existent intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Question: How should one know that this is a false attachment?
Answer: Because the two are mutually adventitious. Why is this so? Because the name does not correspond to the essence of the object. Thus it is said:
Regarding their being "guests," the principle is likewise according to their name: because they possess nothing [of their own], they are said to be guests. The verse says:
Not subsumed by the five categories, And beyond these, nothing else exists; Because names operate upon objects, The two are mutually guests of one another.
△ The three natures encompass the five [categories].
In some places it is said that the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is established according to conventional sentiment as the two things: name (*nāman*) and sign (*nimitta*).
**Commentary on the Meaning:** First, the text is cited; below, the underlying intention of that statement is set forth.
△ Section Four: The Two Natures Encompass the Two [Truths].

Furthermore, there are passages stating that names belong to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); [these] refer to the fact that while the substance is not truly existent, the designation of the object is conventionally established.

**Commentary on the Meaning:** First, the text is cited; below, the underlying intent of that statement is revealed: it demonstrates that the dependent nature encompasses those expressive designators (*vācaka*).
The name [itself] is the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), which subsumes the referential objects it denotes; for the object is itself the characteristic (*nimitta*).
△ Third, the summary and indication:
The five categories (*pañcavastu*) as explained in various sacred teachings—up to [the point where they are] as extensively taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*—should be understood accordingly.
Commentary on the Meaning (*Yinyì*): The five categories taught in the four preceding scriptural passages, though their phrasing differs, do not in fact contradict one another in meaning;
therefore, all are consistent with reason. Nevertheless, the first explanation is particularly exhaustive. As it says in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
"Among the five dharmas, how many are subsumed within the first intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? The answer is: "None at all."
How many [factors] are subsumed under the second nature? Answer: Four are subsumed. How many are subsumed under the third nature?
Answer: One is subsumed. The details are as explained in volumes 72, 73, and 74 of that treatise.
△ 5. The Mutual Inclusion of the Five [Characteristics] and the Five Aspects (2). First, the Question:
Furthermore, in the holy teachings it is said that there are five aspects; how are these related to the inclusion of the three natures?

Explanatory Notes on the Terms: Regarding the five characteristics: first, the characteristic of that which is expressed; second, the characteristic of that which expresses; third, the characteristic of the relationship between these two;
fourth, the characteristic of attachment; and fifth, the characteristic of non-attachment. Their meanings are as explained in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
△ Next, the answer:

Both the expressed (the signified) and the expresser (the signifier) each possess the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), because [the ultimate] has untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*) and so forth as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Commentary on the Meaning: First, the characteristics of both the expresser and the expressed are clarified. The first phrase provides the heading; the section beginning with "namely, the delusory... provides the detailed explanation.

The three natures (*trisvabhāva*). That is to say, if one falsely clings to the existence of real characteristics of the signifier and the signified, these belong to the category of the imagined (*parikalpita*).

The characteristic (*nimitta*), the name (*nāman*), and conceptualization (*vikalpa*)—these three, as they correspondingly establish the relationship between the signifier and the signified, belong to the category of the dependent (*paratantra*). True suchness (*tathatā*) is the signified.
Correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) serves as the signifier; therefore, it is said that "according to what is appropriate," there are two kinds, like wisdom itself.
The characteristics of the signifier and the signified established according to their respective applications are subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Question:

Since correct wisdom and suchness (*tathatā*) are free from mental activity and names, how can there be the name of a signifier? Explanation: Although correct wisdom and suchness are free from names, nevertheless...
Subsequently, when wisdom explains the Dharma for others, it is designated by the name "wisdom as such" (*yathā-jñāna*); thus, there is that which expresses it (*vācaka*).

Regarding the phrase "the two are mutually connected," this next section clarifies that the third characteristic belongs exclusively to the first nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because the characteristics of the expressed (*vācya*) and the expresser (*vācaka*), which are falsely grasped, are invariably and mutually bound together. Regarding the phrase "being clung to," this clarifies the fourth characteristic: being clung to.

The "clinging" refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) themselves; because they are grasped by the imaginatively constructed mind (*parikalpa-citta*), they constitute the "object of imagination" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and are therefore subsumed solely within the "dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Below, the phrase "non-clinging" clarifies the fifth characteristic.

"Non-clinging" refers to the mind and mental factors that, being free from imaginative construction (*parikalpa-graha*), become untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and so forth; thus, they belong exclusively to the "perfected nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
△ 6. The Subsumption of the Four Realities within the Three Natures (2). First, the question:
Furthermore, regarding the teachings in the Noble Scriptures, how are the four realities subsumed within these three natures?
**Explanatory Notes on the Four Realities:** The *Xianyang lun* (Manifestation of the Doctrine) states: First, the reality of the world; second, the reality of principle;
third, the reality that is the object of knowledge purified of the afflictive obscurations; and fourth, the reality that is the object of knowledge purified of the cognitive obscurations.
Regarding the "reality of the world": this refers to all worldly beings who, through habitual practice, [perceive] various phenomena as they appear.
The conventional nature of the designations for the knowledge and vision attained through realization is as follows: regarding earth, one says it is "only earth" and not fire or other elements;

likewise for water, fire, wind, form, odor, taste, and tangibility. These are determined by names and expressions transmitted from antiquity, and are mutually accepted as real through the conceptualizations of oneself and others.
They are not objects apprehended through the investigation of false mental constructions. This is...

This is called worldly reality (*loka-tattva*). Regarding the reality of reasoning (*yukti-tattva*): it refers to those who possess correct knowledge; those who are wise regarding matters that accord with reason;
those who possess their own eloquence while remaining in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); and those who practice according to investigation.

It consists of the objects known and the sphere of activity of the definitive wisdom that has been well-analyzed by means of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, direct perception, inference, and authoritative scripture. By means of these...
Because it is established by means of the principle of proof through causes and conditions as they truly are, this is called the reality of principles (*yukti-tattva*).
Regarding the reality of the sphere of activity of the purified wisdom that removes the afflictive obscurations:

this refers to the objects of engagement for the untainted preparatory wisdom, the untainted correct wisdom, and the mundane wisdom subsequently attained from the untainted [wisdom] of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
This is called the reality that is the object of knowledge purified of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

As for the reality that is the object of knowledge purified of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it refers to the domain of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) which pertains to all phenomena as being of an ineffable intrinsic nature;

this is [the object] for Bodhisattvas and Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who are entering into the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), as well as those who have already entered it and are utterly pure.

The realm (*dhātu*). This is called the reality that is the object of the purified wisdom regarding the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa-viśuddha-jñāna-gocara-tattva*). It is explained at length as stated therein.

△ Next, the answer [to the question] concerning the reality established by worldly reasoning (*loka-yukti-siddha-tattva*) [extends] until [the point where it is stated that] the latter two realities belong exclusively to the third.

Explanation of Terms: The first two realities are subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because they are comprised of the three factors of characteristics, names, and conceptualization.

The latter two realities are subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because they are comprised of the two factors of correct cognition and suchness. This concludes the discussion on the superior and inferior [levels].
Citing the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, this explains the meaning of the different categories:

the principle that "defilement and purification, whether involving grasping or being free from grasping, are pervasive" means that the sense of defilement involving grasping pertains to the *parikalpita* (imagined) and *paratantra* (dependent) natures, while purification free from grasping belongs to the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) nature.
△ 7. The Mutual Inclusion of the Seven [Categories] and the Four Noble Truths (2) First, the Question:
How do the three natures and the four noble truths mutually include one another?
△ Next, the Answer (3) First, the General Statement.
Each of the four truths possesses all three natures.
Next, the specific explanation [of the four truths]: first, the three natures within the truth of suffering.

Regarding the four aspects of the truth of suffering, such as impermanence and so forth, their intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is that which is manifested by the absence of a self (*anātman*).
Commentary on the Terms: The first sentence provides the general outline. From "Impermanence" (*anitya*) downward, the four contemplations are explained individually, each with three aspects.

First, regarding the three aspects of impermanence: (1) contemplating that both self and phenomena are of an impermanent nature; (2) contemplating that dependent origination involves arising and ceasing;

(3) contemplating that there is no purity during times of defilement and no defilement during times of purity, as they transform according to their respective stages. Regarding suffering (*duḥkha*)...

Next, regarding the three aspects of the contemplation of suffering: first, one contemplates that the five appropriated aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are suffering, because they are the basis for the grasping of the self and of phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).

Second, one contemplates that the phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are suffering, because these are the phenomenal characteristics of the three types of suffering (*tri-duḥkhatā*).

The conjunction of the three contemplations is suffering, meaning that the true dharma is conjoined with suffering. Regarding "emptiness has three [aspects] below," the next section on the three types of emptiness contemplation is as follows:
first, the contemplation of the emptiness of non-existence, because the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist;

second, the contemplation of the emptiness of other-nature, meaning that dependently originated phenomena (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are different from the nature of pervasive conceptualization; third, the contemplation of self-nature.

"Emptiness" refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because its intrinsic nature is suchness (*tathatā*) as manifested by the two kinds of emptiness. Regarding "selflessness" and below, there are next three types of contemplation on selflessness:

first, the contemplation of the selflessness of signlessness (*animitta-nairātmya*), meaning that the signs of a self as imagined by the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) are fundamentally non-existent;

second, the contemplation of the selflessness of the distinct characteristics of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-viśeṣa-nairātmya*), meaning [the absence of a self] in relation to the signs of a self as imagined by the nature of pervasive conceptualization.

Because they are distinct, one contemplates the selflessness of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-nairātmya*). This means that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) has as its intrinsic nature that which is revealed by the absence of "mine" (*nirmama*).

By means of these four contemplations—impermanence and so forth—one counteracts the four types of perversions, such as the notion of permanence and so forth. This is what the practitioner should know.
△ II. The Three Natures of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
The three aspects of the truth of origination are: first, the accumulation of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-samudaya*) (up to) "the suchness (*tathatā*) that has not yet abandoned obstructions.
[Commentary: Regarding the habitual tendencies of grasping at the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), this refers to the grasping at a self and phenomena as being identical, different, or both.
The non-existence of [subject and object] simultaneously and so forth is called the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature). "Grasping" refers to the views that cling to those selves and phenomena.

Regarding the establishment of the term "grasping at their habitual tendencies": although those selves, phenomena, and so forth lack any real substance, when the mind that performs universal imagination (*parikalpa*) clings to the five aggregates and so forth as being a self or phenomena, it perfumes and forms seeds of grasping; these are called "grasping at their habitual tendencies."

"Vāsanā. Thus, although that which is grasped does not exist, it is provisionally established based on the mind that performs the conceptualization; the mind receives the name of the "object," and is therefore called its "vāsanā.
Consequently, the previous explanation of the vāsanā of self-grasping stated: "Question: Is the 'self' a parikalpita (imagined) nature?"
How is the seed planted? The answer is: when one clings to the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth as a self, seeds are infused within those aggregates;

this is called the "habitual tendency of self-clinging" (*ātmagrāhavāsanā*). Regarding karma and afflictions being called "co-arising" (*samutthāna*): it means that karma is initiated by afflictions, and afflictions increase because of karma.
These two act as mutual causes, and thus they experience the same retribution of suffering together; therefore, they are called "co-arising."
Those who have not yet abandoned the hindrances refer to *tathatā* (suchness) while still enmeshed in bondage.
△ Third, the three natures regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
There are three aspects of the Truth of Cessation: first, cessation by intrinsic nature; [omitted]; third, cessation by original nature, which refers to *tathatā*.

Explanatory Notes on the Terms: 1. Cessation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nirodha*): This refers to the non-arising of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). 2. Cessation of the two graspings (*dvaya-grāha-nirodha*):

This refers to the wisdom of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-jñāna*), which causes the non-arising of both the grasped object and the grasping subject. 3. Cessation of original nature (*prakṛti-nirodha*):
This refers to the essence of suchness (*tathatā*), which is primordially quiescent and extinguished.
△ The Three Natures of the Truth of the Path.
Regarding the three aspects of the Truth of the Path: first is the Knowledge of Pervasiveness (*parijñā-jñāna*). [The text continues:

"However, the Knowledge of Pervasiveness also extends to the latter two. (Commentary on the Terms: Regarding how the Knowledge of Pervasiveness also extends to the latter two, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "It should be known that herein...")
Regarding the thoroughly imagined nature, there is only thorough knowledge; regarding the dependent nature, there is both thorough knowledge and permanent abandonment;
regarding the perfected nature, there is both thorough knowledge and realization. Therefore, this one [category] also extends to the latter two.
△ 3. Matching the Three Categories.

The seven [categories], the three, and the three natures are matched and explained in their respective order (up to the end). One should understand according to principle whether they are provisional or substantial.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: "the seven, the three" refers to the four sets of three within the category of suffering (*duḥkha*), because there are three each for origination (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*).

There are seven sets of three. To explain them by assigning them in order: for example, in the first set of three, "impermanence of lack of intrinsic nature" is subsumed under the *parikalpita* (imagined);
"impermanence of arising and ceasing" is subsumed under the *paratantra* (dependent); and "impermanence of the exhaustion of defilements" is subsumed under the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected).

The remaining three sets of six can be understood by analogy with this example. Regarding whether they are provisional or real: among the seven sets of three, only the three belonging to the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) are real and correspond to the three natures (trisvabhāva);
the others are merely assigned to the three natures according to their meaning and are thus provisional. Therefore, it is said that "they should be understood accordingly."
△ 8. The Inclusion of the Three and Eight Liberations (2). First, the question:
How are the objective spheres traversed by the three gates of liberation subsumed within these three natures?
*Hexiang Qingliang Shu*, Scroll 37, Part 2, states: "The three gates of liberation are also called the three samādhis.
'Samādhi' is a name derived from its own essential nature (*svabhāva*), while 'liberation' is a designation based on its function (*paratantra*).
Because these three can lead to the liberation of nirvāṇa, they are called 'gates. (Text; *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Scroll 45).
[The Buddha] said: "What is the bodhisattva’s samādhi of emptiness?

It refers to when bodhisattvas contemplate all phenomena as being devoid of any intrinsic nature of verbal expression, such that there is only the ineffable intrinsic nature of all dharmas, and the mind dwells correctly therein;
this is called the bodhisattva’s samādhi of emptiness. What is the bodhisattva’s samādhi of wishlessness? [It refers to when bodhisattvas...]
"Sā" refers to the equal contemplation of the ineffable intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Because they are grasped by afflictions arising from false discrimination and by various sufferings, they are defiled by immeasurable faults.
With the non-aspiration for the future as the precursor, the mind dwells correctly; this is called the bodhisattva’s *apranihita-samādhi* (the concentration of wishlessness).
The Ground. What is the bodhisattva’s signless samādhi?

It refers to the fact that when bodhisattvas correctly contemplate all phenomena as having an ineffable intrinsic nature, all conceptualizations, proliferations, and signs are forever extinguished and stilled.
To understand things as they truly are, with the mind dwelling in right composure—this is called the bodhisattva’s signless samādhi.
Question: Why are exactly three samādhis established, neither more nor less? Answer: There are two kinds of phenomena, namely existence and non-existence.
Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are termed "existence. The self and what belongs to the self are termed "non-existence. Regarding existence...

Regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*): because it possesses the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and because it is to be reviled and rejected, one should know that the signless (*animitta*) samādhi is established based upon this.
Regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): because one aspires for nirvāṇa and because it is correctly embraced by delight, one should know that the signless samādhi is established based upon this.
Regarding that which is not a functional thing (*avastuka*): the bodhisattva neither aspires nor is without aspiration; however...
Regarding that which does not exist, the bodhisattva perceives it as non-existent according to reality. Based on this perception, one should know that the samādhi of emptiness is established (text).

△ Next, the response: In principle, all three are pervasive; according to their specific characteristics, each is one (up to: because these three, respectively, are the objects of those [three gates]). *Hexiang* (Combined Resonance):
Speaking in terms of ultimate principle (*li*), the three gates of liberation each pervade the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). However, according to their phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)...

Furthermore, each corresponds to one [nature]. The seventy-fourth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Moreover, the three gates of liberation are also established by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
That is to say, the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) is established by virtue of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);

the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*) is established by virtue of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); [the gate of liberation of signlessness is established] by virtue of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)."

Because it is established as being without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) is established. Question: As stated in the sūtras, how is the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) established?

Answer: It is established by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). That is to say, by means of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the patient acceptance of the original non-arising of nature (*prakṛty-anutpatti-kṣānti*) is established;
by means of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), [the patient acceptance of self-] ...is established. (The remainder of the sentence is incomplete in the source text.)

However, the patience regarding non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is established by virtue of the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) as the patience regarding the non-arising of afflictions, suffering, and defilements;

it should be understood that this patience is irreversible (text). As for the statement "these three, in their respective order, are its objects," it means that these three natures are, respectively, the objects of apprehension (ālambana) for these three types of patience.
△ 9. The Subsumption of the Nine [Categories] by the Two Truths (2). First, the question:
How are these three subsumed under those two truths?

*Hongyang lun* (Exposition of the Manifestation of the Doctrine), Fascicle 2, states: "The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) refers to the bodies of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*)."
Furthermore, it includes all verbal expressions based on those meanings, as well as the meanings understood through those verbal expressions;
it also includes the worldly minds and mental factors previously attained, along with the objects and meanings within their sphere of activity.

Ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), however, refers to noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*) and the objects and meanings within its sphere of activity, as well as the minds, mental factors, and so forth associated therewith. (Text)
△ Next, the response:
It should be understood that the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) possesses these three types [of nature], and therefore all are subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

[This is] the "Resonance" (*hexiang*): first, a general indication; "the conventional has three" below is the detailed explanation. As for the "conventional as designation" (*prajñapti-saṃvṛti*), it is precisely the designation (*prajñapti*).
The first is the conventional truth of names without reality, referring to things such as armies, forests, jars, and chariots.

The second is the conventional truth of the differentiation of phenomena, referring to the aggregates, bases, and elements. The third is the conventional truth of manifest establishment, which refers to the truths established through skillful means.

This refers to the truths of suffering, its origin, and so forth, as well as phenomena (*dharma*); these are conventional designations and non-established truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*). This refers to the true reality of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā-tattva*).

They are assigned in the following order: the first is the conventional; external objects do not exist apart from the mind, and names are established based on mental states, with pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) as their essence.

Therefore, the first [nature] subsumes [the first aspect]. The second is the conventional, the objects transformed by the mind, which have the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as their essence;
therefore, it is subsumed by the second nature. The latter is also conventional, the principles transformed by the mind, which are established through conceptual differentiation (*prajñapti-viśeṣa*);

therefore, it is subsumed by the third nature. This is based on the explanation in the tenth fascicle of the *Huìxuán*. Regarding the statement that "there are three types of ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*), one should know that there are two meanings.
Meaning (*artha*). First is the object of meaning; second is the principle of meaning.

Herein, *tathatā* (suchness) is called the "ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha*) because suchness is the object of supreme wisdom (*parama-jñāna*); it is thus an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound), meaning "the meaning of the ultimate.
Regarding *nirvāṇa* being named the "attainment of the ultimate," the *Vyākhyāyukti* on the *Śataśāstra*, fascicle nine, states: "Thus, nirvāṇa is not non-existent..."
It is not existent; it is that which is realized by sublime wisdom and is thus called the ultimate (*paramārtha*).

Furthermore, because it is the most excellent among all objects, and because there is no further object to be sought beyond it, it is called "excellent" (*parama*). Since the "excellent" is itself the "object," this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

The noble path is called "that which has the ultimate as its object" (*paramārtha-gocara*). This refers to the fundamental and subsequent wisdoms (*mūla-anvaya-jñāna*) and so forth belonging to the noble stages (*ārya-avasthā*), because they take the supreme dharma as their objective referent (*ālambana-artha*).
The *Huìxuán* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), fascicle ten, states:

"That untainted true wisdom (*anāsrava-tattva-jñāna*), regardless of which truth it resides within, also takes 'the supreme' as its meaning, because it takes true suchness (*tathatā*) as its object" (text). Because it takes the supreme as its meaning, [it is so designated].

This is the explanation by Master Ci'en. The former two [natures] are based on principle (*li*), while the latter one is based on wisdom (*zhi*). This refers to the unconditioned perfected nature (*asaṃskṛta-pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature that is free from inversion (*viparyāsa-pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);
accordingly, they subsume the third nature [the dependent nature].
△ Ten: The Objects of Knowledge for the Wise and the Ordinary (2). First, the question:
Of what wisdoms are these three natures the objects?
△ Second, the answer.

The thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is entirely not the domain of cognition; [it continues] until: the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is exclusively the object of noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*).
(Echoing the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 74): Question: Regarding the thoroughly imagined nature, what kind of cognition is its domain?
Is it the cognition of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) or the cognition of noble ones (*ārya*)? Answer: It is entirely not their domain, because it is devoid of characteristics (*animitta*).
Question: By what kind of knowledge is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) the object of its activity? Answer: It is the object of activity for two kinds of knowledge;

however, it is not the object of supramundane noble knowledge (*lokottara-āryajñāna*). Question: By what kind of knowledge is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) the object of its activity?
Answer: It is the object of activity for noble knowledge alone (text).
△ 11. The Analysis of the Conventional and the Real (2). First, the question:
Among these three natures (*trisvabhāva*), how many are conventional and how many are real?
△ Second, the answer.

Because the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is falsely established, it can be said to be "provisionally non-existent"; because its characteristic is not provisional, it is neither provisional nor real.
Because the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) exists as reality and exists as the provisional—due to its nature as a collection, a continuity, and various states—it is said to be "provisional.
Because mind, mental factors, and form arise from conditions, they are said to be "real."

(2) First, the general explanation that the three natures are taught with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
The treatise states: "Based precisely on the three natures previously explained... [it] generally explains the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) with respect to both existence and non-existence."

Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: First, the initial two lines are explained. Then, from "Therefore, the Buddha... onwards, the final two lines are explained. Regarding "esoteric intent" (*samdhāya*):
if it were explained explicitly, it would clarify both the three natures and the two absences of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) simultaneously;

this alone constitutes the state that is neither existent nor non-existent. From "That is to say, later... onwards, the subsequent explanation clarifies that although the dependent and perfected natures possess substantial reality, [ordinary] fools...

Based on these [imagined and dependent natures], one falsely gives rise to the attachment that the self and phenomena truly exist. This attachment to a self and to phenomena is precisely the parikalpita (the imagined nature).
To eliminate this, the Buddha taught that both are non-existent.
*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance), *Xuantan* (Profound Discourse), Fascicle Five, states:

"In the third period, according to the correct principle of the Mahāyāna, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the three absences of nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*), and so forth, are fully explained; only then is the principle exhausted. The *Chao* (Excerpts) commentary explains:

"Regarding the 'full explanation of the three natures, the three absences of nature, and so forth,' there are two layers. First, concerning the three natures: in the first period, it was taught from the perspective of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)."

There are two [ways of explaining this]: first, by positing emptiness in relation to the *parikalpita* (imagined nature); second, by fully explaining all three natures, wherein the *parikalpita* is empty and the *paratantra* (dependent) and *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) are existent, thereby constituting the Middle Way.
Furthermore, there are two [other ways]: first, by asserting that all three natures are existent; and second, by asserting that all three lack-intrinsic-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) are empty.

In the first period, it was taught that all three natures exist. In the second period, the general teaching that all phenomena are devoid of nature was spoken with the intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) of the three absences of nature.
This means that if one were to speak in an explicit manner, only by clarifying both the three natures and the three absences of nature would it constitute the Middle Way;
thus, it is the most thorough expression of the principle. Furthermore, the Commentary states: "Therefore, regarding..."
Regarding those three periods: the first falls into the extreme of existence, and the second falls into the extreme of emptiness; neither is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

In the final period, it is fully explained that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is empty, while the other two [natures] exist; thus, by acceding to the Middle Way, it finally becomes definitive meaning.

According to this, the teaching of the three natures of non-existence in the sūtras is the Buddha’s intentional terminology (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*). If discussed in terms of the periods, it is indeed the [third].
The two [earlier] periods fell into teachings that lean toward the extreme of emptiness; these are not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Now, clarifying the correct principle of Mahāyāna Vijñaptimātra, one must understand that among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the dependent (*paratantra*) and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) are existent, while the imagined (*parikalpita*) is empty—only then is this the Middle Way of definitive meaning.
