and third, the morality of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*). Among these, one should understand that the morality of restraint is established for the sake of the [other] two types of morality; thus, it gathers virtuous dharmas...
Regarding the ethical discipline (*śīla*): one should understand that the ethical discipline for gathering all Buddha-dharmas has the sense of establishing them;

the ethical discipline for benefiting sentient beings should be understood as having the sense of establishing the maturation of all sentient beings. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, fascicle seven, explains:
"The distinction of excellence means that Bodhisattvas possess three types of ethical discipline, namely the vows of restraint (*saṃvara*) and so forth, whereas Śrāvakas..."

Regarding the vehicles and so forth, there is only one kind of restraint, which is ethical discipline (*śīla*). Therefore, in comparison to those [other vehicles], the Bodhisattva’s discipline is superior.
The restraint of the vow (*saṃvara-śīla*) refers to correctly undertaking the distancing from all categories of evil and unwholesome phenomena.

The restraint of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) refers to correctly cultivating all Buddha-dharmas, such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). The restraint of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*)...

This means that, disregarding one's own pleasure, one leads others—according to their respective capacities—to enter the three vehicles, so that they may abandon the suffering of saṃsāra and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

Regarding the statement that "the ethics of restraint (saṃvara-śīla) should be understood as the basis for the establishment of the two types of ethics," this is because it is the cause of those two ethics;
that is to say, if one guards the body, speech, and mind, one is then able to practice all forms of purity without error.
The Buddha-dharma can also bring all sentient beings to maturity and cause them to enter the three vehicles; other [teachings] cannot do so. The treatise states:

Regarding the distinction between common and uncommon training rules, it means that because Bodhisattvas do not manifest any natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), they share these with the Śrāvakas;
yet because they do manifest certain similar prohibited transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), they differ from them. In this regard...
Regarding these training rules, there are those that a śrāvaka violates while a bodhisattva does not, and those that a bodhisattva violates while a śrāvaka does not.
This is because a bodhisattva possesses the ethical discipline of body, speech, and mind, whereas a śrāvaka possesses only the two disciplines of body and speech.
Therefore, a bodhisattva may also commit a transgression of the mind, which is not the case for śrāvakas. In brief, all that is for the benefit of sentient beings [is the domain of the bodhisattva].
Bodhisattvas should practice and train in all instances where bodily, verbal, and mental actions are blameless;
this is how it should be understood. This is called the distinction between the common and the uncommon. The treatise states:

Regarding the distinction of profundity, it refers to the fact that through such categories of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), bodhisattvas perform the ten types of actions, including killing and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no fault; immeasurable merit is generated, and one swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Moreover, it should be understood that when Bodhisattvas manifest the two types of karma—transformed body and speech—these are also śīla (ethical discipline). For this reason, [they are included].
Or he may become a king, manifesting various acts that afflict sentient beings in order to establish them within the discipline (*vinaya*).
Furthermore, he manifests various *jātaka* tales, appearing to oppress and distress other sentient beings while truly gathering them in;
first causing their minds to give rise to deep pure faith, and subsequently bringing them to maturity. This is...
This is called the profound and supreme ethical discipline (*śīla*) studied by Bodhisattvas.

The treatise states that it is "vast and supreme" because it possesses four kinds of vastness. An-hui’s commentary explains: "The vastness of the various and immeasurable training rules (*śikṣāpada*)."
It refers to the various categories and immeasurable distinctions of the ethical discipline (*śīla*) studied by bodhisattvas, which is so vast because it encompasses immeasurable merit.
It is vast because this ethical discipline can encompass the provisions of immeasurable merit;
it is vast because it encompasses the intention to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
Regarding "vastness": it means that this ethical discipline (*śīla*) encompasses all sentient beings;

it pertains to this world and other worlds, to the mundane and the supramundane, and to the abandonment of evil and the adoption of good, whether in terms of cause or fruit. It is vast because its underlying intention is to bring benefit.
Regarding the "vastness" of establishing unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment: it means that this ethical discipline establishes great enlightenment; therefore, it is vast.
Great! The various śrāvakas and others do not possess such things; therefore, it is "superior" (text).
Next, the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*).
There are four types of concentration: first, the Mahāyāna Radiance Concentration (*mahāyāna-prabhāsa-samādhi*)... [up to] the elicitation of activities as explained elsewhere.

**Explanation of Terms:** The meaning of "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle) is explained as usual. "Radiance" (*prabhā*) is a name derived from a metaphor; the metaphor itself fully integrates both essence (*tattva*) and function (*vṛtti*).
It is that which can produce and illuminate the wisdom of principle, teaching, practice, and fruit. "Principle" refers to the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two kinds of emptiness.
"Teaching" refers to sounds, names, phrases, and syllables. "Practice" refers to the various *pāramitās*. "Fruit" refers to *bodhi* (enlightenment) and *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the "Samādhi of the King Who Accumulates Merit" (*Puṇyasaṃbhārarāja-samādhi*): "King" (*rāja*) signifies the sense of sovereignty.
This samādhi can accumulate boundless merit, just as a king possesses great sovereignty and great power, enabling him to amass vast wealth such that none can equal him.

As for "Worthy Protector" (*Bhadrapāla*) and "Vigorous Practice" (*Kṣemankara*), these two are as explained in their respective texts. Regarding the statement that "the objects of these four are as described elsewhere," it refers to what has been taught in other passages.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: Regarding the distinction of the object of focus (*ālambana-viśeṣa*), it refers to the Mahāyāna Dharma as the object of focus.

Regarding the distinction of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-viśeṣa*), it refers to the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), according to the principle of "using one wedge to extract another wedge."

Regarding the differentiation of capacity: it refers to the ability to abide in the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and to take rebirth according to one’s wish, because all heavy burdens of affliction (*dausthulya*) within the *ālayavijñāna* have been eliminated. Regarding the differentiation of manifestation:
it refers to the ability to manifest unimpeded supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) throughout all worlds. Regarding the differentiation of activity: it refers to the ability to... shake... [the world].
It is mobile, blazing, pervasive, and manifest; it undergoes transformation, comes and goes, and expands and contracts. All forms and images enter into his body.

Among those of similar kind whom he approaches, he may appear or remain hidden. His actions are sovereign, subduing the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of others, bestowing eloquence, mindfulness, and joy, and emitting great radiance.
Because he has brought forth such great supernormal powers, the meaning is as explained in the *Nirabhilāpyadharmatā-sūtra*.

The *Comprehensive Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (Shèlùn Guǎngjiě), "Harmonious Resonance" (Héxiǎng), explains that there are four [stages] of training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*), with three interpretations. Master Ying states: "The first concentration eliminates the obstacle of unwholesomeness;

the second eliminates the obstacle of attachment; the third eliminates the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); and the fourth eliminates the obstacle of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Master Xuánxī states: "The first..."

1. It can eliminate the obstacle of karmic hindrances associated with the outflows and defilements. 2. It can eliminate the obstacle of attachment to the flavor of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

3. It can eliminate the obstacle of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). 4. It can eliminate the obstacle to the pure fruit-wisdom (*phala-jñāna*). These are largely the same as previously explained. Qingliang says:

"This means that by means of the wisdom that realizes the reality within phenomena (*dharmatā*), one remedies the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi, accomplishing the first bhūmi so that one attains 'Worthy Guard' (*Bhadra-pāla*)."
Concentration (*samādhi*). Because by means of this samādhi, one is able to maintain the virtuous and wholesome dharmas of both the mundane and the supramundane:

the first three stages constitute the mundane, while the fourth stage constitutes the supramundane. This is because, having realized that phenomena are themselves reality, one is able to remain concentrated even amidst distraction.
Second, through the wisdom of the function inherent in the essence, one counteracts the fourth stage’s inability to initiate activity, thereby enabling it to attain [such capacity].

In the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), one enters into the mundane world and achieves the Samādhi of the King who Accumulates Merit. Third, by means of the wisdom of equality and signlessness, one counteracts [the obstacles of] the fifth stage;
although one can conform to worldly conventions, one has not yet attained equality, so this brings about the sixth and seventh stages.

Through the functional power of the great light of Prajñā, one achieves the Mahāyāna Radiance Samādhi. Fourth, by means of the wisdom of equality and effortlessness (*anābhoga*), one counteracts the seventh stage.

The effort of the stages (bhūmi-prayoga) causes one to enter the eighth stage and proceed up to the fruit of Buddhahood, whereby one attains the Śūraṅgama-samādhi and brings all that is to be done to completion.
Since the fruit possesses these four [qualities] and the cause likewise involves the cultivation of them all, this interpretation is correct.
△ Section Three: Training in Wisdom (2). First, the correct elucidation of the characteristics of the three types of wisdom.

There are three types of training in wisdom: first, the wisdom of application and non-conceptualization (*prāyogika-nirvikalpa-jñāna*)... [the objects, modes of activity, and so forth, as explained elsewhere].
Regarding the meaning of the terms: "Preparatory non-conceptual wisdom" (*prayoga-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is explained in Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* as the wisdom of investigation (*vitarka*).
It is also said to be the wisdom of aspiration. Because it can give rise to non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), it also receives the name "non-conceptual.
"Fundamental non-conceptual wisdom" (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is explained in the *Saṃgraha-bhāṣya* as the wisdom of direct realization (*sākṣāt-kriyā*). It is also said that...

This is the wisdom of internal realization (*pratyātma-jñāna*). Furthermore, it is said that preparatory application (*prayoga*) is the cause of this wisdom, while subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is its fruit.

Regarding subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* explains it as the wisdom that initiates activity (*vyavahāra-pravartaka-jñāna*), and further describes it as the wisdom that maintains and upholds (*dhāraṇa-jñāna*).
This is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) following non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); therefore, it is also designated by the name "non-conceptual.

Regarding these three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the *Wuxing* (Exposition of Non-nature) states: "It means that with respect to the true meaning (*tattvārtha*), one does not engage in divergent conceptualization (*parikalpa*), taking this as their nature.

As for the basis (*āśraya*) of these three, it refers to non-conceptual wisdom; because the mind that serves as its basis is beyond discursive thought (*acintya*), it is neither [conceptual] nor non-[conceptual].

The mind is the basis of support because it is of the same nature as the mind; taking the mind as its cause, through the power of repeated cultivation, one attains this state, which is called "of the nature of the mind.
This demonstrates that the mind which is the support of wisdom transcends all conceptualization and discrimination.
Regarding these three causes and conditions, Wu-xing’s commentary states: "This means being perfumed by the sounds and words of the Mahāyāna."

It is the cultivation of hearing. Through the specific virtues induced by this, as well as through correct mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*) and so forth—these three objects of focus (*ālambana*) are:
all persons (*pudgala*), and the suchness (*tathatā*) manifested by the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) of all phenomena (*dharma*).
Liberation is the transcendence of the two extremes of increase and decrease; this is the objective sphere (*ālambana-viṣaya*) of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Regarding these three modes of activity (*ākāra*), Asvabhāva’s commentary states: "Because it acts in accordance with its objective sphere, it is called a mode of activity of non-conceptual wisdom.
Because it acts in accordance with the sphere of suchness (*tathatā*), it is free from all mental attention to signs (*nimitta-manasikāra*)."
Regarding the aspect of practice (*ākāra*): as for the distinctions among the aspects of the three wisdoms, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"For example, it is like a mute person who seeks to experience an object but is unable to experience it, nor can they express it.

In this way, non-conceptual wisdom of application (*prayoga*) seeks to realize suchness (*tathatā*), yet is unable to realize it; it is quiescent and beyond verbal expression. One should know that it is likewise so. Furthermore,
Just as a mute person, while experiencing objects, has nothing to express, so too should one know that fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*),
which directly realizes *tathatā* (suchness), is likewise free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Just as a non-mute person experiences various objects and also gives rise to speech,
so too does subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) reflect back upon *tathatā* and realize it through direct manifestation.
The objective sphere (*viṣaya*) that can give rise to verbal teaching should be understood in the same way. As for the term "equal" (*sama*), it refers to these three [aspects]:
whether as support (*ādhāra*), as accompaniment (*sahāya*), or as maturation (*vipāka*), etc., as explained at length in the eighth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*;
they are not recorded here in detail to avoid prolixity.
△ Next, the presence or absence [of these wisdoms] is explained according to the stages.

Thus, regarding the three types of wisdom, within the first two stages (up to the point where it says) because both the seeds and the manifest states of the preparatory application have already been abandoned.

*Commentary on the Meaning*: "The first two" refers to the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*) and the stage of application (*prayoga*). Within these two stages, the seeds of all three types of wisdom are present.

There are [wisdoms present], because they possess the naturally existing (dharmatā) untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*). As for why only the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*) is manifest [in the stage of preparation]:

it is because one has not yet realized *tathatā* (suchness), and thus lacks both the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭha-jñāna*). As for why only the fundamental and subsequent wisdoms are manifest during the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*):

it is because, within the fifteen moments of mind of the initial path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one has just realized *tathatā* and thus lacks the wisdom of application. Within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), there are both.
Regarding the distinction in meaning: from the sixteenth moment of mind in the path of seeing up through the seven stages (*bhūmi*), both seeds and manifestations are all threefold.
This is because within each stage prior to the seventh, there exist the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and special progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
From the eighth stage onward, manifestations are only twofold, because they are effortless (*anābhoga*) and do not depend upon preparatory application (*prayoga*).
"Because of superior progress. If that is so, by means of what wisdom does one advance toward the subsequent stage? The commentary states:

"By means of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one performs uncontaminated contemplation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*) and spontaneously advances to enter the remaining stages. Regarding the phrase "in the ultimate stage, both the manifest and the seeds are abandoned":

this refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) following the vajra-path (*vajra-mārga*), wherein both the seeds of preparatory application (*prayoga*) and [the seeds of the afflictions] are relinquished.
△ Next, the mutual inclusion is explained.

If categorized by their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), ethical discipline (*śīla*) includes only ethical discipline; concentration (*samādhi*) includes meditative absorption (*dhyāna*); and wisdom (*prajñā*) includes the final five [perfections].
In this context, there are four types of mutual inclusion. Regarding inclusion by intrinsic nature: that which co-arises is not taken [as the defining characteristic].
Regarding the meaning of "associates" (*sahāya*): these are stated merely by citing their respective essential natures; thus it is said that "precept only encompasses precept," and so forth.
If they were to encompass one another including their associates, then each of these three would encompass all ten of the preceding [perfections].

If, however, they encompass one another according to their specific functions, then precept encompasses the first three: giving is the provision (*sambhāra*), while precept is the essential body (*svabhāva*).

Patience is a concomitant attribute of ethical discipline (*śīla*). If one were to categorize them according to their manifest characteristics, ethical discipline would subsume the first four perfections.
The first three are as previously described; furthermore, it includes diligence (*vīrya*), because through the power of diligence, one guards against and prevents wrongdoing.
This is for the purpose of purifying the precepts.
△ Eleven: The Gate of Cultivating All Five Stages.
These ten stages are all complete within the five stages (extending to): whether manifest or latent, they are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: Among the characteristics that are most manifest within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), it is as the Sūtra says:

"For a Bodhisattva of the first ground (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is preeminent," and so forth, up to the tenth ground, which states: "In this stage, the Bodhisattva..."
Regarding the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*), it is "supreme" and so forth; this signifies its preeminence.
However, from the beginning downward, these ten practices are further explained through five stages to show that they encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

As for the statement that the sudden-awakening bodhisattva’s seeds belong to both types while their manifestations are exclusively contaminated, one should understand that there is a class of bodhisattvas who, within the first two stages, are [overcome] by afflictions (*kleśa*).
Knowing that the seeds and manifest forms of the two obstacles have not yet been subdued or extinguished, one directly ascends to the first bhūmi;

because one suddenly severs both the seeds and manifest forms of the two obstacles of conceptualization, this is called "sudden awakening. Within the first two stages, the superior practices cultivated—whether manifest or latent—are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).
As for the statement that "seeds also include the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)," this refers to the innate uncontaminated seeds (*dharmatā-anāsrava-bīja*).

Furthermore, regarding the Bodhisattvas of gradual awakening whose seeds and manifestations in the first two stages are both associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) and free from outflows (*anāsrava*): this refers to those prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*).

Because they have already suppressed the manifest arising of conceptual afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*), and because their ten practices (*daśapratipatti*) are associated with the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-darśana*), they are thus associated with the state free from outflows.

Nevertheless, as for the manifest arising of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), these have not yet been eternally extinguished; therefore, they are also associated with that which possesses outflows.

"Leakage is subsumed [by the two obstacles]. In the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*), they manifest as exclusively non-leaking (*anāsrava*) because the seeds of the two obstacles of conceptualization have already been severed.
In the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), they are again divided into two:

from the first through the seventh grounds, the superior practices cultivated—whether emerging from or entering into the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) or the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)—must pertain to both. From the eighth ground onward, they manifest as exclusively non-leaking."
The fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons arises; because it is purely untainted (*anāsrava*), its status as that of a Buddha may be known.
△ Twelfth: The various names for the causal stages.
These ten causal stages have three types of names (up to the point where they are not yet ultimate because the seeds of affliction remain).
**Explanation of Terms:** The Sanskrit term is *asaṃkhyeya*; this is translated here as "innumerable. It is one of the nine great numerical units.

This means that during the first *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa, although the power of the practices such as giving cultivated by the Bodhisattva over immeasurable time was still slight, they were merely termed *pāramitās*.
At this stage, he had not yet seen their underlying principle; he practiced them through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).

Because they merely possess the name "reaching the other shore" while practicing various sublime deeds, in terms of the stages (*bhūmi*), they belong to the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*).
The second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* is called "near" because at that time the power of giving and the other perfections gradually increases;
however, since one still relies on mental attention (*manasikāra*) to initiate giving and so forth, one has not yet attained effortless abiding (*anābhoga-vihāra*) and does not proceed spontaneously.
Therefore, it is merely called "proximate. In terms of the stages, this refers to the stages of penetration (*prativedha*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*), specifically those prior to the seventh bhūmi.

The practice of giving and so forth cultivated during the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa is called "great" because it can permanently subdue all afflictions (*kleśa*), as the giving and other practices cultivated therein are purely untainted (*anāsrava*). In terms of the stages, this refers to [the stages] from the eighth bhūmi onwards.

"Proceeding" refers to reaching the tenth stage (*bhūmi*). This is explained in detail in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. It should be understood that there is still a distinction between this [stage] and the ultimate state;
the meaning may be inferred accordingly. *Hexiang*:
The second part of the fifth fascicle of the *Cheng weishi lun liaoyi deng* (Clear and Cool Commentary) states: "At the beginning, it is merely called a *pāramitā*."

First, "limited" refers to practicing one type of practice within a single category of practice. Second, "proximate" refers to practicing all types of practices within a single category of practice, as it is close to Bodhi.
Third, "vast" refers to practicing all types of practices within all categories of practice, as its essence is comprehensive and expansive.
However, as long as one has not yet entered the [final] eon, it is equivalent to the first; once Buddhahood has been fully attained, it is equivalent to the third.
(Text). △ Third, the summary and distinction of the practice.
These ten categories of meaning are infinitely diverse, yet they are all subsumed within the ten pāramitās.

Commentary on the Meaning of the Text: First, the formal conclusion of the preceding section; second, the specific determination regarding the "ten" below; third, the subsumption of the extensive details following "although there are ten," etc.—all of which can be understood by the reader’s own reflection.
△ Third, the explanation of the severance of the ten heavy obstacles (in two parts): first, the heading.
Regarding the ten layers of hindrances:

△ Next, the explanation [is divided into] two parts. First, the explicit clarification of the ten hindrances (ten sections). First, the hindrance of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) (three sections).
First, the explicit explanation (two sections). First, a brief explanation of the hindrance.

First, the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*): this refers to [the fact that] among the two obstacles, the nature of an ordinary being is established based upon their seeds.
△ Next, the actual explanation of abandonment (in three parts). First, the detailed explanation of abandoning the two types [of obstacles]. (2) First, the direct exposition.
When the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the two vehicles manifests (up to the point where they) fully sever the two types [of seeds], they are said to have attained the nature of an ārya.

To explain: this obstacle of the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) is established based on the seeds of the two obstacles that arise from conceptual construction (*parikalpita*).
By severing these two types, one attains the nature of an ārya; however, within the stage of the path of seeing of the two vehicles, one severs only those arising from conceptual construction.

The afflictions are of one kind; in the Mahāyāna path of vision (*darśanamārga*), both kinds are severed simultaneously. Thus, there is a distinction between the extensive and the concise regarding the severance of delusions in the Great and Small Vehicles.
△ Next, the objections are explained.
When the second true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) manifests, [the nature of an ordinary being is abandoned]; therefore, there is no fault of the two natures existing simultaneously.
Regarding the meaning of the terms, Master Qingliang’s commentary states: "However, the intention of this treatise is to differ from the Sarvāstivāda school.

According to that school's position, prior to the path of seeing, the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) is abandoned; when the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) arises, it is said to coexist with the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions."

This concludes the refutation. Therefore, to address the objection, one says: If the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) were abandoned prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), then when the untainted fruit arises, there would be no fault of both the ordinary person and the noble one (*ārya*) being simultaneously established.
Now, since it is established based on the seeds to be abandoned by vision, there are still seeds of affliction present during the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*).
Since the ordinary person has not yet abandoned them, how could there be no fault of both the ordinary person and the noble one being simultaneously established? Thus [the objection stands].
It is said that when the Path of Seeing arises, those seeds are no longer established, just as when light appears, it does not coexist with darkness;

thus, there is no fault of the two natures—the ordinary and the noble—being established simultaneously. If, however, the Uninterrupted Path were to coexist with the acquisition of afflictions, there would instead be the fault of the ordinary and the noble being established together.
The seventh fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* also clarifies this point.
Regarding "Harmonizing Resonance" (Hexiang), concerning the two types of True Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the *Qingliang Chao* states:

"It should be that the Great and Small Vehicles constitute the two, because it was stated immediately prior that 'the path of seeing of the two vehicles,' etc.; for both the Great and Small Vehicles sever [afflictions] through the True Path of Seeing. (Text)
△ Next, a concise clarification of the distinct functions of the two paths (2). First, the question:

Since the seeds of afflictions have already been eliminated at the time of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), what further purpose is served by arising the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)?
△ Next, the explanation:

Because the mental orientations regarding the timing of abandoning afflictions and realizing cessation differ... [up to] ...and realizing the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of this category.

(Syllable Meanings): Due to two reasons, after the arising of the *ānantarya-mārga* (path of non-obstruction), one further gives rise to the *vimukti-mārga* (path of liberation). First, the *ānantarya-mārga*.
The goal is the severance of afflictions (*kleśa*); liberation is the goal of realizing the principle (*tattva*). The intended aims of these two minds differ.

The second [mind] is for the sake of abandoning the heavy-obstruction (*dauṣṭhulya*) of those categories of afflictions; here, "heavy-obstruction" refers to lack of functional capacity (*akarmanyatā*), which is abandoned only when the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) arises.

The subsequent section on the "uninterrupted path" (*ānantaryamārga*) explains the preceding meaning by clarifying that one realizes the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding this category [of afflictions].

This clarifies that although the seeds of the afflictions are severed when the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) arises, it is through the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that the principle revealed thereby can be realized.
△ Third, the resolution of the doubt regarding why karma and its results are not mentioned.

Although the arising of the Path of Seeing also severs the evil destinies (up to the point where they can arise), this is because [the Path of Seeing] is the root that gives rise to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding the meaning of the terms: someone asks, "The Sūtras state that when a Bodhisattva attains the Path of Seeing, they also sever the various fruits of the evil destinies as well as the various karmas that induce those evil destinies.
Why, then, is it said here only that one severs the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*)? The intent of the explanation is that [it is because] the afflictions...
These two are the fundamental roots of karma and its fruit. Since the root subsumes the branches, karma and its fruit are omitted here and not explicitly mentioned.
△ Next, the scriptural evidence is cited:

"By this, it is said that in the first stage (*bhūmi*) one abandons two delusions... (up to the words) "...the subsequent mention of 'coarse residues' (*dausthulya') should be explained by analogy with this."

Commentary on the Terms (*Yinyì*): This refers to the text of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. First the citations are presented, followed by their explanation. The first is the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*).

The second is the karma and its results pertaining to the miserable realms (*apāya*). Question: Attachment to a self and to phenomena may be termed "delusion," but how can the karma and results of the miserable realms be so designated?
Why is it also called "delusion"? The answer is: one should know that the karmic fruits of the evil destinies arise from delusion;

because they belong to the category of delusion, they are collectively termed "delusion. In the subsequent nine stages, instances such as the mistaken commission of the three types of action are all categories of delusion;
therefore, it is said that the latter follows this explanation. Alternatively, that [text] speaks only of the lower [stages]. Another interpretation is that it refers to the first stage.
Regarding the statement that two types of delusion (*moha*) are abandoned: this refers to the two forms of ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with sharp and dull obstacles.
"Sharp" refers to the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*); "dull" refers to craving (*rāga*) and so forth.

The term "coarseness" (*dausthulya*) refers either to the seeds of those two delusions, or to the unserviceability (*akarmanyatā*) of those two delusions. How is this known? For example, as when entering the second *dhyāna*.
It is said that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is abandoned. However, although this faculty of suffering is neither manifest nor a seed, it is termed "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*).

In this context, "coarseness" is synonymous with "unfitness" (*akarmanya*); the meaning is the same. One interpretation holds that coarseness is itself the seed; another interpretation holds [that it is not].

"Dysfunction" (*dauṣṭhulya*) refers to the state of being unserviceable (*akarmanyatā*). Within each successive stage (*bhūmi*), the dysfunction that is abandoned possesses both of these two meanings.
*Hedyang* (Combined Explanation):
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "If it is comprised within the category of the wholesome, it possesses serviceability; if it belongs to the category of the indeterminate..."
Those included within the category of defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are all termed "seeds" (*bīja*).

If they are included within the category of defiled phenomena or the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they are termed "dysfunctions" (*dausthulya*), because they lack functional capacity. If they are included within the category of defiled phenomena, they are termed only "latent dispositions" (*anuśaya*).
The second fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Furthermore, among all personal existences (*ātman*), whatever seeds there are..."
If it is comprised within the category of afflictions (*kleśapakṣa*), it is called "heavy dysfunction" (*dausthulya*) and is also called a "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*).
If it is comprised within the category of maturation (*vipākaja*) or other categories of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is called only "heavy dysfunction," not a "latent tendency.
If it is a seed comprised within the category of wholesome factors such as faith (*śraddhā*), it is neither called "heavy dysfunction" nor a "latent tendency. Why is this? Because...
This dharma arises and maintains its basis, which is the self-substance (ātman); it possesses only capability, not incapability. (Text).
△ Third, the detailed analysis (in two parts): first, distinguishing [this] from what is abandoned by the Two Vehicles.

Although the afflictions subsumed under the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) actually pertain to both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), they are not mentioned here because their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) have not been severed.

Regarding the meaning of the term "sound" (*svara*): it means that among the delusions to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the first stage, although they actually pertain to both obstacles, the intention here takes only the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as primary.
Why? Because the Sūtra states that the ten stages sever the ten categories of obstacles; this refers precisely to the [cognitive] obstacles.

This clarifies that it is of an obscured nature (*nivṛta*). It does not state that it is of a defiled nature (*kliṣṭa*) because afflictions (*kleśa*) can also be abandoned by those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Why is this not mentioned?
Because it is common to the two vehicles; it is not discussed within the context of the obstructions abandoned by these Bodhisattvas, and thus it is omitted here.
Furthermore, as for the ten types of ignorance (*avidyā*) that are not defiled, they pertain solely to the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

This refers to abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), not that which is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-heya*). It is also termed "non-defiled" because, upon entering the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), one transcends the two minds and thus belongs to the path of cultivation.
Question: In this stage of cultivation, one also suppresses the afflictions (*kleśa*) as well as their underlying latencies (*dauṣṭhulya*).

Why is it not mentioned? The explanation of this intent is as follows: for those Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), their direct aim is *bodhi*, and their primary intention lies solely in the abandonment of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).

Since the latent tendencies of the afflictions (*kleśānuśaya*) are only abandoned at the stage of the "diamond-like concentration" (*vajropama-samādhi*), these two points of meaning lead to their being omitted here.
In this context, "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) refers to the coarseness of manifest activity. This is the intended meaning.
This refers to the lack of functional adaptability (*akarmanyatā*).
Next, [the text] distinguishes this from the innate afflictions (*sahaja*) which are also severed at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
In reality, these are severed all at once only when one is about to attain Buddhahood during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the first stage.

*Yinyi* (Explanatory Notes): Question: Since the ten types of ignorance are explained as being abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), it follows that there is also the sense of abandoning a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) [afflictions] in the first stage.
Why, then, was it previously stated only that the first stage abandons the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) arising from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)?
Therefore, the commentary says: "In reality... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the latter nine are to be understood accordingly": this is because the [stages]...

Each stage (*bhūmi*) possesses three moments of mind: the moment of entry (*praveśa-citta*), the moment of abiding (*sthiti-citta*), and the moment of emergence (*niṣkramaṇa-citta*). In the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), these three moments correspond respectively to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). The obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) is already abandoned at the initial moment of the path of seeing.

The two minds of abiding and emerging both belong to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); in principle, they also sever a portion of the innate [afflictions]. For now, however, we speak of severing the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) based on its initial severance.
The "initial mind" is the mind of entry; the "middle mind" is the mind of abiding; the "subsequent mind" is the mind of emergence. One proceeds to sever the afflictions of the subsequent stages.

As it is with the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), so it is with the remaining nine; therefore, it is said that one should know this by analogy. Having fully perfected the stage of abiding, one emerges from the first stage.
The reason for abandoning that which is co-emergent (*sahaja*) is as follows: "abiding" refers to the mind abiding, while "fulfilling the mind" refers to the mind emerging.

The obstacles to be abandoned are a portion of the co-emergent cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Regarding the "path of the three times," this refers to the stages of entering, abiding, and emerging.

This intends to clarify that within the mind of abiding and fulfilling during the first bhūmi, if one does not proceed to abandon the obstacles that ought to be abandoned, then [the path] would lack its beginning, middle, and end—these three.
The Path should be without distinction; since distinctions are indeed made, we know that it merely severs one portion of the innate (*sahaja*) obstacles.

Therefore, the following citation is introduced as proof: "Having attained realization" (*prāptābhisamaya*). Among the six types of realization (*abhisamaya*), the fourth and fifth realizations—the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)—have already been clarified; hence, it says "having attained."

Supplement: Regarding the statement that "one should proceed to abandon the obstacles that ought to be abandoned," an examination of the meaning of the text reveals that this applies generally to the final moments of mind (*cittakṣaṇa*) of all ten stages (*bhūmi*), wherein one should act accordingly in each case.
Therefore, at the final moment of mind of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), one should naturally proceed to abandon a portion of the innate cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This passage precisely explains and clarifies that, in reality, one also abandons [such obscurations] during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the first stage.
The aspect of the knowable that is innate to the mind.
△ Second, the obstacle of wrong practice (in two parts): first, the formal explanation;
second, the obstacle of wrong practice refers to the obstacle of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which one is able to sever forever upon entering the second stage (*bhūmi*).

*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance): The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) states that this refers to the obstacle of improper conduct regarding the body and so forth within the various realms of existence (*bhava*).
Because great joy arises from the preceding stage, any transgressions of the three karmas are termed "improper conduct" (*mithyā-pratipatti*). The *Qingliang chao* states:

"The ten unwholesome actions of the three karmas—body and so forth—are called the obstacle of improper conduct. This explains the essential nature (*svabhāva*) as derived from the "objects of knowledge" (*jñeya*), thereby distinguishing it from other categories.

These are distinct from the afflictions that arise simultaneously [with birth]. This specifies them as being distinct from the conceptualized [afflictions], because the latter have already been completely severed at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
As for those that belong exclusively to the severance of this specific stage:
△ Next, the scriptural evidence is cited.

"By this, it is said that in the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmiḥ*), two delusions (*moha*) are abandoned" (up to) "...or only the delusion of initiating karma and the delusion of not understanding karma.
[The commentary] *Qingliang* says: "The two obstacles mentioned above are opened up and established as two delusions. 'Delusion' refers to active manifestation (*samudācāra*); it is coarse."
Heaviness is the seed. Regarding the second [type], the delusion concerning the various courses of action (*karmagati*) is termed "reproach" (*nindā*);

since one does not take up evil fruits, how could it be called "various"? Within karma, that which is not uniform is precisely what is "various. That which is various and not one is itself reproach. The treatise further explains:
"Alternatively, there is only the arousal of karma, which is the delusion regarding the non-comprehension of karma; that is to say, the first [of the two] is the arousal of karma."
The latter one is the delusion of not understanding karma; it is not the karma that is actually produced.

Since these two do not necessarily initiate karma, these two delusions are exclusively [cognitive] delusions. According to the commentary, even the latter single delusion belongs to the category of delusion.
Question: Regarding the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), since it cannot produce or moisten [karma], how can it produce the three types of karma within this context?

The answer is found in the first fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: "The afflictions that link rebirth give rise to karma that violates the precepts; this applies to both cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This is stated with reference to transgressions committed through error, and therefore there is no contradiction."
△ Third, the obstacle of dullness and darkness (2): First, the direct explanation.
The three obstacles of dullness and darkness refer to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); upon entering the third stage, one is able to sever them forever.
Regarding the explanation of the terms: Qingliang (Chengguan) states that one is called "dark and dull" because of having lost the three types of wisdom (*tri-prajñā*).
While these three wisdoms have specific obstacles as detailed below in the section on "ignorance," here they are treated collectively.
△ Next, the scriptural evidence is cited.
"By this, in the third stage, two delusions are said to be abandoned" (up to) "...that which obstructs the dhāraṇī of the wisdom of hearing and reflection.
Regarding the meaning of the terms, Qingliang’s commentary states: "The first is the delusion of desire and greed. This merely mentions the delusions in brief; one might ask: [why is this so?]
The preceding section indicated that which is to be known (*jñeya*). Why, then, is the affliction of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) now raised? Therefore, the subsequent explanation states:

"In the past, it was frequently associated with sensual desire," and so forth. The meaning is this: because of sensual desire, one frequently dwells in distraction; thus, it obstructs meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

Since this sensual desire functions by depending upon these obstructions, when the obstructions are exhausted, the desire perishes. Below the section on the "two fulfillments" (*paripūri*), this [verse] maintains...
It encompasses four types: first, retention of the Dharma; second, retention of the meaning; third, retention of mantras; and fourth, retention through the attainment of patience (*kṣānti*).

Because *śruta-dhāraṇī* (retention through hearing) and *śruta-dhāraṇī* (retention by means of hearing) are extremely close to one another, the former is specifically mentioned; it is not that the latter does not obstruct cultivation.
△ Section Four: The Obstruction of the Manifestation of Subtle Afflictions (2). Part One: The Direct Explanation (3). Part One: A Brief Explanation of the Obstruction.

Regarding the obstruction of the manifestation of subtle afflictions (*sūkṣma-kleśa-samudācāra-āvaraṇa*): [it is called "subtle"] because it manifests in accordance with [the state of] the practitioner.
*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance). Qingliang’s commentary states: The mention of the "sixth consciousness" serves to distinguish it from the seventh consciousness.

Because the seventh consciousness is subtle in both its nature and its mode of activity, it has not been severed at this stage. Now, when we speak of "subtlety," it is said in relation to the preceding stages. There are three reasons for establishing the name "subtle":
first, within the sixth consciousness, the discrimination of the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) is termed "superior" (*adhimātra*). Only...

Because it is unwholesome (*akuśala*), greed that occurs independently (*mukhya*) is termed "middling. Because this [subtle greed] is exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*), while the former pertains to both wholesome and unwholesome states, it is termed "inferior.
Second, because it arises spontaneously (*svarasena*) due to the absence of deliberate mental attention (*amanasikāra-pratyaya*), it has the sense of arising effortlessly.

Third, because it follows the manifest activity (*samudācāra*) from afar—having pursued the body since beginningless time—it possesses these three aforementioned meanings and is therefore called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*).
△ Next, the actual explanation of abandonment.
Because those [afflictions] obstruct the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) of the fourth stage, they are able to permanently destroy this view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth.
Regarding the meaning of the terms, the *Qīngliáng* commentary states: "Regarding 'those which obstruct the fourth stage,' because of the view of a self-body, one is unable..."

One contemplates the body as impure and so forth. Question: Regarding the aforementioned statement that a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is called "affliction" (*kleśa*), how is this so?
Answer: In the past, this cognitive obstruction for the most part arose as a single entity with the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

The designation "affliction" is established by virtue of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) correctly severing the objects of knowledge; for even that view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not function [in those stages].
Might this not also apply to the preceding three stages? Because they share characteristics with the mundane, it is only now, upon becoming supramundane, that one is able to abandon them.
△ Section Three: Further Investigation (2) Part One: Investigation of its Association with the Sixth Consciousness (2) Part One: The Question.
How is it known that this [self-view] coexists with the sixth consciousness?

[Commentary on the Meaning of the Sound]: The intent of the question is as follows: Both the sixth and seventh consciousnesses possess innate *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (the view of a self-identity). By what principle is it determined...
Is it known that these views of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth are associated exclusively with the sixth consciousness?

△ Next, [the text] explains that the grasping at a self-view (*ātmagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and so forth associated with the seventh consciousness— [omitted]— therefore, these are associated only with the sixth [consciousness].
"Resonating together" refers to the affliction of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) associated with the seventh consciousness.

Because its nature is diametrically opposed to the path of pure outflow (*anāsrava*) regarding the emptiness of persons, it can still manifest prior to the seventh stage, as the path of pure outflow has not yet been attained.
It is only from the eighth stage onward that it no longer functions. Why is this? This view of a self, along with the other three—self-love (*ātmasneha*) and so forth—[is thus characterized].
Because they serve as the basis and support for the various afflictions, these four afflictions must reach the full stage of the seventh bhūmi before they can coexist with the sixth consciousness;
this is because the lowest-of-the-low afflictions are suppressed simultaneously. Those associated with the sixth consciousness are coarse, while those associated with the seventh are subtle.
Because they differ in coarseness and subtlety, their suppression occurs sequentially; therefore, the afflictions suppressed at this stage are associated only with the sixth consciousness.
Next, the phrase "view of self" (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth is selected for exclusion.

The phrase "the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth" also includes [afflictions] from beginningless time up to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), because they are specifically contrary to them.
Regarding the meaning of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*): it also includes the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

This inclusion of the cognitive obstructions refers to attachment to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and attachment to the Dharma (*dharma*). These two types of attachment—attachment to concentration and attachment to the Dharma—are originally...

Afflictions (*kleśa*) arise together with two types of ignorance; therefore, they are subsumed within the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). Consequently, it is stated below that they are comprised within the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Because these two ignorances are abandoned, the two types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) associated with affliction also cease to function forever. "Craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) carries the meaning of indulging in and not forgetting.
Indulging in the cultivation of hearing, reflection, and meditation is called "craving for the Dharma" (*dharmatṛṣṇā*). Indulging in the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)... [and so forth].

The "taste" refers to craving for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Since the craving that delights in the dharmas of concentration is not absent in the [first] three stages, it is said to "still increase.
Next, the scriptural proof is cited:
"By this, in the fourth stage, two delusions are said to be abandoned... [and] the two cravings of affliction also never again arise."
Commentary on Terms: Regarding "equipoise" (samāpatti), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "The manifestation of correct reception (samyak-pratipatti) is called equipoise.
The rest is as in the text. △ Fifth:
The Obstruction to Parinirvāṇa in the Lesser Vehicle (2). First, the direct explanation.
Fifth, the obstacle to entering parinirvāṇa via the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna) is permanently severed upon entering the fifth stage (*bhūmi*). Regarding the meaning of the terms:
this refers to the preceding four stages, wherein one dwells in supramundane consciousness, feels revulsion for the suffering of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and takes pleasure in attaining nirvāṇa.

The meaning is the same as that of the Two Vehicles who loathe suffering and long for quiescence. As long as this longing and loathing have not been forgotten, grasping and rejecting remain in opposition.
Therefore, this can obstruct the path of non-differentiation which simultaneously contemplates both the ultimate and the conventional truths. Regarding "non-differentiation," Qingliang says:

"In this stage, the *tathatā* (suchness) is called 'non-distinct' because its categories are without difference; thus, the path that takes that as its object is called 'non-differentiated. Now, one enters the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional."
The path of differentiation is then able to sever them.
△ Next, the scriptural evidence is cited:
"By this, it is said in the Fifth Stage that two delusions are severed" (up to) "this refers to those who delight in nirvāṇa within this context."
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: The explanation of severing the two delusions refers to *abhinandana* (delight) and *vidveṣa* (aversion).
△ Sixth, the obstacle of the active manifestation of the six coarse characteristics (2): First, the formal explanation.
The obstacle of the active manifestation of the six coarse characteristics refers to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)... which can be permanently severed upon entering the sixth stage.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: That which manifests in the subsequent stage is called a "coarse characteristic" (*sthūla-nimitta*). Because it is distinguished from being a seed, it is termed "active manifestation" (*samudācāra*).

Regarding the absence of the path of defilement or purity: this means that by virtue of ignorance as a condition, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) arise, and so on, up to birth as a condition for old age and death;
thus there are defiled phenomena. When ignorance ceases, the formative forces cease, and so on, up to the cessation of birth.
The cessation of old age and death is the dharma of purity. In the sixth stage, the most excellent prajñā manifests before one;

there is absolutely nothing to be apprehended, and one thus realizes the uncontaminated and pure *tathatā*. Therefore, one is able to realize the Path and also attains the name "uncontaminated and pure."
△ Next, the scriptural evidence is cited.
By virtue of this, it is said in the Sixth Ground that two delusions are abandoned... [up to] "unable to dwell for long periods in the contemplation of signlessness.

Regarding the meaning of the sounds: "clinging to the existence of a defiled agent" refers to clinging to the existence of the causes and conditions that lead to rebirth, because of the gateway of cyclic existence (saṃsāra). Clinging to the existence of... [the rest of the sentence].

"Purity" refers to the practice of contemplating the gates of cessation and the reversal of dependent origination while maintaining the perception of existence. "One who frequently practices the contemplation of signs" indicates that there is not even a brief moment during which one does not grasp at signs.
△ The Obstacle of the Manifestation of the Seven Subtle Characteristics (2). First, the direct explanation:

The obstacle of the manifestation of the seven subtle characteristics refers to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which one is able to sever forever upon entering the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).
Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms: It manifests before one's eyes upon the ground; therefore, it is described as "subtle.

What distinguishes this from what preceded it is that the former [refers to] the marks of defilement and purity regarding the process of transmigration and cessation, whereas this refers to the marks of arising and ceasing regarding the process of transmigration and cessation.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of marks: first, existence; second, non-existence. That which exists is coarse, while that which does not exist is subtle; thus, it differs from what preceded it.
△ Next, the scriptural evidence is cited:
"By this, it is said that in the seventh stage one abandons two delusions... [up to] being unable to initiate superior practice within emptiness.

(Commentary on the Meaning of the Sound): "The subtle marks manifesting" refers to the arising of the mark of birth due to the grasping at the flow [of saṃsāra]; thus, one applies mental attention to seek [it].
Regarding "signlessness" (*animitta*): because one clings to cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), one seeks signlessness;
yet, being unable to give rise to superior practice within emptiness (*śūnyatā*), this refers to the delusion of one who diligently seeks signlessness through such mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Consequently, they are unable to skillfully employ the activities of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as expedient means (*upāya*) within the signless emptiness.
△ Section Eight: The Obstacle of Applying Effort Toward the Signless (2). First, the direct explanation.
Among the eight types of signlessness, this is the obstacle of applying effort; because that [obstacle] is permanently severed, one attains the two masteries.

Regarding the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Terms), Qingliang’s commentary states: "When the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*) does not arise spontaneously, it is called 'acting according to [the path]' (*yathācaryā*).

Because the contemplative mind is inferior in the fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*), the contemplation of signlessness is slight; because one contemplates the equality of defilement and purity in the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī bhūmi*), the contemplation of signlessness is abundant;
and because one applies preparatory effort (*prayoga*) in the seventh stage (*saptamī bhūmi*), it is so. However, according to Dharmapāla, there is still application within signlessness."
The wisdom of practice (*caryā-jñāna*) is not inherently an obstruction; rather, it is because one dwells well [in it] that it is so.
It is solely due to the obstructions to be abandoned that effort (*prayoga*) must be applied, and for this reason it is called the "obstruction to application.

Because of this seventh stage, although the various marks such as the golden [color] and the buddha-fields appear, they do not manifest spontaneously (*svarasena*). Therefore, this constitutes an obstruction.
△ Next, the scriptural evidence is cited:
"By this, it is said that in the eighth stage two delusions are abandoned" (up to) "...because the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons does not contradict that. [Commentary:

First, the delusion regarding the activity of signlessness (*animitta-kriyā-moha*), which refers to the application of effort in every moment (*kṣaṇa-prayoga*) for entering the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*).
Regarding the two characteristics, there is the delusion of lack of mastery. This is because, while manifesting the body and the land, one is unable to do so spontaneously (*anābhoga*);

it is only from the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) onward, through the purely untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), that one becomes spontaneous. At this stage, one is finally able to relinquish the name of the *ālayavijñāna*.

The afflictions of the three realms (*traidhātuka-kleśa*) never again arise, as one has departed from birth by means of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti*) and transcended the three realms. Only the seventh consciousness remains subtle...

The subtle co-emergent [afflictions] can still manifest because one has only realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is not yet pure or uninterrupted.
Question: Why does the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) still persist when the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons arises? Answer:

Because the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons does not contradict the seventh consciousness’s attachment to a self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya-grāha*). The fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) induced by that wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons.
And [this applies to] the attainment of cessation as well.
△ Ninth: The obstacle of being unwilling to act for the benefit of others (2). First, the formal explanation:
Among the nine types of obstacles to benefiting others, the obstacle of being unwilling to act is permanently severed upon entering the ninth stage.
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: Regarding the obstacle of not wishing to practice for the benefit of others. As the Sūtra states:

When a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā), enters the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), the three periods of time become equal and quiescence manifests before them.
If the Buddhas did not grant this Bodhisattva the gateways of immeasurable wisdom-arisings, he would at that moment enter ultimate *nirvāṇa* and abandon [the world].
All matters concerning the benefit of sentient beings are precisely this hindrance.
*Hexiang* (Harmony of Echoes) quotes the *Qingliang Shu* (Commentary by Qingliang), fascicle 38, as saying:

"This takes as its essential nature the seeds of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that can obstruct the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). This is because from the eighth stage upward, the cognitive hindrances within the six consciousnesses no longer exist."
Because they are currently active.
△ Next, the scriptural evidence is cited:
"By this, it is said that in the ninth stage one abandons two delusions" (up to) "...all of which are subsumed within the ninth obstacle herein."

Commentary on Terms: First, the characteristics of the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) are clarified. *Dhāraṇī* is translated here as "total retention" (*zongchi*). "Meaning" (*yi*) refers to the principle that is expressed;
"phenomena" (*fa*) refers to the names and so forth that express it. Because the many are manifested within the one, they are called "unimpeded.

To provide glosses and explanations for immeasurable words and sounds within a single word or sound is called "unimpededness regarding language and terminology" (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*). The [first] three all rely upon...

That which is capable of maintaining and establishing names is called "unimpeded eloquence" (*pratibhāna*); this is a designation established based on the capacity for speaking, referring specifically to the aforementioned three [unimpeded knowledges].
Next, the phrase "the deluded can descend" explains the meaning of "delusion. This function of delusion is capable of obstructing the four unimpeded knowledges;
it is the subtle cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the seventh consciousness.

Supplement: Regarding "subsequent wisdom," this refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). This is because, within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) flows forth.
10. The obstacle to attaining mastery over all phenomena (2): First, that which is abandoned in the *Maulī Bhūmi* (the Fundamental Stage), not yet [attained] by oneself.
Regarding the second [category], the initial formal explanation:
the obstacle consisting of not yet having attained mastery over all phenomena (up to the point mentioned) is permanently severed upon entering the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).

△ Next, the scriptural evidence is cited: "By this, the ten stages are said to sever two delusions... [and] the obstruction to the great cloud of Dharma-knowledge and that which it contains. Regarding the meaning of the terms:

"The activities that arise" refers to the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) for transforming others. That their wondrous function is difficult to fathom is called "divine" (*śen*). As for "self... [the text continues].

To be unobstructed is called "penetration. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas on this stage possess clear and penetrating wisdom and sovereign supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
According to their mental intentions, they can transform a narrow world into a vast world, and a vast world into a narrow world.
Or, according to their mental intentions, they can manifest all Buddhas within a single pore."
The adornment of the objective realm and so forth are explained in detail as stated therein. "The great cloud of Dharma-wisdom" refers to the wisdom that is capable of containing;

"that which is contained" refers to the qualities of the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Their subtle and secret nature is also as described in the "Chapter on the Ten Masteries of Adornment.
Ignorance can obstruct these two types; by severing this obstruction, one is able to realize the self-nature of karma.

Regarding the *tathatā* (suchness) that serves as the equal basis: this refers to the mastery over supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the performance of activities (*karmakriyā*), the dhāraṇīs, and the gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
△ Next, the remaining obstacles to be severed at the completion of the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*) (2): first, the formal explanation.
Although one has attained mastery over the dharmas on this stage (up to the point where) those [obstructions] are all suddenly severed and one enters the stage of a Tathāgata.

[Commentary on the Meaning of the Sounds]: This first concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one in order to clarify the remaining obstructions. As it says in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
"Although one has attained great mastery in proclaiming the Dharma across all categories of phenomena, one has not yet attained the perfect Dharmakāya."
It is directly realized and experienced; it also carries the meaning of being "other obstacles" (text).
Supplement: Regarding the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:

It refers to the samādhi present at the final stage of severing the fetters while abiding in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which is comprised either within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) or the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).

(Commentary). Regarding that which is subsumed under the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) herein: in the Mahāyāna, the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) are distinguished. The two types of innate grasping (*sahaja-grāha*) are severed all at once in a single moment at the initial mind of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
As for the two types of innate grasping, one portion of each is severed in each successive stage (*bhūmi*), continuing until the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samābodhi*).

There still remain two types of delusion which are exhausted all at once in the final moment of the Vajra-like Samādhi. Therefore it is said that the conceptualization of self and phenomena is completely eliminated.

In the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā*), the innate [delusions] of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses do not exist; in each successive stage, the seventh consciousness is removed; through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), both the seeds and the manifest forms are removed;
and from the moment following the Vajra Path onwards, they are entirely absent.
△ Next, the scriptural evidence is cited:
"By this, it is said that on the Buddha-ground two delusions are severed" (up to) "...because one realizes Great Nirvāṇa and Great Bodhi.
*Qingliang Shu*, Fascicle 40, states: "The various teachings differ in their methods of opening and closing [the categories]. In the *Renwang*..."
Combining these stages of supreme progress, one enters the ten bhūmis; therefore, the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) is not established separately.

Thus, in the Chapter on Teaching and Transformation, the levels are categorized according to the five patiences (kṣānti). Within the patience of quiescence (śānti-kṣānti), there are only two divisions: superior and inferior.

Practicing within the inferior patience is termed a Bodhisattva, which corresponds to the tenth bhūmi. Practicing within the superior patience constitutes sarvajñā (omniscience); this refers to the Tathāgata.

If one follows the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (or *Yogālaṃkāra*), this stage of "superior progress" (*viśeṣagamana*) is opened up as the "Stainless Ground" (*vimalā-bhūmi*), which is precisely Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

Now, Equal Enlightenment is the illumination of stillness, while Wondrous Enlightenment (*prajñā-sambodhi*) is the stillness of illumination. Furthermore, within the "Chapter on the Awakening and Contemplation of Worthies and Sages," six types of natures, as well as the six worthies and six patiences, are taught.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* possesses two meanings; in the seventy-eighth [fascicle], it cites the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* to explain the ten [stages].
The first stage; the tenth is the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*); the eleventh is designated as the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*).

It is said that there are only twenty-two delusions (*moha*), and upon attaining the Buddha-stage (and so forth), no further separate explanation is given regarding the abandonment and realization of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Furthermore, there is a passage in the *Śāstra* which also establishes Equal Enlightenment.
Moreover, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "Although this bodhisattva has already fulfilled the ocean of merit through cultivation, because..."
Because one has not yet abandoned three types of dharmas, it is not called "sublime awakening" (*miao-jue*). First, because one has not yet abandoned inferior untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas;
second, because one has not yet abandoned pure indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas; and third, because one has not yet abandoned tainted wholesome (*kuśala*) dharmas.
Only upon reaching the stage of sublime awakening does one abandon these three, as clarified later in the tenth fascicle. The *Chao* states: "The treatise further says... and so forth.

This is the fiftieth treatise, which elucidates the one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). Within its analysis of the distinctions according to the stages of cause and fruit, it states:

"When a bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), dwelling in his final existence, having brought the provisions for awakening (*bodhi-sambhāra*) on the bodhisattva path to complete perfection, he then—without a teacher—cultivates the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣyā dharmāḥ*)."
One attains a single moment called the "Samādhi of Unobstructed Wisdom. This is the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) included within the Bodhisattva’s path of training.
The commentary on that [text] states: "This clarifies the fulfillment of the cause; it is the final stage within the Bodhisattva stages.
This stage is also called the 'Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment' (*samyaksambuddha-bodhisattva*), meaning that immediately following this, in the second moment, [one suddenly...]"

One attains the remaining unshared Buddha-dharmas, beginning with the ten powers of the Tathāgata and ending with the wondrous knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), all of which are utterly pure and have attained the unsurpassed.
The commentary states: "This obstructs the attainment of the fruit. The explanation says:
According to this treatise, following the ten stages (daśabhūmi), within the single moment of the diamond-like samādhi (vajropamasamādhi), it is termed Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi);
the second moment is Sublime Enlightenment (pravarabodhi).

△ Next, the summary and classification under the two obstacles (2). First, the formal summary of their inclusion within the two obstacles:
These eleven obstacles are subsumed under the two obstacles.
△ Second, explaining the meaning of the abandonment of the two obstacles (2). First, the stage of abandoning the seeds and manifestations (2). First, the formal explanation (2).
First, the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the obstacle of afflictions, the seeds to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) [cease to function] from the eighth bhūmi upward, never manifesting again.

*Yinyi* (Explanations of Terms and Meanings): First, the abandonment through seeing (*darśana-heya*) is clarified. Regarding that which is abandoned at the initial moment of the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), this refers to a portion of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*).

As for those obstacles that have already been suppressed prior to that stage—namely, during the stages of the Requisites (*sambhāra*) and Application (*prayoga*)—this refers to what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Below this, the abandonment through cultivation is next explained. Master Qingliang’s commentary states: "Reading the treatise directly, [this applies] from the first stage upward."

One is able to suddenly suppress and exhaust the active manifestations of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, such that they are no longer present, just as an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted has no further afflictions.
Next, it says that by the power of intentional resolve, although [the afflictions] may temporarily manifest within the seven stages, they do not constitute a fault.
This is a separate section that addresses an objection. It states:

Someone asks, "If [the view of self] is rendered permanently non-arising as in the case of an Arhat, how is it that you previously stated that the view of self still arises, and that greed, hatred, and so forth still arise prior to the seventh bhūmi?

The answer is: They arise through the power of intentional effort (*abhiprāya*). That is to say, prior to the sixth bhūmi, there is still the possibility of emerging from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna*). Furthermore—

They arise erroneously. Within the seven stages, they constantly abide in the signless; yet, for the purpose of transforming sentient beings, they intentionally manifest them, which does not constitute a fault.
From the eighth stage upward, they ultimately do not engage in them because the power of the Path is superior.
△ Next, the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Among the cognitive obstructions, the seeds to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*)—whether as seeds or as manifest states—are suppressed by the untainted (*anāsrava*) [path], such that they do not arise.

[Regarding] the meaning of the terms: first, the abandonment through insight is explained; whether as seeds or as manifest states, their nature is the same as that of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Below this is the abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Next, the cultivation and abandonment [of obstacles] is explained. Whether in their latent seeds or as manifest states, these correspond to a portion of the innate [obstacles] clarified among the eleven obstacles previously mentioned.
From the eighth stage upward, and further regarding the final three stages, it is explained whether the objects of knowledge associated with the various consciousnesses are manifest or unmanifest.
As for the "mind of untainted contemplation," this refers to the mind of the sixth consciousness. Regarding the "continuity of the fruit," it arises...

The fruit of the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*) is that which can oppose those [obstructions]. This refers to the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) arising from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, as well as the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) upon which it relies;
because these have all been transformed into the untainted (*anāsrava*), they are in opposition to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) with which they coexist.

Therefore, they no longer manifest. As for the four types of manifestations, such as the view of a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) of the seventh consciousness, because they are subtle, [they persist until the eighth stage]. Eight.

Above the [first] stage, these still manifest in active conduct; it is only upon reaching the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), when the fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*) arises, that they are finally suppressed and exhausted.
The three types of cognitive objects—attachment, aversion, and ignorance regarding phenomena—which accompany the first five consciousnesses, [are likewise suppressed] from the eighth stage upward.
