Although the basis has not yet been transformed (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), because it is suppressed by the sixth untainted contemplative mind (*anāsrava-citta*), it likewise does not manifest.
△ Next, the resolution of objections:
Although [these afflictions] exist throughout the ten stages of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), they are specifically mentioned here because they are prominent during these three stages.
**Commentary on Terms:** Question: Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), regarding the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one merely suppresses them but does not sever them.
Why, then, in the first three stages of the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), are both obstructions and their residual latencies (*dausthulya*) severed? Answer:

Although [severance occurs] during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and so forth, here "residual latency" refers specifically to the state of being unserviceable (*akarmanyatā*). As for the three stages: the first is the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Second, the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*); third, the Buddha Stage (*buddha-bhūmi*). Question: All stages involve the abandonment [of afflictions]; why are only these three stages mentioned? Answer:
These three stages are explained specifically because they are particularly manifest.
The *Ching-liang-ch'ao* (Commentary on the Clear and Cool), Fascicle Two, Part One, states: "The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* speaks of three types of grossness (*dausthulya*)."

The first resides in the skin and is severed at the first stage (*bhūmi*). The second resides in the flesh and is severed at the eighth stage. The third resides in the bone and is severed only at the Buddha stage.
Although these heavy obscurations (*dausthulya*) are also severed at other stages, these three positions are particularly manifest; therefore, they are specifically mentioned.

This is because at the first stage one abandons the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and enters the stage of a noble one (*ārya*), at the eighth stage the untainted state (*anāsrava*) is constantly continuous, and at the Buddha stage [all obscurations are exhausted].
The fruit of the stage is fulfilled because one simultaneously attains [the state of] relinquishment (text).
△ Next, the gradual and simultaneous abandonment of the seeds (2): first, the inquiry.
How are the seeds of the two obstacles abandoned—gradually or simultaneously?
△ Second, the explanation [of the two parts]: First, the explanation of the obstacles to be abandoned (2). First, the seeds of the two obstacles associated with the seventh consciousness.
Regarding the seeds of the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) associated with the seventh consciousness: [up to] because they arise spontaneously within and lack coarse or subtle [distinctions].
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: "Those beyond training" refers to Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas.

It does not mention those from the eighth stage upward because they have not yet severed this seed. "Spontaneously arising within, without coarseness or subtlety" explains the meaning of simultaneous and instantaneous severance;
that is, the views and so forth associated with this consciousness exclusively grasp the eighth [consciousness] as a real internal self and real phenomena.
Because it does not take external objects as its conditions, there is neither coarseness nor subtlety. Since there is neither coarseness nor subtlety, it is therefore severed instantaneously.
△ Next, regarding the seeds of the two obstacles associated with the remaining six consciousnesses (2): first, the seeds of the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The seeds of the afflictive hindrances associated with the remaining six consciousnesses (up to) are suddenly severed across the three realms within a single moment.

[Regarding] the Explanatory Notes on Terms: First, the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) are clarified; that is to say, the seeds arising from discrimination within the sixth consciousness are all suddenly severed during the stage of seeing in the Three Vehicles.
Next, the afflictions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are clarified; regarding the abandonment by the Three Vehicles, there are both gradual and sudden modes. Therefore...
It is said: "In accordance with what is appropriate. Regarding the gradual and successive severance of each of the nine grades:

this refers to a certain class of dull-facultied followers of the Two Vehicles who, in terms of seven births, sever [the afflictions] by dividing each of the nine stages of the three realms into nine grades. This concerns those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).

One who has severed the afflictions of the desire realm up to the fifth grade is termed a candidate for the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*). Having severed the sixth grade, one is termed the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*);

because three grades of remaining afflictions still exist, one returns to the human world. If one severs up to the eighth grade, one is termed a candidate for the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmi-pratipannaka*).
Having completely severed all nine grades, one is termed the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmi-phala*); because the afflictions of the desire realm are exhausted, one is no longer born among humans.
Therefore, those who have attained the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmin) take birth in the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa).

Furthermore, by severing the nine grades of afflictions (kleśa) of each of the upper eight stages, up to the seventy-first grade, they are termed candidates for Arhatship (arhattva-phala-pratipannaka). Upon exhausting the final grade, they realize the fruit of Arhatship.

Moreover, there is another class of those with sharp faculties among the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) who consolidate the afflictions of the nine stages into a single aggregate, treating them collectively as nine grades; although...

There are nine grades. One eliminates them individually over a single lifetime, as they do not depend upon seven lifetimes. If one possesses superior faculties, one eliminates all nine grades instantaneously.
If one possesses middling faculties, one first eliminates the upper three grades, next eliminates the middle three grades, and finally eliminates the lower three grades.
If one possesses dull faculties, one eliminates each of the nine grades individually; first eliminating the highest-of-the-high grade, then the high grade...
The middle grade [of afflictions], and so on, up to the final severance of the lowest-of-the-low grade and its like, are of various types, as explained extensively elsewhere.

Thus, a sūtra states: "Among those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), there are some who attain arhatship in one lifetime, some in two lifetimes, five lifetimes, or even seven lifetimes. This is precisely that meaning. Below the bodhisattvas, next...
The Bodhisattva may be known.
Next, regarding the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*):
from the first thought-moment of the first stage (*bhūmi*) until their various categories and distinctions, they are manifold.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: First, clarify the abandonment through seeing (*darśana-heya*). This refers to the seeds of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) that arise simultaneously with the six consciousnesses through conceptual discrimination;

these do not concern the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), but pertain exclusively to Bodhisattvas. They are abandoned within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) at the initial moment of the first stage (*bhūmi*).

As for abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), it does not involve the simultaneous abandonment of afflictions across the three realms, as is the case with the former; rather, it occurs gradually throughout the ten stages of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
They are severed. This seed is completely severed during the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*). Why are they severed gradually?

It is because those associated with the six consciousnesses arise by universally taking internal and external, coarse and subtle objects as their conditions; since their categories and distinctions are manifold, they are severed progressively.
△ Next, the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*) is explained.

When those of dull faculties among the two vehicles gradually abandon the hindrances, [the paths] from beginning to end may all be present in relation to one another. Regarding the meaning of the terms:

according to the ancient *Tongshi* (General Explanation), the four paths—such as the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) and so forth—are distinguished as follows. As for the "path of preparation": [The text continues with the definition of the path of preparation.]

This refers to the preparatory application (*prayoga*) preceding the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*). The path of uninterrupted transition refers to the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*).

The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) follows the path of uninterrupted transition; it is called the path of liberation because one has already been liberated from the obstacles that were to be abandoned.
Regarding the "path of superior progress" (viśeṣamārga) that arises initially: it refers to all remaining paths other than the aforementioned three, because they progressively advance.
Specifically, these are the various paths that arise subsequent to the path of liberation (vimuktimārga). Because they are the road to nirvāṇa, they are called "paths."

In the text, the statement that the two vehicles gradually eliminate obstacles refers exclusively to the elimination of the innate afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) within the seven evolving consciousnesses.

Regarding the "preparatory" (*prayoga*) and "superior progress" (*viśeṣa*) stages—whether taken collectively or individually: collectively, they occur simultaneously; individually, they are distinguished as preceding and succeeding.

Alternatively, what constitutes superior progress in a prior stage is precisely the uninterrupted preparatory application (*anantarya-prayoga*) of the subsequent stage; therefore, it is termed "collective. In comparison with... [text continues].

The preceding preparatory practices (*prayoga*) differ in quality and substance; therefore, they are termed "distinct" (or, because the superior progress of a prior stage cannot induce the immediate succession of a subsequent stage, one must again cultivate the preparatory practice of the later stage, they are thus called "distinct").

When it is said that a Bodhisattva gradually abandons the obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), this refers exclusively to the abandonment of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the seven consciousnesses.
This is not the same as the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), for whom all four paths exist moment by moment. That is to say:
Question: It is said that the fruit of Buddhahood is attained only after immeasurable kalpas.

Since such a vast period of time has elapsed, how can it be said that one is able to sever [afflictions] and realize [enlightenment] moment by moment (*kṣaṇa*)? The ancient masters replied: This interpretation is not correct.

That time has passed for so long is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). As a verse says: "In a dream, one thinks a year has passed; yet upon waking, it is but a brief moment. So too with the passing of time."

Although immeasurable, it is subsumed within a single kṣaṇa. Furthermore, it is said that because the bodhisattva’s diligence is so intensely blazing, even though many kalpas have passed, they are regarded as a brief moment.
As a verse says: "Though the fool practices for only a short time, his lazy mind suspects it has been long;
the Buddha, throughout immeasurable kalpas, regards his diligent vigor as but a moment."

*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance). The fifth fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "What is the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*)? It refers to that path by which one is able to abandon the afflictions;
this is called the path of preparation within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). What is the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*)?
It refers to that path by which, immediately thereafter, one eternally severs the afflictions so that nothing remains. What is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)? It refers to that..."
The Path. Regarding the liberation attained through the realization and abandonment of afflictions: what is the path of further progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*)?

It refers to all paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for the purpose of abandoning remaining categories of afflictions; this is called the path of further progress.

Furthermore, having relinquished the application for abandoning afflictions, one either diligently applies skillful means to contemplate all phenomena, or diligently applies skillful means to settle [the mind]...
Abiding in all dharmas, or further cultivating other samāpattis— whatever paths there may be— are called the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
Furthermore, for the purpose of eliciting superior qualities, or for abiding in whatever paths lead to such states, they are called the path of superior progress (text).
△ Fourth, the explanation of the ten true suchnesses (in two parts): First, the heading.
Regarding the ten true suchnesses:
△ Second, the explanation (in two parts): First, the actual explanation of the meanings (in ten parts). First, the all-pervading true suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*).
First is the *tathatā* of universal pervasion (*sarvatraga-tathatā*), meaning that this *tathatā* reaches [to the point where] there is not a single dharma that does not exist within it.
Regarding the explanation of the terminology: it refers to the *dharmadhātu* realized in the first stage (*bhūmi*). It is called "universal pervasion" because its meaning is such;
it is a portion of ultimate truth manifested by the elimination of the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*).
*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance): The *Qingliang Chao*, fascicle 34, part 4, states: "By severing the aforementioned hindrances, one realizes the pervasive true thusness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*).
This means that this true thusness is revealed by the two kinds of emptiness; there is not a single dharma that does not exist within it.

In the *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra*, it is termed 'pervasive' (*vyāpin*), because it pervades all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). The intent is to clarify that there is nothing [that is not it]."
Because the single dharma is not dual, it is empty. This is the initial stage of this ground, wherein one universally realizes and universally pervades.
The *Chao* states: "There may be an objection: 'Do the nine subsequent suchnesses not also pervade? Are they not likewise manifested by the two emptinesses? Therefore, this clarification is provided.

The intent clarifies that the suchness of universal practice is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), whereas the nine subsequent suchnesses are distinguished according to their specific virtues."
Established. Now, at the very beginning of attainment, one attains the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), thereby receiving its specific name (text).
△ Second, the most excellent *tathatā*.
Regarding the second, the most excellent *tathatā*: it is called such because this *tathatā* is the most supreme among all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).
Commentary on Terms: The dharma-realm realized in the Second Ground is called the "Supreme Meaning" (*paramārtha*).

It cannot be measured and is beyond comparison, for it is far removed from the defilements of wrong conduct and transgressions of the precepts. As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says: "Among great and evil maladies, the precepts are the excellent medicine;
amidst great terrors, the precepts are the protection; in the darkness of death's ignorance, the precepts are..."
The bright lamp. Within the evil realms, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is the fierce general; within the waters of the sea of death, ethical discipline is the great ship.
This is the most supreme meaning.
*Hexiang Qingliang Shu*, Fascicle 35, Part 1, states: "This also results from reversing [the consequences of] violating ethical discipline..."
[This is] lost. [It refers to] "boundless virtues. The *Chao* states: "Because one possesses the precepts, one realizes the most supreme *tathatā* (suchness).
This means that this suchness-in-reason (*yathābhūta*) is the most supreme. It is like saying that 'freedom from desire' is called the most supreme."
△ Third, the *tathatā* of supreme outflow.
The *tathatā* of supreme outflow refers to this *tathatā* (up to) because it is extremely superior to other teachings.
[Commentary on the Meaning of the Sounds]: The dharma-dhātu realized in the third stage (*bhūmi*) is named "supreme outflow. This refers to the third stage.

It severs the obstacle of dullness and obtuseness; it is unimpeded regarding all phenomena (*dharma*); and it serves as the eye of the Dharma for the multitude by means of attaining the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*), thereby illuminating the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the teachings that flow from suchness (*tathatā*), the *Liang* commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "From suchness flows the fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*);
from fundamental wisdom flows the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); and from the subsequently attained wisdom flows the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)."
The twelvefold canon flows forth from great compassion and is called the "Superior Flow of True Suchness" (*tathatā*).
If other teachings do not flow forth from that which realizes true suchness, they are therefore not superior.
*Hexiang Xuantan*, Scroll Seven. It cites an ancient commentary (*gushu*), which states:

"Because within this stage one attains the three types of wisdom (*trividya*) that illuminate the Mahāyāna Dharma, and contemplates the fundamental *tathatā* (suchness) of these Dharma-teachings, it is called the 'Superior Flow *Tathatā*' (*śreṣṭha-niṣyanda-tathatā*).
Alternatively, because the teaching of the Dharma is superior once this *tathatā* is realized... (*Wen*). *Hui Xuan*, Scroll Thirteen, states: "That explanation has two parts."
[Commentary: First, this is explained in terms of the teachings that flow forth [from it]. "By virtue of this stage" refers to the third stage, named the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).
The treatise states: "Because one accomplishes supreme meditative concentrations and great dhāraṇīs, and is able to emit the light of boundless, wondrous wisdom.

This refers to the illumination of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) by means of the three types of wisdom. Contemplating the root of these teachings is called the "True Flow of the Supreme" (*śreṣṭha-niṣyanda-satya*).
"Suchness" (tathatā): when viewed through the three types of wisdom as the fundamental basis of the Dharma teachings, it is termed "the Suchness of the Supreme Flow" (viśeṣa-niṣyanda-tathatā).
This refers to tracing back to the source. Alternatively, it may be explained in terms of the Dharma being taught:

because Bodhisattvas of this stage realize this suchness, they attain excellence in teaching the Dharma; since the source is supreme, the derivative is also supreme. This is the suchness of the supreme flow.
"Rú" (如) is interpreted in both cases as a *tatpuruṣa* compound. The first instance establishes the name based on the "outflowing" (*pravāha*) of the teachings;

the latter establishes the name based on the "supreme Dharma" (*dharmottama*) that is expounded. Furthermore, it says: Suppose someone were to ask, "In that school, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is immutable;

how can there be the sense of 'outflow'? Therefore, the Commentary states: "Although that school does not posit that True Suchness follows conditions (*pratyaya-anuvartana*), they do speak of the Buddha’s essential body (*svabhāva-kāya*)."
Wisdom realizes the most pure dharma-realm, and subsequently establishes the teachings; this is called "flowing like a stream.
Fourth is the *tathatā* without appropriation.
The *tathatā* of non-appropriation (upādāna-rahita-tathatā): because it is not the basis for the grasping of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) and so forth.
[Commentary on the Meaning of the Terms]: The dharma-dhātu realized in the fourth bhūmi is called "the meaning of non-appropriation.

This means that the *tathatā* realized when the subtle afflictive obstructions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) are severed in the fourth bhūmi is not bound by dharmas such as form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), existence (*bhāva*), or non-existence (*abhāva*).

Because it belongs to that [category], it is also not the basis for or the object of appropriation by self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*), the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*), self-love (*ātma-sneha*), ignorance (*avidyā*),
extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*),
or the notion of "mine" (*mamakāra*). △ Fifth, the five categories have no distinction from True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The True Suchness of the Non-distinction of Categories (up to): because it is not like the eye and other [senses] which have distinct categories.
*Yinyi* (Exegesis): The dharma-realm realized in the fifth stage is called "the non-distinction of categories.
This means that the true suchness realized upon abandoning the obstacle of parinirvāṇa in the Lesser Vehicle in the fifth stage is ultimately inexhaustible and without change.
Therefore, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equal; thus, there is no distinction between them.
[This is] the "Echo" (Hōkyō) section of the *Ching-liang-ch'ao* (Clear and Cool Commentary), Volume 36, Part 2. It quotes the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, which states:
"It is called the dharma of continuity without distinction. Vasubandhu’s commentary explains: "That is to say, within this, the essence is not different; it is not like the eye..."

[The preceding] and so forth [indicate that] according to the differences in the mental continuums (*saṃtāna*) of various sentient beings, each is distinct; yet their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is the same.

As for the statement in the *Liang* commentary: "By means of this dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is able to cause the succession of the bodies of all Buddhas of the three periods of time to be non-different," this is because sentient beings are deluded regarding this [realm], resulting in the differences among the myriad classes [of beings]. When the Buddhas realize this, it remains inherently unchanging. (Text)
△ Sixth, the *tathatā* of non-defiled purity.
Regarding the sixth, the *tathatā* of non-defiled purity: it cannot be said that it becomes pure only later.
[End of] Explanatory Meaning. Within the sixth stage (*bhūmi*), the *dharmadhātu* realized is termed "non-defiled purity"; this refers to the sixth stage.

Because it eliminates the obstacle of the manifestation of coarse characteristics, one realizes *tathatā* (suchness) and contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), thereby knowing that the phenomena of dependent arising are neither defiled nor pure;
this is not what is meant by "suchness" itself. It is because of *tathatā* that phenomena are without defilement or purity;
thus, this *tathatā* is termed "the absence of defilement and purity."
*Hexiang* (Harmonizing Resonance), *Huixuan* (Assembling the Profound), Volume 11, states:

According to the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*, because a bodhisattva realizes this *tathatā* (suchness), they attain neither defilement nor purity regarding all phenomena. The name of the realized *tathatā* is manifested from this [realization].
If it is the Treatise on Consciousness-Only, then its very substance reveals the name "True Suchness" (Tathatā). It remains unstained by obstacles and unpurified by wisdom;
it is like the nature of jade, which is pure and cannot be defiled by mud. (Text)
△ The non-differentiation of the *tathatā* of the seven dharmas.
Because the *tathatā* of the seven dharmas is established in various ways yet remains without distinction.
(Commentary on the Meaning): The dharma-realm realized in the seventh stage is called the "non-differentiation of dharmas. This refers to the seventh stage.
This is the obstacle to the manifestation of subtle characteristics, which is severed; it is the *tathatā* (suchness) that is realized. As the ancient commentary states:

"Although all teachings are established based upon suchness, suchness itself has no differentiation. Furthermore, within these teachings, various names are established, such as 'dharma-dhātu' (dharma-realm) and 'dharmatā-lakṣaṇa' (the characteristic of reality)."
Yet they are non-different, like an echo.

*Hui-xuan* says: "According to the teaching of *Vijñapti-mātra*, 'dharmas' refers to the teaching that expresses [the truth] (*abhidhāna-dharma*). 'Non-distinct' refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) that is expressed.
This is because *tathatā* does not possess differentiation according to the teaching that expresses it. If one were to analyze this:

In the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, it is stated that once a bodhisattva has realized this suchness (*tathatā*), they attain the sublime path of signlessness (*animitta-mārga*) and is thus able to penetrate the distinctions among the essential natures of all dharmas;
for this reason, its name is established.
△ The Tathatā of Neither Increase nor Decrease.
Regarding the Tathatā of Neither Increase nor Decrease: because both the manifestation of signs and the manifestation of lands are sovereign.
Commentary on the Meaning: The dharma-realm realized within the eighth stage is called "neither increase nor decrease. This refers to the eighth stage.

It severs the obstacles to application regarding the signless (*animitta*). As for the *tathatā* that is realized, it does not decrease when defilement (*saṃkleśa*) diminishes, nor does it increase when purification (*vyavadāna*) increases;
therefore, it is said to be free from the attachment to increase and decrease. As the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states:
"By penetrating this, one fully realizes the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) regarding all purifications and defilements."
Within the Dharma, one does not perceive even a single phenomenon as having increase or decrease.
This is also called the *tathatā* (suchness) that serves as the basis for mastery over signs and lands. The commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains:
"This dharmadhātu is the locus of mastery over signs; because one attains mastery among all signs, it is called 'mastery over signs. Accordingly, whatever sign is desired, it immediately manifests."
Regarding the "mastery over the land" (*bhūmy-vaśitā*): this refers to the *dharmadhātu*, which is the basis for mastery over the land. One attains mastery with respect to the manifested lands;
thus it is called "mastery over the land. For example, as when one wishes for the land to become gold, jewels, and so forth.
"Because they are accomplished according to one's will. The commentary explains: "Phenomenal marks (*lakṣaṇa*) refer to the manifested body; lands (*kṣetra*) refer to the manifested realm. 9.
The *tathatā* that is the basis for mastery over the nine knowledges.
[The text continues: "...because one attains mastery over the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)."
Commentary on Terms: The dharma-realm realized in the ninth stage is called "Mastery of Wisdom" (*jñāna-vaśitā*).
This means that the suchness (*tathatā*) realized upon severing the obstacle to the lack of desire to act for the benefit of others in the ninth stage is the basis for this mastery of wisdom.
Therefore, among the assemblies of humans and devas, one is able to skillfully expound the Dharma with effortless mastery through the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).
[This concludes] *Hexiang* (Harmonizing Echoes), *Qingliang Chao*, Fascicle 38-2. It quotes the *Asvabhāva-ṭīkā*, which states: "That is to say, this stage..."
Because it serves as the basis for attaining the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), one partially realizes the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*).

Regarding all phenomena, one does not follow their mere words but is skillfully able to understand their underlying intentions and meanings, thereby truly bringing all sentient beings to the attainment of the sublime joy of the Dharma. (Text)
Supplement: Huìxuán says: Wisdom is that which relies [upon something], while True Suchness (tathatā) is that which is relied upon.
Once the wisdom that relies [upon it] has realized this True Suchness which is its support, it then attains mastery over the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
△ The *tathatā* that is the basis for mastery over the ten karmas.
Because one attains mastery over everything from the *tathatā* that is the basis for mastery over the ten karmas up to the gates of *dhāraṇī* and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: The dharma-realm realized in the tenth stage is called "Mastery over Karma.

This means that in the tenth stage, one eliminates the obstacles to mastery regarding all phenomena; the suchness thus realized serves as the basis for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and other qualities.
Because this basis is preeminent, the performance of supernormal feats and so forth all attain mastery. As stated in the *Śītalā-sūtra*: [text follows].
It is said: "Abiding in all stages and accomplishing all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth" refers to the meaning of mastery over karma (*karmavaśitā*).
To explain this in detail, one should consult such works as the "Inconceivable" chapter of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Supplement: *Huìxuán* states: "Karma" refers to the bodhisattva’s activities—namely, supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), dhāraṇīs, and samādhis, as well as the three types of physical and other actions.
This means that when this bodhisattva manifests various deeds for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, they are entirely without obstruction; this is termed "mastery" (*vibhutva*).
△ Next, the establishment of the intent is explained.
Although the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is in reality without differentiation... (up to) ...it is for the sake of bringing [the stages] to completion that each subsequent stage is established.
Commentary on the Meaning: Question: The principle of *tathatā* is the single *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm); its essence is without distinction or difference. How can there be...
"Ten. The commentary says: These names are established according to their qualities; they are provisionally designated as ten kinds. Furthermore, it is asked:

Since one has already known all things upon seeing the principle in the first stage (*bhūmi*), why must these ten be established based on the successive subsequent stages? The commentary replies: Although [the truth] is realized in the first stage...
Yet, the practice that can bring about realization is not yet perfected. To bring that practice to fulfillment, it is established in successive stages.
That which can bring about realization consists of the ten pāramitās.
Harmonizing Resonance (Hexiang). Although it is as stated below regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*), the *Qingliang Shu* (Commentary by Qingliang), Fascicle 34, Part 3, states:

"This is based on the differences in the qualities realized; therefore, there is direct realization in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). The *Chao* (Excerpts) quotes an ancient commentary explaining this:

"True Suchness is in reality without distinction, but according to the superior qualities of the realizing subject that arise from what is realized, ten types are provisionally established. The explanation says: "Since it is stated..."

The superior qualities that arise from this realization are conventionally established as ten types; thus, there is a distinction between the clarity and obscurity of wisdom. Furthermore, the Commentary asks:

regarding the direct realization in each stage (*bhūmi*), if, for instance, in the first stage one directly realizes *tathatā* (suchness) through correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), then one should not need to realize it again in the subsequent nine stages, because suchness is non-dual and without differentiation. An ancient master explains: although suchness is...
It is of a single flavor. In terms of the clarity or obscurity of wisdom, there are ten types of direct realization (*pratyakṣa-sākṣātkriyā*). This also accords with the principle. The *Chao* states:

"One should know that the term 'direct realization' refers only to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of its own respective level; it is called 'direct' because it does not refer to subsequent levels."
It is said that this constitutes direct realization; therefore, there is no contradiction. Although it is at the initial stage of the first ground (*bhūmi*), the *Qingliang shu* states:

"This also concerns the meaning of the clarity or obscurity of the realizing capacity. The *Chao* says: "This passage clarifies the principles of abolition and establishment for itself. One might ask:
within the first ground, if one does not yet fully comprehend the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*), would there not be no fruit of setting forth? [The answer is that] one is able to comprehend..."

Regarding the subsequent mutual attainment and the realization of the fruit: if one has already attained thorough penetration (*prativedha*), why is it that one does not simultaneously realize the ten virtues of *tathatā*?
Therefore, the answer is now given: although penetration is indeed simultaneous, because the practice (*caryā*) has not yet reached completion, there are ten stages of practice;
thus, there are ten kinds of perfectly complete *tathatā*, culminating in the Tathāgata, all of which can be fully understood. This is as explained extensively in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*.

There is conceptual differentiation. Furthermore, the Commentary states: "It is like a person contemplating emptiness; when young, it does not extend far, but as they grow older, it gradually increases.
Although emptiness itself has no difference, the eyes have varying degrees of clarity and dimness" (text).
△ Next, the fruit of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is explained. (2) First, the transition from the preceding to the subsequent:
Thus, when the bodhisattva, within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), [reaches] the two transformations of the basis, he is able to realize them.

△ Next, the formal explanation of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti). (II) First, the explanation of the distinctions among the stages of transformation. (III) First, the general heading:
There are briefly six types of distinctions regarding the stages of the transformation of the basis.
△ Second, the detailed explanation (in six parts). First, the transformation through the impairment of power and the enhancement of capacity. 1.

The transformation through the impairment of power and the enhancement of capacity refers to the first two stages (*yogabhūmi*). [It continues] until... and the gradual subduing of active manifestations (*samudācāra*) is also termed "transformation."

Commentary on the Terms: This refers to the two stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and the application (*prayoga*). It is called the "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) through the diminution of power and the enhancement of capacity.

Regarding "diminution of power": by means of these two stages, through superior resolve (*adhimukti*) and the permeation of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*), one diminishes the permeations of afflictions (*kleśa-vāsanā*) that reside within the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*).
Furthermore, by virtue of superior resolve and the permeation of hearing, one feels shame for one’s transgressions and evils, thereby...
Because various afflictions manifest only to a small degree or do not manifest at all, it is said that their power is diminished.

Regarding the "augmentation of capacity," this refers to the fact that through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and other factors, one increases the functional capacity of the pure dharmas cultivated within the *vipāka-vijñāna* (retribution-consciousness) to which they adhere;

hence, it is called the augmentation of capacity. If this is so, and the seeds of the obstacles have not yet been severed, how can this be termed the "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*)? Therefore, he replies: "Although..."
"Those who have not yet severed the obstructions," etc.
Supplement: "Deterioration" (*hāni*) means reduction; "power" (*bala*) means potency; "benefit" (*anuśaṃsa*) means augmentation; "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) means functional efficacy.

This refers to the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), wherein one possesses four kinds of power, cultivates six kinds of practices, and generates three kinds of refined minds (*citta-parikarma*). Faith (*śraddhā*).

Because one understands that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), it is called "cultivating resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*). This refers to the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-avasthā*), wherein one gives rise to the four types of investigation and reflection (*vitarka-vicāra*) and brings forth the four types of true knowledge (*bhūta-jñāna*).

One contemplates the emptiness of the two graspings (*grāhya-grāhaka*). Among humans in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), this cultivation of the mind of revulsion is particularly sublime, as they possess both shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).

By means of the power of these two stages— namely, the perfuming of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and the sense of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*)— one is able to diminish defilement and increase purity (and so forth).
△ Second, the transformation through thorough penetration (*prativedha-parāvṛtti*).

The second is the transformation through penetration (*prativedha-parāvṛtti*), which refers to the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*) up until the realization of a portion of the true transformation of the basis (*tattva-āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Regarding the meaning of the term: it refers to the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), which is called the transformation of the basis through penetration.
This is because, by severing the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*), one realizes a portion of the true principle.
△ Third, the transformation through cultivation (*bhāvanā-parāvṛtti*).
The transformation through cultivation refers to the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), wherein [the practitioner] extensively causes that which is not real to no longer appear.

[Regarding the term] "penetrating the ultimate and the conventional" (*tattva-saṃvṛti-prativedha*): first, the direct explanation; second, the reconciliation with the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. [The phrase] "penetrating the ultimate and the conventional" means...
Master Qingliang’s commentary states: By means of contemplation with signs (*sanimitta*), one attains access to signless contemplation (*animittābhigama*) and penetrates reality.

Regarding "causing the real and the unreal to appear or not appear": when entering signless contemplation, reality appears and the unreal does not appear; upon emerging from contemplation, reality does not appear.
Because they still enter into that which possesses signs, it is not a true manifestation. Regarding the statement that in the latter four stages, that which is not true mostly does not manifest:

this is because one constantly dwells in signless contemplation, and thus [the false] mostly does not appear. Since one is still mixed with afflictions and has not yet attained purity, that which is not true still manifests;
hence the use of the word "mostly."
△ Fourth, the transformation of fulfillment.

The transformation of fulfillment regarding the four fruits refers to the stage of ultimate consummation (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*), wherein benefit and happiness for others continue inexhaustibly until the end of the future.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: "ultimate" is called the "fulfillment of the transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) because the practice throughout the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* has reached completion.
The diamond-like samādhi exhausts all coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*). From this point on, one’s own benefit is fully accomplished;
henceforth, it consists solely in saving sentient beings until the end of the future, and is therefore called the "perfect transformation of the basis" (*pariniṣpannāśrayaparāvṛtti*).
△ Five types of inferior transformation (*hīna-parāvṛtti*).
The five types of inferior transformation refer to the stages of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*); because they lack superior capability, they are termed "inferior transformation.

Regarding the phonology and meaning, Master Qingliang’s commentary states that there are six reasons for designating them as "inferior transformation": first, exclusively seeking one's own [enlightenment].

1. They incline toward limited enlightenment (*hīna-bodhi*). 2. They feel aversion for the suffering of birth and death and take delight in *nirvāṇa*. 3. They realize only the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
4. They sever only the seeds of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). 5. They realize only true analytical cessation (*bhūtā pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). As for "true analytical cessation":
There are two kinds of nirvāṇa: with remainder and without remainder. "Lacking the sixfold supreme capability" is a phrase that encompasses the meaning of the preceding five phrases.
△ Sixth, the vast transformation.
The sixth, the "vast transformation" (*vipula-parāvṛtti*), refers to the stage of the Mahāyāna; reaching a state of superior capability is called the vast transformation.
Regarding the phonology and meaning: this term "vast transformation" is the opposite of the preceding six phrases; its significance is as stated in the text.
△ Third, the specific clarification:
The meaning intended here is that one realizes the vast transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) by abandoning the two types of heavy obstructions (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Regarding the commentary on the verse: as for the statement that "by abandoning the two heavy obstructions, one realizes the transformation of the basis," the intended meaning is as follows:

Among the six [types of transformation], it is the vast transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and not the other five. Question: Why is the transformation of the perfection of the fruit (*phala-paripūri-parāvṛtti*) not included?

Answer: It is because this is explained in relation to the stage of the cause (*hetu-avasthā*); therefore, it is not included. Furthermore, regarding the classification of stages, they do not exceed the two categories of Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Since we do not take the Hīnayāna here, only the sixth is taken.
△ Next, the explanation of the distinct meanings of the transformation of the basis (three sections). First, the general heading:
There are briefly four kinds of distinct meanings regarding the transformation of the basis.
△ Next, the detailed explanation (four sections). First, the path that effects the transformation (two sections). First, the heading:
First, the path capable of transformation; this further has two parts.
Next, the explanation [of the second part]. First, the path capable of subduing:
the path capable of subduing refers to the subduing of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), which, according to their respective natures, subdues them either gradually or instantaneously.
In the *Yinyi Qingliang* (Cooling Explanation of Phonology and Meaning), it is stated: "The six classes of practice suppress the afflictions; this is called 'with outflows' (*sāsrava*).

This is because while the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) suppresses them gradually, the fundamental [meditative] state and its subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) are able to suppress them instantaneously."

Supplement: The contaminated preparatory stage (*sāsrava-prayoga*) can only gradually suppress [the afflictions]. As stated previously, when those obstacles manifest, they are gradually suppressed prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).

The uncontaminated fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms (*anāsrava-mūla- and prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) can both suppress them instantaneously. As stated previously, from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward, they can suppress them entirely and instantaneously.
△ II. The Path of Abandonment (2): First, the direct explanation.
The path of abandonment refers to that which can permanently sever [the afflictions] because what is to be realized and what has been induced have not yet been fully accomplished.

Commentary on the Meaning of Terms: This path is certainly not a contaminated (*sāsrava*) preparatory practice (*prayoga*). Two paths exclude the contaminated; three knowledges (*jñāna*) exclude preparatory practice.
Regarding the phrase "contaminated [states] such as those previously practiced," this explains why it is not contaminated. There are two reasons why it is not a contaminated path:
first, it is induced by the grasping at signs (*nimitta-grāha*) from previous practice; second, because the signs have not yet been extinguished. As stated in the preceding text: namely...
Ordinary beings, even when their minds are of the three natures, continue to internally grasp at a self despite externally engaging in various activities.

Because they grasp at a self, the acts of giving and so forth arising within their six consciousnesses cannot transcend conceptual signs; therefore, these are tainted and cannot serve as the path that severs [afflictions].
Regarding the phrase "exertion and pursuit," this explains what is not the path of application (*prayoga*). That which is realized is *tathatā* (suchness). As for...

"Leading" refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Because preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) has not yet accomplished this wisdom of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), it is not the path capable of severing [the afflictions].
△ Next, the analysis (in two parts): First, regarding whether there is severance or no severance, the first master [holds that]...
There is an interpretation that fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (up to the point where it is said) is not the path of abandonment because subsequent wisdom is not so.

Regarding the commentary on the terminology: the intention of this master is that fundamental wisdom is taken as the path capable of abandoning [afflictions], whereas subsequent wisdom is not, because it cannot directly realize suchness by observing transformed images.
△ Next, the Master [Asaṅga] maintains that both types of wisdom possess the capacity for abandonment.

One interpretation holds that subsequent non-conceptual wisdom (prsthalabdha-nirvikalpa-jñāna)—[extending to the point where it] joins with fundamental wisdom—is capable of correctly abandoning [afflictions].

Regarding the meaning of the terms: first, the primary explanation establishes that subsequent wisdom is also called "capable of abandonment. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Vol. 75) cites scriptural evidence to support this.

The mundane path of abandonment refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). The mundane and supramundane paths of abandonment refer to the two wisdoms of the fundamental and subsequent (*mūla-paścāt-jñāna*).
The purely mundane path is the contaminated preparatory application (*sāsrava-prayoga*). This concludes the section by way of summary and demonstration.
The *Hexiang Huixuan* (合響會玄), Volume Ten, states: "Regarding the non-cessation of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*):

it cannot sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that delude one regarding the principle (*tattva*), because it does not directly realize the principle. However, with respect to the principle of the established Four Noble Truths, it realizes them without inversion;

knowing that their essence is dependent origination (*paratantra*), it merely severs the latent tendencies that delude one regarding phenomena (*vastu*). Its commentary states: "Regarding the latent tendencies that delude one regarding the principle..."

Dormant afflictions (*anuśaya*) regarding the [ultimate] mode of being (*lakṣaṇa*) are profound and far-reaching; one must realize that principle in order to be able to sever them. Dormant afflictions regarding phenomena (*vastu*) are shallow and near;
even through the contemplation of signs (*nimitta*), they can be severed. According to the *Bǎifǎchāo* (Commentary on the Hundred Dharmas), it is asked:

"If subsequent wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) can sever delusions, what kind of delusions does it sever? The answer is that there are two interpretations in the Cien school. The first says: "It is merely based on..."

The subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) can sever the innate (*sahaja*) latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) regarding delusions concerning phenomena; this is not said with reference to bodhisattvas.

This clearly demonstrates that afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are severed by both the fundamental (*mūla*) and subsequently attained wisdoms. As for cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they are severed solely by fundamental wisdom.
Second, it is said that the subsequently attained wisdom of bodhisattvas can also sever cognitive obstructions. Regarding these cognitive obstructions...

There are delusions regarding principles (*tattva*) and delusions regarding phenomena (*vastu*). Because delusions regarding principles involve clinging (*abhiniveśa*), they are difficult to sever; only the fundamental [wisdom] can sever them. If one is deluded regarding phenomena, it does not involve clinging and is thus easy to sever;
even subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) can sever them. Therefore, in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the commentary by Hui-xuan explains:

"This Dharmapāla cites the supramundane path of abandonment from the *Yogācārabhūmi* to prove that fundamental wisdom severs the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of delusion regarding principles. He further cites the mundane...
The mundane path of abandonment simultaneously realizes both the fundamental and the subsequently attained [wisdoms] to sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that delude one regarding phenomena.
Regarding "mundane and supramundane": this distinguishes it from purely mundane states; the meaning is that it is "supramundane within the mundane," hence it is called "mundane-supramundane.

This refers to the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Here, the delusions regarding phenomena are termed "mundane" to distinguish them from purely mundane states, while they are further termed "supramundane" because they transcend such states.

Since this path of abandonment (prahāṇamārga) applies to both types of knowledge, it is cited as proof. Alternatively, this delusion regarding phenomena is abandoned by the subsequently attained knowledge (pṛṣṭhalabdha), so the path is called "mundane" (laukika);
yet, because it is also abandoned by the fundamental [knowledge] (mūla-jñāna), it is further described as "supramundane" (lokottara).
Supplement: The *Kaimeng* (Opening the Ignorant) states: "The path of abandonment refers to the non-conceptual faculty and the two subsequent wisdoms.

Because they abandon the root and secondary afflictions that delude one regarding both principle and phenomena, they are called the 'path of abandonment. Regarding the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that delude one regarding principle and phenomena, Qingliang says:

'They slumber and lie hidden within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), following conditions to entangle and wrap around the objects of phenomena and principle; therefore, two names are established. Their essence is [the same]..."
The seeds of the two obstructions.
△ Second, the basis that is transformed (in two parts): first, the heading;
second, the basis that is transformed. This, in turn, has two [aspects].
△ Second, the explanation [of the two types of āśraya]: First, the support that maintains the seeds (*bīja-dhāraṇa-āśraya*).
First, the support that maintains the seeds refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*). [This continues until: ...because it cannot maintain the seeds, it is not mentioned here.
**Commentary on the Meaning of Terms:** Regarding the phrase "the Noble Path causes one to abandon defilement and attain purity": this refers to Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*).

When they cultivate the Noble Path, they transform and abandon the defiled portion of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) that serves as the basis for the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and they transform and attain the pure portion of the *paratantra-svabhāva* that relies upon the fundamental consciousness.

Therefore, the consciousness that maintains the seeds possesses the meaning of "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Question: Are not the first seven consciousnesses and so forth all *paratantra*?
[It] arises; it is also that which the Noble Ones rely upon as the Dharma. Why is it not the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*)?

The meaning of the explanation is as stated in the text. Supplement: Qingliang says: "This means that while in the state of the cause, one maintains both the defiled and the pure simultaneously. Now, having attained the Noble Path, one abandons the defiled and attains the pure;
this is precisely what is called the transformation of the basis."
△ Second, the basis of delusion and awakening.
Regarding the basis of delusion and awakening, it refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*). [The text continues] up to: "and because it is not the fundamental [cause], this is not mentioned here.
*Commentary on the Phonology and Meaning:* As for "True Suchness is called the basis of delusion and awakening," True Suchness is the actual nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. It exists...
Being entangled is delusion; emerging from entanglement is awakening. When one is deluded, defiled phenomena arise based upon it; when one awakens, pure phenomena are produced from it.
When the noble path arises, one abandons the defiled and attains the pure. Therefore, True Suchness possesses the meaning of "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Question:
Other types of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) are also bases for both delusion and awakening; why are these not mentioned? Answer: (It is said:)
[End of quote]. Supplement: The *Zongjing* states: Although it is said that delusion and awakening depend [upon it], this does not mean that the mind and its objects maintain the seeds.
Because True Suchness is unchanging, it does not follow the mind to transform into the myriad objects; rather, it is merely that which is deluded about. Later, it returns to purity.
Because time does not itself encompass [the nature of] phenomena as being identical to True Suchness (*tathatā*); it is merely that which is realized.
△ Third, that which is transformed and abandoned (in two parts): First, the heading.
Third, that which is transformed and abandoned; this further has two [parts].
△ Next, the explanation [of the second part] has two sections. First, the abandonment of what is to be abandoned.
1. Abandonment of what is to be abandoned refers to the seeds of the two obstacles (up to: ...by this it is called the abandonment of the imagined nature).

Commentary on the Terms: Regarding "the contradiction between the obstacles and their remedies": the true path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) is the remedial wisdom, while the seeds of the two obstacles are the afflictions to be remedied.
Just as light and darkness cannot coexist, it is said that "they are thereby severed and extinguished."

The preceding section clarified that the severance of seeds is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*); because those seeds are severed, [the result is abandoned]. Next, the following section reveals that the suppression of the manifest is called "abandonment.
The *Qīngliáng* commentary states: "A real self and real dharmas have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) from the outset;

they only appear to exist due to deluded cognition. Now, as deluded cognition is severed, there is no object confronting the mind. To speak metaphorically of this object is also called 'severance. By this principle..."
This is termed "the relinquishing of what was grasped. Wherever it is stated that "universal imagination (*parikalpita*) is severed," the meaning lies herein.
Supplement: The *Kaimeung* states: "The relinquishing of what is to be severed refers to the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
Each time one encounters the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) of each stage (*bhūmi*), they are thereby extinguished."
△ II. That Which Is Abandoned (2): First, the formal explanation.
Second, that which is abandoned refers to other contaminated [phenomena] (*sāsrava*)... by means of this, one is said to abandon the inferior dharmas of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Commentary on the Terms: First, it is clarified that "abandoning" (*prahāṇa*) refers to the name for discarding seeds. The *Qīngliáng Chāo* (Cool Grove Commentary) explains:

"The remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) factors" refers to the remaining contaminated wholesome dharmas belonging to the two obstacles. "Inferior uncontaminated seeds" (*anāsrava-bīja*) refers to the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) produced within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

"Complete" (*paripūrṇa*) means fully perfected; "clear" (*vibhūta*) means the discernment of their modes of activity (*ākāra-vikalpa*). This is distinct from [the state of] a Bodhisattva, who has not yet attained such complete clarity.
These purified eight consciousnesses are not the basis for other outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) or inferior untainted (*anāsrava*) states; therefore, they are all relinquished.

Furthermore, the *Chao* (Commentary) states that "inferior untainted" refers to the manifest activities (*pravṛtti*) produced within the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), which can only be relinquished during the vajra-path (*vajramārga*).

Second, regarding the fact that the white and neutral [states] have not yet been relinquished: this refers to the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), [which persists] through the eighth stage.

The name *ālaya* is relinquished. In the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), it is still called the *vipākavijñāna*; only upon reaching the state of a Tathāgata is the *vipāka* relinquished and it is named the *amala-vijñāna*.
Third, regarding "not having relinquished contaminated wholesome dharmas": this means being accompanied by the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
These seeds of the two obstacles are what are to be abandoned and relinquished (text). Once those seeds have been relinquished, [the following] clarifies the manifest [defilements].
Non-arising is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*). [The text] opens the deluded mind. Question: What is it that is abandoned? Answer:

It refers to contaminated wholesome states, the maturation-unspecified (*vipāka-avyākṛta*), and inferior uncontaminated states—the inferior dharmas of the transformation body (that is, the inferior uncontaminated dharmas of the *parināmika-saṃsāra*).

To summarize, these consist merely of contaminated seeds and manifest states, as well as inferior uncontaminated seeds and manifest states. At the time of this final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they are all completely abandoned.
This is called the "four matters" (text).

Supplement: By this single phrase, "thereby abandoning the inferior dharmas of birth and death," the four matters—the inferior contaminated seeds and manifestations, as well as the contaminated and uncontaminated seeds and manifestations mentioned above—are summarized.
△ Next, the critical analysis (in two parts). First, the initial master [holds that] they are abandoned by the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
According to one interpretation, the remaining seeds of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are abandoned simultaneously with the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).

In the *Hexiang* (Harmonious Resonance), Qingliang’s commentary states: "These outflows (*sāsrava*) and the inferior outflow-free states (*anāsrava*) are abandoned simultaneously with the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
This is because these two [categories] exist due to the seeds of the two obstacles" (text).
Supplement: The *Kaimeng* states: "When one contemplates the vajra-mind of the preceding moment, it is called the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*).
At this stage, all subtle dual obstructions are completely severed. Upon reaching the second moment, one abandons the four matters."
△ Next, regarding the Master’s [explanation of] relinquishment in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*):
there is an interpretation that at that time one has not yet relinquished those [afflictions], because the eighth pure consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) is not their support.

Regarding the meaning of the sounds: first, the correct interpretation is stated. That is to say, when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) arises, one merely relinquishes the seeds of the obstructions, but [has not yet relinquished the afflictions themselves].

How can it be that one is able to abandon those seeds of the outflows (*sāsrava*) and so forth? At the time of severing the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), this occurs during the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Since these outflows and the like are not incompatible with the path of immediate succession, the Bodhisattva would consequently lack the lower [levels]. Thus, by means of reasoning, the preceding position is refuted.

Regarding the statement that "a Bodhisattva should be devoid of the phenomena of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*)," this refers to the time of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*). Even at that stage, one is still a Bodhisattva.

If it were said that they simultaneously abandon the seeds of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and so forth, then this Bodhisattva would be devoid of even a portion of the phenomena of transformation-rebirth (*pariṇāmi-janma-saṃsāra*);

therefore, in this state, there should be no consciousness that serves as the object of perfuming (*vāsya-vijñāna*). By "object of perfuming," one means the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*). [The author] intends to say: [the seeds of] the contaminated...

The seeds of the [defiled] categories are likewise maintained by maturation (*vipāka*). It is only after the vajra-path has arisen that the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) emerges, and only then does this consciousness become empty.
If one were to claim that at the time of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), that which is supported is already abandoned, then the supporting maturation would also be abandoned;
consequently, in that state, there would be no consciousness to serve as the basis for perfuming (*vāsana*). If the uninterrupted path had already abandoned the maturation, then...
Because a bodhisattva at the stage of the cause would then have to be called a Buddha; and once he is already called a Buddha, the arising of the path of liberation would be useless.
To say it is useless is because the arising of the path of liberation has two functions: first, to discard the seeds of outflows (*āsrava*) and so forth;
second, to realize the true principle of the ultimate fruit. If one were to claim that the seeds have already been abandoned at the time of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), then...

The Path of Liberation (vimukti-mārga). Because it would lack the function of abandoning the seeds [of afflictions], from this point downward, the conclusion is presented to indicate the correct explanation.
△ Fourth, that which is attained through transformation (3): First, the general heading.
Regarding the four [aspects] attained through transformation, there are further two.
△ Next is the detailed explanation (in two parts): first, the manifestation through realization (in two parts). First, the general explanation of the manifestation through realization.
One manifestation is called Great Nirvāṇa (up to the point where it is said that) its essence is the Pure Dharmadhātu.

Regarding the meaning of the terms: *Nirvāṇa* is here translated as "Perfect Quiescence" (*yuánjì*). It is also called "Extinction and Deliverance" (*mièdù*). In the language of Qin, it means "Unconditioned" (*wéiwéi*).
It is also named "Peaceful Security. Its meaning is as explained in the standard commentaries. In sum, it is the One True Dharmadhātu. Suppose someone were to ask: "Nir..."
The essence of *ālayavijñāna* is inherently pure by nature; it pervades the entire *dharmadhātu* and is possessed by both the holy and the ordinary.
How, then, can one speak of its being "manifested" or "attained"? Therefore, the commentary states: "Although this is originally so," and so forth. Furthermore, it is asked:
"If there are obstructions and coverings that prevent it from manifesting, how can it be called 'originally pure'? Thus, the answer states: "This is based on *tathatā* (suchness)," and so forth.
The *Heryang Huixuan* (合響會玄), Volume Four, states: "The nature of nirvāṇa is, in its essence, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It exists from the beginning, and its self-nature is pure. Later, upon encountering virtuous friends, it is manifested through the severing of hindrances.
Although it is the single True Suchness (*tathatā*), it is differentiated according to conditions and realized; thus it is termed the four types of nirvāṇa. (Text)
△ Next, the four types of nirvāṇa are explained individually (3). First, the general introduction:
Regarding the meaning of nirvāṇa, there are four distinct categories within the dhātu.
While the principle of nirvāṇa is fundamentally non-dual, they are distinguished merely by the relative superiority and inferiority of ordinary beings and sages.
Briefly divided, there are four distinctions.
△ Next, the detailed explanation (2): First, the formal explanation (4). First, *prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of original self-nature purity).
[From] "First, *prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa*" [to] "because its nature is originally quiescent, it is called nirvāṇa."
*Yinyi* (Explanatory Notes on Pronunciation and Meaning): "Regarding 'all that is below'" refers to the explanation of the meaning of the intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) of the nature.
This refers to the principle upon which all phenomena—namely the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—rely.

Although it is obscured by adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*), its essence is inherently pure, like a bright, clear pearl situated in mud. As a sutra says: "Though stained, it is unstained; it is difficult to comprehend."
This principle does not distinguish between the noble and the ordinary; it is equally shared by all sentient beings. [The following] explains the meaning of *nirvāṇa* for all those below.
As for its being neither identical to nor different from all phenomena: if it were different, then True Suchness (*tathatā*) would not be their true nature;
if it were identical, then this nature would be impermanent. "Free from all marks and all conceptualization" means that it cannot be...
Regarding the four propositions such as existence and non-existence: "the path of thought is cut off" indicates that the objective realm cannot be reached by verbal expressions;
"the path of names and words is severed" signifies that the referential meaning cannot be attained through verbal designations.

Supplement: The *Kaimeung* (Opening the Ignorant) states: "The fundamental nature is unstained; this is called purity (*viśuddhi*). The fundamental nature is quiescent; therefore it is called *nirvāṇa*.

The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* states: "From time immemorial, the self-nature is pure (*prakṛti-viśuddha*), fully endowed with various qualities of essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-guṇa*) as numerous as the atoms in the worlds of the ten directions. No names or designations whatsoever can [fully express it]."
It is attained; it is exclusively pure, having as its intrinsic nature the *tathatā* (suchness) manifested by the two kinds of emptiness realized through noble wisdom.
It is partially realized by the various noble ones and perfectly realized by the Buddhas.
△ Second, *nirvāṇa with remainder*. Regarding *nirvāṇa with remainder*:

it refers to when true suchness (*tathatā*) emerges from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), yet a remainder still persists. Because the obstacles are eternally stilled, it is called *nirvāṇa*.
(End of quote). [Combined Explanation]: As for *nirvāṇa with remainder*, it means that while true suchness has emerged from the obstacle of afflictions, there still remains...

Because it is the basis for the suffering of分段生死 (paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa, segmented birth-and-death). This is because the final body of suffering belonging to the various noble ones (*ārya*) has never yet been extinguished. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"Dwelling in the state of having a remainder of support (*sopadhiśeṣa*), one falls within the category of the multitude (*saṃkhyā-gata*). There still exist various sufferings;

the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parivṛtti*) that has been attained is still associated with the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). 'The category of the multitude' refers to the body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-kāya'). Because this exists..."
Because the body possesses manifold sufferings. Question: Since there are manifold sufferings, why is it called *nirvāṇa*? Answer:

Although there is still a subtle suffering with which it is associated, because the obstacles have been eternally extinguished, it is also called *nirvāṇa*. This is because while the "bond of the fruit" (*phala-bandhana*) remains, the "bond of the seed" (*bīja-bandhana*) has already been exhausted.
Since there is that upon which it depends, it is not without transition and cessation; how then can it be called *nirvāṇa*? The *Kaimeung* says: "That which can summon defilement..."
Because [all suffering] is exhausted, it is called *nirvāṇa*.
△ Third, *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvāṇa without remainder):
because all sufferings are eternally stilled, it is called *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the phonetic meanings: when both the body and wisdom are extinguished, the basis of suffering (*duḥkha-āśraya*) likewise ceases to exist; this is called "nirvana without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
The great affliction is forever extinguished and all sufferings are eternally stilled; this is the meaning of *nirvāṇa*. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"Abiding in nirvana without remainder, one does not fall into the categories of sentient beings, is forever free from all suffering, and is eternally dissociated from the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)."
Supplement: Qingliang says: "These categories of 'with remainder' and 'without remainder' apply to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;
however, in asserting that True Suchness (tathatā) is their essence, they differ from the Hīnayāna."
△ Fourth, non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*).
Regarding "non-abiding nirvana": because it functions while remaining eternally quiescent, it is called nirvana. Commentary on the terminology:

"That is, when true suchness (*tathatā*) emerges from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)" intends to show that [the Bodhisattva’s] afflictions are distinct from those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Therefore, it is not explained in detail. Regarding "Great Compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) below: this explains the meaning of non-abiding.

Because one is constantly assisted by the mind of great compassion, one observes that all sentient beings are deluded by the three types of suffering and are submerged in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Thus, by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), one rescues conscious beings;
for this reason, one does not abide in *nirvāṇa*. Because one is constantly assisted by the wisdom of *prajñā*, in every thought-moment...
In the interim, one severs all hindrances and abides in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). For this reason, one does not abide in saṃsāra;

because one abides in neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa, it is called "non-abiding. Question: To bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future is the sublime function of benefiting others;
how can this be called "nirvāṇa"? Answer: It is said: "Though functioning, it is eternally quiescent."
△ Next, the critical analysis (in two parts). First, a general analysis regarding ordinary beings and sages:
All sentient beings possess the first [of the four]; only our World-Honored One can be said to possess all four.
△ Next, the questions and answers are presented to distinguish [the states] specifically (5). First, distinguishing that the Sugata possesses the remainder of the basis (2). First, the question:
How does the Sugata possess the remainder of the basis?

*Yinyi* (Explanatory Notes on Pronunciation and Meaning): This follows upon the preceding sentence to pose a question regarding how only our World-Honored One can be said to possess the four intentions.

"Sugata" (Well-Gone) is one of the ten epithets of the Buddha. The intention of the questioner is this: since he has already departed from the two types of death and all suffering is forever stilled, he is called a Buddha.
How could there be a nirvana in which even a trace of the basis for suffering has not been exhausted?
△ Next, the response:
Although there is no actual basis, it appears as if there were (up to) "therefore the World-Honored One may be said to possess the four. [Commentary on the Meaning of the Sounds]:
The intent of the response is twofold. First, it clearly demonstrates that [the Buddha] possesses [the marks], being the same as those of the Two Vehicles, as in the *Kṣīrābhāsya-sūtra*.
It is said that when the World-Honored One was ill, he commanded Ānanda to seek milk to cure his thirst; this is one such instance.
Furthermore, there are reports of his back pain from being pierced by a golden spear and so forth. All such matters as these have the sense of appearing to exist phenomenally.

Alternatively, in the section on suffering, it is later clarified that the untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) constitute the "remainder of the basis" (*sopadhiśeṣa*); therefore, it is said that the basis of suffering does not remain, as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
It says: "This body of mine is now the eternal body, the Dharma-body, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "harmonizing with resonance," the *Kaimeng* (Opening the Ignorant) states: "The body of the Tathāgata has a remaining basis for bliss; because it is a non-outflow body (*anāsrava-kāya*), it is not a basis for suffering, and is thus called 'having a remaining basis.
This differs from the 'remaining basis of suffering' of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), as their bodies still possess [the seeds of] attachment."

Question: How is it known that there is no suffering? Answer: By relinquishing impermanent form (*rūpa*) and attaining permanent form; feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise so.

Therefore, one knows there is no suffering, for there is a basis for further bliss. Question: Although the aggregates (*skandha*) are untainted (*anāsrava*), they are not devoid of transition and cessation.
Why then are they called *nirvāṇa*, given that they are not [ultimately] tranquil? Answer: Because they can bring about the exhaustion of defilements (*kleśa*), they are called *nirvāṇa*.
△ 2. Distinguishing the Two Vehicles as Potentially Possessing the First Three [States] (2): First, the Question.
If śrāvakas and others possess the state of nirvāṇa without remainder, how could they possibly possess the state of nirvāṇa with remainder? They do not possess it either.

*He-xiang* (Harmonizing the Resonance). This follows upon the preceding text’s inquiry regarding whether the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) can possess the first three [types of] intentions.

Herein are two questions. The first concerns the Śrāvakas and others: since they already possess the nirvāṇa without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*), how is it that some passages state there is only the nirvāṇa with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and no nirvāṇa without remainder?
This uses the fact that other places lack the nirvāṇa without remainder to challenge the claim made here.

Furthermore, it is said that in another passage it states: "If there were absolutely nothing at all, how could there be a *sopadhiśeṣa* (remainder of substrate)? Would not even those Arhats of the Two Vehicles who have attained *aśaikṣa* (no-more-learning) likewise be non-existent?
This uses the fact of absolute non-existence in another context to challenge the claim that there is a *sopadhiśeṣa* state in this context.
△ Next, the response (in two parts). The first part (two sections): First, answering the previous question by way of the meaning of "perfect quiescence" (parinirvāṇa).
Now, when the body and wisdom of the śrāvakas and others still exist—[up to]—the true reality manifested therein is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder).

Regarding the explanation of the terminology: when it is said in certain places that "nirvāṇa does not exist at all," this is spoken in reference to the time when the body and wisdom of śrāvakas and others have not yet been extinguished.
Because the physical body—which serves as the basis for the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—has not yet been exhausted, it is said that nirvāṇa does not exist at all.
This does not mean that they truly lack the nirvāṇa with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) attained through the exhaustion of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Appendix: That which serves as the basis for suffering is precisely the bondage of the fruit. The body and mind of the two vehicles properly belong to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
△ Next, regarding the answer to the first question based on the state of not yet having realized the remainderless [nirvāṇa]:
At that time, [he] had not yet realized *parinirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*), up until the exhaustion of the basis of suffering, *nirvāṇa* without remainder.

Regarding the meaning of the term: it is said in some places that "he has no *nirvāṇa* without remainder" because, while the body and wisdom of those śrāvakas and others still remain, they have not yet realized *nirvāṇa* without remainder; therefore, it is said that he does not have it. However, at a later time...
